claim: Section 5.3 uses pathway enrichment to argue that relationships uniquely retrieved by Semi-Clipped reveal biological synergy beyond the transcriptomic and microscopy baselines. Apply its stated \(p<0.01\) cutoff to the reported Table 3 values and source-set labels; the table does not specify a separate raw-versus-adjusted significance convention.

Let \(S\), \(\mathrm{Tx}\) and \(\mathrm{Img}\) denote the relationships retrieved by Semi-Clipped, the transcriptomic baseline and the microscopy baseline. The claimed unique set is \(U=S\setminus(\mathrm{Tx}\cup\mathrm{Img})\); the morphology-transfer set is \(V=(S\cap\mathrm{Img})\setminus\mathrm{Tx}\).
analysis: Every element of \(U\) lies outside \(\mathrm{Img}\), while every element of \(V\) lies inside \(\mathrm{Img}\). Therefore \(U\cap V=\varnothing\): a pathway sourced from \(V\) cannot supply the claimed unique-set evidence.
The only displayed Table 3 row sourced from \(U\) is REACTOME cell-cycle checkpoints, with reported \(p=0.0323\). Since \(0.0323>0.01\), that row fails the stated significance filter.

The REACTOME post-translational protein-modification row has \(p=0.0002<0.01\), but its source is \(V\). It satisfies the numerical cutoff while failing the unique-source requirement. All other displayed rows are likewise sourced from \(V\).

No displayed row therefore satisfies both necessary conditions: source set \(U\) and \(p<0.01\). The table does not establish the unique-pathway enrichment used to distinguish emergent synergy from transfer of information already present in microscopy.
result: The \(19\) uniquely retrieved known relationships and the reported recall gains remain. At a nominal \(0.05\) cutoff, \(0.0323\) would pass, but that is a different cutoff and does not change the source set of the \(0.0002\) row. Raw-versus-adjusted values, multiplicity handling and additional unreported qualifying rows are unresolved; the displayed evidence supports additional retrieval and morphology transfer without establishing the stronger unique-pathway conclusion.
brief: The only displayed unique-set pathway has \(p=0.0323>0.01\); the \(p=0.0002\) pathway comes from morphology transfer.
The \(19\) uniquely retrieved known relationships and the recall gains remain; raw-versus-adjusted significance is unresolved.

source_report_paragraphs.text: Semi-Clipped trains a transcriptomic adapter against frozen morphological embeddings using a contrastive loss. Biological metadata define weak pairing, while inference uses transcriptomics. PEA randomizes batch-correction transforms, retained correction steps and the control samples used to estimate the transform. The paper admits at least two controls per biological batch, and its student representation has dimension 256 in Appendix A.2. Its principal downstream outcomes are known-relationship retrieval and an expression-reconstruction/structure preservation metric.

Problem 1 (The pathway evidence uses the wrong significance threshold and source set: Major).  Section 5.3, pp. 8–9, analyzes relationships unique to distillation, states a filter \(p<0.01\), and uses cell-cycle and post-translational enrichment to argue for biological insights absent from either unimodal source. Table 3, p. 19, does not supply that evidence.

Let \(S\) be the relationships retrieved by Semi-Clipped, \(T\) those retrieved by the transcriptomic baseline, and \(I\) those retrieved by the microscopy baseline. The stated emergence test concerns \[U=S\setminus(T\cup I).\] This is different from morphology-specific transfer, \[V=(S\cap I)\setminus T.\] Indeed \(U\cap V=\varnothing\): every element of \(V\) belongs to \(I\), whereas every element of \(U\) lies outside \(I\).
The original table explicitly gives the following decisive rows:
Pathway | Source set | Reported \(p\)
REACTOME cell cycle checkpoints | \(U\) | 0.0323
REACTOME post-translational protein modification | \(V\) | 0.0002

The cell-cycle-checkpoints row is the only displayed row sourced from \(U\). Its \(p\)-value is 3.23 times the stated cutoff and does not meet \(p<0.01\). All other displayed rows are sourced from \(V\). The post-translational row meets the cutoff, but concerns relationships already retrieved by microscopy and cannot witness emergence beyond the union of the two baselines.

Thus, among the displayed enrichment results, zero pathways simultaneously have the required unique source set and satisfy the stated significance filter. This conclusion uses the actual source-set labels and reported \(p\)-values; it does not require recreating GSEA or making assumptions about unreported gene lists. The independent `check.py`/`check.json` records the threshold arithmetic and set distinction.

Changing the cutoff to 0.05 would admit the cell-cycle-checkpoints result at a nominal level. It would not change the post-translational result’s membership in \(V\), and it would not establish correction for searching many pathways. A raw-versus-adjusted \(p\)-value distinction could in principle explain different thresholds, but the table labels only P-value and supplies no such distinction. Additional unreported qualifying rows would require their actual source sets, statistics and analysis records. These possibilities are Needs Evidence, not verified corrections.

The Venn diagram in Figure 4 still supports substantial overlap and some newly retrieved relationships. For Semi-Clipped the displayed regions give \(|S|=19+21+17+35=92\) and \(|S\cap T|=21+35=56\) out of \(|T|=61\). The 19 relationships in \(U\) are newly retrieved relative to these baselines. Their existence alone does not establish significant pathway enrichment, causal synergy or previously unknown biology; the retrieval task uses known database relationships.

The dependency is direct: Section 5.3 invokes this enrichment analysis to distinguish emergent synergy from ordinary transfer, and Section 6 repeats the conclusion about cell-cycle and post-translational synergies. The supplied evidence fails the very source-set and threshold test used for that distinction. This is a Major defect in a central biological interpretation, even if all recall improvements remain numerically correct.

claim: Appendix C.3 defines full-dimensional TVN as \(T=WD^{-1/2}W^\top\), where \(D\) contains the eigenvalues of the control covariance. The recipe admits randomly selected control sets with only \(c\ge2\); retain the full TVN branch and allow positive variance in every individual coordinate. The student representation has \(m=256\) dimensions.
The printed unregularized inverse square root must be defined on those admitted control sets; the formulation gives neither a full-rank condition nor a rule for singular directions.
analysis: Center the \(c\) control vectors in \(\mathbb R^m\). Their rows now sum to zero, so the rows are linearly dependent and the centered data matrix has rank at most \(c-1\), as well as at most \(m\). Its covariance consequently satisfies \(\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma)\le\min(m,c-1)\). When \(c\le m\), the \(m\)-dimensional covariance must have a zero eigenvalue.

A concrete admitted witness is \(X=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}\). There are two controls, both coordinate means are zero and both coordinate standard deviations are one under the stated convention. Centering and coordinate scaling are therefore defined and leave \(X\) unchanged.

Its covariance is \(\Sigma=\tfrac12X^\top X=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\), with eigenvalues \(2\) and \(0\). The prescribed \(D^{-1/2}\) would require \(0^{-1/2}\), which has no finite real value. Using the unbiased covariance convention changes the positive eigenvalue but leaves the zero eigenvalue.

In the stated \(256\)-dimensional setting, the two controls \(\mathbf1_{256}\) and \(-\mathbf1_{256}\) again have positive variance in every coordinate, but their covariance has rank one and \(255\) null dimensions. These controls meet the admitted sample-count condition while making the retained full-TVN branch undefined. Randomly omitting other correction steps does not define this allowed branch when it is selected.
result: The counterexample concerns the mathematical definedness of the printed unregularized map on its admitted inputs. The actual normalization implementation and its effect on published scores remain unresolved; the available evidence does not establish whether singular directions were handled in the historical pipeline.
brief: The admitted control sets can have singular covariance; for \(c=2\) and \(m=256\), at least \(255\) directions are null.
The printed inverse square root is then undefined. A regularized implementation could avoid this, but its use and historical score effects were not established.

source_report_paragraphs.text: Semi-Clipped trains a transcriptomic adapter against frozen morphological embeddings using a contrastive loss. Biological metadata define weak pairing, while inference uses transcriptomics. PEA randomizes batch-correction transforms, retained correction steps and the control samples used to estimate the transform. The paper admits at least two controls per biological batch, and its student representation has dimension 256 in Appendix A.2. Its principal downstream outcomes are known-relationship retrieval and an expression-reconstruction/structure preservation metric.

Problem 2 (Random-control PEA lacks the rank condition required by its inverse: Major).  Appendix C.3, p. 16 (printed p. 3), defines the full-dimensional TVN map \(T=WD^{-1/2}W^\top\) from the control covariance eigenvalues. The formulation requires only at least two controls and randomizes their number, without a full-rank condition or a stated regularization rule.

Let \(c\) be the number of selected controls and \(m\) the feature dimension. After centering, their data matrix has rank at most \(c-1\). Consequently its \(m\times m\) covariance satisfies \[\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma)\le\min(m,c-1).\] When \(c\le m\), at least one covariance eigenvalue is zero, regardless of numerical precision. Positive variance in each individual coordinate does not ensure a full-rank covariance.

A complete two-dimensional witness is \[X_{\rm control}=
\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.\] There are two controls, the mean is zero, and both coordinate standard deviations are one under Appendix C.2’s convention. Centering and scaling are therefore well-defined and leave this matrix unchanged. Its covariance is \[\Sigma=\tfrac12X_{\rm control}^{\top}X_{\rm control}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \operatorname{spec}(\Sigma)=\{2,0\}.\] The prescribed \(D^{-1/2}\) requires \(0^{-1/2}\) and has no finite real value. This example isolates the inverse failure from any zero-coordinate-variance problem. Using an unbiased covariance changes the positive eigenvalue, not the zero.

For the actual 256-dimensional student setting, take the two controls \(\mathbf1_{256}\) and \(-\mathbf1_{256}\). Every coordinate again has positive variance, but the covariance has rank one and nullity 255. More generally, any centered control set with \(c\le256\) has singular covariance. No extra constraint in the inspected formulation excludes these counts or requires affine spanning. Selecting the full TVN sequence is an allowed branch of the augmentation recipe; dropping random steps does not define that branch when it is retained.

The independent check constructed the two-dimensional covariance and verified its rank and eigenvalues numerically alongside the exact calculation. The defect is mathematical definedness of the supplied normalization, not a claim that the author implementation was observed producing an error.

This is tied to PEA’s central mechanism: control sampling determines the augmentation delivered to the student, and TVN is also used in the teacher/inference/evaluation description. The stated mapping is undefined for admitted inputs, so its operational assumptions must be strengthened or its formula changed. Under the core-contribution calibration, this supports Major for the described method’s definedness.

There is a substantive counterargument: the appendix could be shorthand for a regularized implementation, making this a missing specification rather than an executed failure. No source code, regularizer, retained-rank parameter or control-count distribution was available to verify that reading. The exact implemented normalization and any effect on the published scores remain Needs Evidence. The assessment does not rely on a difficult repair or claim that all PEA runs fail.

claim: The annotations in Listing 2 formally verify that the returned Boolean agrees with the palindrome specification.
The array is non-null, has length \(N\ge0\), and is unchanged by the displayed loop. Use only the printed precondition and loop invariants. The exact Dafny version and flags were not supplied.
analysis: Location: Appendix A.4.2, p.19, Listing 2 and its surrounding verification claim. The postcondition equates the returned Boolean with the predicate that every first-half array element equals its mirror. Let N be the nonnegative array length. The listing initializes left = 0 and right = N-1; on each iteration it compares arr[left] and arr[right], returns false on mismatch, otherwise increments left and decrements right. It returns true on loop exit.

The declared output res is not assigned before the invariant res == true. Under Dafny 3.11 automatic initialization, the verifier treats an uninitialized auto-initializable value as arbitrary; the historical function method syntax makes these semantics relevant [2,3]. Take a non-null array [1,2,1] and res = false: the precondition holds, but the entry invariant fails. Strict definite-assignment checking would instead reject an unassigned read. Neither reading establishes res == true. The exact author tool version and flags were not supplied.

An invariant-based loop proof must justify the early return for every state satisfying its invariant and guard [2]. The missing relationship is left + right = N-1. The following countermodel checks every displayed condition, without assuming reachability:
Condition at loop head | Countermodel evaluation
State | arr = [1,2,1]; N = 3; left = 0; right = 1; res = true
Non-null array; bounds | True; 0 <= 0 <= 1+1 <= 3
Result invariant | res == true holds
Processed prefix | 0 <= i < left has no indices; universal statement is true
Processed suffix | Only j = 2 satisfies right < j < N; arr[2] = arr[0] = 1
Guard and branch condition | left < right is 0 < 1; arr[0] != arr[1] is 1 != 2
Required versus returned result | IsPalindrome is true, since arr[0] = arr[2]; branch returns false

Thus the early-return verification condition is false for the displayed annotations. This state is unreachable from the actual initialization: the actual updates preserve left + right = N-1, which this state violates. It is a countermodel to the proposed proof obligations, not a runtime counterexample to the algorithm. The supported consequence is loss of the worked example’s claimed formal verification. Section 5 and the conclusion use the examples to substantiate the integrated trustworthy-action approach, and p.19 specifically claims executable fidelity through formal verification. The false verification condition therefore damages core supporting technical evidence and supports Major. It does not establish an incorrect initialized execution, a failure of formal methods, or a refutation of the general integration position.
result: The displayed annotations do not establish the worked example's claimed formal verification. The initialized algorithm and the broader integration position remain separate surviving claims.
brief: The displayed invariant permits an early-return countermodel and lacks an establishing assignment for the result invariant.
The countermodel is unreachable from the initialized algorithm; the finding concerns its claimed proof, not a runtime failure.

fields.source_location: Section 2.2, example 9, p. 3; Definition 2.3, p. 2
claim: The closest counterfactual \(\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{z:f(z)\ne f(x)}\|x-z\|_1\) supplies a point-valued statistic without an explicit attainment or selection condition.
Use the displayed optimization for a measurable binary classifier; the background distribution does not enter its objective.
analysis: Source claim and location. Under Definition 2.3, p. 2, statistics of functions have vector-valued outputs. Section 2.2, example 9 on p. 3, lists the nearest point with a different prediction as an example, using the following argmin. The missing step is ensuring that the feasible set contains a distance minimizer and that the expression selects one point when ties occur.

\[\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{z:\,f(z)\ne f(x)}\|x-z\|_1.\] Complete counterexample. Set d = 1 and f(z) = 1{z > 0}, and explain x = -1. If a distribution argument is required, fix D to the uniform distribution on [-2,2]; it does not affect the displayed optimization. This is an ordinary measurable binary threshold classifier, with x inside the data support. We do not exploit a nonmeasurable function, infinite loss, or regression output.

\[f(-1)=0,\qquad \{z:f(z)\ne f(-1)\}=(0,\infty),\qquad |-1-z|=1+z\quad(z>0).\] The feasible set is nonempty, yet no candidate is closest. For every feasible z, the point z/2 is also feasible and has strictly smaller distance. Meanwhile the feasible sequence z_n = 1/n has distances 1 + 1/n converging to 1. Thus the infimum is 1, but it is not attained, and the argmin is empty. The same problem remains if candidates are restricted to the distribution support: the feasible set becomes (0,2], with the same unattained infimum.

\[\inf_{z>0}(1+z)=1,\qquad \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{z>0}(1+z)=\varnothing.\] This contradicts the unrestricted use of the expression as a point-valued example. It does not contradict the claim that properly specified counterfactual algorithms can be useful statistics, and no later theorem or experiment in this position paper depends on the unrestricted optimization.

Strongest alternative reading and severity. The example may be intended as a sketch with existence, finite numerical precision and tie handling understood. Those assumptions are often supplied in implementations. However, this failure occurs for a routine classification boundary and should be explicit when the example motivates a formal domain and output type. Judgment: Minor, a local well-posedness gap.
result: A nonempty feasible set need not contain a closest counterfactual. The example needs attainment and output-selection conditions; this does not refute properly specified counterfactual algorithms or the broader position.

repair.heading: Correction and verification scope
paragraphs: For Euclidean inputs with the displayed \(\ell_1\) distance, specify a nonempty closed target region and a fixed tie rule or set-valued output. The distance attains a minimum by restricting to a nonempty bounded sublevel set, which is compact.

For this witness, \(z\ge\varepsilon>0\) gives the unique minimizer \(z=\varepsilon\); at \(\varepsilon=1/10\), the distance is \(11/10\). An explicitly approximate counterfactual is another option. These mathematical checks do not certify an implemented algorithm.

fields.source_location: Section 3.1, bottom of p. 3, unnumbered meta-posterior equation
claim: Write theta = (\(\theta_I\), \(\theta_E\)) for internal and external knowledge variables, F for a reasoning strategy, A for a reasoning trajectory and O for observed feedback. Section 3.1 gives strategy generation p(F|theta), trajectory generation p(A|F), and feedback p(O|A). We hold any external goal/context fixed. The counterexample uses independent knowledge priors, exactly as the product prior on the printed right side allows.
The central meta-level update identifies \[p(\theta_I,\theta_E\mid O,F)\propto\left[\int p(O\mid f)p(f\mid\theta_I,\theta_E)\,df\right]p(\theta_I)p(\theta_E).\]

The witness has independent Bernoulli knowledge priors and binary strategy, trajectory and observation variables. Use the admitted submodel \(p(i,e,f,a,o)=p(i)p(e)p(f\mid i,e)p(a\mid f)p(o\mid a)\); direct knowledge-to-observation effects may vanish.
analysis: Source claim and exact location. At the bottom of p. 3, Section 3.1, under ’Updating knowledge priors at the meta-level’, the paper labels the following quantity as the posterior over knowledge priors. The original rendered page was visually checked. [E1]

\[p(\theta_I,\theta_E\mid O,F)\ \propto\ \left[\int p(O\mid f)\,p(f\mid\theta_I,\theta_E)\,df\right]p(\theta_I)p(\theta_E).\] Suspect step. Integrating over f removes the realized strategy from the evidence. Under the stated Markov simplification, the right side is an unnormalized p(theta|O), not p(theta|O,F). Its dependence on theta cannot generally be repaired by a scalar normalizing constant. This is a target-distribution mismatch.

Dependency. This is the second level of the paper’s central two-level Bayesian learning scheme, immediately following Eq. (2) and Table 1. Section 3.2 uses meta-reflection to update knowledge and strategies, and Section 4.4 describes refining F and then optimizing the meta-parameters. Consequently the incorrect expression affects the proposed mechanism for consolidating knowledge across tasks. It is not a peripheral numerical example or a bibliography defect.

All five variables I=\(\theta_I\), E=\(\theta_E\), F, A and O are binary. I and E are independent Bernoulli(1/2). The remaining conditional tables are below; probabilities of value zero are the complements. E is a genuine random variable but its effect on F is set to zero.
Conditional probability | Parent value 0 | Parent value 1
P(O=1 | A), parent A | 1/8 | 7/8

\[p(i,e,f,a,o)=p(i)p(e)p(f\mid i,e)p(a\mid f)p(o\mid a).\] Assumption check. Each conditional table sums to one. Exact enumeration gives total joint mass 1, all 32 joint assignments strictly positive, and minimum mass 1/3200. No zero-likelihood event, undefined conditioning, dependent prior, invalid strategy value or negative weight is used. The event O=1,F=1 has probability 2/5. The independent reviewer script uses Python Fraction arithmetic and does not import or execute author code. [E4]

\[\Pr(O=1\mid F=0)=\frac9{10}\frac18+\frac1{10}\frac78=\frac15,\qquad \Pr(O=1\mid F=1)=\frac45.\] Correct result when F=1 and O=1 are given. Conditional independence makes the O likelihood common to both values of I. The posterior probability of I=1 is therefore 9/10. Equivalently, its numerator is (1/2)(9/10)(4/5)=9/25 and the event probability is 2/5.

\[\Pr(I=1\mid O=1,F=1)=\frac{9/25}{2/5}=\frac9{10}=0.90.\] Printed-right-side result. Marginalizing F yields likelihood 13/50 for I=0 and 37/50 for I=1. Multiplying each by its 1/2 prior and normalizing gives 37/50=0.74 for I=1. The exact joint meta-parameter probability is also different: the correct P(I=1,E=1|O=1,F=1)=9/20=0.45, whereas the printed normalized right side gives 37/100=0.37.

\[\frac{(1/2)(37/50)}{(1/2)(13/50+37/50)}=\frac{37}{50}\ne\frac9{10}.\] The disagreement survives normalization: the correct odds for I=1 versus I=0 are 9, while the printed odds are 37/13. When the conditioned strategy is changed to F=0, the correct posterior is 0.10, but the integrated expression still gives 0.74. Thus the formula loses information that its left side explicitly conditions on. Analytic Bayes calculations and exact finite enumeration agree.
result: The printed update and the stated conditional target give different normalized posteriors in an admissible positive-probability model.
A marginal interpretation can be stated explicitly, but neither the intended complete algorithm nor empirical performance is verified by that correction.

repair.heading: Correction and verification scope
paragraphs: For strategy evidence \(F=f\), use \[p(\theta\mid O,F=f)\propto p(O\mid f,\theta)p(f\mid\theta)p(\theta).\] For a marginalized strategy, use \[p(\theta\mid O)\propto p(\theta)\int p(O\mid f,\theta)p(f\mid\theta)\,df.\] These are distinct inferential targets.
Both Bayes identities were checked analytically. Author intent, evidence accounting, calibrated likelihoods, the complete learning rule and empirical gains remain unresolved.

claim: The constant-sensitive derivations in D.7 and D.9 require \(\sum_{n=1}^Nn^{-1/2}\le\sqrt N/2\), while Appendix E effectively uses \(\sum_{n=1}^Nn^{-1/2}\le\sqrt N\). Appendix E also substitutes \(2H\sqrt{L/N}\) for the stated \(2HL/\sqrt N\).
The summation index satisfies \(N\ge1\); keep the stated stage and logarithmic factors when relating the scalar check to regret bounds.
analysis: Lemma D.7, p.25 after Eq.(34), turns 2H^2 sqrt(SL) times a state-action sum of n^(-1/2) into \(H^{2}\) S sqrt(A T_k L). With the displayed balanced upper limit N=T_k/(SA), this requires the false bound sum_{n=1}^N n^(-1/2)<=sqrt(N)/2. The same factor error occurs in term (c) on that page and in D.9, p.31, Eqs.(56)-(57). Appendix E, pp.34-35, instead effectively uses sum n^(-1/2)<=sqrt(N).

\[\begin{aligned}\sum_{n=1}^N n^{-1/2}&\ge\sqrt N>\frac{\sqrt N}{2}&& (N\ge1),\\ \sum_{n=1}^N n^{-1/2}&>\sqrt N&& (N>1).\end{aligned}\] The first inequality holds because every summand is at least 1/sqrt(N); no probabilistic or MDP assumption can make this scalar step valid. For a concrete large-count choice, take H=2,S=2,A=1,K=1000000,delta=0.05. Then T=2000000, N=1000000 and L=20.5001223; K exceeds 250HS^2AL. The sum is 1998.54014549 while the D.7 implied upper bound is 500. This diagnostic concerns the displayed intermediate sum, not an assertion that a stochastic variance attains that sum.

\[\sum_{n=1}^Nn^{-1/2}\le1+\int_1^N x^{-1/2}\,dx=2\sqrt N-1\le2\sqrt N.\] Using this bound in the displayed reindexing changes D.7’s coefficients from 1+4+2 to 4+4+8, giving a conservative combined coefficient 16 instead of 7. D.7 feeds the empirical-variance sum in D.9, which feeds Eq.(75) and the 24e/616e constants in Theorem 3.2. Appendix E has an additional bonus substitution: its summation uses 2H sqrt(L/N), although Theorem 3.1 specifies 2HL/sqrt(N). These are material errors in a contribution explicitly focused on constants.
result: The final constants are not proved false by these failures. Conditional on the remaining counting steps, replacing 7 by 16 still gives an Eq.(51) normalized envelope of about 2.1438 at the typical threshold, below its stated 4. A corrected CH envelope can also fit within the main 10HL term for nontrivial H>=2 and L>=log(20). These explicit slack checks are retained rather than asserting that every final coefficient must increase.

Other intermediate counting conventions need separate work: D.9 drops a stage index when aggregating stage-specific harmonic sums, and its b’ definition varies between \(H^{2}\) and \(H^{3}\). The scalar correction alone does not validate those steps, the probability event, or Problem 1. Major describes the invalid derivation of central constant-sensitive results; a complete repaired theorem remains unverified.

Evidence: primary p.25 image; independent_root_checks.py/json; agent_math/analysis.txt and independent_results.json. These calculations are analytic bounds with finite arithmetic checks, not empirical regret experiments.
The reciprocal-root summation constants in the central derivations are false under their displayed ranges.
Explicit slack checks preserve the possibility of some final bounds. A complete corrected probabilistic proof and all final constants remain unverified.

analysis: The official repository linked by the publisher is pinned to commit `3434b55b735d674d144eefce392b545425816ca1`. In agents.py, UCBVI.newEpisode (lines 79, 83) and MVP.newEpisode (line 216) compute population variance across the entries \(p_i\) \(V_i\). The formulas in the paper require the variance of V under probability weights p.
\[\mu=\sum_i p_iV_i,\qquad \operatorname{Var}_{p}(V)=\sum_i p_i(V_i-\mu)^2.\]

Code:
Released statistic: np.std(Phat[s,a,:] * Vstar[:,h+1])**2

Take p=(1/2,1/2), V=(1,0), admissible next-stage values with deterministic rewards and H>=2. The required variance is 1/4. The entrywise products are (1/2,0), whose population variance is 1/16. More generally, for uniform p over S states, the released statistic is the required variance divided by \(S^{2}\); the variance-dependent bonus component is therefore divided by S. This is a mathematical function mismatch, not a numerical tolerance issue.
Item | Inspected release | Paper specification
Terminal UCBVI bonus | Positive B/C still computed; terminal stage-count slot never updated | Footnote 5: zero bonus at stage H
UCBVI initialization/cap | H at all stages | Algorithm 1 starts at H-h+1
UCBVI log factor | log(5SAKH)=log(5SAT) | L=log(5HSAT/delta)
CH flag | improved=True gives 7; False gives 2 | The refined coefficient is 2
BF constant choices | 4, 7 and 84^2 versus 8, 14 and 100^2 | These coefficient choices agree

Minor is assigned to the confirmed released-code discrepancy; the paper-level numerical effect is a separate Needs Evidence item. The released computation is not a faithful evaluation of the displayed weighted-variance bonus, and its confidence setting differs. Because both BF variants share several differences, the effect on their empirical ranking or ratio cannot be inferred from the algebra.

The weighted-variance expression above is a precise local correction and was checked by independent rational arithmetic. It is not a validated repair of the entire implementation. No author file was edited or executed. Establishing the reported empirical effect requires the generating revision and raw results, followed by a corrected comparison if authorized.
The original implementation is preserved for static replay.
result: The released variance statistic is mathematically different from the required probability-weighted variance, with the exact uniform-state witness above. Historical empirical impact remains unestablished.
brief: The released code takes the variance of probability-weighted entries instead of probability-weighted value variance.
The exact uniform-state witness and additional release discrepancies do not determine historical curve changes.

claim: Theorem 3.2, pp.3-4 and its Appendix F restatement on p.35, defines the Bernstein-Freedman bonus with correction term C below. Lemma F.1 also omits an exterior factor L in its correction, although its minimum is outside the expectation. Write N=max{N_k(x,a),1}, and let expectation be under the empirical next-state distribution.

\[\begin{aligned}L&=\log(5HSAT/\delta),\\ b'(y)&=\min\!\left\{\frac{84^2H^3S^2AL^{2}}{\max\{1,N'_{k,h+1}(y)\}},H^{2}\right\},\\ C&=\sqrt{\frac{4\mathbb E_{\widehat P}b'}{N}}.\end{aligned}\] In Eq.(74), p.40, the substitution for this same bonus instead contains sqrt(4 L E_Phat[b’]/N)=sqrt(L) C. The subsequent variance comparison on p.41 relies on this enlarged term to cancel the term containing L times the squared value-estimation gap. Since L>1 and b’ is positive for finite counts, the inserted term is strictly larger. The \(L^{2}\) already inside b’ does not supply the additional exterior L.

\[\begin{aligned}\text{Stated:}\quad &\sqrt{4L\widehat{\mathcal V}/N}+C-\sqrt{2L\widehat{\mathcal V}^{*}/N},\\ \text{Eq. (74):}\quad &\sqrt{4L\widehat{\mathcal V}/N}+\sqrt L\,C-\sqrt{2L\widehat{\mathcal V}^{*}/N}.\end{aligned}\]

Take a stationary one-state MDP with two actions, both returning deterministically to that state with known reward zero. Set \(S=1\), \(A=H=2\), \(K=100000\), \(T=200000\), and \(\delta=0.05\), so \(SA=H=2\) and \(T\ge H^3S^3A=16\). The log factor is \(L=\log(80000000)\). In episode one choose \(a_0\) at both stages; later choose \(a_1\) at stage one and \(a_0\) at stage two. Terminal bonuses are zero, as footnote 5 requires. The unique transition law supplies the consistent zero-count convention. All true values are zero; transition and martingale errors vanish, and the relevant event and optimism conditions hold deterministically.

Rewards | R(s,a0)=R(s,a1)=0, known, deterministic and in [0,1]

Tie schedule | Episode 1: a0 at both stages. Later: a1 at stage 1, a0 at stage 2
Stage 2 | Footnote 5 sets terminal bonus to zero; estimated and true values are zero
Other regime conditions | SA=H=2; T>=\(H^{3}\) \(S^{3}\) A=16

For the sole state, the unique transition distribution also gives a consistent zero-count convention. Before episode K, N(a0)=K=100000, N(a1)=K-2=99998, and the stage-2 state count is K-1=99999. The raw b’ expression is approximately 373.859, so its cap is \(H^{2}\)=4. These counts follow from the stated schedule, not from freely assigning inconsistent counters.

All stage-2 actions tie at value zero. At stage 1, after the initial cap stops binding, the bonus B(n)+C(n) is decreasing in its visit count n. Action a1 has the smaller count and therefore the larger optimistic value. Earlier episodes can follow the same choices while the initial cap produces ties. Monotone Q clipping preserves this ordering. The independent reviewer calculation checked the closed-form greedy comparisons through all 100000 episodes; no author implementation was executed.
\[B(n)=\frac{7HL}{3(n-1)},\qquad C(n)=\frac{2H}{\sqrt n},\qquad n=99998.\]

Both empirical variances in Eq.(74) vanish. Transition-estimation and martingale deviations are zero, so event E and optimism hold deterministically. Yet the printed lower bound exceeds the actual left-hand side. The discrepancy is much larger than numerical rounding and follows directly from the distinct closed forms.

The actual regret is zero because all rewards are zero. This is deliberately an example of a false proof inequality under the algorithm’s assumptions, not a counterexample to the final regret bound or to optimism. Evidence: `verification/0070/agent_math/independent_checks.py`, independent_results.json, and rendered source pages 3, 37, 40 and 41.
result: Lemma F.1 is the optimism step used to replace true regret by optimistic regret and invoke the bonus/model-error bounds in Theorem 3.2. The substitution changes the quantity being analyzed. A complete execution on the next page makes the printed lower bound itself false, rather than merely identifying a notational ambiguity. Major is warranted by this invalid derivation of a central technical guarantee; empirical score deterioration is not required for that judgment.

There is no stated convention that absorbs the extra L: the main bonus, repeated lemma statement and released correction term agree in omitting it. The counterexample is also insensitive to the H^2/H^3 inconsistency and min/expectation order because it has one state and the b’ cap is active. Retaining a nonnegative future-value gap cannot justify the enlarged lower bound in that execution, where the future gap is zero.

Azar et al. (2017), main Algorithm 4 and supplement Lemma 19, already contain a related missing-L step: their variance-difference lower bound drops L. The current issue therefore has inherited lineage; the 2025 proof inserts L into the correction instead. Both primary versions and exact locations are preserved. No allegation about intent or historical discovery priority is made.

claim: The vector and matrix Frequent Directions algorithms have the advertised uniform data-dependent regret orders under their stated convexity, rank and comparator assumptions, with lagged-preconditioner stability factors absorbed into constants. Keep the original fixed algorithm parameters and comparator bounds; a uniform hidden constant cannot grow with the horizon or realized stability ratio. Honor the stated Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse convention, intended symmetric fast reconstruction, and the favorable correction from max to min.
analysis: Write G_t=sum_{i<=t} g_i g_i^T, bar g_t=sum_{i<=t} g_i, and rho_{1:t}=sum of the FD-discarded eigenvalues. FTSL uses A_t=B_t B_t^T+rho_{1:t} I and x_{t+1}=-eta A_t^{-1/2} bar g_t. FTFSL implements the analogous update through a larger basis and delayed compression. Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 assume convex losses and ||x*||<=D, choose eta=D/sqrt(2), and claim O(tr(G_T^{1/2})+sqrt(rho_{1:T})). D is fixed throughout the counterexamples.

Appendix A, p. 12, explicitly defines inverse notation to mean the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse when a matrix is singular. We honor that convention. Startup singularity is therefore not alleged as an undefined-algorithm defect. The counterexamples either use an ordinary positive inverse after the first gradient or act wholly within the observed gradient span.

The matrix theorem assumes convexity, gradient rank at most r, and ||X*||_F<=D_M. It uses eta=D_M/sqrt(r), epsilon>0 and the cumulative-gradient update X_{t+1}=-eta Ltilde_t^{-1/4} bar G_t^X Rtilde_t^{-1/4}. No gradient-norm cap is included among those theorem assumptions.

The uniform interpretation of big-O is essential: with the stated parameters and assumptions fixed, its hidden multiplicative constant cannot grow with the horizon or the realized gradient/preconditioner ratio. Merely renaming an unbounded sequence-dependent factor as a constant changes the claimed data-dependent guarantee.
Fix any d>=2, sketch size tau=1, D=1 and eta=1/sqrt(2). Let T=N+1, e1 be the first coordinate vector, and choose the following differentiable convex losses:

\[f_t(x)=-\frac{x^{(1)}}{N}\quad(1\le t\le N),\qquad f_{N+1}(x)=x^{(1)}.\] Every loss is convex and globally Lipschitz with gradient norm at most 1. The cumulative loss of every fixed x is zero, so x*=0 is an attained optimum and satisfies the comparator assumption. Nonuniqueness is permitted by the source. A smooth unique-optimum strengthening is given below.

In FTSL with tau=1, FD discards the only eigenvalue each round, so B_t=0 and rho_{1:t}=sum_{i<=t}||g_i||^2. For the first k gradients, rho_{1:k}=k/N^2 and bar g_k=-(k/N)e1. Hence A_k=(k/N^2)I and the actual next decision is x_{k+1}=eta sqrt(k)e1. These matrices are positive definite for k>=1.

In FTFSL the gradients stay in one direction, so the maintained rank remains 1<2tau and no compression occurs. Its escaped mass is zero; the preconditioner is the exact rank-one G_k. Its prescribed pseudoinverse gives exactly the same decision trajectory. Thus the example also covers the fast method without any sketch approximation error.

\[R_N=\eta\left(\sqrt N-\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\sqrt k\right)\ge\frac{\eta}{3}\sqrt N.\] The inequality follows from sum_{k=0}^{N-1}sqrt(k)<=integral_0^N sqrt(u)du=(2/3)N^{3/2}. At the final horizon G_T=(1+1/N)e1 e1^T. The expression in Theorem 4.1 is exactly 2sqrt(1+1/N)<=2sqrt(2), while that in Theorem 4.2 is sqrt(1+1/N)<=sqrt(2). Actual regret diverges like sqrt(N), while each claimed controlling expression stays bounded. No horizon-independent constant can make the advertised orders hold.
N | Actual vector regret | FTSL claimed expression | Regret / expression

The table is reviewer arithmetic for the displayed formulas, not an author-code experiment. The analytic unbounded ratio is the proof; a finite ratio exceeding one alone would not refute an unspecified big-O constant.

The failure is not restricted to a nonunique optimum. The total fixed-comparator objective is then sqrt(1+||x+e1||^2)-1, uniquely minimized at x*=-e1, with ||x*||=D=1. All losses remain smooth and convex, and every gradient is globally bounded by 2. The prefix trajectory is unchanged; terminal squared-gradient mass is at most 5, while regret is the preceding \(R_N\) plus a nonnegative term and still diverges. This removes both a uniqueness objection and a concern about choosing D larger than a zero comparator’s norm.

For fixed sketch sizes tau>=2, the same rank-one sequence is retained exactly, with zero discarded mass and the same pseudoinverse trajectory. Thus the mechanism is not a one-column sketch artifact. It concerns the unconstrained cumulative-gradient update and its missing stability control.

Appendix A.2, p. 13, compares the lagged preconditioner A_{t-1} with the current covariance G_t through a_t, then sets C1=max_t 1/sqrt(a_t). The publisher PDF actually prints a_t=max{rho_{1:t-1}/(||g_t||^2+rho_{1:t-1}),1} and claims a_t<=1. For nonnegative masses that maximum is 1; the required matrix comparison generally fails. Replacing max by min corrects the immediate expression but does not bound C1.

For the normalized tau=1 counterexample, before the last gradient rho_{1:N}=1/N and ||g_{N+1}||^2=1. Even after ignoring the initial zero-mass issue, the corrected ratio is a_{N+1}=1/(N+1), so C1>=sqrt(N+1). It cannot be absorbed into a uniform constant. In the no-compression fast case rho remains zero, making the same escaped-mass comparison even less informative.

There is also an initialization problem in the imported lagged-regret lemma as printed. For T=1, tau=1, D=1, eta=1/sqrt(2), take f1(x)=|\(x^{(1)}\)+1|, x1=0 and x*=-e1. The queried gradient is e1, A1=I and A0=0. Actual regret is 1. Lemma A.1’s right-hand side is Psi1(x*)/eta+(eta/2)||g1||^2_{A0^{-1/2}}=1/sqrt(2), because the prescribed zero pseudoinverse makes the second term zero. The displayed lemma therefore fails in this admissible instance. A positive initial regularizer requires a different statement and proof treatment.

These diagnostics explain the theorem failure, but the complete trajectory counterexample is independently decisive. Correcting the max/min symbol or an omitted transpose does not alter that trajectory and cannot repair its divergent ratio.

Fix m=n=2 and tau=r=D_M=epsilon=eta=1. Let E11 denote the matrix with a single 1 in position (1,1). For N>=8 use the first N losses -X_11 and the final loss N X_11+(1/2)||X||_F^2. Their sum is exactly (1/2)||X||_F^2, so X*=0 is the unique optimum. Every gradient queried along the trajectory has rank one, satisfying Assumption 3.3. No gradient-norm bound is assumed by Theorem 4.4.

With tau=1, each left/right sketch discards its sole nonzero eigenvalue. Consequently Lhat=Rhat=0, rho^L=rho^R=S_t (the cumulative squared scalar-gradient mass), and Ltilde=Rtilde=(1+S_t)I_2. After k of the first gradients, the exact decision is X_{k+1}=k/sqrt(k+1) E11. All inverse powers are ordinary positive definite matrix functions.

\[R_N=\frac{N^{2}}{\sqrt{N+1}}-\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{k}{\sqrt{k+1}}+\frac{N^{2}}{2(N+1)}\ge\frac14N^{3/2}\quad(N\ge8).\] Let q=N+N/sqrt(N+1) be the final scalar gradient and S=N+\(q^{2}\). The true terminal left and right covariance matrices each have eigenvalues 1+S and 1. With rho^L=rho^R=S and r=1, the factor displayed in Theorem 4.4 is:

\[B_N=\left((1+S)^{1/4}+1+S^{1/4}\right)^{2}\le25N,\qquad \frac{R_N}{B_N}\ge\frac{\sqrt N}{100}\longrightarrow\infty.\] A simple bound suffices: q<=2N and S<=5N^2, so the displayed factor is O(N); meanwhile k/sqrt(k+1)<=sqrt(k) and N^2/sqrt(N+1) is at least sqrt(8/9)N^{3/2} for N>=8, giving the stated regret lower bound. Reviewer calculations independently reproduce the exact recurrence. At N=512, 2,048, 8,192 and 32,768 the exact regret/factor ratios are approximately 1.853, 3.734, 7.503 and 15.045.

Page 22 identifies the same missing control explicitly: C3=[min_t sqrt(r epsilon/(||g_t||^2+r epsilon))]^{-1}. Here it grows with N. A separately imposed, horizon-independent gradient cap, or an explicit retained C3 term, would change the matrix theorem and can block this family. The source’s current convexity/rank/comparator assumptions do not supply that cap. This is grouped with the vector failure as one fundamental issue, not counted as a second unrelated discovery.
result: Complete admissible loss sequences make actual regret divided by the advertised controlling factor unbounded. Horizon-dependent stability factors cannot be hidden in a uniform constant.
The conclusion concerns the targeted mathematical guarantees and dependent corollaries; it does not establish failure of all empirical runs or regularized variants.
brief: The actual regret grows without bound relative to the advertised controlling factors on admissible vector and matrix loss sequences.
The vector witness already has a fixed gradient cap. FD approximation, empirical outcomes and restricted regularized variants remain outside this refutation.

repair.heading: Correction and verification scope
paragraphs: A restricted vector repair adds a fixed ridge \(\delta>0\): \(A_t=\delta I+B_tB_t^\top+\rho_{1:t}I\), with \(A_0=\delta I\), and assumes a fixed \(\|g_t\|\le G\). With \(G_T=\sum_{t=1}^Tg_tg_t^\top\), the retained proof gives \[R(T)\le\frac{D^{2}}{2\eta}\left(\sqrt\delta+\sqrt{\rho_{1:T}}+\operatorname{tr}G_T^{1/2}\right)+\eta\sqrt{1+G^{2}/\delta}\,\operatorname{tr}G_T^{1/2}.\]

This changes the original vector algorithm and retains explicit ridge and gradient dependence. No repaired matrix theorem, preservation of the original scale behavior, or empirical invariance was established.

fields.source_location: Sections 4.2 (p. 5) and 5.5 (pp. 8–9); Appendix cost evaluations
claim: The changing-cost scalar evaluation diagnoses whether a model recovers the optimal graph alignment \(P^*\). The check uses the zero-substitution settings \(C_0=(1,1,0,1,1)\) and \(C_3=(1,1,0,11,12)\) from Table 5, with simple connected undirected graphs. The inspected \(C_0\)-trained branch retains its scalar predictions when the target costs change; the cost-feature \(C_1\) branch is separate.
analysis: Source claim. Sections 4.2 (p5) and 5.5 (p8) present the cost-variant tests as assessing whether models recover the optimal alignment P*. Page 9 interprets performance through alignment capability. The stated target is stronger than end-to-end prediction under a changed cost vector.

The inspected C0-trained baseline branch omits cost features, reloads the same learned checkpoint at each cost setting, and changes the GED targets. This is visible in inference_with_diff_ged_cost.ipynb cells 3-5 and utils/data_utils.py lines 223-268 [E2]. GraphEdX separately applies cost coefficients to its output. The manuscript itself acknowledges unchanged predictions on p9, so this is a disclosed interface difference, not an alleged hidden implementation bug. The C1-trained branch supplies four cost features and must be distinguished.

Admissible failure with perfect alignments. Use the paper’s C0=(1,1,0,1,1) and C3=(1,1,0,11,12). For K2 to P3, an optimal alignment adds one node and one edge; exact costs are 2 and 12. A model can recover that alignment perfectly but continue reporting its C0 cost 2, producing squared error 100 at C3. Thus changed-cost error does not imply incorrect alignment.

The two-pair example below also reverses Kendall ordering, so the problem is not merely MSE units. Every graph is simple, connected, undirected and unlabeled. Pair A preserves the source edge and attains the mandatory additions of three nodes and three edges. Pair B deletes exactly the edge-count difference 10-6=4. Each construction attains cardinality lower bounds and is therefore optimal under both cost settings. A perfect C0 predictor returns 6>4, whereas C3 truth is 36<48: Kendall tau is -1 despite exact alignments [E4].

Success is not alignment identification either. Let D0 be exact C0 GED, a=(n’-n)+, d=(n-n’)+ and DeltaE=|E’|-|E|. In the valid zero-substitution regime, edge additions plus deletions equal D0-a-d, and their difference is DeltaE. The identity below therefore converts an exact scalar D0 and graph counts into every compatible GED_C, without producing a node correspondence.

Impact and strongest counterreading. These tests validly assess joint cost-generalization under the chosen model interface. They do not by themselves identify learned alignments, and their failures cannot justify the stronger alignment-specific diagnosis. That invalid inference affects a central advertised purpose of the adversarial benchmark, supporting Major at that claim level. It does not show that actual baselines recover perfect alignments, that numerical results are false, or that the cost-conditioned C1 results are all invalid.

A precise alignment-specific evaluation would require a feasible predicted correspondence and compare its induced edit cost with a known optimal cost, allowing all optimal mappings. By definition, equality then establishes optimality of the submitted path. For scalar-only models, describe the task as cost-conditioned GED prediction and consider the scalar transport identity as a theoretical control. These criteria are analytically supported; no empirical rescoring, retraining or adoption is claimed.
\[\operatorname{GED}_{C}=c_{\rm NA}a+c_{\rm ND}d+\frac{c_{\rm EA}+c_{\rm ED}}{2}(D_0-a-d)+\frac{c_{\rm EA}-c_{\rm ED}}{2}\Delta E.\]
Graph pair | Optimal operations | C0 truth / fixed prediction | C3 truth
A: K2 to P5 | 3 node additions + 3 edge additions | 6 | 36
B: K5 to C5 plus one chord | 4 edge deletions | 4 | 48
result: The scalar cost-shift benchmark cannot by itself identify alignment recovery. This limits a central advertised diagnostic purpose while preserving its numerical cost-generalization task.

analysis: The Proposition 4.1 proof on pp4-5 also uses an invalid degree-only equality for substitution cost. Equal degrees do not ensure equal aligned neighborhoods. With source edges {(0,1),(1,2)}, target edges {(0,2),(1,2)}, identity alignment and labels (A,C,D)/(B,C,D), the matched vertex 0 has degree 1 in each graph. Unit substitution/addition/deletion costs give a true cost of 3 (one substitution and two edge edits), whereas the displayed degree formula gives 1. This invalid derivation is a Major subfinding (F1b). The false equality is used to prove Proposition 4.1; Theorem 4.2 invokes that proposition to fix node-edit counts; the theorem then supports reuse of alignments in the augmentation method. The witness can take all five costs equal to 1, so cNS=1<\(c_{\rm NA}+c_{\rm ND}\)=2. The proposition itself survives the independent repair below. Ease of repair does not reduce the severity of the invalid core proof step.

A correct exchange proof merges one deleted source node with one inserted target node while retaining every other real match. No previously matched edge is destroyed. Node addition and deletion counts each drop by one, while substitutions increase by at most one. Nonnegative edge costs therefore give a total change at most cNS-\(c_{\rm NA}-c_{\rm ND}\)<0. This proves the no-paired-insertion/deletion result under its original assumptions.

For cNS=0, optimal node counts are consequently fixed by graph-size differences. If m(P) counts preserved edges, the cost is Cnodes+\(c_{\rm ED}\)|E|+\(c_{\rm EA}\)|E’|-(\(c_{\rm EA}+c_{\rm ED}\))m(P). Positive \(c_{\rm EA}+c_{\rm ED}\) means every allowed cost vector selects exactly the same maximum-common-edge alignments. This supplies the missing invariant behind the weighted-edge minimization step and proves the theorem heading’s restricted statement.

The supported correction is to retain cNS=0 with the other four costs positive, or independently solve/validate positive-substitution configurations. Restricting the domain restores a valid guarantee; it does not prove the false broader one. No author files or published experiments were modified.
claim: The proof of Proposition 4.1 uses an equality depending only on vertex degrees to evaluate the matched-edge term. The equality must hold for the actual alignment and graphs in its domain.
result: A valid exchange bound DeltaC<=cNS-\(c_{\rm NA}-c_{\rm ND}\)<0 proves the same proposition without that equality. Existing matched edges remain matched when a deleted source vertex and inserted target vertex are merged. The cNS=0 invariance theorem also has a valid independent proof.

claim: The broader cost-invariance claim requires the same optimal graph alignment to remain optimal when the admitted edit-cost parameters change, under the stated graph and cost assumptions. Simple connected undirected labeled paths. All five costs positive. cNS<\(c_{\rm NA}\)+cND. Sufficient padding for partial mappings.
analysis: Source and operative assumptions. Theorem 4.2’s heading on p5 requires cNS=0 and \(c_{\rm NA}\),\(c_{\rm ND}\),\(c_{\rm EA}\),\(c_{\rm ED}\)>0. Its proof-closing sentence instead claims invariance for all five positive costs satisfying cNS<\(c_{\rm NA}\)+cND. Section 4.2 uses invariance to justify reusing an optimal alignment to generate ground-truth labels across cost settings. Appendix A.2.1, p14, repeats the weaker inequality. The demonstrated failure concerns the explicit broader conclusion on p5, not the theorem heading.

Complete counterexample. Both graphs are the simple connected undirected path 0-1-2, with source labels (A,A,B) and target labels (A,B,A). Use cost order (node addition, node deletion, node substitution, edge addition, edge deletion). Each graph is padded to six vertices with three isolated artificial vertices, so every partial matching is representable. In both settings below every cost is strictly positive and cNS=1<20=\(c_{\rm NA}\)+cND. Ordinary undirected edges are counted once.

All 720 padded permutations were independently enumerated for each cost vector using exact fractions [E3]. The two optimal real-map sets are disjoint. Each has 12 padded optima, accounting for dummy permutations. The minimum cost among alignments with any real-node deletion/insertion is 20.5 in the low-edge setting and 24 in the high-edge setting, so partial mappings do not defeat the example.

A high-edge-cost optimal alignment reused at low cost returns 2 rather than the true GED of 1/2. Reusing a low-edge-cost optimum at high cost returns 4 rather than 2. This is a concrete wrong-label mechanism for the broadened compatibility rule supporting the core augmentation method. Major follows from this dependency, independently of whether any released experiment used the invalid regime.

Counterevidence and exact limits. Every C0-C6 configuration in Table 5 sets cNS=0. Section 5.4 also expressly invokes the zero-substitution regime. Appendix p14 can be read narrowly as referring only to those seven settings. These observations preserve the demonstrated applicability of the restricted theorem to the published configurations; they do not make the p5 universal positive-substitution conclusion true. No corruption of Table 5 labels is inferred from this counterexample.
Cost vector | Optimal real maps | Operations and exact GED
(10,10,1,2,2) | (0,1,2), (2,1,0) | 2 substitutions; no edge edits; GED=2

claim: The released filtered training and test graph split is intended to exclude leakage visible to the graph model. The check compares graph structure and model-visible labels up to isomorphism, rather than file identity alone. Stored graphs symmetrized by checked PyG path. Constant node features. Released snapshot only.
analysis: The pinned release’s Linux_filtered data contain two train-test isomorphism classes after the edge symmetrization used by the PyG input builder (utils/data_utils.py, lines 95-100). The raw objects are directed graphs; they are distinct under directed isomorphism. The model input builder adds both directions for every stored arc. All inspected train/test node-feature storage contains only 1.0, so features do not distinguish these examples. This establishes a release-level failure of the advertised isomorphic-separation invariant for that model path, independently of whether it affected the published run.

An exact seven-node witness uses zero-based train index 41 and test index 1. Ignoring stored direction, train edges are {(0,1),(0,3),(1,2),(2,4),(2,6),(5,6)}. Test edges are {(0,1),(0,3),(0,5),(1,2),(3,4),(4,6)}. The train-to-test map (0,1,2,3,4,5,6) -> (4,3,0,6,5,2,1) sends the first set exactly to the second. Constant features are preserved. The second witness is train 32/test 18. The full edge lists, mappings, data hashes and inert parsing method are saved in code_directed_graph_results.json and code_feature_check.json.

The narrow conclusion is that 2 of the 19 test graphs in this released filtered set have model-equivalent training counterparts under the checked path. Some adjacency consumers treat direction differently; do not generalize to every architecture. The release contains 98 filtered LINUX graphs, while the paper reports 89 undirected unique graphs, reinforcing the need for a run/version map. Without that map or reruns, the magnitude of any historical Table 2 effect is Needs Evidence. Minor is supported for the verified release inconsistency, without promoting it to a demonstrated paper-wide experimental failure.

A precise prevention rule is to normalize graphs to the actual model-visible edge/feature semantics, form exact feature-preserving isomorphism classes, and split whole classes. By construction, this prevents a class from crossing splits. That invariant is logically verified; no dataset or author implementation was changed and no corrected score is claimed.
result: Verified release-level split invariant failure; published Table2effect not established.

claim:
Section 3 assumes \(W=W_\phi\in {\rm GL}_D(\mathbb R)\) and a shared univariate affine foundation model \[f_{\rm FM}(X)=W_{\rm FM}^{\mathsf T}X+b\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}.\] No nonzero-rank assumption on \(W_{\rm FM}\), no restriction on \(Y\), and no nonorthogonality requirement involving \(b\) and \(Y-W_{\rm FM}^{\mathsf T}X\) are stated. Put \[A=Y-W_{\rm FM}^{\mathsf T}X,\qquad B=b\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}.\] The loss reduces exactly to \[L(W)=\|A-BW^{-1}\|_F^2.
 \] The paper proposes \[W_*=(B^{\mathsf T}A)^+B^{\mathsf T}B.
 \] Appendix A.1 explicitly writes the optimization domain as \({\rm GL}_D(\mathbb R)\).

The domain is \(W\in\operatorname{GL}_D(\mathbb R)\), with \(A=Y-W_{\rm FM}^{\mathsf T}X\), \(B=b\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}\), and \(L(W)=\|A-BW^{-1}\|_F^{2}\). No extra rank or nonorthogonality condition is assumed. The explicit instance uses \(L=H=1\), \(D=2\), \(X=(0,0)\), \(W_{\rm FM}=0\), \(b=1\), and \(Y=(1,2)\).
analysis: Proposition 3.3, Eq. (4), and its proof in Appendix A.1 claim an optimizer over invertible adapters but produce a singular matrix whenever \(D>1\). The ridge expression in Remark 3.4 does not remove this obstruction.

Because \(B=b\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}\), its rank is at most one. Consequently \[\operatorname{rank}(W_*)\leq
 \operatorname{rank}(B^{\mathsf T}B)\leq1.\] For every \(D>1\), the displayed formula is outside the optimization domain; the inverse required by the displayed formula is undefined. This is an exact structural obstruction, not a numerical conditioning issue. Whenever the left inverse in the proposed ridge modification exists, \[W_\lambda=(B^{\mathsf T}A+\lambda I)^{-1}B^{\mathsf T}B\] also has rank at most one.

For a fully specified admissible instance, take \(L=H=1\), \(D=2\), \(X=(0,0)\), \(W_{\rm FM}=0\), \(b=1\), and \(Y=(1,2)\). These satisfy the paper’s model assumptions. Then \(A=(1,2)\), \(B=(1,1)\), and independent exact arithmetic gives \[W_*=\begin{pmatrix}1/5&1/5\\2/5&2/5\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 W_{\lambda=1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/4&1/4\\1/4&1/4\end{pmatrix}.\] Both determinants are zero. In contrast, \[W_{\rm feasible}=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/2)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 BW_{\rm feasible}^{-1}=(1,2)=A,\qquad L(W_{\rm feasible})=0,\] while \(L(I)=1\). Thus an invertible optimum exists in this example, but the reported formula does not produce it.

The theorem does not always have any attained minimum. With the same dimensions, \(A=0\), and \(B=(1,1)\), every invertible \(W\) gives \(BW^{-1}\ne0\), hence \(L(W)>0\). The sequence \(W=tI\), \(t\to\infty\), has \(L(W)=2/t^{2}\to0\). The infimum is zero and is not attained.

The final paragraph of Appendix A.1 asserts convexity in \(W\), citing the inverse operation. Even on a convex positive scalar domain this is false. For \(A=B=1\) and \(w>0\), \[f(w)=(1-w^{-1})^{2},\qquad
 f''(w)=\frac{6-4w}{w^{4}},\qquad f''(2)=-\frac18.\] Equivalently, \(f(2)=1/4>53/225=[f(3/2)+f(5/2)]/2\). The loss is a quadratic in \(M=W^{-1}\), but this does not make it convex in \(W\), and invertibility still restricts the admissible \(M\).

The stationary equation \(B^{\mathsf T}AW=B^{\mathsf T}B\) does not justify discarding its null-space freedom and selecting a singular minimum-norm matrix. The omitted freedom is precisely what can make a solution invertible. Remark A.4 proposes channel-dependent biases to obtain full-rank \(B\). This changes the shared-univariate-model assumption and therefore does not establish Proposition 3.3 as stated. Full-rank \(B\) by itself also does not guarantee a full-rank \(B^{\mathsf T}A\).

A corrected characterization for the stated shared-bias case is simple. If \(b\ne0\), write \(q^{\mathsf T}=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}W^{-1}\), which must be nonzero. Every nonzero row \(q^{\mathsf T}\) can be realized by some invertible \(W\), by extending nonzero row vectors to bases. The unconstrained least-squares row is \[q_*^{\mathsf T}=\frac{b^{\mathsf T}A}{b^{\mathsf T}b}.\] If \(q_*\ne0\), any invertible completion satisfying \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}W^{-1}=q_*^{\mathsf T}\) attains the minimum. If \(q_*=0\), the infimum is not attained. If \(b=0\), the loss is constant on all invertible \(W\). This characterization is an analytic correction, not an author-adopted repair.

The paper explicitly identifies theoretical foundations as a contribution on page 2, calls Proposition 3.3 its foundational motivation on page 3, and claims to evaluate Eq. (4) in Figure 2 on page 4. The demonstrated invalid derivation therefore affects a core theoretical contribution and its synthetic optimality interpretation. This supports Major. It does not establish that the separately trained encoder–decoder method fails or that any real-data score is wrong. The useful existence of better adapters in some cases is compatible with this counterexample; the theorem and its advertised optimizer are nevertheless invalid. Historical Figure 2 code and outputs would be needed to determine how an inverse of the displayed singular expression was handled.
result: The advertised optimizer and its ridge modification are inadmissible for \(D>1\) under shared bias. Existence and convexity also need additional conditions; the separately trained practical method and empirical scores are not refuted.
brief: The claimed shared-bias optimizer has rank at most \(1\), so it is singular for \(D>1\).
An invertible optimum can exist, but is not always attained; the practical encoder–decoder results remain separate.

repair.heading: Correction and verification scope
paragraphs: For \(b\ne0\), optimize over the nonzero row \(q^{\mathsf T}=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}W^{-1}\). Its unconstrained optimum is \(q_*^{\mathsf T}=b^{\mathsf T}A/(b^{\mathsf T}b)\). If \(q_*\ne0\), an invertible completion attains the optimum; if \(q_*=0\), the infimum is not attained. If \(b=0\), every invertible adapter has equal loss. This analytic characterization and explicit numerical case do not establish author adoption or an experimental repair.

result: \(\operatorname{Decode}(\operatorname{mean}U)\) differs from \(\operatorname{mean}(\operatorname{decode}U)\): samples0,2 give .761594 vs .482014 for tanh. \(g(u)=-u\) maps latent mean0,sd1 lower/upper endpoints to 1,-1. Current returned moments/bounds lack the advertised general interpretation; published scores/plots remain Needs Evidence.
claim: ADAPTS.predict_multi_step returns predictive mean and lower/upper summaries after decoding.
Nonlinear decoder for mean discrepancy. Negative linear decoder permitted for bound reversal. Synthetic transformations are independent mathematical diagnostics, not executions of the author model.
analysis: The acquired `ADAPTS.predict_multi_step` summarizes latent predictions before applying the decoder, although a nonlinear or sign-mixing decoder does not preserve those summaries. The effect on the proceedings experiments remains Needs Evidence.

In `src/adapts/adapts.py`, lines 217–254, the program obtains latent sample means and standard deviations, then applies `inverse_transform` to the mean and to componentwise mean-plus/minus-standard-deviation vectors. With decoder \(g\) and latent forecast \(U\), it therefore returns \(g(\widehat{\mathbb E}U)\), whereas the Monte Carlo predictive mean is \(\widehat{\mathbb E}[g(U)]\). These differ for nonlinear \(g\). For equal samples \(U=0,2\) and \(g(u)=\tanh u\), independent arithmetic gives \[g(\bar U)=0.761594,\qquad
 \frac{g(0)+g(2)}2=0.482014.\] The released VAE decoder contains nonlinear LeakyReLU and Tanh layers, so the required affine identity is not imposed.

Even an affine decoder can invalidate the returned bounds. For \(g(u)=-u\), latent mean zero and standard deviation one, the returned lower value is \(g(-1)=1\), and the upper value is \(g(1)=-1\). A negative decoder weight is permitted by the released linear decoder classes. More generally, a multivariate linear decoder requires propagation of the covariance, not simultaneous transformation of componentwise endpoints.

The proper computation is to decode each joint sample with consistent decoder and normalization state, then calculate the desired means, standard deviations, or quantiles in the original space. The supplied `compute_ks_metric` already decodes individual draws before its calibration calculation; this is material counterevidence against claiming that the identified summary-order defect automatically invalidates every ECE value. No historical plot or score was reproduced. The established result concerns the current returned summaries and their interpretation, not a measured loss of the paper’s empirical advantage.

claim: Hyperparameter optimization uses outer-fold validation of the fitted forecasting pipeline.
Moment branch with trainable forecast head (freeze_head=False). Default outer3fold construction. Head fitting receives full pooled X_train/y_train and no explicit validation arrays.
analysis: The current hyperparameter-search script constructs outer folds but fits the Moment forecasting head on the complete pooled data, including the current outer validation fold.

In `scripts/hyperopt.py`, lines 145–148 combine the original training and validation arrays. Lines 290–316 construct fold-specific train and validation subsets. However, lines 334–345 call `fine_tune_iclearner` with `X=X_train` and `y=y_train`, not the fold-training arrays. The subsequent adapter fit does use the fold subsets. The forecast model and learner are created before the fold loop; only the adapter is re-created inside it.

This is supervised label access, not merely fitting a feature scaler on contexts. The Moment wrapper creates a tensor dataset from every supplied pair and, without explicit validation arguments, randomly splits that entire dataset 90/10 before optimizing the unfrozen forecasting head. For a concrete 30-example, three-fold case, each outer validation set has ten elements and the inner head-training set has 27. Their intersection must contain at least \(27+10-30=7\) elements, regardless of the random split. Thus at least 70% of that outer validation set’s labels enter supervised head training. The independent check verifies this set bound; no training was executed.

This defeats the interpretation of the resulting fold metric as validation of the entire fitted forecasting pipeline. It does not prove that test labels were trained on: the separate test arrays remain outside this pool, and the inspected search objective selects by validation MSE, not the saved test score. The corrected procedure must reinitialize the trainable head and adapter for each outer fold and confine all supervised fitting to the outer training portion, with a suitable inner validation split. The released snapshot demonstrates the protocol defect; experiment-time configurations and logs are needed to determine whether it affected the paper’s selected hyperparameters or final scores.
result: Outer validation labels enter supervised head training. Example n30: head inner train27, outer validation10 => intersection>=7 independently of inner random split. Only adapter is rebuilt each fold; learner/head created before loop. Released outer-fold score is not held out for the entire pipeline; historical hyperparameter/result consequences Needs Evidence.

claim: The stated \(\ell_1\)-penalized objective yields the printed quadratic mask update and its asserted optimization guarantees.
Use the specified \(S(r)=|r|\), including zero residuals permitted by the initialization. For the separate normal-equation check, freeze the other variables as the derivation stipulates.
analysis: Equation (4), p. 3, explicitly defines \(S\) as an \(\ell_1\) norm. Equations (10)–(12), p. 4, replace it by a quadratic Taylor model whose justification assumes that \(\nabla S\) is Lipschitz continuous. For the scalar restriction \(S(r)=|r|\), the derivative is undefined at zero, and for \(r=\varepsilon\) and \(s=-\varepsilon\), the derivative difference divided by \(|r-s|\) equals \(1/\varepsilon\). No finite global gradient-Lipschitz constant exists.

This obstruction is directly relevant to the proposed initialization: zero masks and the piecewise mapping in Equation (5) permit zero residuals. Choosing zero as a subgradient at zero does not supply a differentiable function or a valid tangent quadratic upper model: \(|r|>Lr^{2}/2\) for sufficiently small nonzero \(r\) and any finite \(L\). An additive constant that makes a quadratic a loose bound cannot restore the missing first-order equality required by the stated Taylor argument. A deliberately smoothed penalty could fix the premise, but its definition, smoothing scale, approximation error and resulting update are absent.

Even if Equation (12) is taken simply as a chosen quadratic surrogate, its printed solution is wrong. Interpret image products charitably as pointwise operations and consider one scalar pixel, freezing \(w_k,\widetilde m_k,R_{k-1}\) as stipulated. The coefficient of \(\widehat m\) in the normal equation must be \[C^{2}+\mu+\alpha L_S w_k^{2},\] whereas Equation (13) sets \(Q_a=C^{2}+\mu+L_Sw_k^{2}\), omitting \(\alpha\). The numerator retains \(\alpha\), so a uniform redefinition of \(L_S\) does not remove the discrepancy. For \(C=1\), \(B=0\), \(\mu=1\), \(\alpha=2\), \(L_S=10\), \(m_{k-1}=0.2\), \(\widetilde m_k=0.1\), \(w_k=w_{k-1}=1\), and \(R_{k-1}=0.1\) with gradient one, Equation (12) has \[J(m)=\tfrac12(1-m)^{2}+\tfrac12(m-0.2)^{2}+10(m-0.1)^2.\] Its unique minimizer is \(3.2/22\approx0.145455\). Equation (13) instead gives \(3.2/12\approx0.266667\), where \(J'(m)=2.666667\ne0\). This scalar case already disproves the displayed closed-form claim. If one scalar mask is shared across RGB channels, the data-term coefficient additionally needs the appropriate channel sum; averaging independent channelwise solutions is not generally the same minimization.

The supplied `get_m_hat.py`, lines 39–49, differs further: its denominator adds a constant \(L_S\) without \(w_k^{2}\) or \(\alpha\), while its numerator retains their product. The constructor’s \(L_s\) argument is stored but the formula resets \(L_s\) to an all-ones tensor. Those choices may define a useful learned architecture, but they do not verify the claimed exact optimization correspondence.

This is Major because the paper emphasizes mathematically strict connections in Figure 3 and explicit theoretical guarantees on p. 8. It is a derivation failure, not a proof that the learned model must perform poorly. Use a valid nonsmooth proximal update or state and analyze a smooth surrogate; rederive the normal equations; define all pointwise operations, channel reductions and initial states, including \(M_{-1}\) needed at \(k=1\). If arbitrary learned blocks replace proximal maps and gradients, identify which guarantees survive and under what assumptions. Otherwise describe the method as optimization-inspired and remove unsupported convergence or optimality wording. The background scalar update in Equation (17) was checked and does solve its stated quadratic surrogate; that local correctness does not repair the mask derivation.
result: The stated nonsmooth objective does not support the smooth Taylor argument, and the printed mask update fails its own normal equation. The learned architecture may still be useful; its strict optimization correspondence requires correction.

repair.heading: Correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use a valid \(\ell_1\) proximal method or explicitly define and analyze a smoothing model; rederive coefficients, channel reductions and initial states, including \(M_{-1}\). State the assumptions under which guarantees survive learned replacements, or qualify the architecture as optimization-inspired. The local algebraic checks and correct background update do not establish an empirical repair or author adoption.

claim: The released training and inference implement persistent learned RSS blocks and joint reconstruction-guided segmentation unfolding.
Use the acquired default loss, forward graph and inference return value; correspondence to the historical experimental program is not established.
analysis: Equation (22), p. 5, includes stage-wise reconstruction loss, and Figures 2–3 and Algorithm S1 require a refined background to influence the next segmentation stage. In the advertised `Train.py`, lines 80–82, a reconstruction quantity is computed, but line 83 sets the differentiated objective to `loss_init + loss_final + loss_edge + 2 * ual_loss`. The reconstruction quantity is absent; it is only logged afterward.

The extra uncertainty loss is defined in `utils.py`, lines 29–33, as the mean of \(1-(2\sigma(z)-1)^{2}\), rather than the reconstruction term in Equation (22). Moreover, in the default `Network.forward`, `Network.py` lines 646–682, the mask pipeline and selective Mamba branch modify only the coarse returned mask after `REM11` has already computed all four masks. Reconstructed backgrounds are then computed at lines 669–680, with no call returning them to another segmentation update. `REM11`, lines 998–1025 of `Modules.py`, was read to confirm the ordering and independent returned tensors. `Test.py` line 55 selects return element four, the fine mask `f1` computed before those modifications. Thus the reconstructed background branch is absent from the final forward dependency and, with the reconstruction term omitted, its own parameters have no path to the optimized loss. Auxiliary supervision on the modified coarse mask can still affect shared encoder training; this review does not claim that every added branch has no training effect.

A further implementation defect affects the central RSS component. `Network.py` line 655 creates a local `Selectivemamba()` on each call; its own forward method creates local `VSSBlock` instances at `Modules.py` lines 324 and 329. These are newly initialized module objects, not registered persistent children of the model used by the optimizer at `Train.py` line 214 or by checkpoint loading. They are therefore not learned and restored as the paper’s fixed trained RSS blocks. Calling `model.eval()` cannot turn newly created, unregistered objects into persistent evaluated submodules. This statement follows from object construction and registration, not an executed training trace.

These discrepancies constitute a Major obstacle to reproducing the central joint reconstruction/segmentation mechanism. A different historical program or accidentally released development branch could explain them; the published tables are not proved fabricated or numerically wrong. Publish the source and configurations that generated them, register state-space modules in constructors, make every intended background-to-mask dependency explicit, and include the intended reconstruction term in the training objective. Recompute the mechanism ablations with matched checkpoints and verify gradients reach the reconstruction branch. The present loss and graph cannot substantiate the claimed reconstruction-guided causal explanation merely because an intermediate image is displayed in Figure 2.
result: The acquired default graph omits reconstruction supervision and background-to-mask feedback, while its transient RSS modules do not implement the advertised persistent trained blocks. Historical metric impact remains unresolved.

repair.heading: Correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Identify the historical source and configurations, register persistent modules in constructors, restore the intended feedback and reconstruction term, verify gradient reachability, and rerun mechanism ablations with matched checkpoints. Static checks establish the present discrepancies; no corrected training run is claimed.
