claim: The potential gives a uniform \(O(\log\Delta)\) amortized bound for every permitted fractional clustering input.

Use the fixed metric \(F=M=\{a=0,b=1,c=2\}\), unit opening costs, \(\Delta=\beta=2\), and \(0<s<0.1\). Initially the client is \(a\), with \(x_a=y_{aa}=1-s\), \(x_b=y_{ba}=s\), and other entries zero. Coverage, \(y\le x\), and cost \(1+s\le2\operatorname{OPT}^{1}=2\) all hold. Fractional recourse measures changes in \(x\); assignment changes are free. The rounding theorem permits any fractional path satisfying its stated conditions, not only a particular chasing implementation.
analysis:
The facility-location algorithm on p. 6 assigns a newly selected client radius \(r_j=\gamma R_j\), where \(R_j=\sum_i d_{ij}y_{ij}\). With \(\alpha=11,\gamma=10/9,\delta=2\), Eq. (3.4), p. 7, has the form \[
\Phi=K\sum_{j\in A}\max\{0,1/10-x(B_j)\}
-\eta\sum_{j\in A}\log_2(\Delta/r_j),\] where \[\eta=\frac1{\log_2(69/20)},\qquad
K=110(1+\eta\log_2\Delta).\] Equation (3.5) asserts \[
\Delta N_1+\Delta N_2+\Delta\Phi
\le O(\log\Delta)\|x^t-x^{t-1}\|_1.\] The proof also asserts a lower bound \(\Phi\ge-C\log\Delta\sum_i x_i\). Both assertions fail under the printed assumptions.

The minimum positive distance between distinct points being one does not imply \(R_j\ge1\): \(R_j\) is a fractional weighted average that can include self-distance zero. The following construction keeps \(\Delta,\beta\), the number of points and all opening costs fixed.

Let \[M=F=\{a=0,b=1,c=2\},\qquad d(u,v)=|u-v|,\qquad f_a=f_b=f_c=1.\] This is a metric with minimum positive distance one and aspect ratio \(\Delta=2\). Set \(\beta=2\), start from the prescribed empty state, and insert the single client \(a\). For any \(0<s<0.1\), choose \[x_a=y_{aa}=1-s,\quad x_b=y_{ba}=s,\quad x_c=y_{ca}=0.\] Assignments sum to one, \(0\le y_{ia}\le x_i\), and the cost is \(1+s\le2\,\mathrm{OPT}^{1}\), where \(\mathrm{OPT}^{1}=1\). The fractional optimum is exactly one because coverage requires \(\sum_i x_i\ge1\), all opening costs are one, and opening at \(a\) attains one. Initial fractional movement is one.

The algorithm adds \(a\), whose service cost is \(s\), radius is \(r_a=\gamma s<1\), and ball is the singleton \(B_a=\{a\}\). Its mass \(1-s>1/10\) satisfies all mass invariants; separation is vacuous and the sole client is covered by the cheapest facility \(a\). The nonnegative term in the displayed formula vanishes, so \[
\Phi^{1}=-\eta\log_2\frac{2}{\gamma s}.\] As \(s\downarrow0\), this tends to minus infinity while \(\Delta=2\) and \(\sum_i x_i=1\). Therefore no claimed universal terminal bound of that form holds.

The same failure can be obtained without an empty second state. Insert \(c\) instead, and set \(x_b=1,\ y_{ba}=y_{bc}=1\). The cost is 3, within the \(\beta=2\) budget \(2\mathrm{OPT}^{2}=4\). Here \(\mathrm{OPT}^{2}=2\): opening at both endpoints attains 2, and dual client values \(1,1\) certify the lower bound since \(\sum_j\max\{1-d_{ij},0\}\le f_i=1\) for every facility. The old singleton ball is dropped. Whichever current client is selected next has radius \(\gamma\) and a ball containing \(b\) with mass one. Any cheapest facility chosen there covers the other client within distance \(2<11\), so exactly one replacement ball suffices. The resulting change is \[\Delta N_1+\Delta N_2+\Delta\Phi
=1+\eta\log_2(1/s),\qquad
\|x^{2}-x^{1}\|_1=2(1-s)<2.\] This also contradicts a universal bound the displayed formula, independently of tie choices.

For \(s=2^{-400}\), direct reviewer-authored arithmetic gives \(\eta=0.5597235175\), \(\Phi^{1}=-224.3640508\), whereas even the weaker explicit bound \(-110(1+\eta)\sum_i x_i\) is \(-171.5695869\). The deletion-step left side is 225.3640508, and the insertion-step left side is 224.8894070. The symbolic family \(s=2^{-m}\), rather than any single large value, establishes failure for every universal constant. Exact rational inputs and numerical outputs are retained in `check.py`/`calc.json`.

The faulty potential step is used to prove Theorem 3.4’s principal facility-location recourse guarantee. Theorem 3.7 explicitly inherits the \(k\)-median recourse bound from Theorem 3.4. The error therefore concerns the core competitive-recourse derivation, supporting Major under the specified calibration.

The \(k\)-center potential (3.2), p. 5, has the same logarithm. For one client and \(k=1\), the allowed \(F=M\) gives \(\mathrm{OPT}=0\), so its created radius is zero and \(\log(\Delta/r)\) is undefined. Exact self-service also produces zero radii in the facility-location and \(k\)-median formulations. This is not fixed by separating distinct metric points.

At the other end, facility-location radii are not capped: \(r=\gamma R\) may exceed \(\Delta\). The p. 8 add-only argument \(-\eta\log_2(\Delta/r)\le0\) then also needs a separate justification. For example, on the same metric a singleton at \(a\) can be fractionally served entirely from \(c\) with opening cost 1 and service cost 2; with \(\beta=3\) this is feasible, and its new radius is \(2\gamma>2\).

These observations do not demonstrate excessive actual recourse. The deletion construction makes just one opening and one closing, total recourse 2, matching its total fractional movement 2. Nor does the review show that the particular positive-body-chasing implementation must produce this fractional path. Theorem 3.4 and its proof purport to round any fractional input satisfying the stated conditions, which the example does.

A bounded scale potential together with a separate singleton-ball argument may repair the proof. Merely replacing \(r\) inside the logarithm is not a verified repair: replacement-event credits and all boundary transitions must be re-established. No complete corrected amortization is claimed. The geometric coverage and approximation arguments may survive independently.

analysis: Major. The unrestricted estimator lemma is false as stated, and a core step-size lower bound is false. The batch regime used for the main complexity result has a verified restricted repair.

For Lemma 2.3 itself, take \(n=20\), \(b=19\), \(\gamma=3/4\), \(G_1x=x\) and \(G_ix=0\) for \(i>1\). Initialize \(x^{-2}=x^{-1}=x^{0}=0\) and the table at zero. Draw independent uniform 19-subsets. Choose the adapted sequence \[x^{1}=28/3,\qquad
 x^{2}=\begin{cases}28/3&1\in B_1,\\8&1\notin B_1,\end{cases}\] and let \(x^{3}=x^{2}\), except that \(x^{3}=8+760/99\) if both \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) omit index 1. Use precisely the paper’s table update. These are valid adapted iterates for the generic estimator lemma, which imposes no VFR update. The operators are Lipschitz (\(L^{2}=1/20\)) and their average is monotone with root zero. This is explicitly not a VFR trajectory.

The counterexample uses \(b>n^{2/3}\), outside the complexity corollaries. Their variance recurrence can be proved without the false independence step. Set \(q=b/n\) and let \(I_i\) indicate non-refresh. Writing \(r_i\) for the previous component residual, \(s_i=G_ix^{k-1}-G_ix^{k-2}\) and \(d_i=G_ix^k-G_ix^{k-1}\), the exact identity is \[a_i^k=d_i+I_i(r_i-\gamma s_i).\] Only \(r_i,s_i\) are fixed before the previous draw; \(d_i\) may depend on it. For \(D=Cb=4/q-2-q>1\), Young’s inequality bounds this by \(D\|d_i\|^{2}+D(D-1)^{-1}I_i\|r_i-\gamma s_i\|^{2}\). After averaging \(I_i\), its second coefficient is \(A=(4-2q-q^{2})/(q+4)\). The required domination \[A\|r-\gamma s\|^{2}
 \le(1-q/2)\|r\|^{2}+\gamma^{2}(4/q-2-2q)\|s\|^{2}\] has first principal minor \(q(q+2)/[2(q+4)]\) and determinant \(\gamma^2q(8-6q-3q^{2})/[2(q+4)]\). It therefore holds for \(0<q\le(\sqrt{33}-3)/3\). Dividing by \(nb\) recovers the printed constants. Every \(b\le n^{2/3}\) with \(n\ge2\) lies in this range; \(n=b=1\) is checked directly. This is a verified repair of the relevant recurrence, not of the unrestricted lemma.

Corollary 3.3 (p. 6) asserts \(\eta=1/(L\sqrt M)\ge0.1494b^{3/2}/(nL)\). For \(n=1000\), \(b=100=n^{2/3}\), \(\gamma=3/4\), all \(G_ix=x\), \(L=1\) and \(\kappa=0\), its own constants give \[\rho=1/20,\quad C=379/1000,\quad
 \widehat C=1701/8000,\quad M=54913/1200.\] Hence \(\eta=0.14782675297<0.1494\), although all assumptions hold. The symbolic \(\sigma\) on pp. 22–23 evaluates to \(0.1341808523\), not \(0.14948\). The symbolic \(\Gamma\) evaluates to \(841.8947368\), not \(2815.8\); the chosen 2816 is nevertheless conservative.

claim: Lemma D.8 bounds \(\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(X)\) below by \((\mathbb E_\mu\nabla^2U)^{-1}\) on arbitrary convex support; this supplies the uniform Lipschitz lemma and improved rate.

Take \(\Omega=[0,1]\), \(Z=\int_0^1e^{-y^{2}/2}\,dy\), and \(U(y)=y^{2}/2+\log Z\). The potential is smooth and convex, and the positive density is normalized. For the on-support target interpretation use \(\alpha=2\) and an independent Gaussian prior, as in the report.
analysis: Lemma D.8, p. 28, asserts \(\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(X)\succeq(\mathbb E_\mu\nabla^2U)^{-1}\) for a density \(e^{-U}\) on an arbitrary convex set, assuming only twice continuous differentiability. This statement is false on a bounded interval. It is used explicitly in Eq. (69), p. 29, and therefore invalidates the supplied derivation of the core uniform Lipschitz lemma.

Take \(d=1\), \(\Omega=[0,1]\), \(Z=\int_0^1e^{-y^{2}/2}\,dy\) and \[U(y)=\tfrac12y^{2}+\log Z,\qquad \mu(dy)=Z^{-1}e^{-y^{2}/2}\,dy\quad\hbox{on }\Omega.\] The set is convex; \(U\) is smooth and even strictly convex; the density integrates to one; and \(U''=1\), so the asserted lower bound is one. But any random variable in \([0,1]\) satisfies \[\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb E(Y-\tfrac12)^{2}-(\mathbb EY-\tfrac12)^{2}\leq\tfrac14<1.\] This is an exact contradiction independent of numerical precision. Reviewer quadrature additionally evaluates the variance as approximately \(0.07965\). The usual boundary-free integration-by-parts reasoning cannot simply be applied on this interval; the boundary density is nonzero.

If \(V\) is finite and \(C^{2}\) on all of \(\mathbb R^d\), \(e^{-V}\) is everywhere positive, contradicting bounded support. Then the simultaneous assumptions of the improved-rate theorem have no examples. If smoothness is intended only on the support, the truncated Gaussian above satisfies Assumptions 1.1–1.2 in that interpretation with \(\alpha=2\). It nevertheless defeats the uniform Lipschitz conclusion, as follows.

For \(d=1\), write \(s=1-t\). At \(x=0\), the conditional target density is proportional to \(\exp(-Ay^{2}/2)\) on \([0,1]\), with \(A=1+t^{2}/s^{2}\). Direct differentiation of the conditional-mean formula gives the valid identity from Lemma D.5: \[
 \partial_xv^*(0,t)=\frac{t}{s^{3}}\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X_t=0)-\frac1s.\] After setting \(z=\sqrt A\,y\), the conditional variance is \(A^{-1}\) times that of a standard Gaussian restricted to \([0,\sqrt A]\). As \(t\uparrow1\), this latter variance tends to \(1-2/\pi\). Consequently, \[\lim_{t\uparrow1}(1-t)\partial_xv^*(0,t)=-2/\pi,\] so the derivative is unbounded. At \(t=0.99\) independent quadrature already gives magnitude above 63, whereas the printed \(\zeta(2,1)=\frac12(2+\sqrt{2+2})^{2}=8\). The conditioning is legitimate: for every \(t<1\) the Gaussian convolution has a positive smooth density at \(x=0\). This is not a counterexample to the logically empty global-potential interpretation; it shows why restricting the potential to the cube does not repair the result.

The assessment is Major because the false lower bound supplies the essential cancellation in Eq. (69) and Lemmas D.9/1.4, which Theorem C.5/1.7 uses explicitly. The weaker Lemma D.6 does not use this lower bound. Extending the target to full support with suitable integrability and boundary conditions may support a different argument, but also removes Assumption 1.1 and requires new approximation/tail analysis. No such complete repair is verified here; the improved rate is not established by its present proof.
result: The covariance lower bound is false on bounded convex support. The present proof does not establish the uniform Lipschitz constant or improved rate, under either interpretation of its target assumptions.

claim: The displayed globally Lipschitz ReLU construction is uniformly accurate on the closed cube and identically zero immediately outside it.
Use \(d=1\), \(X_1=0\) almost surely, \(T<1\), and tolerance \(\epsilon<R\). This satisfies the bounded-support assumption.
analysis: Appendix A.1, pp. 12–13, uniformly approximates \(v^*\) on \(K=[-R,R]^d\) and says that the constructed ReLU network is identically zero outside \(K\), from which global Lipschitz continuity is asserted. Those simultaneous construction properties are impossible for admissible targets whose velocity is nonzero on the boundary.

Let \(d=1\) and \(X_1=0\) almost surely. This satisfies Assumption 1.1 and gives \(v^*(x,t)=-x/(1-t)\), which is spatially Lipschitz on every \([0,T]\) with \(T<1\). At \(t=0\) its value at \(R\) is \(-R\). Every finite ReLU network is continuous; if it is zero for all \(x>R\), it must also be zero at \(x=R\). Its uniform approximation error on \(K\) is therefore at least \(R\), contradicting the claimed arbitrary tolerance \(\epsilon<R\). This is a counterexample to the stated construction properties, not to the existential \(L^{2}\) approximation theorem.

The explicit partition has a separate visible endpoint defect. The notation \([N]=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\) is defined on p. 3. At \(x'=1\) all terms \(\psi(3N(x'-m/N))\) vanish, because \(3(N-m)\geq3\) and \(\psi\) vanishes beyond two. Thus the proposed sum is zero, not a partition of unity. At \(x'=-1/(6N)\) its \(m=0\) term equals one, so the factors do not vanish immediately outside the cube either. Both facts are checked exactly for \(N=1,2,4,10\) by a reviewer-written rational calculation.
result: Adding endpoint nodes and tapering on an enlarged cube are plausible ways to change the construction, and the cited approximation literature may contain suitable constructions. They were not established by the displayed proof. A taper needs a new Lipschitz bound and tail estimate; merely imposing a hard cutoff is discontinuous. This is a Major gap in the construction used by Theorems 3.1 and 4.4 and hence both main guarantees. No impossibility of learning bounded-support targets is claimed, and no full network-class repair is certified.
The displayed sharp-cutoff construction cannot have all its stated properties, leaving a core approximation proof gap in both main guarantees.

claim: The condition \(h=O(n^{-4a})\), with \(a=1/[3(d+5)]\), makes the supplied discretization bound \(\widetilde O(n^{-a})\).
Conditionally grant the preceding lemmas, set \(s=1-T=n^{-a}\), and use the allowed uniform mesh. The network bounds are \(K=\widetilde O(s^{-1})\) and \(\gamma_2=\widetilde O(s^{-4})\).
analysis: Even conditionally granting the preceding lemmas, the last substitution in Theorem C.5, pp. 24–25, does not establish its asserted rate using the parameters in Theorem 3.1.

Let \(a=1/[3(d+5)]\), \(s=1-T=n^{-a}\) and \(h=\max_k(t_{k+1}-t_k)\). The theorem chooses \(h=O(n^{-4a})\). Its network class allows \(K=\widetilde O(s^{-1})\) and \(\gamma_2=\widetilde O(s^{-4})\). On a uniform mesh, \(\sqrt{\sum_k(\Delta t_k)^{3}}=h\sqrt T\). Thus the displayed discretization estimate yields only \[\widetilde O((K+\gamma_2)h)=\widetilde O(n^{4a}n^{-4a})=\widetilde O(1),\] whereas the early-stopping term is \(n^{-a}\) and the estimation term is \(s^{-2}n^{-1/(d+5)}=n^{-a}\). Exact fraction arithmetic in the script confirms these exponents for several dimensions; the symbolic expression holds for every \(d\geq1\).

This is failure of the given upper-bound argument, not a lower bound on actual Euler error. A smaller mesh \(h=O(n^{-5a})\) makes that same discretization upper bound \(\widetilde O(n^{-a})\), conditional on the other lemmas. Such a smaller mesh also belongs to \(O(n^{-4a})\), so an existential interpretation of “choose” can accommodate it. The printed condition alone and the claimed direct substitution do not ensure it. The impact is Major for the supplied core rate derivation, separately from Problems 1–2. The stronger mesh repairs this algebraic step only; it does not restore the false covariance argument or complete the approximation proof.
result: The supplied mesh condition establishes only \(\widetilde O(1)\) through the displayed bound, rather than the claimed improved rate. A stronger mesh repairs this calculation conditionally.

Take \(d=\kappa=1\), \(U=[1]\), \(x=2\), fixed \(\gamma=1\), \(\sigma>0\), and unconstrained decoder coefficient \(w\). Constant encoders are admissible for this one-point input; no exclusion of \(\mu=0\) or \(\sigma=1\) is imposed.
analysis: The uniqueness claim on p. 6 is contradicted by an admissible local minimum of the full three-variable scalar objective. The omitted branch is removed by the division by \(1-\sigma\) on p. 22 of Appendix E.3.

Set \(d=\kappa=1\), \(U=[1]\), \(x=2\), and \(\gamma=1\). The decoder is exactly the theorem’s linear decoder and its coefficient \(w\) is unconstrained. Subtracting the irrelevant normalizing constant \(\tfrac12\log(2\pi)\) from the loss on p. 21 yields \[
F(w,\mu,\sigma)=\frac12\left[
 (2-w(1-\sigma)\mu)^{2}+w^{2}\sigma^{2}(1-\sigma)^{2}
 +\sigma^{2}-2\log\sigma+\mu^{2}-1\right].\] At \((w,\mu,\sigma)=(0,0,1)\), \(F=2\). This is a local minimum in all its variables, not only on a selected slice. For \(\sigma>0\), \(\log\sigma\leq \sigma-1\) implies \[\sigma^{2}-1-2\log\sigma\geq(\sigma-1)^2.\] Writing \(t=1-\sigma\) and dropping only the nonnegative term \(w^2t^{2}(\mu^{2}+\sigma^{2})\) gives \[\begin{aligned}
2(F-2)&\geq \mu^{2}+t^{2}-4|w|\,|\mu|\,|t|\\
&\geq(1-2|w|)(\mu^{2}+t^{2})\geq0
       \qquad (|w|<1/2).\end{aligned}\] The region \(|w|<1/2,\sigma>0\) contains a neighborhood of the specified point, so this proves local minimality. Flatness along part of the dormant branch does not disqualify it as a local minimum.

Now use the equally admissible point \[w=2\sqrt3,\qquad \mu=\sqrt3/2,\qquad \sigma=1/2.\] Its reconstruction bias squared is \(1/4\) and its reconstruction variance is \(3/4\). The remaining contribution inside the brackets in the displayed formula is \(\log4\), so \[F(2\sqrt3,\sqrt3/2,1/2)=\frac{1+\log4}{2}
 \simeq1.19314718056<2.\] The dormant local minimum is therefore suboptimal. The independent standard-library calculation `c.py`, with results in `calc.json`, reproduces these values. Its 10,000 finite neighborhood evaluations are only a diagnostic; the proof is inequality the displayed formula.

The first stationary-point elimination on p. 22 writes \(w=\mu x/[(1-\sigma)(\sigma^{2}+\mu^{2})]\) and the next elimination also cancels \(\mu\). Neither operation covers the dormant branch. Direct visual inspection of p. 22 confirms that this is in the typeset source rather than an extraction artifact. The paper’s active stationary point remains a valid lower-loss point in this example. Its footnote allows multiple sign-equivalent global minima, whereas the new point has a strictly larger loss. Optimizing out \(w\) changes local geometry: leaving the dormant neighborhood can require a large change in \(w\). No strict-minimum qualifier is present.

There is a separate ambiguity about \(\gamma\). Section 2.2 permits learning it, whereas Appendix E.3 differentiates only with respect to \(w,\mu,\sigma\). The counterexample above addresses precisely that fixed-\(\gamma\) argument. If \(\gamma\) is jointly optimized, the same dormant point has \(\partial L/\partial\gamma=-3/2\) and is not a local minimum. It must not be used to claim joint-optimization spurious minima.

Joint optimization also has a non-sign continuum of global minimizers, a different failure of literal uniqueness. For \(x\ne0\), write \(a=w(1-\sigma)\) and \(r=\mu^{2}+\sigma^{2}\). Minimizing the reconstruction error over \(a\) gives \(R=x^{2}\sigma^{2}/r\), and minimizing over \(\gamma>0\) sets \(\gamma=R\). The resulting lower bound is \[L\geq \tfrac12\{\log(2\pi x^{2})-\log r+r\}
 \geq \tfrac12\{\log(2\pi x^{2})+1\}.\] For each \(s\in(0,1)\), equality is attained by \(\sigma^{2}=s\), \(\mu^{2}=1-s\), \(\gamma=x^2s\) and \(w=x\mu/(1-\sqrt{s})\). Thus the joint reading does not restore literal uniqueness, but this continuum is global, not suboptimal.

The invalid fixed-variance derivation is Major: Section 4.3 and p. 7 explicitly use Theorem 4.7 as the unique-minimum half of their exponential SAE/VAEase local-minima comparison. The claimed elimination of suboptimal minima in that setting fails. The VAEase architecture, empirical comparisons, and the separate manifold-recovery claim are not refuted by this example. No replacement uniqueness theorem or full correction is established here.
result: The fixed-variance proof omits an admissible suboptimal dormant local minimum. The joint-variance reading has a different global nonuniqueness, and must not inherit the fixed-variance spurious-minimum claim.
brief: The fixed-variance uniqueness argument omits a provably suboptimal dormant local minimum.
With jointly optimized variance that point is not locally optimal; a separate continuum of equal global optima remains.

claim: The released logarithmic threshold utility implements the minimum-variance active-dimension partition for admissible ReLU codes.

analysis: The inspected release does not implement a finite minimum-variance partition for inputs containing a zero activation.

Section 5.1 (p. 7) describes partitioning active and inactive dimensions by minimizing within-group variance. In the pinned release, `activation_sae.py`, lines 121–124, and the corresponding block in `activation_sae_log.py` pass \(\log |z_j|\) into `utils.py:find_optimal_threshold_torch`, lines 211–245. For example, let \(|z|=(0,0.01,1,2)\). The logarithmic input includes \(-\infty\). Every candidate lower partition contains it, so its variance includes \(\infty-\infty\); the upper calculation also subtracts nonfinite cumulative sums. These comparisons with the initial best variance cannot succeed. The threshold remains \(-\infty\) and the final strict comparison counts all three positive entries. A choice of zero-handling policy would need to be specified and checked before a corrected empirical comparison could be assessed.
result: For inputs containing zero codes, the acquired release can return a positivity count instead of a finite minimum-variance partition. No historical score change is established.

claim: The released lattice-path generator orders groups numerically by their Lagrange invariant before constructing covers.
Use the acquired notebook and singleton invariant groups. The independent finite calculation uses exact integer matrix products and rational comparisons, without running the author notebook or Sage.
analysis: In `lattice_path_posets/lattice_path_data_generation_with_sage.ipynb`, cell 14, the code sorts `D_l.items()` using `operator.itemgetter(1,0,-1)`. Each item is \(((D,q),[(p,L(p)),\ldots])\). The key is therefore the tuple consisting of the whole path list, the \((D,q)\) key, and the whole path list again. It is not the nested Lagrange number. Cell 13 then creates covers between adjacent groups in that incorrectly sorted list. This contradicts the numerical ordering required by Appendix C.2.5, p. 37.

The calculation uses an independently written exact continued-fraction computation: prepend 2 to the sequence that replaces equal adjacent path bits by \((1,1)\) and unequal bits by \((2)\); for every cyclic rotation multiply matrices \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}c&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). If the product is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), compare the rational values \(((a-d)^{2}+4bc)/c^{2}\) and take their maximum. Fractions are compared exactly; decimal values above are illustrative. This checks the invariant specified in the supplied generator, not a new theorem identifying it with all external number-theoretic conventions.

Impact and counterevidence. This is a Major release-code defect in a core label-generation step. The argument proves the constructed group order is wrong; it does not assert that this particular pair survives every later filtering step or appears in the historical train/test files. A corrected historical notebook could explain valid published data. Such a notebook, data hashes and exact label audits are needed to resolve that possibility.
result: The tuple key orders path-containing fields rather than numerical invariants, reversing the exact order of the checked singleton groups. Historical dataset membership and downstream survival of that pair remain unresolved.
brief: The released lattice generator sorts path data instead of the numerical invariant used to define covers.
An exact singleton-group witness reverses the required order; historical dataset impact is not established.

claim: The reported best test scores independently evaluate the selected models and generated programs.

The numerical illustration has \(100\) independent candidates of true accuracy \(1/2\), each tested on \(20\) independent trials. These assumptions are not asserted for the paper's actual experiments.
analysis: Appendix B.10 (p. 27) says the best test score was recorded across 60 epochs and describes hyperparameter optimization. Appendix B.11 (p. 29) expressly chooses the best of 100 generated programs by evaluating each on the test set. These test values are selection criteria, not independent assessments of the selected solution. The current `dataloaders.py` also returns the test dataset from both validation loaders.

For an explicit illustration, let 100 independent candidate classifiers each have true accuracy \(1/2\), and let their test counts be independent \(\operatorname{Binomial}(20,1/2)\). The expected maximum test accuracy is \[\frac1{20}\sum_{k=1}^{20}\left[1-\Pr\{\operatorname{Binomial}(20,1/2)<k\}^{100}\right]
 \approx0.773197.\] This is a finite demonstration of selection optimism, not an estimate of this paper’s inflation; its candidates and errors need not be independent. Three initialization repeats do not turn a previously used selection set into an untouched test set.

The paper openly frames these as exploratory diagnostics and says performance alone does not establish a useful conjecture (p. 2). That is meaningful counterevidence against treating the numbers as a claimed definitive leaderboard. Accordingly the finding is Minor in this framing: label the scores as best-on-selection-set diagnostics and restrict the relative-difficulty interpretation, or introduce a separate validation set and assess selected models/programs once on an untouched test set. No such rerun was performed.
result: Selection and evaluation reuse the test set, so the selected score is not an independent holdout assessment. The disclosed exploratory framing limits the inference; no actual inflation magnitude or false conjecture is established.
brief: Best-epoch and best-program scores are chosen on the same test data used for reporting.
The paper discloses exploratory diagnostics; the finite optimism example is not an estimate of its score inflation.

claim: The stated smoothness assumptions and demonstration condition guarantee decreasing test loss for the proposed in-context attention update.

Use scalar squared loss \(\ell_y(F)=\tfrac12(F-y)^{2}\), with \(d=d^\prime=1\), \(h_t=h=W_K=W_V=z_0=1\), demonstration label \(0\), and test label \(2\). Pretraining copies of input \(2\), label \(2\), give \(W_0=1\) and Hessian \(H=4\). Every per-label output gradient is globally \(1\)-Lipschitz.
analysis: Theorem 1 and its proof, equations (11)–(12) on page 4 and (33)–(34) on page 12, use within-loss smoothness as a bound between gradients from different labeled samples. Equations (3)–(9) also identify incompatible parameter updates.

The notation section says that labels are omitted for brevity. Under this ordinary supervised reading, Lipschitz continuity of \(
abla_F\ell_y(F)\) in \(F\), for each label \(y\), does not imply \[
 \|
abla_F\ell_{y_t}(Wh_t)-
abla_F\ell_{y_0}(Wz_0)\|
 \leq\mu\|W(h_t-z_0)\|.\] There is an uncontrolled label-dependent term. Take scalar squared loss \(\ell_y(F)=	frac12(F-y)^{2}\) and \[d=d'=1,\quad h_t=h=W_K=W_V=1,\quad z_0=1,
 \quad y_0=0,\quad y_t=2.\] Let the pretraining set have \(n\) copies of input \(2\) and label \(2\). Its average loss is \(	frac12(2W-2)^{2}\), so \(\widehat W=1=W_0\) as required by (4), and \(H=4>0\). Each output-loss gradient is globally 1-Lipschitz. The demonstration satisfies (5), since \(
abla_F\ell_0(1)=1=W_Vh/\sqrt d\).

The two gradients with respect to \(W\) are \(g_t=-1\) and \(g_0=1\). The eigenvalue ratio in (7) is one. Its left side is \(1\), while its right side is zero because \(h_t=z_0\). Thus its strict sufficient condition holds. Nevertheless, \[\widehat W_{\epsilon,z_0}=\frac4{4+\epsilon}<1,
 \qquad \ell_2(\widehat W_{\epsilon,z_0})>\ell_2(1)=\frac12
 \quad(\epsilon>0).\] For \(n=1000\), \(\epsilon=1/n\), the exact new loss is \(8008002/16008001\), an increase of approximately \(0.00024997\). The derivative at zero is \(+1/4\), so making the upweighting arbitrarily small does not help. The failed step [missing] (#missing) tries to bound \(2\) by zero.

Distinct labeled problems are not assumed to have injective representations in the paper. This example uses the permitted coincidence of representations, not contradictory labels for one stipulated deterministic mathematical problem. If the intended theorem instead assumes one common, label-independent loss function or explicitly assumes the cross-sample bound [missing] (#missing), this particular example is excluded. That would be a materially narrower hypothesis than ordinary per-label smoothness and must be stated and justified for the reasoning task.

Set the test label to zero in the preceding construction and leave everything else unchanged. The theorem condition still holds. The surrogate minimizer now does reduce the test loss, so this variant is not a counterexample to that surrogate conclusion. However, equation (3) has zero-shot output \(1\) and one-shot linear-attention output \(1+1=2\). Its squared test loss rises from \(1/2\) to \(2\).

This directly refutes the claimed identification of the two procedures inside the paper’s own linearized model. Under (5), the attention increment is a positive gradient outer product; [influence] (#influence) is a negative Hessian-preconditioned increment. Calling the former a conceptual analogy does not make their loss changes equal. Reversing the loss-gradient convention would also require changing (5) and the influence calculation. Moreover, no approximation error bound connects softmax attention (2), linear attention (3), contextual representations and the final answer loss.

The proof’s first-order Taylor step (9)/(30) also supplies no remainder bound ensuring that the particular finite choice \(\epsilon=1/|D_{\rm pre}|\) stays in a loss-decreasing neighborhood. A valid negative derivative establishes a sufficiently small neighborhood under regularity, not an unquantified universal finite-step guarantee. This is an additional proof-scope limitation; the two exact examples above do not rely on it.

Page 5 states that examples failing the condition will have a negative effect. Theorems 1 and 2 are presented as sufficient conditions, not necessary ones. Even in the retraining surrogate with a shared zero-label squared loss, put \(h=3\), \(h_t=W_K=W_V=1\) and keep the same pretraining objective. Equation (5) holds, \(C_1=1\), and (7) reads \(1>8\), which fails. Yet \(\widehat W_\epsilon=4/(4+9\epsilon)\) reduces test loss for every \(\epsilon>0\). Failure of the bound therefore cannot establish harmfulness. Replacing unknown absolute quantities by a percentile threshold, as LMS3 does, is a practical heuristic that needs empirical validation.

The assessment of Problem 1 is Major. It affects the advertised theoretical explanation and guarantee, not a peripheral presentation detail. A defensible repair must state the required loss/label regularity, derive the loss change for the actual attention update or explicitly limit the theorem to retraining, control finite-step/approximation errors where a guarantee is claimed, and describe rejection as a heuristic unless a separate necessity result is established. This review does not supply or certify such a replacement theorem. The empirical success of the score is not refuted by these examples.
result: The published assumptions do not establish the advertised loss-decrease guarantee or justify equating attention with retraining. Rejection from failure of the sufficient condition is separately unsupported.
brief: The guarantee uses an unstated cross-sample assumption and identifies incompatible parameter updates.
Exact examples separate retraining, attention and rejection behavior; reported benchmark success is not refuted.

paragraphs: State the required loss/label regularity, analyze the actual attention update or restrict the theorem to retraining, and control finite-step and approximation errors. Treat rejection as heuristic unless necessity is established. No replacement theorem or empirical repair is certified.

claim: For general Bregman divergence, realizability, convexity and the stated sequential consistency suffice to make every sufficiently near-optimal student satisfy the approximate misfit–gain inequality.

Write \(J(s)=\mathbb E D_\psi(s,w)\) and \(R(s)=\mathbb E D_\psi(g,s)\). The witness has singleton input support and a realizable target. Use \(\psi(x,t)=x^{2}/t+t^{2}\) on \(U_\psi=\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\), extended by \(\psi(0,0)=0\) and \(+\infty\) elsewhere outside that domain.
analysis: Convexity, realizability, and the stated sequential consistency do not suffice for the claimed approximate misfit–gain inequality for arbitrary Bregman divergences.

Use a single-point input distribution, so finite support holds. Set \[U_\psi=\mathbb R\times(0,\infty),\qquad
 \psi(x,t)=x^{2}/t+t^2.\] Extend \(\psi(0,0)=0\) and \(\psi=+\infty\) at other points with \(t\leq0\). This is a proper, lower-semicontinuous convex function, strictly convex and smooth on \(U_\psi\). Its Hessian has first principal minor \(2/t>0\) and determinant \(4/t>0\). Direct differentiation gives \[D_\psi((x,t),(u,s))
   =\frac{(x-ut/s)^{2}}{t}+(t-s)^2.
 \] For every fixed \((u,s)\in U_\psi\), convergence of this divergence to zero implies \(t\to s>0\), followed by \(x\to u\). Thus the theorem’s sequential-consistency assumption is satisfied.

Take the strong class of constant functions with output in \[C=\{(x,t):t>0,\ x\geq2t\},\] which is convex. Let \(g=(2,1)\in C\) and \(w=(0,1)\in U_\psi\). The target is realizable. Moreover, \[R(w)=D_\psi(g,w)=4,\qquad
 D_\psi((x,t),w)\geq4t+(t-1)^{2}=1+2t+t^2.\] The infimum of \(J\) on \(C\) is therefore 1, approached along \(x=2t,\ t\downarrow0\). For \(j\geq2\), the student \(s_j=(j^{-3},j^{-4})\) lies in \(C\) and satisfies \[\begin{aligned}
 J(s_j)&=j^{-2}+(1-j^{-4})^{2}\longrightarrow1,\\
 R(s_j)&=(j-2)^{2}+(1-j^{-4})^{2}\longrightarrow\infty.\end{aligned}\] For any optimization tolerance \(\delta>0\), sufficiently large \(j\) is \(\delta\)-optimal, but \(R(s_j)+J(s_j)\leq4+\epsilon\) fails for any fixed \(\epsilon\). At \(j=10\), suboptimality is \(0.00980001\) and target risk is \(64.99980001\); at \(j=100\), these are approximately \(0.00009998\) and \(9604.99999998\).

The proof on p. 15 applies Fact 3.4 to the closure of the strong class. Here its minimizing point is \((0,0)\), outside \(U_\psi\). The divergence with that point as its second argument is not defined, and the claimed interior projection argument cannot be used. On the unclosed class itself, the minimum is not attained. This directly refutes the main arbitrary-Bregman theorem under the printed assumptions. It does not refute every suitably strengthened Legendre-generator theorem.

The finite-support KL specialization is protected from this particular boundary failure. Its closed-simplex objective attains a minimum; if a minimizing coordinate were zero, moving toward the strictly positive realizable target gives a negative-infinite entropy directional derivative. Hence the minimizer is interior. The KL corollary is not invalidated by this non-KL counterexample.

Require an attained minimizing projection \(z\in\overline{F\circ h_s}\cap U_\psi^{\mathcal X}\), with the usual differentiability and convex projection inequality. Then \[\mathbb E D_\psi(s,z)\leq J(s)-J(z).\] For finite support, fixed-\(z\) sequential consistency makes near-optimal students converge coordinatewise to \(z\). Continuity then gives \(R(s)+J(s)\to R(z)+J(z)\leq R(w)\), establishing the asserted \(\epsilon\)–\(\delta\) form. This repairs the theorem under an explicit extra interior-projection hypothesis; it does not establish that the original assumptions imply it.
result: The printed general-Bregman assumptions allow arbitrarily near-optimal students with unbounded target risk, contradicting the claimed approximate guarantee.
The failure is the missing interior-projection condition, not the finite-support KL specialization.
brief: A boundary projection lets \(J(s_j)\to\inf J\) while \(R(s_j)\to\infty\), refuting the general-Bregman approximate guarantee.

fields.source_location: Appendix A.3, pp. 21–22; Pinsker completion claim on p. 22
claim: Pinsker-based \(L^p\) sequential consistency completes the approximate KL misfit–gain extension to infinite input support.

Let \(\Pr(X=j)=2^{-j}\), \(g(j)=w(j)=1/2\), and \(a_j=e^{-2^j}\). Use the convex class \[F=\left\{f_\alpha(j)=\tfrac12-\alpha_j(\tfrac12-a_j):\alpha_j\ge0,\ \sum_j\alpha_j\le1\right\}.\]. The class is closed in \(L^{2}(P_X)\), contains the exact projection \(g=w\), and every individual target risk is finite.
analysis: The claimed extension of the approximate KL inequality requires control of target risk near zero probabilities. Pinsker-based \(L^p\) convergence alone does not supply it.

Let \(\Pr(X=j)=2^{-j}\) on the positive integers, and \(g(j)=w(j)=1/2\). Put \(a_j=e^{-2^j}\) and define the class \[F=\left\{f_\alpha(j)=\tfrac12-\alpha_j(\tfrac12-a_j):
       \alpha_j\geq0,\ \sum_j\alpha_j\leq1\right\}.\] It is convex, contains \(g\), and has strictly positive probabilities. It is closed in \(L^{2}(P_X)\): convergence implies coordinatewise convergence at every positive-mass atom, and Fatou’s lemma preserves the sum constraint. The exact projection of \(w\) is \(g=w\), with misfit zero. All target risks are finite: convexity of \(-\log\), together with \(2^{-j}(-\log a_j)=1\), bounds the logarithmic contribution by a constant plus \(\sum_j\alpha_j\).

Select \(f_m\) by \(\alpha_m=1\), with all other coordinates zero. Set \(q_m=2^{-m}\). Then \[\begin{aligned}
 M_m:=J(f_m)
   &=q_mD_{\rm KL}(a_m\|1/2)
     =q_m\{\log2-H(a_m)\}\longrightarrow0,\\
 T_m:=R(f_m)
   &=\tfrac12-q_m\log2-\tfrac{q_m}{2}\log(1-a_m)
     \longrightarrow\tfrac12.\end{aligned}\] Thus for every \(\delta>0\), a sufficiently large \(m\) is \(\delta\)-optimal, but the claimed inequality would require \(T_m+M_m\leq\epsilon\), which fails for any fixed \(\epsilon<1/2\). At \(m=8\), \(M_m=0.0027076062\) and \(T_m=0.4972923938\).

Here \(\|f_m-g\|_p^p=q_m|1/2-a_m|^p\to0\) for every finite \(p\), exactly as the cited Pinsker reasoning suggests. A shrinking rare event carries an increasingly confident mistake, whose logarithmic loss compensates its shrinking probability.

Page 22 states that Pinsker sequential consistency completes the extension of Corollary A.1. The example shows the missing target-risk continuity even when projection existence, uniqueness, closedness, and finite individual risks are not obstacles. Appendix A.3 also gestures toward Legendre functionals without spelling out a complete theorem; the finding concerns the extension under the conditions actually supplied, not an independently formulated theorem with stronger functional hypotheses. It does not refute the exact projection inequality, the finite-support KL corollary, or Theorem 4.3 under its additional inverse-probability condition: this example fails that latter condition.

A stronger usable setting is a nonempty closed convex subset of \(L^{2}\) of probability functions uniformly bounded away from zero, with the weak predictor also so bounded and \(g\) in the set. Weak compactness, convexity, and lower semicontinuity give a minimizing projection \(z\). If every probability coordinate is at least \(\alpha>0\), Pinsker and the mean-value bound for \(\log\) imply \[|R(s)-R(z)|\leq\alpha^{-1}\sqrt{2\,\mathbb E D_{\rm KL}(s\|z)}.\] For \(J(s)\leq J(z)+\delta\), the projection inequality then gives \[R(s)+J(s)\leq R(w)+\delta+\alpha^{-1}\sqrt{2\delta}.\] This verifies a bounded-probability extension, not the unrestricted assertion.
result: Near-optimal misfit and finite-\(p\) convergence do not control target KL risk near the probability boundary.
An infinite-support approximate guarantee needs further target-risk continuity or probability-boundary control.
brief: The witness has \(J(f_m)\to0\) but \(R(f_m)\to1/2\), despite convergence in every finite \(L^p\).
Exact projection, finite-support KL and the separately regularized finite-mixture theorem are not refuted.

paragraphs: For a nonempty closed convex \(L^{2}\) class, require all probability coordinates and the weak predictor to be bounded below by a fixed \(\alpha>0\), with the target in the class. Projection, Pinsker and the logarithm's mean-value bound give \[R(s)+J(s)\le R(w)+\delta+\alpha^{-1}\sqrt{2\delta}\quad\text{when }J(s)\le J(z)+\delta.\]
This verifies the uniformly positive restricted setting, not the unrestricted infinite-support assertion.

fields.source_location: Appendix A.2.2, p. 20, final expectation estimate
claim: The expected inverse-probability quantities \(\rho_i=\mathbb E\sup_{f\in F}1/f_i(X)\) can bound the correlated random denominator inside the proof's target-KL risk estimate.

Use two-point input support with rare mass \(0.01\), \(a=10^{-6}\), and a convex class whose rare positive probability lies in \([a,2a]\) and is \(1/2\) elsewhere. Let \(g=w=q\) take rare probability \(a\), and student \(p\) take \(2a\). The exact projection is \(q\), all probabilities are uniformly positive, and \(p\) is in every finite-mixture class.
analysis: The final estimate treats \(\rho_i=\mathbb E\sup_{f\in F}1/f_i(X)\) as a pointwise bound inside a correlated expectation. That step is false even for two-point input support satisfying the theorem’s regularization condition.

The estimate is a central step in the proof of the finite-mixture \(k^{-1/2}\) guarantee. An invalid derivation tied directly to that contribution warrants Major under the assigned standard. Its repairability is separately assessed below; no collapse of the final theorem or benchmark scores is required.

Let \(r_i(x)=\sup_{f\in F}1/f_i(h_s(x))\), \(R_0=\sum_i\mathbb E r_i(X)\), and \(A(x)=\max_i r_i(x)\). Both the student and the convex-hull projection \(z\) satisfy \(\min_i(s_i(x),z_i(x))\geq1/A(x)\). The Hellinger bound \[\sum_i(\sqrt{p_i}-\sqrt{q_i})^{2}\leq D_{\rm KL}(p\|q)\] follows by Jensen applied to the \(\log\) affinity and \(-\log u\geq1-u\). Applying the mean-value theorem to \(\log\sqrt{p_i}\) gives \[\max_i|\log p_i-\log q_i|
 \leq2\sqrt{A(x)D_{\rm KL}(p\|q)}.\] Cauchy–Schwarz therefore yields \[|R(s)-R(z)|
 \leq2\sqrt{R_0\,\mathbb E D_{\rm KL}(s\|z)}.
 \] The paper’s Jensen approximation argument, Lemmas A.4–A.5 and Corollary A.6, gives \(\eta=R_0/(8k)+\delta\) as an upper bound on both \(J(s)-J(z)\) and \(\mathbb E D_{\rm KL}(s\|z)\). Combining the projection inequality and the displayed formula proves \[R(s)+J(s)\leq R(w)+\eta+2\sqrt{R_0\eta}.
 \] Choose \(\delta=R_0/(8k)\). The error becomes \(R_0/(4k)+R_0/\sqrt{k}\), independent of input-support size. Since \(R_0\leq c\rho\) and \(\rho\geq c\), this also recovers the advertised \(O(\rho^{3/2}\sqrt{c/k})\) form up to a universal constant. Thus the finite-support classification rate is independently supported after replacing the faulty estimate. The original square-root bound in Lemma A.7 is valid and is not the source of this failure.
result: The displayed averaging estimate fails on an admissible two-point example.
A verified replacement proof recovers the inverse-square-root finite-mixture rate; the final theorem and valid auxiliary lemmas are not declared false.
brief: The actual intermediate expectation is \(8.7897083128\), exceeding the printed bound \(0.6216496999\).
A replacement proof recovers the \(k^{-1/2}\) rate; this finding refutes a proof step rather than the final theorem.

claim: Reported forward misfit XE(weak,strong) and contrast with reverse KL establish quantitative directionality.
Pinnedsource/staticcallchain; preserved notebook CIFAR forward loss.405211538,accuracy.898133636,misfit1.10241437matchTable1rounding.
analysis: The empirical argument for quantitative directionality compares an entropy-containing cross-entropy with KL. For the numerically identified CIFAR-10 forward row, the released measurement additionally reverses the cross-entropy arguments relative to the paper’s definition.
The paper defines \(\operatorname{XE}(u,v)=-\sum_i u_i\log v_i\), and says that the forward experiment’s misfit is \(\operatorname{XE}(w,s)\). Parent static inspection finds the following call chain:
- `vision/src/measurements/estimate_losses.py:272--275` selects weak output first, strong output second, and `CrossEntropy`.
- Lines 87–95 pass those outputs in that order.
- `vision/src/metrics/losses.py:124--136` treats the second argument as the target distribution and applies cross-entropy to the first argument’s logits.
This computes \(\operatorname{XE}(s,w)\), not the reported \(\operatorname{XE}(w,s)\).
The preserved notebook `vision/notebooks/11-am-read_results_vision_icml.ipynb`, zero-based cell 6, gives an unusually direct numerical binding:
Quantity | Stored output | Table 1
Strong test loss | 0.4052115381 | 0.4052
Strong accuracy | 0.8981336355 | 0.8981
Reported forward XE misfit | 1.1024143696 | 1.1024

The same stored output gives the correctly oriented forward KL \(D_{\rm KL}(w\|s)=0.2681628565\), reverse KL \(D_{\rm KL}(s\|w)=0.3681456645\), and weak loss \(0.5824153622\). Thus the forward run’s gain is \[G=0.5824153622-0.4052115381=0.1772038241.\] The reported-XE-minus-gain gap is \(0.9252105455\), whereas the correctly oriented forward-KL-minus-gain gap is \(0.0909590324\). Table 1’s reverse-series gap is \(0.3185-0.2447=0.0738\). These arithmetic comparisons materially change the magnitude of the advertised discrepancy; they are not a rerun or a matched-teacher statistical test.

Even with the XE argument order repaired, the comparison remains confounded because \[\operatorname{XE}(w,s)=D_{\rm KL}(w\|s)+H(w).\] With \(g=w=s=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\), gain and both KL divergences are zero, while XE equals \(\log2\). Thus failure of gain to track XE does not establish directional failure of a KL-based Pythagorean relation.

Section 5.6 interprets the dramatic mismatch as empirical evidence of directionality central to the proposed recipe. The demonstrated error concerns that measurement and interpretation. It does not refute the correctly oriented reverse-KL theorem or the reported accuracy values. Reverse accuracy is higher in five of six Table 1 datasets, with ImageNet the disclosed exception. Auxiliary inspection found that the training branch itself selects the intended forward or reverse objective.

The notebook outputs were read as preserved evidence; no cell was executed. The exact numeric match supports the CIFAR row, but the commit is not independently authenticated as the historical revision for every table, and the NLP implementation is absent from this snapshot. Correcting the evaluator requires choosing the intended KL argument order and comparing divergences, or subtracting the appropriate target entropy from an accurately identified XE. The stored CIFAR arithmetic is verified; a complete corrected empirical comparison requires matched predictions, teachers, and reruns.
result: Reported misfit gap.925210545 becomes forward KL gap.090959032; even correct XE includes Hweak and cannot establish KL directionality by that change alone. Material harm to core empirical quantitative directionality argument.

fields.source_location: Lemma G.2, p. 18, Eqs. (12)–(13); Theorem 4.2 proof, pp. 16–18; finite-volume assumption, p. 3
claim: The alternative space \(S\subset\mathbb R^d\) is assumed to have finite volume, and the observed set \(M\) is finite. Annotator rewards are \(K\)-Lipschitz in context distance; pairwise probabilities are population averages of Bradley–Terry–Luce probabilities. A representative dataset has exactly those pairwise probabilities. The clone-robustness definition asks for qualitative continuity when a new alternative approaches an existing one.

Let \(\sigma(t)=(1+e^{-t})^{-1}\). Write the unweighted ordered-pair negative log likelihood as \[L_M(r)=-\sum_{x,y\in M}p_{xy}\log\sigma(r_x-r_y).\] Equation (1) minimizes \(F_\lambda(r)=L_M(r)+(\lambda/2)\sum_xr_x^{2}\). The weighted objective in Equation (2) is \[
 f_w(r)=-\sum_{x,y\in M}w_xw_yp_{xy}\log\sigma(r_x-r_y)
       +\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_xw_xr_x^{2},\] where \(w_x\) is the normalized volume of the Voronoi cell, splitting ties. The examples in Problems 1–3 all have positive cell weights, positive \(\lambda\), and valid representative probabilities. Thus none relies on a zero-weight ambiguity.

Lemma G.2, p. 18, states \(|\widehat r_w^D(y)-r_1(y)|=O(\sqrt\epsilon)\) when a clone is within \(\epsilon\) of its original. Its Equation (13) first asserts that merged Voronoi weights change by \(O(\epsilon)\). Here \(r_1\) is the weighted optimizer after replacing the old weight of the cloned alternative by the combined weights of it and its clone, while retaining the old alternatives and probabilities. Theorem 4.2’s proof on pp. 16–18 uses this rate to choose \(\epsilon=c\delta^{2}\). The model on p. 3 assumes finite volume, not boundedness of \(S\).

Use the fixed measurable domain \[S=([0,1]\times[-1,1])\cup\left\{(u,v):v\ge e^{2},\ \tfrac34\le u\le\tfrac34+\frac1{v(\log v)^{2}}\right\},\] whose volume is \(V=5/2\). Take \(a=(0,0)\), \(b=(1,0)\), clone \(a'=(0,\epsilon)\), and \(0<\epsilon<e^{-2}\). All cells have positive volume. The annotator reward \(r^*(u,v)=(\log3)u\) is globally Lipschitz; use \(\lambda=1\).
analysis: Assessment: Major; outcome: issue found.

Consider the fixed two-dimensional domain \[\begin{aligned}
 S&=([0,1]\times[-1,1])\cup T,\\
 T&=\left\{(u,v):v\ge e^{2},\quad
       \frac34\le u\le\frac34+\frac1{v(\log v)^{2}}\right\}.\end{aligned}\] It is measurable with positive finite volume \(V=2+\int_{e^{2}}^{\infty}[v(\log v)^{2}]^{-1}dv=5/2\). Let \(M=\{a=(0,0),b=(1,0)\}\) and add \(a'=(0,\epsilon)\), where \(0<\epsilon<e^{-2}\). All three Voronoi cells have positive area within the rectangle. The distance between \(a'\) and \(a\) is exactly \(\epsilon\).

Use one annotator with reward \(r^*(u,v)=(\log3)u\), globally Lipschitz with \(K=\log3\), and set \(\lambda=1\). Then \(p_{ab}=1/4\) and the clone has exactly the same preferences as \(a\). All comparison probabilities are \(1/4\), \(3/4\), or \(1/2\), so finite representative datasets exist.

For any two positive weights \(w_a+w_b=1\), the first-order conditions for the displayed formula give a fixed reward gap \(d=r_a-r_b\) satisfying \[d+\sigma(d)=\tfrac14,\qquad
 r_a=w_b d,\quad r_b=-w_a d.\] The unique root is \(d=-0.2001330666939489\ldots\ne0\). Increasing \(w_a\) by \(q\) therefore shifts both original rewards by \(-qd\). By the displayed formula, \[|r_1(y)-\widehat r_w^D(y)|
 \ge\frac{|d|}{V\log(1/\epsilon)},\qquad y\in M.\] Dividing by \(\sqrt\epsilon\) diverges as \(\epsilon\downarrow0\). This directly falsifies Lemma G.2, with every relevant original assumption and positivity condition satisfied. The geometry and algebra are exact; `check.json` records supporting root and rate evaluations.
result: The lower bound still tends to zero. The example refutes the asserted rate and the proof’s quadratic choice of neighborhood size, not the qualitative continuity in Definition 3.1. For finite-volume measurable domains, dominated convergence can support qualitative continuity of merged cells away from the null tie hyperplanes. A bounded-domain restriction would also change the geometry behind the claimed rate, but would be an additional assumption. No unconditional repaired version of Theorem 4.2 is certified here. The demonstrated false lemma is directly used in its central proof, supporting Major.
An explicit positive-cell finite-volume domain violates the weight and reward rates used in the central robustness proof.
The rate counterexample does not refute qualitative convergence; its global domain and repair conditions remain separate questions.
brief: A finite-volume tail gives \(q\ge1/[V\log(1/\epsilon)]\) and a reward shift that is not \(O(\sqrt\epsilon)\).
This contradicts the quantitative lemma used in Theorem 4.2, while leaving qualitative continuity possible.

paragraphs: Revise the domain assumptions and quantitative rate, or replace the rate-dependent argument with a qualitative continuity proof. Finite volume alone does not supply the printed rate.

claim: The harmonic schedule and squared-ratio condition in Theorem 7 yield \(O(1/t)\) mean-square convergence.

Replace the squared \(\gamma_{t+1}\) on the right by a linear one. Even then a gain condition is missing. Let \[\ell(\theta;Z)=\tfrac12(\theta-Z)^{2},\quad
 \Pr(Z=\pm1)=\tfrac12,\quad \theta_0=\theta_{\rm PS}=0,\] with \(\mu=L=G=B=1\) in Eq. (19), \(\beta=0\), \(\sigma_0=1\), \(\sigma_1=0\), no DP noise, and \(C_1=C_2=2\). Take \(a_0=1/4,a_1=64,b=8\). The exact variance recurrence is \[v_t=(1-\gamma_t)^2v_{t-1}+\gamma_t^2.\] Its solution is \(\Theta(t^{-2a_0})=\Theta(t^{-1/2})\): after division by the product of \((1-\gamma_i)^{2}\), the positive forcing series has terms of order \(i^{2a_0-2}\) and converges. Parent numerical evaluation gives
\(t | v_t\) | Printed bound \(8\gamma_t\) with \(M=0\)
This is a counterexample to an exponent-only repair, not an instance satisfying the impossible original condition.

Use the full past history as filtration, including error states. Let \(K=L(1+\beta)\), \(u_t=\theta_t-\gamma_te_t-\theta_{\rm PS}\), \(V_t=\mathbb E\|u_t\|^{2}\), \(\gamma=\gamma_{t+1}\), \(r=\gamma_t-\gamma\), and \(A=K\gamma\gamma_t+r\). A^{2}\|e_t\|^{2}/(\kappa\gamma)\) yields \[\begin{aligned}
 V_{t+1}\le{}&(1-\kappa\gamma+4B^{2}\gamma^{2})V_t
        +2\gamma^{2}(G^{2}+d\sigma_{\rm DP}^{2})\\
 &+\left[\frac{A^{2}}{\kappa\gamma}+2r^{2}+
                  4B^{2}\gamma^{2}\gamma_t^{2}\right]M^2.\end{aligned}\] For harmonic steps, \(r=O(\gamma^{2})\) and the bracket is \(O(\gamma^{3})\). claim: The explicit noise \(\sigma_{\rm DP}=c\sqrt{T\log(1/\delta)}/(m\epsilon)\) ensures \((\epsilon,\delta)\)-DP for every \(\epsilon\le T/m^{2}\).

Take \(m=T=c=\epsilon=1\), \(\delta=0.01\), \(\gamma_1=1/2\), \(\theta_0=0\), adjacent datasets \(\{+1\}\), \(\{-1\}\), loss \((\theta-z)^{2}/2\), projection onto \([-4,4]\), and no distribution shift.
analysis: Assessment: Major. Anchors: p. 5, Corollary 1; p. 17, Appendix E.

The corollary claims \((\epsilon,\delta)\)-DP for every \(\epsilon\le T/m^{2}\) when \(\sigma_{\rm DP}=c\sqrt{T\log(1/\delta)}/(m\epsilon)\). Set \(m=T=c=\epsilon=1\), \(\delta=0.01\), \(\theta_0=0\), and \(\gamma_1=1/2\). Use adjacent singleton datasets \(\{+1\}\) and \(\{-1\}\), no distribution shift, loss \(\ell(\theta;z)=(\theta-z)^{2}/2\), and projection set \([-4,4]\). The clipped first gradients are \(-1\) and \(+1\). The two unprojected outputs are Gaussian with means \(\pm\gamma_1\) and common standard deviation \(\gamma_1\sigma\), where \(\sigma=\sqrt{\log100}\).

For the event \[S=\{\theta_1\ge \gamma_1\sigma^{2}/2\},\] the threshold \(1.15129255\) lies inside the projection interval, so projection does not alter either event probability. Direct normal integration gives \[\Pr_+(S)=0.2719279741,\qquad
 \Pr_-(S)=0.0619053689,\] and hence \[\Pr_+(S)-e^\epsilon\Pr_-(S)=0.1036517348>0.01.\] All explicitly stated privacy parameters are admissible, and the mechanism violates the definition. The witness even satisfies the convex analysis assumptions on this compact domain with \(\mu=L=1,G=5,\beta=0\).

Appendix E invokes additional small-sampling conditions and asymptotic constants that are not retained in the corollary. Such constants cannot be silently discarded from an explicit DP guarantee. This materially affects the privacy/utility calibration central to the proposed remedies.

The experimental guarantees also do not follow from the displayed condition: quadratic \(T=m=10^{5}\) gives \(T/m^{2}=10^{-5}<\epsilon=0.1\); logistic \(T=10^{6},m=15776\) gives approximately \(0.004018<\epsilon=1\). This applicability failure does not independently prove privacy violation for those historical runs.
result: The admissible one-step mechanism violates the claimed privacy definition. Separate applicability failures in the displayed experimental parameters do not independently prove historical privacy violations.

       -e^\epsilon\Phi(-c/\sigma-\epsilon\sigma/(2c)).\] This one-step calculation does not supply a multi-step subsampled/adaptive accountant.

claim: The prescribed constant step minimizes expected error for every positive horizon.
Take fixed data \(z=0\), \(\ell(\theta)=\theta^{2}/2\), domain \([-1,1]\), \(\kappa=G=1\), \(c=1/2\), \(\theta_0=0.1\), \(m=T=\epsilon=1\), and \(\delta=0.01\).
analysis: Assessment: Major. Anchors: p. 6, Corollary 2/Eq. (15), and the subsequent asymptotic argument.

Corollary 2 prescribes \(\gamma^\star=-\log\Delta/(\kappa T)\) for all \(T\ge1\), without requiring \(\Delta<1\) or imposing the admissible step interval. Choose a constant dataset \(z=0\), \(\ell(\theta;0)=\theta^{2}/2\), \(\mathcal X=[-1,1]\), \(\kappa=G=1\), \(c=1/2\), \(\theta_0=0.1\), \(m=T=\epsilon=1\), and \(\delta=0.01\). Its stated noise formula gives \(\sigma_{\rm DP}^{2}=\tfrac14\log100\). Equation (15) yields \[\Delta=730.2585093,\qquad \gamma^\star=-6.59339859.\] The prescription is not an admissible nonnegative SGD step. This is an invalid claimed optimum in a core remedy, rather than only an imprecise convergence constant.

The expression is the unconstrained minimizer of an exponential surrogate bound \(R_0e^{-\kappa T\gamma}+C\gamma+\text{constant}\). On \([0,\gamma_{\max}]\), elementary differentiation instead gives \[\gamma_{\rm opt}=
 \min\{\gamma_{\max},\max\{0,-\log\Delta/(\kappa T)\}\}.\] This verified repair optimizes that surrogate only; it does not establish the minimum of the actual expected error. In addition, setting \(\gamma=(1+c_2)/(\kappa T)\) gives \((1-\kappa\gamma)^T\to e^{-(1+c_2)}\), not zero. The initial-error term must be retained in the Corollary 3 derivation. That observation alone does not refute its loose big-\(O\) expression, since other bounded-domain constants may absorb the term.
result: The prescription can be negative and inadmissible. Its constrained correction optimizes a surrogate bound, not actual expected error, and the finite-horizon transient must be retained.

Clamping repairs the constrained surrogate calculation, while an initial-error transient remains.

analysis: Assessment: Major for the released measurement path; historical figure impact remains Needs Evidence.

In `logistic/main_getps.py:39--57`, the outer `theta` is copied from the ERM solution and never updated inside the deployment loop. Every shifted dataset is consequently \(D(\theta_{\rm ERM})\). The optimizer updates `gd.theta`; `gd.py:52` rebinds it with a fresh array, so aliasing does not update the outer variable. The result is saved as `theta_PS`. `main_clip.py:19--25` loads it as the stability-gap reference. Repeatedly solving the same deployed problem does not enforce \(F(\theta_{\rm PS})=0\).

The independent check independently checked a two-feature logistic example using the released mathematical weighting and shift convention, without importing author code. The five feature rows are \((2,0),(0,1),(-0.3,0),(0,-3),(1,-2)\), with labels \((1,1,0,0,0)\), weight \(1+3y\), regularization \(0.2\) on feature coefficients, an unregularized intercept, and positive-class shift \(-0.5\,\theta_{1:2}/\|\theta_{1:2}\|\). Independent Newton minimization on the frozen deployment gives a point whose actual PS-gradient norm is \(0.00431826\); updating the deployment to self-consistency reduces that residual to \(1.62\,10^{-12}\). The reference points differ by \(0.00810283\). These are reviewer example values, not credit-dataset results.

A second target mismatch affects the risk plot. Both `clipsgd.py:74--75` and `dicesgd.py:57--58` record loss on the unshifted base features. Notebook `plot-clip.ipynb`, zero-based cell 5, plots that saved loss and labels it performative risk, matching the metric description in Appendix H.2/Figure 4, p. 22. The intended metric is \(\mathbb E_{D(\theta)}\ell(\theta;Z)\). In the same reviewer example, base risk is \(0.68925710\) and deployed risk is \(0.80994637\), so the distinction is substantive.

The old pinned commit and configuration differences prevent attributing an exact numerical change to the published figures. The code path itself does not establish the central empirical claim it is intended to measure. claim: With fixed activation patterns \(D_i\) and variables \(\theta=(u'_1,u_1,\ldots,u'_P,u_P)\), the lifted two-layer score is linear: \[f_\theta(X)=\sum_iD_iX(u'_i-u_i).\] The signs of the primed and unprimed variables are interchanged between some earlier and later displays; the examples use the Section 6 convention and are invariant to consistently swapping these roles. Activation constraints require \((2D_i-I)Xu'_i\ge0\) and \((2D_i-I)Xu_i\ge0\).

Theorem 4.1’s splitting of positive and negative output weights, merging inside each activation cone, and reconstruction with at most \(2P\) neurons were checked. The three-layer construction similarly duplicates signed branches under the stated ample-width condition. These are feasibility reformulations; they do not by themselves supply an initial radius, a statistically meaningful label budget, or prediction identification.

For a full-dimensional convex body, an active valid linear cut excluding its centroid retains at most \(1-1/e\) of the volume. Adding activation constraints cannot increase that retained volume. This portion of Theorem 6.3 is sound within its assumptions. It is a per-active-cut statement, not a guarantee for arbitrary queries, arbitrary analytic centers, or convergence to one prescribed real-valued prediction.
Nested nonempty vanishing-volume localization sets identify the retained parameter and imply convergence to its real-valued predictions.
Use compact full-dimensional nested convex bodies, valid active homogeneous cuts and a retained feasible point.
analysis: Assessment: Major.

Appendix G.1, p. 30, asserts that nestedness, nonemptiness, and vanishing volume imply \(\bigcap_tT^{(t)}=\{\theta^*\}\). Appendix G.2, pp. 30–31, then uses the purported implication \(\theta^{(k)}\to\theta^*\) to prove Corollary 6.4’s convergence of real-valued scores on every fixed \(X\).

The geometric implication is false even for active homogeneous cuts. Let \(T_k\) be the closed unit-disk sector with angles \(0\le\phi\le\alpha_k\), where \(\alpha_k=(\pi/2)3^{-k}\). Each is a compact convex body with nonempty interior. Cutting at angle \(\alpha_k/3\) retains \(T_{k+1}\), removes the old centroid (whose angle is \(\alpha_k/2\)), and reduces area by exactly \(1/3\). Nevertheless, \[\bigcap_kT_k=[0,1]\times\{0\},\qquad
 \operatorname{CG}(T_k)=
 \left(\frac{2\sin\alpha_k}{3\alpha_k},
       \frac{2(1-\cos\alpha_k)}{3\alpha_k}\right)
 \longrightarrow(2/3,0).\] The retained feasible point \((1/3,0)\) is not the limit, and the linear output equal to the first coordinate differs by \(1/3\) in the limit. This is an exact counterexample to the geometric inference used by the proof; it is not asserted to be a complete network-query trajectory.

The network setting also preserves scale ambiguity: zero-margin classification and activation constraints are homogeneous, so a feasible nonzero ray segment can remain inside the initial ball. Correct classification does not fix score amplitude. The finite-intersection property guarantees a nonempty intersection, not a singleton. Corollary 6.4 is therefore unproved by the supplied argument, directly affecting a central prediction-convergence claim. No failure of the conditional volume inequality itself is alleged.

A precise sufficient additional assumption would be \(\operatorname{diam}(T_k)\to0\) with \(\theta^*\in T_k\). For a fixed lifted matrix \(A_X\), it then gives \(\|A_X\theta^{(k)}-A_X\theta^*\|\le
\|A_X\|\operatorname{diam}(T_k)\to0\). This conditional repair is valid; the proposed algorithm has not been shown to enforce its new premise.
result: Volume decay does not establish parameter or prediction identification. Homogeneous classification also retains scale ambiguity; the conditional centroid-cut volume inequality remains valid.
brief: Vanishing volume can leave an entire segment of feasible parameters.
The claimed prediction convergence needs an additional identification condition; the active centroid-cut volume bound survives.

Theorem 4.1’s splitting of positive and negative output weights, merging inside each activation cone, and reconstruction with at most \(2P\) neurons were checked. The three-layer construction similarly duplicates signed branches under the stated ample-width condition. These are feasibility reformulations; they do not by themselves supply an initial radius, a statistically meaningful label budget, or prediction identification.

For a full-dimensional convex body, an active valid linear cut excluding its centroid retains at most \(1-1/e\) of the volume. Adding activation constraints cannot increase that retained volume. This portion of Theorem 6.3 is sound within its assumptions. It is a per-active-cut statement, not a guarantee for arbitrary queries, arbitrary analytic centers, or convergence to one prescribed real-valued prediction.
Theorem G.2 supplies its universal inexact-cut volume bound, and dense data yield the Corollary G.3 rate \((1-1/e)^t\).

For G.2 use one-dimensional input \(X=[1]\), label \(+1\), both activation patterns and a four-dimensional lifted body with strict gate constraints and both cut sides nonempty. The construction permits every proposed \(\Theta_4>0\). For G.3 use i.i.d. uniform inputs on \((0,1)\), all labels \(+1\), the specified unit-ball initialization and Algorithm 5.
analysis: Assessment: Major.

Theorem G.2, pp. 32–34, claims \[\frac{\operatorname{vol}(T_1)}{\operatorname{vol}(T)}
 <1-e^{-1}(1-\widetilde\lambda)^d,\qquad
 \widetilde\lambda=
 -\frac{R^dH_{T^-}}{\Theta_d\operatorname{vol}(T)H_{T^+}}h,\] where \(h\) is the centroid’s distance to the cut, \(R\) is the radius of a \((d-1)\)-ball with the cross-section’s volume, and \(\Theta_d>0\) depends only on dimension.

Use input dimension one, \(X=[1]\), label \(+1\), and the complete pattern set \(\{1,0\}\). The lifted parameter dimension is four. In orthogonal coordinates set \[q=(u'_1-u_1)/\sqrt2,\qquad s=(u'_1+u_1)/\sqrt2,\] and define the rectangular body \[-\epsilon\le q\le1,\quad 2\le s\le3,\quad
 -2\le u'_0,u_0\le-1,\qquad 0<\epsilon\le0.1.\] It is compact and full-dimensional. Both active-pattern variables are positive because \(s>|q|\), and both inactive variables are negative. Thus every activation constraint is satisfied strictly throughout \(T\). The classification cut is exactly \(q\ge0\) and removes no additional volume through activation constraints.

Its volume is \(1+\epsilon\), its cross-section at \(q=0\) has three-volume one, and \[R=(3/(4\pi))^{1/3},\quad
 h=(1-\epsilon)/2,\quad
 H_{T^-}/H_{T^+}=-\epsilon.\] Writing \(K=R^{4}/(2\Theta_4)>0\), the printed expression gives \(\widetilde\lambda=K\epsilon(1-\epsilon)/(1+\epsilon)\). For any positive \(\Theta_4\), choose \(\epsilon=\min\{0.1,1/(10K)\}\). Then \[\frac{\operatorname{vol}(T_1)}{\operatorname{vol}(T)}
   =\frac1{1+\epsilon}\ge\frac{10}{11},
 \qquad
 1-e^{-1}(1-\widetilde\lambda)^{4}
   \le1-e^{-1}(0.9)^{4}=0.7586343\ldots .\] The claimed upper bound is contradicted. All quantities are well-defined, both half-spaces meet \(T\), and \(0<\widetilde\lambda\le0.1\). Uniformly scaling \(T\) by \(1/5\) places it inside the unit ball, preserves all signs and the retained fraction, and multiplies \(\widetilde\lambda\) by \(1/5\), strengthening the contradiction. This refutes the theorem’s stated universal convex-body bound; the box is not claimed to be a particular recorded historical iterate.

Corollary G.3, p. 35, claims that uniform, increasingly dense input data and minimum raw margin recover the \((1-1/e)^t\) volume bound for Algorithm 5. Take independent inputs uniform on \((0,1)\) and give every input label \(+1\). Both labels being represented is not assumed. The full activation-pattern set remains \(\{1,0\}\); a strictly correct four-neuron representation exists.

Starting at \(B_2\subset\mathbb R^{4}\), every positive input induces the identical constraints \[u'_1\ge u_1\ge0,\qquad u'_0\le0,\quad u_0\le0.\] The first cut retains one orthant, with half of its active-coordinate ordering, so \(\operatorname{vol}(T^{(1)})/\operatorname{vol}(T^{(0)})=1/32\). All later distinct queries add redundant copies of the same constraints. Hence the ratio remains \(1/32\) for every \(t\ge1\), independently of dataset size or minimum-margin selection. Already at \(t=8\), \[(1-1/e)^{8}=0.02549173\ldots < 1/32=0.03125.\] This is a direct counterexample to the claimed asymptotic bound using the specified initialization and valid ReLU cuts.

The proof also confuses raw margin with normalized distance: \(h=|f_\theta(x)|/\|a(x)\|\). Here \(a(x)=x(1,-1,0,0)\). Small positive \(x\) makes the raw margin small but leaves the hyperplane and its distance unchanged. Dense inputs do not guarantee informative cuts. Theorem 6.3 survives because these later cuts are not active. No complete corrected inexact-cut theorem is certified.

analysis: Assessment: Major.

Section 5, p. 5, claims the unit ball contains optimal parameters by scale invariance, while Algorithm 1’s cut enforces margin at least one, as in Equation (3). Scaling preserves the sign, but not that fixed margin.

The incompatibility persists with explicit bias augmentation and both classes. Let \(x_+=(0.1,1)\), \(x_-=(-0.1,1)\) and labels \(+1,-1\). These independent rows realize all four first-layer patterns, so \(P=4\) and the stated ample-width condition is met by \(m=8\). The original network \[f(z)=10(z_1)_+-10(-z_1)_+\] (padded with zero neurons) has both margins exactly one.

For any lifted parameter with \(\|\theta\|_2\le1\), the reconstructed ReLU function is Lipschitz with constant at most \[\sum_{i=1}^{P}(\|u_i\|_2+\|u'_i\|_2)
 \le\sqrt{2P}\|\theta\|_2\le\sqrt8.\] The two outputs can therefore differ by at most \(0.2\sqrt8=0.565685\ldots\), whereas the two unit margins require a difference of at least two. Thus the radius excludes every solution of a feasible original instance.

This invalidates the initialization argument for the central fixed-margin training scheme. A data-dependent adequate radius, or an explicitly changed margin/domain, is required. The zero-margin cuts in Algorithms 2/4 and in the release avoid this particular contradiction; that distinction is not a repair of Algorithm 1 as printed.
result: The original instance is feasible, but no parameter in the asserted ball meets its unit margins. Sign-preserving rescaling does not preserve a fixed margin.

analysis: Assessment: Major; written algorithm, with different released behavior.

Algorithms 1, 2, and 4 (pp. 4, 6, 16) start from the unit ball and cut only if \(y f_{\theta_c}(x)<0\). Its centroid and symmetric barrier center are zero, and \(f_0(x)=0\) for every input. Therefore no label, including either binary class, can trigger the strict inequality. The localization set and center remain unchanged by induction. In Algorithms 2/4, \(D_{\rm AL}\) stays empty, so a positive budget is never reached. Algorithm 1’s cut counter also stays zero.

This is a complete execution argument for the printed rule, not a rounding issue or an assumption about data separability. It prevents the proposed starting procedure from producing its first cut. The conditional theorem assuming active cuts does not make a zero score negative.

Counterevidence is decisive: the release uses \(\texttt{np.sign(pred)}\ne y\), which treats zero as a mistake for labels \(\pm1\), and therefore can leave zero. Treating zero margins as eligible cuts restores this initial step; a cut through the centroid has a non-strict \(1-1/e\) bound. Neither full termination nor all other guarantees follows from this local change. Historical runs are not alleged to have stalled.
result: The printed strict guard cannot leave zero or reach a positive cut/query budget. The released zero-handling behavior differs, so historical runs are not alleged to stall.

analysis: Assessment: Major for the stated query-budget interpretation.

Algorithms 2/4 query a label before testing correctness, but add the point to \(D_{\rm AL}\) only if the cut is accepted. Their stopping condition counts \(|D_{\rm AL}|\). Algorithm 9’s baselines instead add every newly queried label. This matters directly to Section 7’s comparisons at a fixed number of queries.

The same accounting appears in `src/cpal/cpal.py`: the routine reads both `y[i_mini]` and `y[i_maxi]`, records tried indices, but increments `data_used` only on mistakes. The sentiment application likewise plots and budgets `len(data_used)`. Correctly classified queried labels have already been acquired, although they do not change the feasible set.

A complete local trace uses inputs \(1,2,3,4,5\), all labels \(+1\), both scalar patterns, and requested budget three. At the exact zero center, minimum and maximum scores tie at index zero. Both stale-center tests append that same index, giving `data_used` length two but one distinct label. After these positive cuts, any strict barrier center has positive score on every remaining positive input. The next candidate pairs are indices \((1,4)\) and \((2,3)\); all four labels are inspected and all predictions are correct. Five distinct labels have now been acquired while the counter remains two, below the requested budget three. No numerical solver value is needed beyond the strictly positive cut slack.

The list also allows duplicate initial entries, so it is neither a distinct-label counter nor a reliable oracle-call counter. Fixing only the duplicate does not fix the uncharged correct labels. This demonstrates a core mismatch between the advertised label budget and the proposed accounting. It does not determine the actual number of labels behind the published curves or prove their ranking would reverse. A separate ledger of all queried distinct indices, with each label charged when requested, restores budget semantics; historical comparisons require those logs or fresh experiments. There is no certified numerical correction to the reported curves.
result: The counter measures accepted cut entries, with possible duplicates, rather than all distinct acquired labels or oracle calls. Historical label costs and ranking changes remain unestablished.

analysis: Assessment: Major for the frozen release’s core implementation; historical impact unresolved.

In `src/cpal/utils.py`, `predict` iterates over outer index \(l\) and inner index \(j\), then multiplies both outer sums by `Di[i,j]` instead of `Di[i,l]`. The three-layer query and mistake tests call this routine, while the cut uses the intended outer pattern.

Take \(d=P_1=1\), \(P_2=2\), \(x=1\), \(Q=[1]\), and the generator-compatible sorted outer row \(D=[0,1]\). In the routine’s four parameter blocks choose \[c_1=(.1,.3),\ c_2=(.4,.1),\
 c_3=(.1,.2),\ c_4=(.2,.1).\] Their squared norm is \(.37<1\). All inner weights are positive; the outer preactivations are \((-.3,.2)\) and \((-.1,.1)\), strictly matching \(D\). The intended score is \(.2-.1=.1\). The released expression instead uses \(D_0=0\) for both outer terms and returns zero. This is an admissible sampled-pattern instance, not a violation of an activation constraint. Changing the selected index to \(l\) restores this displayed score and the corresponding general sum. The mathematical reformulation itself is not refuted; historical three-layer figures are not bound to this preliminary implementation.

This is Major for the frozen implementation’s core three-layer algorithm. In `src/cpal/cpal_3layer.py`, line 55 uses this predictor to rank query candidates, and lines 78–83 use it to decide whether to cut and count a sample. The cut in lines 40–43 uses the intended outer pattern, so these central decisions use a different score from the constraint. The preliminary label and missing historical run binding limit attribution to the paper’s figures; they do not remove this demonstrated core implementation failure. A historical benchmark loss is not required to establish the defect in the inspected algorithm.

analysis: Assessment: Major for the frozen release’s application evaluation; historical impact unresolved.

The sentiment application’s query and cut use interleaved pattern-major blocks through a Kronecker product. Its evaluation instead applies default row-major \(\texttt{c.reshape((2*d,m))}\). The required matrix layout has these blocks as columns.

For \(d=m=2\), take data rows \((-1,0)\) and \((1,0)\) with sorted pattern columns \[D=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 c=(.3,0,.1,0,-.1,.8,-.2,0).\] Its squared norm is \(.79<1\). The intended positive and negative weight matrices are \[U_+=\begin{pmatrix}.3&-.1\\0&.8\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 U_-=\begin{pmatrix}.1&-.2\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.\] All signed preactivations on both data rows are strictly positive. At \((1,0)\), the correctly decoded ReLU score is \(.3-.1=.2\). The default reshape yields positive-block rows \((.3,0),(.1,0)\) and negative-block rows \((-.1,.8),(-.2,0)\), producing \(.3-.8=-.5\). Thus evaluation reverses the sign of a valid parameter vector. Column-major decoding restores the specified block correspondence.

The release also crops embeddings to 200 dimensions, whereas the paper reports 2560, and uses a different fixed data seed. These differences further prevent attributing Figure 4’s historical values to this exact code. The demonstrated evaluation defect remains; its historical score effect requires provenance and reruns.

This is Major for the frozen sentiment application’s evaluation path. Lines 168–172 compute and display train/test predictions with the incorrect layout, and lines 175–181 append that accuracy to the returned `score` sequence. The reversed classifier sign therefore reaches the application’s actual evaluation output. Query and cut calculations continue to use the separate Kronecker layout; they are not claimed to share this reshape defect. Historical uncertainty does not repair the demonstrated failure of this core evaluation path.
result: The evaluation reshape can reverse a valid classifier sign and reaches the returned train/test accuracy. Query and cut use a separate correct layout; historical paper scores remain unresolved.
