paragraphs: For the stated nondegenerate model, define \[D=a^2s_Z+s_T,\quad C=a(b-ac)s_Z-cs_T,\quad H=(b-ac)^2s_Z+c^2s_T+s_Y.\] Gaussian conditioning gives \[\mathbb E[Y\mid T=t]=\exp\left((b-ac)\mu_Z+\frac CD(\log t-a\mu_Z)+\frac12\left(H-\frac{C^{2}}{D}\right)\right),\qquad t>0.\] This is the exact conditional log-normal mean, with \(D>0\), rather than a replacement empirical fit.

analysis: Source claim and location. Section 2.1, p. 2, gives a special-case expression for E[Y|T] when c=0. Appendix B.2, p. 14, Eq. (9), gives its general expression. The latter uses the coefficient [a(b-c)\(s_Z\)-c \(s_T\)]/[\(s_Z+c^{2}\) \(s_T+s_Y\)] multiplying (T-a \(\mu_Z\)). The preceding Gaussian conditioning identity on p. 14 and the covariance matrix in Eq. (8) on p. 14 instead imply a different coefficient multiplying log T. Source pages 2 and 14 were rendered and inspected; this is not a text-extraction artifact [S1, E1].

Suspect step. Substitution from Eq. (8) into the immediately preceding correct Gaussian conditioning formula changes both the covariance numerator and the conditioning variance, and drops the logarithm. Define the following quantities directly from the stated model:

\[D=a^2s_Z+s_T,\quad C=a(b-ac)s_Z-cs_T,\quad H=(b-ac)^2s_Z+c^2s_T+s_Y,\quad \beta=C/D.\] \[\mathbb E[Y\mid T=t]=\exp\!\left((b-ac)\mu_Z+\frac{C}{D}(\log t-a\mu_Z)+\frac12\left(H-\frac{C^{2}}{D}\right)\right),\quad t>0.\] Complete analytic check. Since (V,W) is jointly Gaussian, E[W|V=log t]=(b-ac)\(\mu_Z\)+(C/D)(log t-a \(\mu_Z\)) and Var(W|V)=H-C^2/D. The log-normal expectation is the exponential of this conditional mean plus half the conditional variance. This gives the displayed correction without an approximation. D>0 in the stated nondegenerate model.

Assumption-satisfying counterexample. Take a=b=2, c=1, \(\mu_Z\)=0, \(s_Z=s_T=s_Y\)=1. All original positivity and independence conditions hold; doses 1 and 2 both lie in the strictly positive support. Then D=5, C=-1, H=2 and H-C^2/D=9/5. Thus E[Y|T=t]=exp(0.9)t^(-0.2). The correct means at t=1 and t=2 are 2.4596031112 and 2.1412088739, with ratio 0.8705505633. Eq. (9)’s printed coefficient is 1/3; its ratio is exp(1/3)=1.3956124251. Any additive exponent constant independent of T cancels, so no interpretation of ’const.’ repairs this reversal of the trend [E2].

The p. 2 special case is independently wrong even without a trend reversal. For a=b=1, c=0, \(\mu_Z\)=0 and all variances 1, the correct mean ratio between doses 4 and 1 is 2; the printed expression gives exp(3/2)=4.4816890703. In general the c=0 coefficient should be ab sZ/(a^2 \(s_Z+s_T\)), multiplying log t, not t.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. Reading T as an already logged variable conflicts with Eq.(1) and the explicit log T in the preceding derivation, and does not repair the coefficient. Eq.(8) and the general Gaussian-conditioning identity remain correct. At c=0, the corrected mean still increases with dose for a,b>0, preserving the qualitative confounding example. At c>0, the paper claims the possibility of positive association, not that every allowed parameter setting has it; the checked reversal does not refute that existential statement. Eq.(4)’s fixed-dose intervention mean also remains valid.

Calibrated judgment: Major at the claim level. The abstract identifies concrete examples as the paper’s demonstration; Section2 introduces this as its running example, and Section2.1/p.3 explicitly invokes Eq.(9) to explain observational versus interventional response. The wrong quantitative function, including a reversed trend for allowed fixed parameters, is therefore a failed derivation closely tied to the core explanatory contribution. The reversal is established for the saved c=1 example, not the c=0 specialization or the paper’s plotted parameters. The existing analytic replacement remains verified. No figure or empirical effect is claimed; the previously checked later version retains the error [S2].
claim: For the aspirin model, let U=log Z, V=log T and W=log Y. The original model has positive Z,T,Y, independent Gaussian log-noises, a,b>0, and parameters treated as fixed in the conditional-mean calculation. Write \(s_Z\)=Var(U), \(s_T\)=Var(log epsilon_T), \(s_Y\)=Var(log epsilon_Y). In the counterexamples all three variances are strictly positive. The model implies V=aU+E_T and W=(b-ac)U-cE_T+E_Y, with U N(\(\mu_Z\),\(s_Z\)), E_T N(0,\(s_T\)), E_Y N(0,\(s_Y\)).
The displayed substitutions give E[Y|T] for the model in Eq1.
Independent Gaussian log-noises; a,b>0; positive variances; t=1,2 in positive support.
result: Major at the claim level: the principal worked example contains a demonstrated wrong quantitative derivation, and an allowed-parameter instance reverses its observational dose trend. This is closely tied to the paper's explanatory contribution. The broad expressivity thesis and the surviving qualitative claims do not settle the severity.

analysis: Source claim and location. Appendix C.1, p. 17, Eq. (35), and Appendix J, p. 25, Eq. (37), assert q(x_y)=q(x_y|x_t) when discussing interventions whose new parent set is empty. Both explicitly extend the result beyond atomic interventions to any such intervention. The parent-adjustment sum that follows is a conditional treatment response; it is not the unconditional outcome under a nondegenerate random treatment [S1, E1].

Suspect step. Removing incoming edges to T makes T independent of its former parents, but it does not remove the edge T -> Y. Therefore it does not imply q(Y)=q(Y|T=t). An atomic treatment is constant, which is why the equality is valid at the assigned value in that special case.

Complete finite check. Let the original graph be T -> Y. Use p(T=1)=1/2 and unchanged outcome probabilities p(Y=1|T=0)=1/5 and p(Y=1|T=1)=4/5. Intervene with g(T=1)=1/4 and no parents. All four original joint cells and all four intervened joint cells have strictly positive mass. There is no hidden confounder, no cycle, no support problem, and the sole original outcome mechanism is preserved.
T | Y | Intervened joint probability q(T,Y)

\[q(Y=1)=\frac34\frac15+\frac14\frac45=\frac7{20},\qquad q(Y=1\mid T=1)=\frac45\ne\frac7{20}.\] Repair. Under the stated valid parent-adjustment setting and positivity on the treatment values used, the fixed-treatment response is obtained first. A stochastic policy then requires averaging over its treatment distribution:

\[q(y)=\sum_t g(t)\sum_z p(y\mid t,z)p(z).\] Here z denotes the original parents of T; for the two-node counterexample this parent set is empty. Summing the four displayed cells verifies the repair exactly. Alternatively, the paper can restrict the equalities in Eqs. (35) and (37) to the atomic case at its assigned treatment. These are two precise repairs, with different scope.

Calibrated judgment: Major at the claim level. Section2.3, p.5, defines general kernel replacement in Eq.(5)/Figure5 and directs readers to Appendix J for adjustment shortcuts. Appendix J expressly asks for q(y) and extends the atomic result to every empty-parent intervention; Appendix C.1’s proof establishes the conditional response only. This failed generalization drops the policy weights and answers a different query from the advertised stochastic marginal. The two-node example also satisfies Y not being a parent of T, and uses positive joint cells and an unchanged outcome kernel. Reading the notation as a family of atomic outcomes would require withdrawing the explicit stochastic extension.

Counterevidence and scope. Eq.(5)’s general stochastic joint factorization remains valid. Appendix I Eq.(36) identifies the treatment-conditional response on the intervention support. Under an atomic intervention, the marginal equals that conditional at the assigned treatment value only; the main fixed-dose aspirin calculation survives. Restoring the outer policy average repairs the stochastic result. Neither this repair’s simplicity nor the survival of the broad expressivity thesis downgrades the failed core generalization. The previously checked arXiv text retains it [S2]; no empirical policy consequence is asserted.

analysis: Use K2 in both domains, source features (2,2), target features (5/2,5/2), and common label 0. The architecture has identity activation and readout, W1=W2=1, and filters h_a(t)=a \(t^{2}\) for 0<=a<=1. Evaluate the hypothesis a=1 with squared error loss. The graphs, bounded real features, weights, Lipschitz maps and nonnegative loss all meet the stated conditions. The evaluated polynomial has genuine degree 2.

A valid uniform \(K_{\rm Lip}\)=1 is supplied independently of the failed D.5. Let the input space be all K2 graphs with scalar feature entries in [0,5/2]. Because both degrees are 1 and the depth trees are single paths, each of TMD^1, TMD^2 and TMD^3 equals the optimal unit-mass matching cost d_OT between the two feature multisets. For every a in the class, the difference between a times the two feature sums is at most d_OT, hence at most the summed-depth cost 3d_OT. Thus the whole class satisfies the required Lipschitz upper bound; this is not merely a two-point estimate.

Here \(P^{2}\)=I. Outputs are 4 and 5, so risks are 16 and 25. Every depth has two terminal feature differences of 1/2, hence TMD^1=TMD^2=TMD^3=1. The two domain measures are point masses, and W1=3. The joint-risk infimum is zero at a=0. Even if one insists every class member have strictly positive degree-two coefficient, use 0<a<=1 and the same infimum is approached as a tends to zero.
claim: \[H(G;w)=\phi\!\left(\sum_i[h_\alpha(P)\sigma(\sigma(XW_1)W_2)]_i\right),\qquad P=D^{-1}A,\] \[H(G;w)=\operatorname{Softmax}\!\left(h_\alpha(\widehat L)\sigma(\sigma(XW_1)W_2)\right).\] The inductive readout is real-valued; it is not constrained to [0,1]. The assumptions on sigma and phi in Theorems 4.8/D.5 are Lipschitz continuity, without sigma(0)=0, positive homogeneity, or a restriction to ReLU. Weight norms are bounded by \(c_W\) when the main bound is used. The risk setup allows a nonnegative loss, without the loss conditions from Shen et al. being stated [R1, pp. 9, 16–18]. The separate softmax in the transductive architecture cannot supply an unstated probability-range assumption for the inductive one.

The risk setup on p. 9 permits an arbitrary nonnegative loss. Theorem 4.9, Eq. (4), then bounds target risk by source risk plus 2 \(K_{\rm Lip}\) W1 and the best joint source/target risk, citing Shen et al. The imported result uses an absolute-disagreement loss, [0,1]-valued hypotheses, a shared labeling function and a common Lipschitz constant over the class [R2, p. 5, Lemma 1 and Theorem 1]. Those are operative assumptions, not optional provenance details. The counterexample below targets the broader published claim in [R1], not [R2].
\[R_T(w)\le R_S(w)+2K_{\rm Lip}W_1(\mu_S,\mu_T)+\inf_{w'}\{R_S(w')+R_T(w')\}.\]
result: The labels do not change between domains; label shift is not the explanation. The error does not rely on Problem 1 because a common Lipschitz constant has been established directly. Squared error is allowed by [R1]’s nonnegative-loss setup and its real-valued inductive readout. Imposing the separate transductive softmax or the unstated [0,1] restriction would change that setup. Shen et al.’s theorem remains valid within the assumptions inspected here.

The source’s absolute-disagreement proof uses both a triangle inequality and a 2 \(K_{\rm Lip}\) Lipschitz bound for disagreement. Those steps cannot simply be reused for arbitrary loss with the same constant. The failed conversion is central to Section 4.3’s claimed out-of-domain guarantee and its interpretation in terms of polynomial coefficients, so the supported impact is Major. A repair must state a defensible loss/class restriction and rederive constants, in addition to obtaining valid stability assumptions. No complete repaired generalization theorem is claimed. analysis: Theorem F.1 [R1, bottom of p. 22 continuing on p. 23] states lambda_2/2 <= h(G) <= sqrt(2 \(\lambda_2\)), but defines h(G) as min over S subset V of |E(S,Sbar)|/(d|S|), with no half-size or half-volume restriction. To give the statement its most favorable meaningful reading, exclude empty and full subsets. A regular graph removes any ambiguity in the scalar degree d.

For connected unweighted K3, d=2 and \(\lambda_2\)=3/2. A singleton has two cut edges and ratio 2/(2*1)=1. Any two-vertex proper subset also has two cut edges and ratio 2/(2*2)=1/2. These exhaust the six nonempty proper subsets. The printed minimum is therefore 1/2, while lambda_2/2=3/4. The lower inequality fails: 3/4 is greater than 1/2. The normalized-Laplacian convention and all regular-graph conditions hold.

The standard volume definition is h_vol=min cut(S,Sbar)/vol(S) over 0<vol(S)<=vol(V)/2, equivalently using min(vol(S),vol(Sbar)) in the denominator over all nonempty proper subsets. On a d-regular graph this requires 0<|S|<=|V|/2. It gives h_vol=1 on K3. The corrected conventional Cheeger statement is supported by Chung’s primary account [R5, printed pp. 754, 756; PDF pp. 4, 6]. The review independently verifies the lower inequality as follows.

\[\begin{aligned}
z&=D^{1/2}\!\left({\bf1}_S-\frac{\operatorname{vol}(S)}{\operatorname{vol}(V)}{\bf1}\right),
\qquad z\perp D^{1/2}{\bf1},\\
\lambda_2&\le\frac{z^\top\widehat Lz}{z^\top z}
=|\partial S|\!\left(\frac1{\operatorname{vol}(S)}+\frac1{\operatorname{vol}(\bar S)}\right)
\le\frac{2|\partial S|}{\operatorname{vol}(S)} .
\end{aligned}\] The last step uses precisely the missing half-volume condition. The upper Cheeger inequality is checked against the primary source, not independently reproved here. This is a local repair with explicit conditions, not a new generalization result. The defect changes a stated background theorem but is not used in the new stability or risk derivations; its supported severity is Minor. analysis: Take \(G_a\) = K2 and \(G_b\) = P3, with scalar raw features zero on every vertex. Set W1=W2=1, phi(t)=t, sigma(t)=1/(1+exp(-t)), and h(t)=\(t^{2}\). Both graphs satisfy the binary, connected, undirected, positive-degree setting. Their degree lists are (1,1) and (1,2,1). Sigma is globally 1/4-Lipschitz; phi is 1-Lipschitz; both weight norms are 1; the polynomial has genuine degree 2. The original definition permits different graph sizes and explicitly supplies padding for this case.

Write c = sigma(sigma(0)) = sigma(1/2) > 0. Since P maps the all-ones vector to itself, the transformed constant survives \(P^{2}\). Sum readout therefore gives 2c and 3c. Every leaf feature of every computational or blank tree is zero, so every terminal cost is zero. Recursion and optimal transport give TMD^1=TMD^2=TMD^3=0, irrespective of a possible degree-reset interpretation. Thus both the weighted D.5 bound and the main summed-depth bound have a zero right side.

\[\big|H(G_a)-H(G_b)\big|=c=\frac{1}{1+e^{-1/2}}>0,\qquad \text{claimed upper bound}=0.\] The local failure can also be evaluated directly. For F(x)=sigma(sigma(x)), x=y=0, a=1 and b=2, |F(0)/1-F(0)/2|=c/2>0 whereas any proposed Lipschitz multiple of |0/1-0/2| is zero. These denominators occur in depth-three K2/P3 walks. As an exact-arithmetic corroboration, the allowed affine activation sigma(t)=t+1 gives node value 2 and graph outputs 4 and 6, while the same raw-tree distances remain zero.
claim: \[H(G;w)=\phi\!\left(\sum_i[h_\alpha(P)\sigma(\sigma(XW_1)W_2)]_i\right),\qquad P=D^{-1}A,\] \[H(G;w)=\operatorname{Softmax}\!\left(h_\alpha(\widehat L)\sigma(\sigma(XW_1)W_2)\right).\] The inductive readout is real-valued; it is not constrained to [0,1]. The assumptions on sigma and phi in Theorems 4.8/D.5 are Lipschitz continuity, without sigma(0)=0, positive homogeneity, or a restriction to ReLU. Weight norms are bounded by \(c_W\) when the main bound is used. The risk setup allows a nonnegative loss, without the loss conditions from Shen et al. being stated [R1, pp. 9, 16–18]. The separate softmax in the transductive architecture cannot supply an unstated probability-range assumption for the inductive one.

Theorem 4.8 [R1, pp. 8–9, Eq. (3)] and D.5 [p. 18, Eqs. (12)–(13)] claim a TMD control on the output of Eq. (6) for Lipschitz activation and readout. The proof’s decisive unsupported inference is the last inequality of Eq. (20), p. 20: it moves unequal accumulated degree divisions through the nonlinear feature transform using only its Lipschitz constant. That property controls F(x)-F(y), not F(x)/a-F(y)/b when a and b differ. Eq. (18) must not itself be condemned merely for using zero padding: padding missing transformed embeddings by zero can justify that identity. Compatibility with the raw-feature blank tree and the later nonlinear scaling remains unproved.
result: Replacing the actual sum readout with a mean, silently requiring a zero-preserving homogeneous activation, or requiring equal node counts would change the claim. The present witness uses the published architecture and assumptions. The report does not infer experimental failure for an implementation that happened to use a more restricted activation. A separate zero-preserving clipped-activation calculation in Appendix B shows why simply adding sigma(0)=0 has not been verified as a complete repair of D.5.

This is Major because D.5 is the new stability derivation, its corollary is main Theorem 4.8, and Section 4.3 explicitly substitutes its coefficient-dependent constant into the inductive generalization argument. A core theoretical guarantee is false even though other perturbation bounds and localization observations survive. No full corrected theorem is certified. Evidence: verification/0047/independent_checks.json, replay_checks.py, completion_checks.json, and the preserved source images for pp. 18 and 20.
Other perturbation bounds, localization observations and restricted architectures are not refuted.

analysis: Take K2 with m=u=1, scalar feature 1 at both nodes, identity activation, W1=1, W2=(1,0), and h(t)=1+\(t^{2}\). Let w0 contain exactly these parameters and R=0. The closed ball is a nonempty singleton; feature, weight and activation constants can all be 1. The graph is connected, the polynomial has genuine degree 2, and the weight dimensions match Eq. (7). Assign opposite binary labels to the two nodes and use standard nonnegative cross-entropy.

The normalized Laplacian is [[1,-1],[-1,1]], annihilating the constant feature. Both logits are (1,0) and both softmax probability vectors are (e/(e+1),1/(e+1)). The two losses are log(1+e^(-1)) and log(1+e), whose difference is exactly 1. Consequently the test-minus-train gap is +1 or -1 with probability 1/2 each.

\[\|I\|_\infty=1,\quad\|\widehat L\|_\infty=2,\quad\|\widehat L^{2}\|_\infty=4,\quad\|I+\widehat L^{2}\|_\infty=5;\qquad L_1=\sqrt{14},\quad L_2=10.\] All constants are finite, but the displayed bound is zero because R=0. At delta=1/4, a positive gap violates even a favorable one-sided upper-bound interpretation with probability 1/2, exceeding the allowed failure probability 1/4. Interpreting big-O as an absolute bound does not help.

The failure is not confined to a two-node finite-size case. For any odd m>=3, use the connected regular cycle C_(2m), the same constant features and predictor, m nodes of each label, and m training nodes. If J is the number of lower-loss nodes sampled for training, then J is hypergeometric with population 2m and m lower-loss nodes; the gap is (2J-m)/m. Symmetry under J -> m-J and odd m give P(gap>0)=1/2 at arbitrarily large graph sizes. R=0 still forces the displayed term to zero. Exact finite checks for m=1,3,5,9,21 agree with this analytic argument.

Even a positive-radius reading requires qualifications: under the usual interpretation that the displayed dependence is uniform in R, choose R=1/m and retain w=w0 in that ball. Bounds \(c_W\)=2 and fixed feature/activation constants work; the normalized-cycle operator norms stay bounded. The claimed term is O(m^(-3/2)), whereas every positive gap for odd m is at least 1/m and occurs with probability 1/2. This auxiliary observation is conditional on that uniform big-O interpretation; the primary R=0 witness uses the literal stated closed ball.

Tang and Liu [R3, p. 3] work with an open ball of radius r>=1, so the R=0 witness is outside their assumptions. At least one eigenvector at lambda_k has exactly k nodal domains.
analysis: Source claim: the main discussion on p. 6 and Theorem F.3 on p. 23 assert that an eigenvector corresponding to the k-th eigenvalue exists with exactly k nodal domains [R1]. F.3 gives no simple-spectrum assumption and defines domains as maximal connected subgraphs on which sign does not change. The claim is stronger than the qualified upper-bound results in Davies, Leydold and Stadler [R4, pp. 2–3], which distinguish weak and strong nodal domains and multiplicity.

Use the connected unweighted triangle K3. Its normalized Laplacian is (3/2)I-(1/2)J, with spectrum 0,3/2,3/2. Every nonzero vector in the \(\lambda_3\) eigenspace has zero coordinate sum and therefore at least one positive and one negative entry. Both sign supports are connected cliques. There are exactly two strong sign domains; maximal weak domains also number two, with any zero entries allowed in the relevant maximal sign sets. A zero cannot create a third maximal domain. The eigenspace is spanned by (1,-1,0) and (1,1,-2), but the argument applies to every vector in it.

\[k=3,\qquad \lambda_3=3/2,\qquad \max_{0\ne v\in\ker(\widehat L-(3/2)I)}\{\text{nodal-domain count of }v\}=2<3.\] Repeated eigenvalues are allowed by the published statement. Choosing a different basis within that eigenspace cannot restore the exact-three assertion. This is a bounded background strengthening rather than a premise used in D.5, Eq. (4), or F.6. Qualified nodal-domain upper bounds can still support a narrower discussion of low-frequency structure. The supported impact is Minor on that dependency analysis, not because the claim is in an appendix.

Deleting the exact-existence assertion removes the demonstrated false subclaim. A complete replacement must still state the weak/strong-domain and eigenvalue-multiplicity qualifications; this review does not certify the remainder of F.3 verbatim. result: Connected unweighted K3 has normalized spectrum (0,3/2,3/2); every nonzero \(\lambda_3\) vector has zero sum and exactly two maximal strong or weak sign domains, never three. Davies v1 distinguishes weak/strong domains and multiplicity-sensitive upper bounds; those are not universal exact-count existence assertions.

claim: All compositionally sparse functions under the fan-in/node-count-only Definition 3.1 have deep approximation complexity \(O(d\varepsilon^{-2})\), without a further constituent-class constraint.
analysis: Claim and location. On p.3, Theorem 3.3(2), labeled an informal statement of Poggio et al. (2017), assigns a graph-mimicking deep network complexity O(d epsilon^-2) for a compositionally sparse function. Definition 3.1 requires only polynomially many constituents with constant fan-in. The paragraph following Corollary 3.4 expressly says that approximation imposes no further restriction on the node-function class. Corollary 3.4 is then derived by combining Theorems 3.2 and 3.3.

Source check. The cited 2017 paper specifies uniform approximation and derivative-bounded function classes. Its Theorem 2, printed p.5, assumes a binary-tree class with constituents in \(W_{m}^{2}\) and an infinitely differentiable, nonpolynomial activation; its rate is O((n-1) epsilon^(-2/m)). Its proof uses Lipschitz control. The arbitrary-DAG Theorem 3, p.6, still requires regularity classes for individual nodes and gives a sum of rates depending on their dimensions and smoothness. Its ReLU discussion also retains regularity assumptions. None of these statements establishes a fan-in-only theorem for arbitrary real node functions.

Exact scope of the refutation. The target omits a norm and activation class. The following counterexample uses the uniform norm and continuous activations of the cited approximation setting; it also applies to ReLU networks. Under this natural source-based interpretation the unrestricted statement is false. Choosing a different norm or a discontinuous activation class requires a newly specified theorem and proof.

\[X=[-1,1],\quad d=2^k\geq128,\qquad
f_d(x)=\mathbf{1}\!\left\{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_i\geq0\right\}.\] Build a complete binary tree with constituent A(u,v)=(u+v)/2, then append h(t)=1{t>=0}. The averaging tree computes the mean using d-1 binary nodes; the final threshold is unary. This construction depends on every coordinate and avoids any need to interpret unused input slots.
Original hypothesis | Counterexample check
Function X^d -> X | The output is 0 or 1, both in X.
At most O(poly d) constituents | There are exactly d nodes: d-1 averages and one threshold.
Small constant fan-in c | Every node has fan-in at most 2, independently of d.
Node outputs remain in X | Averages of members of [-1,1] remain in [-1,1]; threshold outputs also belong to X.
No extra node-class restriction | Definition 3.1 and the explicit p.3 explanation admit this threshold constituent.
Network interpretation used | Every finite feedforward network with continuous activations computes a continuous function q.
Proof. Let a=q(0). For x^(j)=(-1/j,0,...,0), the target is zero and x^(j) tends to zero. Continuity gives q(x^(j))->a, whereas \(f_d\)(0)=1. Therefore the supremum error obeys:

\[\|q-f_d\|_{\infty}\geq
\max\{|a|,|1-a|\}\geq\frac12,
\qquad 1\leq |a|+|1-a|.\] The constant function q=1/2 attains the lower bound, so the obstruction is exact. Taking epsilon=1/4 contradicts the claimed availability of a finite O(16d)-parameter approximation: no finite continuous-activation network achieves that uniform error, irrespective of size. The proof is analytic. Reviewer-written rational spot checks are supporting arithmetic checks, not substitutes for the limiting argument.

Dependency and severity. This is a substantial invalid derivation in the paper’s central link from compositional structure to approximation complexity, expressly used to obtain Corollary 3.4. That direct dependency warrants Major. The result does not require showing that the entire research agenda fails or that every restricted theorem is false. The position-paper label and informal presentation do not remove the explicit scope mismatch.

Strongest alternative readings. Restricting the claim to the original regular node classes restores a meaningful restricted theorem, but changes the target’s definition-to-theorem implication and its express fan-in-only assertion. A distribution-dependent Lp approximation can behave differently for this discontinuity and is not refuted by this example; it is also not the uniform theorem cited. Threshold activations can represent the example exactly, but require a different network class and an independently justified general rate.

Limits. The threshold function is not claimed to be polynomial-time computable under a Type-2 real-number representation. Thus this example directly refutes the unrestricted Theorem 3.3 reading, not every possible formalization of the real-valued Corollary 3.4. The invalid displayed derivation and a separately false conclusion are distinct claims.
result: Substantial invalid central structure-to-approximation derivation used explicitly forCor3.4. No assertion counterexample is Type2 polynomial-time computable. Not a direct refutation of all formalized real-FP versions ofCor3.4.

analysis: Claim and location. Section 4.2, p.5, attributes avoidance of weight-space permutation symmetries to CNN translational equivariance and links that mechanism to a simpler optimization landscape. Standard convolutional networks retain permutations of hidden channels.

Counterexample with actual parameters. At every spatial site z, let a hidden 1x1 convolution have two kernels K=(1,2), zero biases and ReLU activations. Follow it with a linear 1x1 convolution with channel weights L=(3,5). Simultaneously swap the hidden channels and their corresponding output weights, giving K’=(2,1), L’=(5,3). Then:

\[F(z)=3R(z)+5R(2z)=13R(z)
=5R(2z)+3R(z)=F'(z),\qquad z\in\mathbb{R}.\] The parameter vectors are distinct, all operations remain convolutional, and applying the same rule at each location preserves translation equivariance on a periodic or unrestricted spatial domain. The equality is an algebraic identity, not merely an equality on test examples. Independent reviewer checks used a second choice of kernels and biases and confirmed the same phenomenon.

The weaker interpretation that weight sharing restricts arbitrary permutations of individual spatial units is reasonable. It does not eliminate hidden-channel permutations. A correction should identify which symmetries are restricted, retain the channel symmetry, and qualify any optimization advantage rather than infer it from complete symmetry removal.

Severity is Minor because this is a bounded architectural/optimization explanation, with no demonstrated failure of the Boolean circuit result or additional failure of the main approximation bridge. Ease of correction and the paper’s genre are not the grading basis.
claim: CNNs avoid parameter permutation symmetries through translation equivariance.
result: False local architecture/optimization mechanism;no demonstrated additional central-theorem failure.

analysis: Source claim and suspect step. Algorithm 1 (p.5) and Appendix C (pp.14-15, after Eq.16) define the loss estimator rhat, gain estimate rtilde=1-rhat, m=sum over Ut of \(x_a\) rhat_a, and rbar=1+m. The proof replaces the squared centered gain by a weighted second moment minus \(m^{2}\). With Ut equal to all arms and sum x=1, the supplied definitions instead give a plus 3m^2 term. The next asserted variance bound therefore does not follow. [R1, R4]

Complete feasible-target check. Use K=2, S=1, T=50, epsilon=1/(KT)=0.01, x=(0.99,0.01), rewards (0,0), and graph edges 1->2 and 2->1 with no self-loops. Each vertex receives an edge from every other vertex, so the graph is strongly observable and alpha=1. The target lies in the truncated simplex. Singleton sampling has the required means and automatic negative pairwise correlation. Ut contains both arms because both possible loss estimates are at most 100, its threshold.

Selecting arm 2, with probability 0.01, yields rhat=(100,0), m=99, rbar=100 and centered gains (-199,-99). The actual squared sum is 39303; the claimed variance expression is 99. Selecting arm 1, with probability 0.99, yields rhat=(0,100/99), m=1/99; the corresponding values are 103/9801 and 1/99. Exact averaging gives 38911/99 versus 1, as displayed below.

Precise consequence. This refutes a universally asserted algebraic/conditional step in the proof. Reachability of this exact target from the specified initialization within 50 rounds has not been established. The all-zero reward example has zero actual regret. Consequently this is not presented as a counterexample to OSMD-G’s numerical regret rate.

Core dependency and judgment. Theorem 3.2 explicitly includes S=1 and delegates that case to Appendix C; Theorem 1.1 inherits its all-S guarantee. The variance reduction is an essential step in the supplied proof, so a substantial invalid derivation closely tied to the core upper guarantee supports Major even without an algorithmic regret counterexample.

Alternative reading and repair limit. Changing rbar to 1-m repairs this square expansion locally. A common shift cancels from the projected exponential-weights decision, but the subsequent exponential-moment inequalities still require valid step-size/gain conditions. Centered positive gains can be of order 1/epsilon. A sign replacement alone is therefore not certified as a complete proof repair. The same definitions and false transformation persist in v7 Appendix C, pp.14-16. Evidence: upper_bound_audit.json and exact Fraction calculations in upper_bound_checks.py/results.

\[\sum_a x_a(\widetilde r_a-\bar r)^{2}=\sum_a x_a(\widehat r_a+m)^{2}=\sum_a x_a\widehat r_a^{2}+3m^{2}\ne\sum_a x_a\widehat r_a^{2}-m^2.\] \[\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_a x_a(\widetilde r_a-\bar r)^{2}\right]=\frac{38911}{99}\approx393.0404,\qquad \mathbb E\!\left[\sum_a x_a(1-x_a)\widehat r_a^{2}\right]=1.\]

claim: Any subset and uniform \(T\ge\max(S,\alpha^{3}/S)\), S<=K/2 gives \(\Omega(S\sqrt{T\log(K/S)}+\sqrt{\alpha S T})\).
analysis: Source claim. Theorem 1.3, p.3, states the following bound for any decision subset A0 contained in A, any strongly observable graph, T >= max{S, alpha^3/S}, and S <= K/2. Appendix A, p.12, imports the logarithmic full-information term. [R1, R3]

Subset counterexample. Set K=2, S=1, alpha=1, T any integer at least one, use a complete directed graph with all self-loops, and A0={(1,0)}. The graph is strongly observable; S=K/2 and the horizon condition holds. The learner and comparator are identical on every reward sequence, so the minimax regret is exactly zero. The displayed positive lower bound cannot hold.

Counterevidence to the breadth of that first objection: Section 1.2 and the contribution list explicitly focus on the full set. Restricting the theorem to A0=A removes the singleton example. It does not remove the next example.

Full-set counterexample. For every integer n >= 2, take T=n, S=1, K=2^(\(n^{2}\)), A0=A, and the complete self-loop graph with alpha=1. All printed conditions hold. For every reward sequence the comparator receives at most n and the learner at least zero, so R* <= n. The claimed scale is sqrt(log 2) n^(3/2) + sqrt(n), and n divided by this scale tends to zero. No positive uniform Omega constant can satisfy the stated result.

The correct order on this family is Theta(n), not just an unknown quantity below the claimed expression. Give every arm independent Bernoulli(1/2) rewards across all n rounds. Any learner’s expected reward is n/2. The probability that at least one arm has all n rewards equal to one is at least 1-exp(-2^(\(n^{2}\)-n)), which is at least 1-exp(-4). Thus the expected hindsight reward is at least n(1-exp(-4)). This randomized oblivious construction supplies a lower bound on the worst-case regret by averaging, and the deterministic upper bound supplies the other direction.

Impact and alternatives. Theorem 1.3 supplies the lower-bound half of the paper’s minimax characterization; its explicit full-set parameter guarantee is materially false. This supports Major under the user’s standard. The new graph-dependent sqrt(alpha S T) term is not refuted, nor is the intended sufficiently-long-horizon rate with logarithms suppressed. If Omega meant only fixed K,S,G followed by T tending to infinity, the growing-K family would not challenge that weaker assertion; the stated parameter conditions do not express that restriction.

\[R^*=\Omega\!\left(S\sqrt{T\log(K/\allowbreak{}S)}+\sqrt{\alpha ST}\right).\] \[\left(\tfrac12-e^{-4}\right)n\ \le R^*\le n,\qquad \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log2}\,n^{3/\allowbreak{}2}+\sqrt n}\longrightarrow0.\]
result: Novel graph-dependent term and intended long-horizon scale not refuted.

analysis: Local truncation derivation — Major; scoped correction verified. The S>=2 proof on p.6 explicitly uses the chain (v-v_epsilon) transpose r <= the L1 distance <= K epsilon to obtain Eq.(7). The latter is feasible, has total mass two, and minimizes L1 distance: the three unselected coordinates must receive at least 0.3 total mass, so the selected coordinates must lose at least 0.3. analysis: Source claim. Section 5.1 (p.9) advertises a stochastic elimination algorithm for general decision subsets. Algorithm 3 and Theorem D.1 (pp.16-17) claim an Otilde(S alpha + S sqrt(log(KT/epsilon) alpha T)) guarantee. The proof bounds each minimum-count phase by 50 log(K)(1+log(K)) alpha using greedy domination. [R1, R5]

Suspect step. AN contains active decisions whose minimum constituent-arm observation count is N. Ut is the union of all arms in these decisions. A well-observed arm stays in Ut if it shares a decision with an unobserved arm. Thus the algorithm’s repeated maximum-outdegree choice does not implement a greedy cover that removes already covered vertices.

Parameters and graph. For any integer m >= 2, set S=2, T=m, K=3m+2, A0=A (all pairs), and epsilon=1/4. There is one hub h, a set H={H0,...,H(2m)} of size 2m+1, and L={L1,...,Lm}. Every vertex has a self-loop. Direct h to every H and every L to h. On H use the regular tournament Hi->Hj iff (j-i) modulo (2m+1) belongs to {1,...,m}. On L direct Li->Lj iff i<j. Choose a fixed m-element set Hminus; every L points to Hminus, and all remaining m+1 vertices Hplus point to every L.

All graph assumptions hold. Every distinct pair has exactly one directed edge, hence alpha=1. Self-loops imply strong observability. Including self-loops, h has outdegree 2m+2; Hminus has m+1, Hplus has 2m+1, and Li has 2m+2-i. Therefore h is the unique maximum-outdegree vertex.

Permitted execution. Choose the pairs {h,Lm}, {h,L(m-1)}, ..., {h,L1}. This is allowed by Algorithm 3’s instruction to pull any decision in AN containing the chosen arm. Before each of these rounds at least one L remains unobserved, and N=0. Any other vertex can pair with an unobserved L; that L itself pairs with h. Therefore Ut is the entire graph. The uniquely selected hub remains h. At the round using Li, h reveals H, while Li reveals itself, h, Hminus and Lj for j>i. Those larger-index L vertices have already been observed. Exactly one new L is revealed each round.

By induction the phase lasts m rounds. Elimination is triggered only once every least-observed decision exceeds N, so none occurs before round m. Elimination after that round cannot change the incurred regret. The example does not depend on a tie in the maximum-outdegree arm; only the expressly permitted companion-decision choice is used.

Rewards and exact regret. Every L has deterministic reward one; h and H have deterministic reward zero. These degenerate stationary distributions are in [0,1] and i.i.d. over time. Every pulled pair earns one; a fixed pair of distinct L vertices earns two every round. All available concentration events hold exactly. The regret is therefore deterministically T=m.

Contradiction. With fixed S=2, alpha=1, epsilon=1/4 and K=3T+2, the claimed bound is Otilde(sqrt(T)); fixed powers of logarithms in K,T cannot absorb linear regret. The explicit phase bound also fails finitely: at m=20000, K=60002, its proposed bound is about 6602.4534 while the phase lasts 20000 rounds. The large comparison evaluates the formula, not a huge simulated graph.

Counterevidence, impact and repair. Different companion choices can cover L much faster. The result falsifies the guarantee for Algorithm 3 as specified, which permits the displayed execution; it does not prove all elimination variants fail. Section 5.1 explicitly claims this extension, so its appendix location does not make the failed algorithmic guarantee peripheral. Judgment: Major. No revised exploration/companion rule or regret proof is certified. The main full-set OSMD-G algorithm is a different algorithm and is not falsified by this construction.

Independent reviewer code checked m=2,3,5,10,20, including graph orientation, self-loops, unique hub, legal actions, full Ut, new observations and exact regret. The all-m induction supplies the general argument. Targeted comparison confirms the same rules, theorem and phase bound in v7 Algorithm 3 p.16 and proof p.17. Evidence: capacity_audit.json, capacity_counterexample.py/results.json, capacity_v7_comparison.json.
\[T_0=m,\qquad R_T=\sum_{t=1}^{m}(2-1)=m=T,\qquad \alpha=1,\quad K=3T+2.\]

result: Main OSMD-G existence bound not attacked.

analysis: Adaptive-hindsight inference — Major; numerical rate not falsified. Page 1 explicitly allows rewards to depend on the learner’s past decisions, and Eq.(1) places the hindsight maximum inside expectation. Theorem 3.2’s proof fixes a comparator before Eq.(7), applies fixed-comparator unbiasedness in Eq.(8), and concludes the adaptive-hindsight bound on p.7. That conclusion does not follow from the fixed-comparator calculation. The issue affects the stated adaptive upper guarantee and its inheritance by Theorem 1.1; it is not resolved by the correctness of the variance calculation.

Take K=2, S=1, T=2, the full singleton action set, and the graph with both self-loops and no cross edges (strongly observable, alpha=2). Use the prescribed truncation epsilon=1/(KT)=1/4 and entropy initialization x=(1/2,1/2); the first action A1 is therefore uniform. Let r1=(0,0) and r2=e(A1). These rewards lie in [0,1] and the second vector depends only on the past action, not the current one. The unique best fixed arm in hindsight is A1. Its first-round gain estimate from Eqs.(3)-(4) is -1 although its true reward is zero. In fact the first-round true comparator-regret term is zero, whereas the estimated term against the conditional mean action is -1. The common centering shift cancels because both decisions have unit mass. Thus the required fixed-to-random comparator substitution fails in a permitted execution.

Evidence and scope. The exact two-round estimator result is reused from upper_bound_check_results.json; no unchanged arithmetic was rerun. This is a demonstrated invalid inference in the core adaptive-regret derivation, so the severity is Major under the saved calibration criterion. It does not establish that the numerical regret rate is false. Oblivious deterministic sequences and a fixed comparator avoid this particular obstruction; a valid uniform or martingale analysis could restore the adaptive guarantee, but none is verified here. The correction must either supply that argument or explicitly restrict the proved claim’s comparator/adversary scope.
claim: An expected bound established for each comparator fixed before estimator averaging is concluded as an E[max] hindsight bound against nonanticipating adaptive rewards. Rewards in [0,1]; r2 depends only on the past action. Graph strongly observable by self-loops; full decision set valid. Theorem 3.2 imposes no lower-bound-theorem horizon restriction on this example. Prescribed truncation feasible and entropy minimizer gives uniform first-round action. The comparator is the best fixed arm on the realized reward sequence, as Eq.(1) specifies.
result: Major for an invalid core inference under the saved calibration criterion, not for a claimed numerical-rate contradiction. The inspected S>=2 variance identity and its fixed-comparator scope; no claim that the numerical adaptive rate is false.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: For column updates, use \(\widehat\delta=M^\top(MM^\top)^{-1}M\delta\) when all clusters are nonempty. For row updates, use \(\delta M^\top(MM^\top)^{-1}M\). Replace the inverse by the Moore–Penrose inverse if empty clusters are allowed.

claim:
For a row \(w\in\mathbb R^{1\times c}\), the paper defines \(S\in\mathbb R^{c\times k}\), a one-hot reconstruction matrix \(M\in\{0,1\}^{k\times c}\), and \[z=wS,\qquad \widehat w=zM.\] With a positive definite Hessian \(H\), let \(q_i=(1/(H^{-1})_{ii})^s>0\), where the experimental choice is \(s=3\). Equation (4) minimizes \[
 J(z)=\sum_{i=1}^c q_i\bigl(\operatorname{RTN}(w_i,z)-w_i\bigr)^{2} .\] For fixed nonempty clusters \(C_j=\{i:a_i=j\}\), their weighted least-squares centers are \[
 z_j^*=\frac{\sum_{i\in C_j}q_iw_i}{\sum_{i\in C_j}q_i}.\] The distinction between a scalar center \(z_j\) and the entries of a matrix \(S\) that subsequently multiplies \(w\) is essential.

The gradient in equation (6) is consistent with differentiation through a fixed \(M\). Likewise, the static forward/backward structure in `tailor_utils.py`, lines 13–36, reconstructs a weight matrix and sums weight gradients into shared parameters. This observation does not verify the CUDA kernels, their numerical accuracy, or the provenance of the initial quantization grids.
Appendix B equation (10) provides optimal update projection through \(M\)\((M^\top M)^{-1}\) \(M^\top\).
\(M\) is \(k\) by \(c\) as explicitly defined. \(k<c\), nonempty clusters for ordinary inverse of \(MM^\top\).
analysis: Appendix B, page 14, equation (10), gives the purported optimal update approximation as \[\widehat\delta=M(M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top\delta .\] The paper declares \(M\) to be \(k\times c\) with \(k<c\). Consequently, \(M^\top M\) is \(c\times c\) and has rank at most \(k<c\); its ordinary inverse does not exist. The displayed left factor \(M(M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top\), even if an inverse were possible, would be \(k\times k\), whereas an update in the original row has \(c\) coordinates. A row-versus-column convention alone cannot remove both errors.

For the explicit nonempty assignment matrix with rows \((1,1,0,0)\) and \((0,0,1,1)\), \(M^\top M\) has rank 2 and \(MM^\top=2I_2\). A column update \(\delta=(1,3,2,6)^\top\) projects onto the reconstruction subspace as \((2,2,4,4)^\top\), with residual squared norm \(10\). The independent calculation records these values.

result: The familiar formula in the paper would be valid if its \(M\) meant the transposed design matrix, rather than the explicitly defined reconstruction matrix. analysis: Take \(c=128\), \(k=4\), one group per row, \(s=3\), and \(X=I_{128}/\sqrt2\). Then \(H=2XX^\top=I_{128}\) is positive definite and all \(q_i=1\). Let \(w\) consist of 32 copies each of \(1,2,3,4\), with \(C_j\) containing the copies of \(j\). Every cluster is nonempty, the centers \(z^*=(1,2,3,4)\) are a global minimizer of the displayed formula, and the minimum is zero because every weight equals a center.

Under the literal denominator \(\sum_{l=1}^{128}q_l=128\), equation the displayed formula instead yields \[wS=(1/4,1,9/4,4).\] Keeping the original cluster assignments gives a squared error of \[32\{(1-1/4)^{2}+(2-1)^{2}+(3-9/4)^{2}+(4-4)^{2}\}=68.\] Allowing the round-to-nearest reassignment actually specified in the displayed formula does not fix the discrepancy: \(1\) maps to \(1\), \(2\) and \(3\) map to \(9/4\), and \(4\) maps to \(4\). Thus \[J(wS)=32\{0+(1/4)^{2}+(3/4)^{2}+0\}=20>0.\] If the denominator is read charitably as \(\sum_{l\in C_j}q_l=32\), the resulting centers are \((1,4,9,16)\) and \(J(wS)=64>0\). The extra factor of \(w_i\) therefore causes failure under either interpretation.

claim:
For a row \(w\in\mathbb R^{1\times c}\), the paper defines \(S\in\mathbb R^{c\times k}\), a one-hot reconstruction matrix \(M\in\{0,1\}^{k\times c}\), and \[z=wS,\qquad \widehat w=zM.\] With a positive definite Hessian \(H\), let \(q_i=(1/(H^{-1})_{ii})^s>0\), where the experimental choice is \(s=3\). Equation (4) minimizes \[
 J(z)=\sum_{i=1}^c q_i\bigl(\operatorname{RTN}(w_i,z)-w_i\bigr)^{2} .\] For fixed nonempty clusters \(C_j=\{i:a_i=j\}\), their weighted least-squares centers are \[
 z_j^*=\frac{\sum_{i\in C_j}q_iw_i}{\sum_{i\in C_j}q_i}.\] The distinction between a scalar center \(z_j\) and the entries of a matrix \(S\) that subsequently multiplies \(w\) is essential.

The gradient in equation (6) is consistent with differentiation through a fixed \(M\).  S_{ij}=\frac{q_iw_i}{\sum_lq_l},\] and zero otherwise. The surrounding text says that weighted \(k\)-means produces the sketched parameters and that these parameters are obtained as \(wS\). Algorithm 1 repeats both the entry formula (line 3) and multiplication (line 13) on page 5. The same dimensions are stated in Table 5, page 14.

\(c=128\), \(k=4\), GPR=1, block size 128, \(s=3\). \(H=I\) from \(X=I/\sqrt{2}\); all weights \(q_i=1\). 32 copies each of 1,2,3,4; four nonempty clusters.

analysis: Assessment: Major; failure of the core reweighting mechanism.

Let \(n=m=8\), with matching weight one for every target statement. In \(\mathbb R^{2}\), give conjecture \(j\) the unit embedding \[x_j=\left(-\frac{j}{10},\sqrt{1-\frac{j^{2}}{100}}\right),\quad 1\le j\le8,\] and give each of the eight target statement identifiers the unit embedding \(y_i=(1,0)\). The statements may be distinct while their embeddings agree; injectivity is not an assumption of the algorithm. All norms are one and all costs are finite, with \[d(x_j,y_i)=-\langle x_j,y_i\rangle=j/10.\] The weight increment \(n/m\) is exactly one.
Claim 1.  Algorithm 4 returns weights \((8,0,0,0,0,0,0,0)\) on this input, including four assignments to the first conjecture after its mask has become zero.

Proof. Initially the unique minimum cost is \(1/10\), so the first four targets are assigned to \(x_1\). The fourth assignment makes \(nP(x_1)=4>3\) and sets \(M(x_1)=0\). Thereafter its masked cost is zero, whereas all other masked costs remain at least \(2/10\). It is therefore the unique minimum at every remaining step. Its final weight is eight. ◻

This is failure of the masking mechanism, rather than merely a one-increment overshoot caused by the strict threshold. For arbitrary larger \(n=m\), replacing \(j/10\) by \(j/(n+1)\) yields the analogous concentration on one item.

At the pinned commit, `RL/utils/RL_utils.py`, lines 607–638, normalizes embeddings and selects the largest values of `similarity * mask`. It sets the mask to zero once a weight is at least three. The reviewer independently translated this scalar rule; it has the same output on the construction, setting the mask after the third assignment instead of the fourth. The code uses total matching mass rather than \(m\) when target weights differ; that difference disappears in the weight-one example. The source was read, not executed.

If every unmasked candidate has positive cosine similarity, a zero mask ranks below those candidates. This is a valid favorable regime, but it is not a general property of normalized or mean-pooled embeddings. No sign statistics or training artifacts were acquired to determine whether the counterexample’s regime occurred historically. Therefore no benchmark reduction or training instability is claimed.
claim: Appendix A.5, pp. 16–18, defines matching cost as negative cosine similarity. The discussion after the unconstrained solution says that the practical method limits overly large conjecture weights to avoid unstable weighted training. Algorithm 4, p. 18, line 6 selects the smallest values of \(d(x,y)M(x)\); lines 9–10 set \(M(x)=0\) when \(nP(x)>3\). The source page was rendered and inspected. No restriction to nonnegative cosine similarities is stated.
\(n=m=8\); matching weights all1. \(x_j=(-j/10,\sqrt{1-j^{2}/100})\), \(y_i=(1,0)\), unit embeddings. No injectivity or positive-cosine assumption.
result: Printed and independently translated release rule both return[8,0,0,0,0,0,0,0]; masked item continues to win. The concentration-control component of the central reweighting routine can leave all matching mass on one conjecture and continue selecting it after masking. No historical instability or benchmark damage; no invalid unconstrained transport theorem.

claim: The sampling and symmetrization proof must control the error caused by the stated approximate normalizer, rather than treating a fixed relative normalizer error as a vanishing centered sampling term. Exact valid score oracle; sample count <=m; rank-three family {0,i,j}; all unit weights; \(z=4/(n-2)\); normalizer ratio 21/20 permitted by 0.1 interface; \(\varepsilon=1/100\); sufficiently large n.
analysis: Problem 2 (Constant normalizer error survives sampling and invalidates the symmetrization — Major).

Algorithm 2, line 4 (p. 7), calls SumEstimate with accuracy \(0.1\), while line 8 uses the returned sum in the output weights. Appendix C, pp. 17–19, explicitly retains this fixed accuracy and claims an arbitrarily small \(\varepsilon\)-error after choosing a sufficiently large sample size. The equality introducing Rademacher signs in the uncentered second term on p. 18 is invalid.

Grant an exact valid score oracle, so this finding is independent of Problem 1. Put \(s=\sum_e z_e\), \(p_e=z_e/s\), and let \(\widehat s=(1+\delta)s\). Conditional on this normalizer, the returned energy is \[\widehat Q(x)=\frac1M\sum_{t=1}^M
       \frac{\widehat s\,w_{e_t}}{z_{e_t}}Q_{e_t}(x),
 \qquad \mathbb E[\widehat Q(x)\mid\widehat s]=(1+\delta)Q_H(x).\] Jensen’s inequality already gives \(\mathbb E|\widehat Q(x)-Q_H(x)|\ge|\delta|Q_H(x)\). Increasing \(M\) cannot remove this bias.

A family makes the failure deterministic conditional on an allowed normalizer value. Let \[V=\{0,\ldots,n-1\},\quad
 E=\{\{0,i,j\}:1\le i<j\le n-1\},\quad w_e=1.\] Every hyperedge has rank three. Use the star centered at 0 with conductance \(1/2\) on each of its two edges. The resulting graph is a star whose leaf conductances are \((n-2)/2\). Hence each hyperedge has maximum resistance \(4/(n-2)\). Set \(z_e=4/(n-2)\), a valid overestimate with \[m=\binom{n-1}{2},\qquad s=2(n-1),\qquad p_e=1/m.\] For \(x_0=1\) and all other coordinates zero, every \(Q_e(x)=1\) and \(Q_H(x)=m\). Every possible sampled sequence yields \[\widehat Q(x)=\frac{\widehat s}{s}m.\] The normalizer \(\widehat s=21s/20\) satisfies the stated 10% accuracy guarantee but produces relative error \(1/20\), exceeding \(\varepsilon=1/100\) for every sample sequence. For any fixed hidden constant in \(M=\Theta(n\log n\log3/\varepsilon^{2})\), choose \(n\) sufficiently large that \(M\le\binom{n-1}{2}\); such an integer exists since \(n/\log n\to\infty\). Then the sampling primitive’s \(M\le m\) condition and the sparsification regime \(\varepsilon\ge\sqrt{n/m}\) are both met. No single-edge example outside that regime is needed.

On p. 18, the uncentered mean term is replaced by a Rademacher-signed sum. Those quantities do not have the same expectation: in the displayed family the former is a nonzero constant while the latter decreases with sample size. The preceding triangle-inequality coefficient also needs \(|s/\widehat s-1|\), rather than a signed coefficient.

A particular normalizer implementation could return a much more accurate value on a particular input. The result above disproves the claimed consequence of the stated \(0.1\) interface and the displayed proof, not a universal lower bound on all implementations.
result: The fixed normalizer tolerance does not justify an arbitrarily small final error through the displayed centered-sampling argument.

analysis: Problem 3 (The density conditions do not justify the advertised runtime simplification — Major).

Remark 4.2 (p. 7) drops \(r\sqrt{mnr}\) under \(\varepsilon\ge\sqrt{n/m}\) and \(m\ge nr\). The exact ratio of this term to \(r\sqrt{mn}/\varepsilon\) is \(\varepsilon\sqrt r\); density cancels. With rank growing polynomially, fixed \(\varepsilon\) and a sufficiently dense simple hypergraph, that ratio need not be polylogarithmic. For example, include all three-vertex hyperedges and the full vertex set, with \(n>3\). Then \(r=n\) and \(m=\binom n3+1=\Theta(n^{3})\); both stated inequalities hold for sufficiently large \(n\) and \(\varepsilon=1/2\). The ratio is \(\sqrt n/2\), which is not polylogarithmic in any of the stated parameters.

The abstract (p. 1) advertises the simplified bound as the main algorithmic runtime for rank \(r\), and Remark 4.2 supplies its stated justification. Thus the lost nonpolylogarithmic factor affects a core complexity claim and supports Major. The full two-term complexity in Theorem 4.1 and Table 1 is not contradicted by this arithmetic. Retain both terms in the advertised bound or explicitly restrict, for example, to \(\varepsilon\le1/\sqrt r\) (up to suppressed logarithms). The validity of the unsimplified bound and the availability of this local correction do not validate the stronger claim.

analysis: Problem 1 (Loss of hyperedge mass invalidates the leverage-score construction — Major).

Algorithm 1, lines 3–6 and 9 (p. 7), stores \(\widetilde G^{(t)}\) and passes that stored graph to WeightCompute and QOverestimate. Proposition B.5, equation (7) (p. 14), divides by \[\Delta_e=\sum_{g\in S_e}\widetilde c_{e,g}^{(t)}\widetilde R_g^{(t)}.\] Proposition B.7 (pp. 15–16) treats the averaged sparsified conductances as an underlying graph of \(H\) and telescopes ratios of successive sparsified conductances to establish domination.

Take \(n=201\) vertices. Include every two-vertex hyperedge with weight one, and one additional hyperedge \(e_0=\{1,2,3\}\) of weight \(d=1/100\). This is a simple weighted hypergraph of rank three with \(m=20101\). Choose vertex 1 as the center of the star for \(e_0\). WeightInitialize produces the multigraph \[L_G=L_{K_n}+\frac d2 L_{\{\{1,2\},\{1,3\}\}}.\] All required weights are nonnegative, and the groupwise sums equal the original hyperedge weights.

Consider the graph-sparsifier output \(\widetilde G=K_n\), retaining the unit edges with their original labels and removing the two edges labelled by \(e_0\). On \(\mathbf1^\perp\), \(L_{K_n}=nI\) and the star Laplacian has largest eigenvalue three. Consequently, \[0\preceq L_G-L_{\widetilde G}\preceq
 \frac{3d/2}{n+3d/2}L_G=\frac1{13401}L_G.\] This output is therefore a valid \(0.1\)-spectral sparsifier. The input has 20102 underlying edges, so \(0.1\ge\sqrt{201/20102}\), as required by the stated graph-sparsification interface. The output has 20100 edges, exactly \(n/(0.1)^{2}\), and meets its size requirement.

Nevertheless, both stored conductances for \(e_0\) vanish. Equation (7) is \(0/0\) for that hyperedge. Moreover, already with \(T=1\), QOverestimate returns \(z_{e_0}=0\) regardless of its positive prefactor. Its purported underlying graph has group mass zero instead of \(1/100\). If that graph is interpreted as \(K_n\), its effective resistance between any two distinct vertices is \(2/n\), and \[w_{e_0}R_{e_0}=\frac1{10050}>0=z_{e_0}.\] This is not an issue about floating-point accuracy.

There are two further manifestations of the same failed invariant. A spectral approximation preserves aggregate quadratic forms, not the sum of conductances with each hyperedge label. Also, WeightCompute defines the pre-sparsification next conductances \(c^{(t+1)}\); equality (b) on p. 16 substitutes the independently reweighted \(\widetilde c^{(t+1)}\) into the recurrence. The proposed telescoping identity does not follow.

The example is an admissible output of the stated graph-sparsifier interface; it is not a measurement of the distribution produced by a specific implementation of that primitive. That distinction does not rescue the proof: no group-preservation property is supplied, and a sparsifier with fewer edges than positive-weight hyperedges cannot retain a labelled edge from every group. Retaining the unsparsified conductances could change the construction, but would require a new query-cost and domination argument. No such repaired algorithm is verified here.

The demonstrated failure directly affects Theorem 3.4, which supplies the core overestimates for Theorem 4.1. This supports Major even without claiming that quantum hypergraph sparsification is impossible or that every execution fails.
claim: The leverage-score construction must preserve the relevant hyperedge mass when converting and sparsifying the auxiliary graph. \(n=201\); complete unit pair hyperedges plus {1,2,3} of weight 1/100; rank 3; alpha1=0.1; admissible graph sparsifier drops only two weak labelled star edges.
result: The auxiliary graph sparsifier can lose a hyperedge's mass, invalidating the stated domination and core leverage-score argument. This does not establish impossibility of quantum hypergraph sparsification or failure of every sparsifier execution.

analysis: Problem 4 (Proposition C.2 leaves a core chaining hypothesis unjustified — Major).

Proposition C.2 (p. 17) asserts \(Q_H(L_G^{+/2}x)\ge\|x\|^{2}\) for every \(x\perp\mathbf1\). For the graph with one unit edge \(\{1,2\}\) and isolated vertex 3, take \(x=(1,1,-2)\). This satisfies \(x\perp\mathbf1\) but lies in \(\ker L_G\), giving left side zero and right side six.

The proof establishes only \[Q_H(L_G^{+/2}x)\ge x^\top P_{\operatorname{range}L_G}x.\] Thus \(x\in(\ker L_G)^\perp\) is a sufficient corrected assumption. Even for a connected graph, the set \(T\) on p. 18 as literally defined contains arbitrary kernel directions and is not contained in the Euclidean unit ball. The proof on p. 19 explicitly invokes Proposition C.2 to assert \(T\subseteq B_2^n\), the hypothesis needed to apply Lemma C.1 in the proof of Theorem 4.1. This false statement and its invalid application therefore affect a core derivation and support Major. The range restriction verifies a local domain correction, not the remaining chaining argument. Disconnected inputs are allowed by the paper; connectivity must not be silently imposed.

analysis: Judgment: Major. Corollary 6.2 (p. 5), restated in Appendix \(B\) (p. 14), bounds the minimum expected squared gradient using only the deterministic initial objective gap and \(\Delta_F^*\). Its right-hand side has no independent jittering variance. Appendix \(B\) verifies gradient Lipschitzness but does not justify eliminating the variance of the additive stochastic gradient.

Take \(n=1\), \(A=1\), \(y=0\), \(r(u)=u^{2}/2\), so \(f(u)=u\), \(L=L_{\max}=1\), \(F(u)=u^{2}\), \(u^*=0\), and \(\Delta_F^*=0\). Choose \(K=128\) and the stipulated \(\eta=\sqrt{2/(LL_{\max}K)}=1/8\). Initialize \(u_0=\delta>0\), and take independent \(w_k\sim N(0,64\delta^{2})\), satisfying Assumption 6.1. All functions are smooth and bounded below, and the minimizer exists. Then \[u_{k+1}=\tfrac34u_k-\tfrac18w_{k+1},\qquad
 m_{k+1}=\tfrac9{16}m_k+\delta^{2},\quad m_0=\delta^{2},\] where \(m_k=\mathbb E u_k^{2}\). The moments increase to \(16\delta^{2}/7\); hence \[\min_{0\le k<128}\mathbb E|\nabla F(u_k)|^{2}=4\delta^2.\] The corollary’s right-hand side is instead \[\sqrt{2/128}\bigl(2(F(u_0)-\inf F)+0\bigr)=\delta^{2}/4.\] The violation factor is exactly sixteen. Choosing \(\delta=10^{-4}\) makes the noise standard deviation \(8\cdot10^{-4}\), so describing jittering as small does not remove the example.

This is a direct check of the paper’s asserted corollary, not an allegation about the cited source theorem in its own setting. That external theorem was not separately retrieved. A stationarity bound for an unbiased gradient normally requires a variance contribution or an appropriate structural noise condition. This report does not certify a replacement constant or convergence-to-argmin theorem. The corollary is used on pp. 4–5 to support the claimed preservation of the inverse mapping, making the dependency substantive.
claim: For denoising, \(y=x+z\), with \(z\sim N(0,\sigma_z^{2} I/n)\). The learned gradient is \(f_\theta=\nabla r_\theta\). The noisy iteration is \[u_{k+1}=(1-\eta)u_k+\eta y-\eta f_\theta(u_k)-\eta w_{k+1}.\] Assumption 6.1 specifies independent centered Gaussian \(w_k\); Assumption 7.2 requires twice differentiable \(f_\theta\). At inference jittering is removed. The risks compare the reconstruction to \(x+g\) (generalization) or \(x\) (robustness), with perturbed input \(y+g\) or \(y+e\). Thus these are specific perturbation risks, not a general finite-sample generalization bound.

There is a material distinction between the exact lower-level argmin/limit in Eqs. (5),(8) and the finite \(K\) iterations used by the proofs and implemented architectures. We state explicitly which interpretation each check addresses. The covariance failures hold in the displayed finite-trajectory proof itself. The independent convergence counterexample concerns the corollary exactly as stated.

analysis: Judgment: Major. Theorems 7.4 (p. 5) and 7.5 (p. 6) claim universal superiority over optimal MSE training under the stated assumptions. Appendix C, p. 15, deletes a covariance when expanding the noisy loss, citing zero-mean jittering. Appendix D, p. 16, similarly deletes a covariance between the attack and the network’s response to that attack. These are the steps used to identify the training objective with the purported risk penalties.

Take \(n=1\), \(A=1\), \(f_a(u)=au\), \(r_a(u)=au^{2}/2\), \(\eta=1/2\), and \(K=2\). Initialize both trajectories at \(y\), as in the proof; its auxiliary \(w_0\) is therefore zero. Let \(w_1,w_2\) be independent \(N(0,s^{2})\), independent of data. The learned gradient is smooth, conservative, and Lipschitz for any finite \(a\). The deterministic output is \(u'_2=c(a)y\), where \[c(a)=1-\frac{3a}{4}+\frac{a^{2}}{4}.\] Writing the final perturbation in the paper’s form \(B-N\) gives \[B=\frac a4w_1,\qquad N=\frac14w_1+\frac12w_2,\qquad
 \mathbb E[BN]=\frac{a s^{2}}{16}.\] Thus, independently of the clean reconstruction error, \[\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E(B-N)^{2}&=\left(\frac{(1-a)^{2}}{16}+\frac14\right)s^{2},\\
 \mathbb E B^{2}+\mathbb E N^{2}&=\left(\frac{1+a^{2}}{16}+\frac14\right)s^2.\end{aligned}\] The latter, used on p. 15, exceeds the correct expression by \(as^{2}/8\). Centering \(w_i\) does not make \(B\) independent of them. At \(a=1\) the true additional variance is \(s^{2}/4\), whereas the printed decomposition gives \(3s^{2}/8\).

For \(K=1\), the same scalar model gives \(H_a(y)=(1-\eta a)y\). In the paper’s notation the response term is \(B=-\eta a e\). With \(e\) independent of \((x,y)\) and variance \(t^{2}\), the actual perturbation contribution to robustness is \[(1-\eta a)^{2} t^2.\] The displayed expansion on p. 16 instead gives \((1+\eta^2a^{2})t^{2}\), omitting \(2\mathbb E[eB]=-2\eta a t^{2}\). At \(\eta=1/2,a=1\), the correct coefficient is \(1/4\), and the displayed coefficient is \(5/4\). Both identities fail for arbitrarily small positive noise.

The proof is not rescued merely by saying these are harmless terms. Consider the same \(K=2\) architecture with \(a\in[1,3/2]\), \(x=0\), \(z\sim N(0,s^{2})\), and independent \(w_1,w_2\sim N(0,s^{2})\). Let both \(g\) and \(e\) have variance \(5s^{2}/16\), independently. All noises can be made arbitrarily small by choosing \(s>0\) small. This is a linear neural gradient, with a unique strictly convex lower-level objective, twice differentiability, and independent Gaussian noises as required.

For the finite architecture, the MSE objective divided by \(s^{2}\) is \(c(a)^{2}\), uniquely minimized at \(a_{\rm mse}=3/2\), giving \(c=7/16\). The jittered training objective is exactly \[J(a)/s^{2}=c(a)^{2}+(a-1)^{2}/16+1/4.\] Its derivative is \((2a^{3}-9a^{2}+18a-13)/8\) and its second derivative is \(3(a^{2}-3a+3)/4>0\). The derivative is negative at \(1\) and positive at \(3/2\). Hence its unique minimizer lies strictly inside that interval: \[a_{\rm sgd}=1.3894887313\ldots,\qquad c(a_{\rm sgd})=0.4405531851\ldots>7/16.\] With \(q=5/16\), inference risks are \[G(a)/s^{2}=c(a)^{2}+q(1-c(a))^{2},\qquad R_e(a)/s^{2}=(1+q)c(a)^2.\] Both increase on the relevant interval of gains: the derivative of the first is \(2((1+q)c-q)>0\) for \(c\ge7/16\). Consequently both inequalities claimed by the theorems reverse:
Risk divided by \(s^{2}\) | MSE optimum | Jittered optimum

The final accumulated variance of \(N\) equals \(5s^{2}/16\), matching the chosen test variance. Matching this scalar variance does not identify the joint noisy trajectory with a shared input perturbation.
claim: For denoising, \(y=x+z\), with \(z\sim N(0,\sigma_z^{2} I/n)\). The learned gradient is \(f_\theta=\nabla r_\theta\). The noisy iteration is \[u_{k+1}=(1-\eta)u_k+\eta y-\eta f_\theta(u_k)-\eta w_{k+1}.\] Assumption 6.1 specifies independent centered Gaussian \(w_k\); Assumption 7.2 requires twice differentiable \(f_\theta\). At inference jittering is removed. The risks compare the reconstruction to \(x+g\) (generalization) or \(x\) (robustness), with perturbed input \(y+g\) or \(y+e\). Thus these are specific perturbation risks, not a general finite-sample generalization bound.

There is a material distinction between the exact lower-level argmin/limit in Eqs. (5),(8) and the finite \(K\) iterations used by the proofs and implemented architectures. We state explicitly which interpretation each check addresses. The covariance failures hold in the displayed finite-trajectory proof itself. The independent convergence counterexample concerns the corollary exactly as stated.
Theorems7.4-7.5 guarantee lower generalization and robustness risks than optimal MSE training.

\(n=1\),\(A=1\),\(f_a\)(u)=a*u, \(r_a=a*u^{2}/2\), smooth and conservative. Two-step architecture \(\eta=1/2\), initial \(y\); \(w_0=0\). Independent Gaussian observation, jittering and evaluation noises; all scales arbitrarily small. Parameter a in [1,3/2]; both optima exist uniquely. Finite-\(K\) interpretation explicitly separated from exact argmin.
result: The example is an exact two-step architecture, not a reconstruction of the paper’s ten-step empirical models. It directly addresses the finite-\(K\) interpretation adopted in Appendices C–D. If \(H_\theta\) is instead interpreted exclusively as the exact argmin, the two-step numerical comparison is not a counterexample to that different definition. The printed proof still contains the invalid finite-trajectory identities, and does not establish the proposed exact-argmin theorem. With constant nonzero Gaussian jittering, the noisy iterates generally do not even converge to a deterministic argmin; a fixed-step stationary distribution is a different object.

The last paragraph of Appendix D additionally restricts attention to models performing equally well on clean MSE, a condition absent from Theorem 7.5. Our finite comparison does not assert equality of their clean risks; it refutes the unrestricted finite-unrolling conclusion. Even adding that equality would not repair the missing covariance identities. Empirical improvements in Tables 1–5 remain evidence for the tested settings and are not disproved by this result.

The theoretical simultaneous-improvement guarantee is a core stated contribution. Invalidating its derivation warrants Major without demanding benchmark deterioration. A valid replacement would need controlled joint perturbation laws and explicit risk comparisons; none is claimed here.
Both displayed identities false; finite-unrolling universal comparisons false. Major for invalid central proof; no empirical result asserted false.

Supported impact: Major. Section 3.3, Equation (13), and Appendix E on p. 15 claim that the engineering forward rule achieves Equation (12) while preserving the normal forward value. Write \(\operatorname{sg}\) for a stop-gradient operation. The proposed contribution of an expert is \[
 \sqrt{\operatorname{sg}(g_i)}\,B_iA_i+
 \bigl(g_i-\sqrt{\operatorname{sg}(g_i)}\bigr)
          \operatorname{sg}(B_i)\operatorname{sg}(A_i).\] Numerically this equals \(g_iB_iA_i\). Its autodifferentiation rule with respect to \(A_i,B_i\), however, uses \(\sqrt{g_i}\), not \(g_i\). After Equation (6), the factor increments are therefore \[\Delta A_i=\sqrt{g_i}(B_i^TB_i)^{-1}B_i^TG,\qquad
 \Delta B_i=\sqrt{g_i}GA_i^T(A_iA_i^T)^{-1}.\]

Appendix E’s first line substitutes updated \(A_i,B_i\) only into the first term of [stop] (#stop), leaving the detached product at its old value. This is a local surrogate with frozen numerical constants. It is not the output of Algorithm 1 evaluated after an optimizer step. In that algorithm, `exp_out.detach()` is recomputed from the current `exp_out` on every forward pass. Consequently the next numerical value, with gates fixed as assumed in the paper’s derivation, is \[W+\sum_i g_i(B_i-\eta\Delta B_i)(A_i-\eta\Delta A_i).\] Its correct first-order expansion is \[
 X_{\rm new}=X-\eta\sum_i g_i^{3/2}(P_iG+GQ_i)+O(\eta^{2}),\] not [target] (#target). The error is first order in the step size and survives the paper’s deliberate omission of second-order terms.

The released `moe_lora.py`, lines 97–108, computes the same rule with cloned, detached values on each call. The alternate branch at lines 123–133 does likewise. The released `custom_optimizer.py`, lines 165–208, supplies the simultaneous preconditioned SGD updates. Static inspection therefore corroborates the recomputation semantics, without executing either program.

Let \(d=2,r=1,N_{\rm Expert}=2\), with both experts active, \[A_1=A_2=(1,0),\quad B_1=B_2=(1,0)^T,\quad
 g_1=g_2=\tfrac12,\quad W=0,\quad
 \mathcal L(X)=\tfrac12\|X\|_F^2.\] Thus \(X=G=P=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\) and all four Gram matrices are the scalar one. Gates are positive and normalized; equal softmax logits realize them. Identical expert outputs give zero gradient to those gate logits, so holding them fixed is also consistent with their actual update in this example. The example uses the deterministic algebra of Section 3 and Appendix E, not an assumption about a stochastic benchmark training trajectory.

For each factor, the engineering update multiplies its nonzero entry by \(1-\eta/\sqrt2\). Re-evaluating the ordinary numerical forward gives exactly \[
 X_{\rm engineering}
   =\left(1-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt2}\right)^2P
   =\left(1-\sqrt2\eta+\frac{\eta^{2}}{2}\right)P.\] Equation (11), by contrast, gives \((1-\eta)^2P\), whose first-order coefficient is \(2\). Freezing the detached old products as in Appendix E gives the different surrogate \[\left[\sqrt2\left(1-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt2}\right)^{2}+1-\sqrt2\right]P
 =\left(1-2\eta+\frac{\eta^{2}}{\sqrt2}\right)P.\] At \(\eta=10^{-4}\), the actual engineering value has coefficient \(0.9998585836437626\) on \(P\), while Equation (11)’s value is \(0.9998000100000001\). Reviewer-written symbolic expansion and finite arithmetic verified these formulas and the limit of the engineering descent coefficient, \(\sqrt2\), as \(\eta\to0\). The script and outputs are in and its JSON/stdout companions.

analysis: Supported impact: Major for the central theoretical justification. Section 3.2, p. 5, asserts that Equation (12) further approaches global full fine-tuning. The preceding argument, p. 4, uses the sum-of-squares inequality for the gates to diagnose underestimation. That scalar inequality does not compare the matrix update with \(G\), because each term is a sum of overlapping projections.

In the same admissible example, \(P_i=Q_i=P=G\). The three first-order descent directions are \[D_{\rm ordinary}=G,\qquad
 D_{\rm Eq.(12)}=2G,\qquad
 D_{\rm engineering}=\sqrt2\,G .\] Full fine-tuning at the same learning rate uses \(D_{\rm FFT}=G\). Since \(\|G\|_F=1\), the corresponding errors are
Update | Descent coefficient on \(G | \|D-G\|_F\)
Ordinary preconditioned MoE | \(1 | 0\)
Proposed ideal Equation (12) | \(2 | 1\)
Actual engineering implementation | \(\sqrt2 | \sqrt2-1\)

Thus the proposed ideal rescaling moves an already exact first-order full-gradient update away from that gradient. For completeness, the ordinary finite update is \((1-\eta/2)^2P\), while full fine-tuning gives \((1-\eta)P\); their discrepancy is \(O(\eta^{2})\). The proposed changes instead have nonzero first-order discrepancies.

There is no assumption in the relevant argument that the experts’ subspaces or the row/column projections are disjoint. The two projection terms count their shared component twice. Even a normalized weighted average of these sums is not thereby an orthogonal projection or an unbiased approximation to \(G\). This invalidates the stated inference from gate normalization to systematically better full-gradient approximation.

The scope matters. The prose can be read as a qualitative heuristic about common training configurations rather than a quantified theorem. The example does not disprove such an empirical tendency. It does show that the mathematical reasons offered for the central closeness claim do not establish it under the stated conditions. Retuning the learning rate can match this one direction; that would change the comparison and does not verify a general claim with heterogeneous subspaces or token-dependent gates. The theory therefore needs a specified metric, conditions, and a valid argument. The Major assessment concerns this core justification, not an assertion that the method must train poorly.
