claim: Sections 1, 4.2 and 4.3 interpret smaller-patch gains as recovery of irreversibly compressed visual information. The introduction says patchification often loses information, rather than asserting that every patch projection does. A patch has \(3p^{2}\) scalar coordinates and embedding \(z=Wx+b\in\mathbb R^D\). For the reversible construction take \(D\ge3p^{2}\), full-column-rank \(W\), and, in the square example, \(p=16,D=768,W=I,b=0\).
fields.source_location: Sections 1, 4.2 and 4.3; Table 7, PDF p. 12; models_mamba.py, lines 32–55 and base configuration lines 293–295
analysis: Sections 1, 4.2 and 4.3 repeatedly interpret smaller-patch gains as recovery of visual information irreversibly compressed by patchification. For the base models used in central experiments, patchification need not lose any input information.

A patch has \(3p^{2}\) scalar coordinates and its embedding is \(z=Wx+b\in\mathbb R^D\). If \(D\geq3p^{2}\) and \(W\) has full column rank, a left inverse recovers \(x\). For \(p=16,D=768\), the base-model projection is square. With \(W=I\), patch flattening and rearrangement are exactly invertible. At \(224\times224\), \(196\cdot768=224\cdot224\cdot3=150{,}528\): fewer spatial positions do not imply fewer scalar coordinates. For \(p\leq8\) the same \(D\) is already an expansion. An independently constructed integer image was patchified at \(p=16\) and reconstructed exactly with zero error. The inspected code’s patch layer is a strided convolution followed by flattening, with identity normalization, so this counterexample lies within the described layer class.

The introduction qualifies its claim as patchification “often” incurring irreversible loss; it does not state that every patch projection destroys information. The invertible construction therefore does not refute that empirical claim or establish that the trained embeddings are lossless. It rejects only a deduction of necessary information destruction from fewer spatial tokens. Accordingly, this item is Needs Evidence, not a demonstrated error in the actual learned representations.

This does not prove that the trained matrices are full rank, numerically well conditioned, or sufficient for the downstream task. Tiny and small models at large patches can have genuine dimensional bottlenecks. Finite-precision effects and learned rank collapse are also possible. A justified clarification is to distinguish spatial granularity and computational access to coordinates from irreversible input loss. A rank/singular-value study or reconstruction experiment on the actual learned embeddings is needed before assigning the observed gains primarily to lost information.
result: Information loss in the trained embeddings and its causal role in the gains remain unresolved. The reversible construction is a scope clarification, not a demonstrated learned-model defect or a refutation of the reported improvements.
Resolution requires rank/singular-value or reconstruction checks on the actual learned embeddings, alongside appropriate invertible-projection and matched comparison controls.
brief: At \(p=16,D=768\), a full-rank patch projection can be invertible; \(196\cdot768=224\cdot224\cdot3\) preserves scalar dimension.
That does not show that the trained embeddings are lossless or refute the paper's qualified claim. Actual learned-model information loss remains Needs Evidence.

claim: The token-interpolation ablation is used to identify information recovery as the principal cause of smaller-patch gains. That interpretation requires the comparison to distinguish information loss from its other changed representation and access properties.
analysis: Needs Evidence: causal interpretation of Table 5. The token-interpolation control shows that simply interpolating coarse tokens gives much smaller gains than reducing patch size. It is useful evidence against that particular sequence-extension method. It does not equalize local token geometry, receptive fields, the learned projection, positional parameterization, or the ease with which mixers access fine structure. Even an invertible patch embedding and a pixel embedding can differ in all these properties while containing identical information. Thus the control does not identify information recovery as the principal cause. An invertible space-to-depth baseline, fixed/invertible projection controls and matched parameter/compute experiments would separate these explanations more directly.
result: The interpolation arm is a useful negative control for that sequence-extension method, but does not isolate irreversible information recovery from the other representation and access changes.

claim: The resolution-transfer routine should preserve the class-token position used by this model, which appends the class token after the image tokens.
analysis: The model appends its class token after image tokens (models_mamba.py 260–262), whereas the resolution-transfer routine preserves the first positional entry as the extra token and interpolates the remaining entries (main.py 332–345).

For a symbolic stored sequence \([p_0,p_1,p_2,p_3,c]\), the correct image grid is \([p_0,p_1,p_2,p_3]\) and the retained class position is \(c\). The routine instead retains \(p_0\) and interpolates \([p_1,p_2,p_3,c]\), then concatenates the preserved entry first. Changing grid size thus mixes the old class position into the image grid and does not preserve it as the new last class position. At unchanged grid size the identity interpolation can conceal the issue. The multi-resolution recipe makes this path relevant, but its historical invocation and accuracy consequences remain unknown.
result: The transfer routine assumes a leading class token while this model uses a trailing one. Identity interpolation can conceal the discrepancy at unchanged resolution; historical invocation and accuracy effects remain unresolved.

analysis: Judgment: Major, a false core convergence guarantee.

Use the displayed formula with \(\theta^*=(20,20)\), \(\theta^{1}=(0,20)\), and \(\Omega=\mathbb R^{2}\). Define \[c=\mathbb E|X|=\sqrt{2/\pi},\qquad
 m(a)=\mathbb E[X\tanh(aX/2)] .\] At the initial parameter, \(\mathbb E_{\theta^{1}}[Z\mid x,y]=y\tanh(10x)\). Under the true model, \(\mathbb E_{\theta^*}[Y\mid x]=\tanh(10x)^{2}\). The two exact \(M\)-step moment equations therefore give \[\beta^{2}=20,\qquad
 m(w^{2})=\mathbb E[X\tanh(10X)^{3}].
 \] The function \(m\) is strictly increasing, since \(m'(a)=\tfrac12\mathbb E[X^{2}\operatorname{sech}^{2}(aX/2)]>0\). Its right-hand side in the displayed formula lies strictly between \(0\) and \(m(20)\), so \(w^{2}\) is a unique finite point in \((0,20)\).

These parameters satisfy the Gaussian-feature and symmetric-logistic assumptions exactly. The complete conditional model is a regular minimal finite-support exponential family; \(A\) is strictly convex. The loss is finite and bounded below. Each block of the population \(Q\) objective is a logistic cross-entropy with nondegenerate soft targets, hence is coercive: along either parameter tail, a positive-measure interval of \(X\) contributes a positive linear growth coefficient. Its sublevel sets are compact and the \(M\)-step exists uniquely. Observed-loss strong convexity or identifiability is not assumed in part (1) of the corollary and is not needed here.

For \(u\ge0\), \(1-\tanh(10u)^{3}\le6e^{-20u}\). Bounding the Gaussian density by its value at zero gives \[\mathbb E[|X|\tanh(10|X|)^{3}]\ge
 c-\frac{12}{400\sqrt{2\pi}}=0.985c .\] On \(0\le |X|\le\tfrac12\), \(1-\tanh(2|X|)\ge1-\tanh1\), so \[m(4)\le c\{1-(1-\tanh1)(1-e^{-1/8})\}<0.972c .\] Thus \(w^{2}>4\). Since the expert parameter stays fixed and \(w^{1}=0\), the displayed formula yields \[D_A(\theta^{2},\theta^{1})
 =\mathbb E\log\cosh(w^2X/2)
 >2c-\log2=0.9026219410\ldots .\] The initial observed distribution is uniform on \(Y=\pm1\), hence \(L(\theta^{1})=\log2\). Moreover \(L(\theta^*)\ge0\), so \[L(\theta^{1})-L(\theta^*)\le\log2=0.6931471806\ldots .\] This contradicts the displayed formula for \(T=1\), independently of numerical integration. The distinction is not an iteration-index convention.

Parent Gaussian integration with 24,000 and 48,000 Simpson panels on \([-12,12]\) gives the same displayed values: \[\begin{array}{l|r}
 w^{2}&13.3796422672\\
 D_A(\theta^{2},\theta^{1})&4.6932948710\\
 L(\theta^{1})-L(\theta^*)&0.6095153680\\
 D_A(\theta^{1},\theta^{2})&0.5962829095\\
 L(\theta^{1})-L(\theta^{2})&0.6063297660
\end{array}\] Independent auxiliary quadrature agrees. Numerical checks corroborate the analytic contradiction rather than supply its logical basis.
result: The core forward-order guarantee is false on an admissible exact EM step. Reversing the divergence arguments gives the verified surviving stationarity inequality, while the EM–mirror-descent correspondence remains.
claim:
Corollary B.1(1), Eq. (48), p. 23, asserts without additional convexity conditions that \[\min_{1\le t\le T}D_A(\theta^{t+1},\theta^t)
 \le \frac{L(\theta^{1})-L(\theta^*)}{T}.
 \] Its proof instead establishes \(D_A(\theta^t,\theta^{t+1})\) in Eq. (52), p. 24. These are different quantities: by Theorem 5.1, their associated complete-data KL divergences have opposite directions. The corollary is the symmetric-model convergence result emphasized in Section 5, so the mismatch affects an explicit principal guarantee, not merely notation in an ancillary calculation.

analysis: Judgment: Major for a false lemma used in the core spectral derivation; the criterion itself is repairable.

Theorem B.2, p. 26, converts relative strong convexity into a bound on the eigenvalues of \(M=C^{-1}K\), where \(C=\nabla^{2} A(\theta)\succ0\) and \(K=\nabla^2_1 H(\phi\mid\theta)|_{\phi=\theta}\succeq0\). Its proof invokes Lemma B.3 (pp. 26–27), which asserts \(M=M^\top\). The proof diagonalizes \(C^{-1}\), then commutes that diagonal matrix with the transformed \(K\). A diagonal matrix need not commute with an arbitrary symmetric matrix. Likewise, left multiplication by \(C^{-1}\) alone is not a valid symmetric-matrix congruence for the displayed Loewner inequality.

For an exact model counterexample, use \(d=1\), true and current \(w=2,\beta=1\). Define \(f(u)=\sigma'(u)\) and \(a_v=\mathbb E[X^2f(vX)]\). Then \[C=\operatorname{diag}(a_2,a_1),\qquad
 K=\begin{pmatrix}h&b\\b&h\end{pmatrix}.\] Because \(f\) is even and strictly decreasing in \(|u|>0\), \(0<a_2<a_1\). Let \(U=wX/2,V=\beta X/2\) and \(P_\pm=P_{\theta}(Y=\pm1\mid X)\). The exact model gives \[P_\pm=\frac{\cosh(U\pm V)}{2\cosh U\cosh V},\qquad
 b=\mathbb E\!\left[
 \frac{X^{2}\{\operatorname{sech}(U+V)-\operatorname{sech}(U-V)\}}
 {8\cosh U\cosh V}\right]<0 .\] The inequality is strict because \(w\beta>0\) implies \(|U+V|>|U-V|\) for \(X\ne0\), an event of probability one. Hence \(M_{12}=b/a_2\ne b/a_1=M_{21}\). This proves nonsymmetry analytically within the Gaussian symmetric-model assumptions.

Parent integration gives \[C\simeq
 \begin{pmatrix}.0605275333&0\\0&.1442244802\end{pmatrix},\quad
 K\simeq
 \begin{pmatrix}.0552795015&-.0198487611\\-.0198487611&.0552795015\end{pmatrix},\] \[M\simeq
 \begin{pmatrix}
 .9132951315&-.3279294565\\
 -.1376240780&.3832879234
 \end{pmatrix}.\] The auxiliary’s swapped-parameter example independently gives the corresponding permuted matrix.

claim: H(\(\theta|\theta\))=0 and L(\(\theta\))=\(Q\)(\(\theta|\theta\)); invalid complete-entropy Jensen chain.
analysis: Judgment: Major for the printed core derivation; the corrected result is verified.

Section 3 (p. 4) defines \(H(\theta\mid\phi)=-\mathbb E_{X,Y}\mathbb E_{Z\mid X,Y;\phi}\log p_\theta(Z\mid X,Y)\), then asserts \(H(\theta\mid\theta)=0\). This premise is reused in the proof of Theorem 5.1, Appendix B.2(c), p. 20, Eq. (43), to equate the loss with its unshifted \(Q\) surrogate. Appendix B.3 applies that proof to the logistic case. Part (b) on p. 20 also uses an invalid Jensen chain purporting to make complete-data entropy zero.

Set true and current \(w=\beta=0\) in the displayed formula. Given \(X\), \(Y\) and \(Z\) are independent uniform signs. Therefore, writing \(C_X=-\mathbb E\log p(X)=\tfrac12\log(2\pi e)\) and \(\bar Q=Q-C_X\), \[H(\theta\mid\theta)=\log2,\qquad
 L(\theta)=\log2,\qquad
 \bar Q(\theta\mid\theta)=2\log2 .\] All quantities are finite, the mirror Hessian is \(\tfrac14 I_2\), and the zero parameter is allowed by the symmetric model. The analogous zero-parameter linear model has \(H=\log2\) as well; its full complete-data entropy is \(2C_X+\log2>0\). Thus neither the posterior zero-entropy premise nor the displayed complete-entropy conclusion holds. The omission of the fixed \(C_X\) constant does not account for the nonzero posterior entropy.

Here is a precise repair. Let \(r_\phi(z\mid x,y)=p_\phi(z\mid x,y)\). Then \[H(\theta\mid\phi)-H(\phi\mid\phi)
 =\mathbb E_{X,Y}\operatorname{KL}(r_\phi\Vert r_\theta)\ge0 .\] Using \(L=\bar Q-H\), it follows that \[L(\theta)-L(\phi)\le \bar Q(\theta\mid\phi)-\bar Q(\phi\mid\phi).\] The independently checked \(Q\)-difference identity is \[\bar Q(\theta\mid\phi)-\bar Q(\phi\mid\phi)
 =\langle\nabla L(\phi),\theta-\phi\rangle+D_A(\theta,\phi).
 \] These two relations prove the claimed 1-relative smoothness, with the tangent upper surrogate \(\bar Q(\theta\mid\phi)-H(\phi\mid\phi)\). The KL/Bregman identity can likewise use the normalized score identity \(\mathbb E_\theta\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(X,Y,Z)=0\), without the false Jensen chain.

Interpreting the intended surrogate as implicitly shifted is a charitable reading, but it changes the explicitly supplied definitions and Eq. (43); the correction must be stated. The defect is tied directly to the unit-step justification and convergence analysis. The repair verifies those particular identities, not every local-rate claim. analysis: Theorems 6.1 and 6.2 (p. 7) quantify over \(C<\infty\), but give total error \(\widetilde O(n^{1/5}C^{2/5})\) and mean squared error \(\widetilde O(n^{-4/5}C^{2/5})\), respectively, without a parametric baseline.

For Theorem 6.2 choose \(f=0\), any \(n\ge3\) and \(\sigma>0\). All stated assumptions hold and \(C=0\). For every selected knot set, \(S(K)\) contains constants. Least-squares orthogonality consequently gives, pathwise, \(\overline{\widehat f}=\overline Y=\overline\epsilon\), even though \(K\) is data-dependent. Therefore \[\frac1n\|\widehat f\|_2^{2}\ge\overline\epsilon^{\,2}>0
 \quad\text{almost surely},\qquad
 \frac{n\overline\epsilon^{\,2}}{\sigma^{2}}\sim\chi^2_1.\] The displayed upper bound equals zero; it cannot hold with probability \(1-\delta>0\). For the online claim, the constant signal \(f=1/2\) also has \(C=0\), whereas the empty-history first prediction is zero, already giving total error at least \(1/4\).

Multiplicative constants and logarithms cannot turn zero into a positive upper bound. There is no stated lower bound on \(C\). Counterevidence for the intended interpretation is explicit: Lemma C.1 retains \(\max\{n^{1/5}C^{2/5},1\}\), and Section 5 discusses an \(n^{-1}\) parametric rate. Thus a parametric term was plausibly intended. Nevertheless, it disappears in the theorem statements and later Corollary C.6/C.9 bounds. Retaining a baseline such as \(\widetilde O(n^{-1}+n^{-4/5}C^{2/5})\) is necessary for a uniform offline statement. This report does not certify that amended bound, because Problems 1 and 2 leave other proof obligations open. The assessment is Major for the stated central uniform guarantee; the positive-\(C\) leading exponent is not refuted by this check.

analysis:
Algorithm 5 (p. 13) uses \[B=\max_{1\le i\le n}|Y_i|+
 \max\{\sigma\sqrt{2\log(4n/\delta)},1\}\] to clip the linear experts. Lemma D.6(1) (p. 20), with \(\mathcal F_j=\sigma(Y_1,\ldots,Y_{j-1})\), asserts \[E[(Y_j-z_j)^{2}-(Y_j-\theta_j)^{2}\mid\mathcal F_j,V]
 =E[(z_j-\theta_j)^{2}\mid\mathcal F_j,V].\] The identity fails because \(B\), and consequently \(z_j\), depends on the current response.

Take \(n=3\), \(\sigma=0.1\), \(\delta=0.1\), and \((\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3)=(-1,1,1)\). A permissible underlying function equals \(-1\) up to \(x_1\), rises linearly with slope \(6\) to \(x_2\), and then equals \(1\). Thus it is bounded by one, has the required design values and \(C=6\).

Write \(a=\sigma\sqrt{2\log120}=0.3094347<1\) and \(V=\{|\epsilon_i|\le a\text{ for all }i\}\). First evaluate the conditional law at past responses \(Y_1=-1,Y_2=1\); their noise values satisfy \(V\). The linear expert starting at the first observation extrapolates to \(3\) at \(x_3\). Conditional on the past and \(V\), \(e=\epsilon_3\) has a symmetric normal law truncated to \([-a,a]\), and \[B=2+\max(e,0)<3,\qquad z_3=B.\] All clipping operations are therefore in the stated clipped branch. Subtracting the right side of Lemma D.6(1) from its left side gives \[\begin{aligned}
 -2E[e(z_3-\theta_3)\mid V,Y_1=-1,Y_2=1]
 &=-2E[e(1+\max(e,0))\mid |e|\le a]\notag\\
 &=-E[e^{2}\mid |e|\le a]<0. \end{aligned}\] The exact conditional moment has the analytic form \[v=\sigma^{2}\left(1-\frac{2c\phi(c)}{2\Phi(c)-1}\right),
 \qquad c=a/\sigma,\] and independent evaluation gives \(v=0.0097938491\). Thus the claimed zero difference is approximately \(-0.0097938491\).

The exact past point has probability zero, so it is not itself asserted to be a positive-probability counterevent. Conditional moments and this clipped prediction vary continuously with the two past responses in a small neighborhood of \((-1,1)\), while \(V\) has a positive-density interior there. The strictly negative difference in the displayed formula therefore persists on a neighborhood of positive probability. This establishes failure of the asserted conditional identity as an almost-sure statement.

result: Conditioning on \(V\) alone preserves the symmetric truncated law of each independent noise variable. The failure comes from the response-dependent threshold, not from an automatic claim that every conditioning argument is invalid. The counterexample follows Equation (1)’s Gaussian model and Section 3.1’s \(|f|\le1\) bound. Lemma D.8 (p. 21) uses Lemma D.6 to declare the corresponding noise term a martingale difference and apply a Freedman-type inequality. The counterexample invalidates that justification. This is Major for the ADDLE error proof and the dependent AKORN guarantee. No failure rate of the empirical estimator is inferred; no complete replacement concentration argument has been verified.

analysis:
Lemma C.7, Case 2 (p. 18), sets \[
 s(z)=g(z)+(h(z)-g(z))\frac{z-a}{b-a},
 \qquad a=k_{i-1},\ b=k_i,\] and asserts membership in the linear-spline space. The claimed implication from noncrossing to linearity is false.

Use \(n=8\), \(K_f=\{1/2\}\), \(K_b=\{1/4\}\), and, on \([0,1]\), \[g(z)=\max\{0,z-1/2\},\qquad h(z)=\max\{5/4,1+z\}.\] These are in \(F(K_f)\) and \(F(K_b)\), respectively; continuous piecewise-linear functions are allowed members. The knot sets are disjoint, and \(g\le1/2<5/4\le h\), so there are no crossover points, regardless of whether crossings are tested on the grid or continuously. The first knot \(1/4\) belongs to \(K_b\), so the proof’s base case gives \(s=g=0\) up to that knot. The next knot \(1/2\) belongs to \(K_f\), satisfying precisely the hypotheses of Case 2.

On \([1/4,1/2]\), the displayed formula becomes \[s(z)=4z^{2}+3z-1,\qquad s''(z)=8.\] All three of \(1/4,3/8,1/2\) are design points, but \[s(1/4)=0,\qquad s(3/8)=11/16,\qquad s(1/2)=3/2.\] An affine segment with these endpoints must have midpoint \(3/4\). The discrepancy is \(-1/16\). Thus membership fails even if \(S(K)\) is interpreted only as vectors of evaluations on the finite design. Exact rational arithmetic reproduces these values in `verification/0292/check.json`. The original p. 18 was rendered and inspected to exclude extraction error.

result: The pointwise convex combination in the displayed formula does stay between \(g\) and \(h\); that fact does not make it affine. Equal slopes would be a valid special case, but equal slopes are not a lemma hypothesis. The lemma’s existence conclusion is not disproved by this example. More generally, endpoint interpolation stays in an ordered strip between two affine functions because the relevant differences are affine and nonnegative at both endpoints. This verifies a local repair, not all jump, crossover and collision cases in the full construction.

analysis: Theorem 3.2, page 5, puts the existence of one problem before the universal quantifier over execution time, and claims \(\operatorname{dist}^{2}(x_o(\tau);S_x)>R_x^{2}/8\) for every admissible first-order method and every \(\tau>0\). The fixed finite-dimensional instance used in Appendix F, page 18, cannot have this property.

The theorem assumes Assumptions 2.3–2.5 and \(\delta_x=0\), with arbitrary fixed \(R_x>0\) and accuracy \(\epsilon>0\). It is distinct from the positive-curvature lower bound in Theorem 3.3. Appendix F proposes \[\min_{u,v}\max_y h(u)+\frac{L_x}{2}\|v\|^{2}+\mu_{yx}\langle y,v\rangle-\frac{\mu_y}{2}\|y\|^{2},\] where \(h\) is a finite-dimensional convex \(L_x\)-smooth hard function cited from Nesterov. It explicitly claims the solution is \((u^*,0,0)\) with \(u^*=\arg\min h\), then infers the entire theorem. The issue is the inference to an all-time distance obstruction, not the primal-dual gap comparison in this construction.

Fix any dimension and any \(h\) as in the source’s proposed construction, with a minimizer. Starting at zero, keep \(v_k=y_k=0\) and update \[u_{k+1}=u_k-L_x^{-1}\nabla h(u_k).\] The full primal gradient at \((u_k,0)\) is \((\nabla h(u_k),0)\), so this is allowed by the gradient-span memory in Definition 3.1 and takes a finite time per iteration. No hidden access to \(u^*\) or non-oracle operation is used.

For a convex \(L_x\)-smooth function, cocoercivity with a minimizer gives \(\langle
abla h(u),u-u^*angle\geq L_x^{-1}\|
abla h(u)\|^{2}\). This inequality follows by applying the smoothness descent inequality to \(h\) after subtracting the affine tangent at each of two points, then adding the resulting inequalities. Expansion of the displayed formula yields \[\|u_{k+1}-u^*\|^{2}\leq\|u_k-u^*\|^{2}-L_x^{-2}\|
abla h(u_k)\|^2.\] Consequently the iterates are bounded and their gradients tend to zero. Finite dimensionality provides a convergent subsequence; continuity makes its limit a minimizer. Applying the same Fejer inequality to that minimizer forces the whole sequence to converge to it. Thus \(\operatorname{dist}(u_k,\arg\min h)	o0\). In particular, for the unique minimizer claimed in Appendix F, \(\|(u_k,0)-(u^*,0)\|^{2}<R_x^{2}/8\) at some finite time. This proves that none of the fixed solvable instances of the displayed family can establish the advertised universal-in-time lower bound.

An independent check makes the quantifier distinction concrete. Let \(u\in\mathbb R^{20}\), \(v,y\in\mathbb R\), let \(H\) have diagonal \(2\) and adjacent off-diagonals \(-1\), and set \(h(u)=u^THu/2-c e_1^Tu\), with \(c=\|H^{-1}e_1\|^{-1}\). Take \[(L_x,L_y,L_{xy},\mu_x,\mu_y,\mu_{xy},\mu_{yx})=(4,2,2,0,1,0,1).\] Then \(B=(0,\ldots,0,1)\), \(f(u,v)=h(u)+2v^{2}\), and \(g(y)=y^{2}/2\). The eigenvalues of \(H\) are \(2-2\cos(j\pi/21)\) and lie in \((0,4)\); the full primal Hessian is bounded by \(4I\). The dual Hessian is \(1\), so its declared strong convexity and smoothness bounds \(1\) and \(2\) are valid. The minimum eigenvalue of \(B^TB\) is zero, its positive eigenvalue and that of \(BB^T\) are \(1\), and \(\nabla g(y)\) lies in \(\operatorname{range}B=\mathbb R\). Thus Assumptions 2.3–2.5 hold, the extra equality condition when both coupling lower bounds are positive is inapplicable, and \(\delta_x=0\). The unique saddle is \((H^{-1}ce_1,0,0)\) and \(R_x=1\) by construction.

The independently written 20-dimensional gradient calculation crosses the claimed \(1/8\) barrier at iteration 148: squared distance \(0.1243643237\). At 1,000 iterations it is \(8.9039\times10^{-6}\). These figures verify the illustration, not a disproof by a single easy instance of an existential worst-case theorem. The decisive evidence is the preceding convergence proof for the whole proposed fixed-instance family.
claim: General convergence proof for gradient descent on the independent u block, plus finite 20-dimensional illustration verifying every parameter bound.

Finite-dimensional smooth convex \(h\) with attained minimum, as explicitly used in Appendix F. Oracle model Definition 3.1 permits gradient descent from zero. Only Assumptions 2.3-2.5 required for Theorem3.2; \(\delta_x=0\). Operative assumptions: The whole-family argument uses finite dimension, convex \(L_x\)-smooth \(h\) and attainment as explicitly asserted for Eq.(48). Delta_x=0 is a declared lower bound, not a requirement that the maximal curvature modulus vanish. The m=20 illustration has \(L_x\)=4>0, \(L_y\)=2>\(\mu_y\)=1, \(L_{xy}\)=2>\(\mu_{yx}\)=1, \(\mu_{xy}\)=0; range and singular-value clauses of Assumption 2.5 are satisfied.
result: The intended lower-bound reading is plausibly horizon dependent: for each prescribed number of oracle calls, choose a sufficiently large dimension and a corresponding hard function. That allows class-wide slow convergence while every fixed finite-dimensional function eventually becomes solvable. It does not imply the source’s displayed order “one instance, all times.” Reinterpreting the proof this way changes a substantive quantifier. The later accuracy-dependent gap bound and the lack of a uniform linear rate may survive, but a complete replacement theorem must specify the dimension/horizon dependence and rederive the oracle-time relation. This review has not proved that replacement in all parameter regimes.

The supported assessment is Major for the invalid supporting derivation of the all-time negative claim. Section 2.2 explicitly uses Theorem 3.2 to present a necessary-and-sufficient characterization, making this a technical contribution rather than a peripheral display error. The report does not claim to have disproved every possible existential formulation under only Assumptions 2.3–2.5, especially formulations allowing unattained dual optima. Nor does it infer failure of the optimal positive-curvature complexity theorem. Appendix F’s own solvable witness is sufficient to establish the reported proof defect. No correction or later version is present among the frozen inputs; no exhaustive erratum search is asserted.

Every fixed solvable witness in Eq.(48) eventually crosses the positive distance floor. Invalid proof of claimed all-time nonconvergence used for necessity characterization; full theorem under any alternate existential interpretation not disproved.

analysis: Theorem 5.1, p. 6, states \(\mathbb E|\widehat x_t(k)|^{2}=|\widehat x_0(k)|^{2}+\int_0^t g(s)^2ds\) for an SDE with a general drift \(f\). The proof immediately assumes \(f=0\). The unrestricted statement is false, including for the VP family actually used in Section 4.4.

Use a finite orthonormal transform and a deterministic initial image with one transform coefficient equal to one. Let each pixel solve \(dx=-x\,dt/2+dW\) independently. The transformed coefficient satisfies the same Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation, so \[\mathbb E|\widehat x_t(k)|^{2}=e^{-t}|\widehat x_0(k)|^{2}+1-e^{-t}=1.\] The printed expression gives \(1+t\), hence two at \(t=1\). All coefficients of this SDE are smooth, and there is no transform-normalization ambiguity. More generally, for the VP kernel in Eq. (7), with \(a_t=\exp(-\int_0^t\beta)\), the correct identity is \[\mathbb E|\widehat x_t(k)|^{2}=a_t|\widehat x_0(k)|^{2}+(1-a_t).\] It follows directly by linearity and covariance preservation of a unitary transform; for zero drift the paper’s formula is valid under that normalization. The main proof’s \(\mathbb E|\widehat\epsilon|=0\) should be the zero mean of \(\widehat\epsilon\), as correctly used in Appendix A.3.

This is assessed Minor because the intended restricted claim is explicit in both proofs and the VP correction preserves the frequency-order argument: if the initial spectrum decreases with frequency, \(a_t|\widehat x_0(k)|^{2}/(1-a_t)\) crosses a fixed SNR threshold earlier at higher frequencies. This is an SNR ordering, not an exact factorization into a frequency-autoregressive generator. Appendix A.4 and the released implementation already use the VP kernel. The evidence does not invalidate the training method or its reported FIDs. The finite orthonormal formulation also avoids Appendix A.3’s formal integral over the infinite spatial line, which would need a spectral-density normalization.

analysis: Theorem 5.2 and Appendix A.5 replace a parity-selected cosine by an average of two cosines, yielding Eq. (12) with an approximation sign. No error bound or small-high-frequency assumption is part of the theorem. The approximation can miss the entire low-resolution coefficient for an admissible image.

Let \(C_N\) be the orthonormal DCT-II matrix and let \(P\) average adjacent pairs. For \(0<k<B\), the only nonzero entries in row \(k\) of \(C_BP C_{2B}^{\top}\) are \[M_{k,k}=\frac{\cos\theta_k}{\sqrt2},\qquad
 M_{k,2B-k}=-\frac{\sin\theta_k}{\sqrt2},\qquad \theta_k=\frac{k\pi}{4B}.\] The row \(k=0\) has only \(M_{0,0}=1/\sqrt2\). These identities follow by averaging the two neighboring inverse-DCT cosines and using discrete cosine orthogonality. Hence the exact two-dimensional transformation is \(\overline D=MDM^{\top}\). In particular, \[\overline D(k,0)=\tfrac12\cos\theta_kD(k,0)-\tfrac12\sin\theta_kD(2B-k,0).\] The second term is missing from Eq. (12). Set \(B=2\), add a constant pixel background of 128, and set the sole non-DC coefficient to \(D(3,0)=64\). The resulting \(4\times4\) pixels lie inside \([0,255]\), so this is also a valid bounded grayscale image. Its \(D(1,0)=0\), while \(\overline D(1,0)=-32\sin(\pi/8)\simeq-12.246\). Equation (12)’s retained term is zero. Reviewer-written matrices verify the exact alias identities for \(B=2,4,8\) to floating-point precision; the trigonometric derivation explains the discrepancy independently of rounding.
result: Low coefficient \(D(1,0)=0\) but pooled coefficient=-32 \(\sin(\pi/8)\). Missing approximation regime; no universal performance inference.
claim: Low-resolution DCT approximates scaled low-frequency coefficient for arbitrary matrix.
B2. Orthonormal DCT-II. Exact 2x2 average pooling. Pixel background128 and coefficient \(D(3,0)=64\).

paragraphs: Restore \(\gamma^{2}\) in M-BL precision and \((GF)^{-1}\) in SLP mean.

analysis: These local formula defects are Minor, given the correct adjacent derivations and no demonstrated additional empirical dependency.

Corollary 3.1.1 omits \(\gamma^{2}\) from the precision retained by Theorem 3.1 and its proof; Corollary 3.2.1 prints \(G^F\) rather than \((G^F)^{-1}\) in the mean. For the first, take scalar \(P=\Sigma_0=\Omega^F=\Omega=1\), zero prior and feature centers, \(\alpha=\beta=0\), \(q=1\), and \(\gamma=2\). The correct precision is \(6\), giving mean \(1/3\) and latent variance \(1/6\); the corollary’s precision \(3\) gives mean \(2/3\) and latent variance \(1/3\). For the second, take \(\Sigma_0=\Omega^F=1\), \(\theta_0=0\) and feature center \(a=1\): \(G^F=2\) and \(b=1\), so the printed mean is \(2\) instead of \(1/2\). All variances are positive. Restoring the squared coefficient and inverse, respectively, recovers the completed-square identities. analysis: Remark 3.3 (p. 5), repeated in the conclusion (p. 9), states that \(\Omega\to0\), \(q\to Pr^*\) and \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(0,0,1)\) imply \(\widetilde r\Rightarrow\delta_{r^*}\).

Use \(m=k=1\), \(P=1\), \(\Sigma=\Sigma_0=\Omega^F=1\), \(\theta_0=0\), feature center \(\alpha^F+F\beta^F=0\), \(r^*=q=2\), and \(\Omega=\varepsilon>0\). Every covariance is positive definite, the stated regression parameters are classical, views are accurate, and their uncertainty tends to zero. Theorem 3.1 gives \[\mu_\varepsilon=\frac2{1+2\varepsilon},\qquad
 V_\varepsilon=\frac{\varepsilon}{1+2\varepsilon},\qquad
 \widetilde r\sim N(\mu_\varepsilon,1+V_\varepsilon).\] Consequently \(\widetilde r\Rightarrow N(2,1)\), not \(\delta_2\). For example, its limiting characteristic function at frequency one is \(e^{2i-1/2}\) rather than \(e^{2i}\), directly ruling out the claimed weak limit without relying on convergence of moments. The latent mean \(\theta\) does collapse in this scalar example; the future noisy return \(r\) does not.

The mean claim also needs an identifiability condition on \(P\). For \(m=2,k=1,P=(1,0)\), prior and feature precision both \(I_2\), their centers zero, and \(r^*=(0,1)^T,q=0\), the second posterior coordinate remains \(N(0,1/2)\) as \(\Omega\to0\). The theorem allows this rectangular \(P\). Appendix A’s practical choice \(P=I\) avoids this second obstruction but not the intrinsic-noise obstruction above.

Under full-column-rank \(P\) with \(\Omega=\varepsilon\Omega_1\), \(\Omega_1\succ0\), accurate views and bounded prior/feature terms, the repaired conclusion is \(\theta\Rightarrow\delta_{r^*}\) and \(\widetilde r\Rightarrow N(r^*,\Sigma)\). This follows because the posterior precision diverges in every parameter direction and its covariance tends to zero. A predictive point mass additionally requires \(\Sigma\to0\). This is a major defect in the asserted general recovery property; it does not refute ordinary Bayesian shrinkage or the separate empirical SLP-BL comparisons.

analysis: Equations (1)–(2), Observation 3.1 and Sections 3.2–3.3 (pp. 2–4) are affected. The sign error is directly correctable; the asserted general conversion from gradient outliers to detrimental samples needs substantially more assumptions.

Write \(L_T(\theta)=\sum_i\ell_i(\theta)\), \(H=\nabla^2L_T(\widehat\theta)\succ0\) and \(v=\nabla L_V(\widehat\theta)\). For the paper’s downweighting objective \(L_T(\theta)-\varepsilon\ell_j(\theta)\), differentiation of its first-order condition gives \[
 \left.\frac{d\widehat\theta_{-\varepsilon,j}}{d\varepsilon}\right|_0
 =H^{-1}g_j,
 \qquad
 \left.\frac{dL_V(\widehat\theta_{-\varepsilon,j})}{d\varepsilon}\right|_0
 =v^TH^{-1}g_j,
 \quad g_j=\nabla\ell_j(\widehat\theta).\] Multiplying the whole training objective by \(1/n\) does not change this calculation. Equation (1) defines \(I_j=-v^TH^{-1}g_j\), whereas (2) calls \(I_j<0\) detrimental. With lower loss as better utility, that inequality says that downweighting increases loss, which describes a beneficial sample. One can either remove the minus sign or reverse the harmful/beneficial inequality.

This discrepancy is not merely a limitation of infinitesimal approximations. Consider binary logistic regression with a scalar constant input \(x=1\), no regularizer, four labels \(1\) and two labels \(0\), and cross-entropy loss. The finite optimum is \(\widehat\theta=\log2\), \(p=2/3\), with \(g_j=p-y_j\) and \(H=6p(1-p)=4/3>0\). The objective is strictly convex and smooth, and the model is exactly converged. Use a validation record with label \(1\), so \(v=-1/3\). The resulting quantities are
Removed label | Paper’s \(I_j\) | Refit probability | Exact validation loss change
Thus both printed classifications are reversed even for exact leave-one-out retraining in this admissible convex example.

There are two separate obstacles to the proposed equivalence even after correcting the sign. First, if the evaluation set in (1) is the training set, as the paper explicitly permits and uses in several comparisons, an unregularized interior ERM optimum obeys \(v=\sum_i g_i=0\). Every first-order aggregate influence in (1) is then zero, although the individual gradients need not be zero or have similar norms. In the example they are four copies of \(-1/3\) and two copies of \(2/3\). A gradient-outlier ranking can still be nontrivial, but is not the discrete sign classification of (1). This exact-zero argument does not apply unchanged to an incompletely optimized or separately regularized objective; those require their own analysis and cannot justify the stated ERM observation.

Second, the common factor \(v^TH^{-1}\) remains decisive for signs, even though it is shared across samples. Keep the identical six training records, model and gradient cloud, but change the validation label to \(0\). Removing any of the four positive-label records now reduces validation loss by \(\log(5/6)\), while removing a negative-label record increases it by \(\log(5/3)\). The detrimental fraction is \(4/6\), contradicting Observation 3.1’s conclusion that a much smaller minority is detrimental. An algorithm receiving only the unchanged gradient cloud and budget cannot produce correct sign labels for both validation targets. This does not depend on Hessian approximation or nonconvexity.

Counterevidence and scope. The paper calls statement 3.2 a hypothesis, rather than a formal theorem, and acknowledges distribution adaptation with OneClassSVM in Section 8. No universal failure of outlier removal follows from this review. The demonstrated defect is the claimed logical transformation and Observation 3.1, including the statement that average empirical loss makes it clear. The synthetic and noisy-label experiments can validate a useful heuristic on their distributions without validating that general transformation. A repair should correct the sign, state the target utility, distinguish aggregate training influence from self-influence, and present gradient outlyingness as a conditional empirical hypothesis unless assumptions connecting the target direction and outliers are proved. These restricted repairs do not establish a general equivalence. The impact is Major because this bridge is an explicit principal contribution, even if the practical method and some empirical gains survive.
claim: Negative I=-\(v^T\) \(H^{-1}\) g denotes detrimental samples; average ERM loss implies a small detrimental minority and enables gradient-outlier equivalence.

Scalar logistic model with \(x=1\), labels111100, no regularizer, exact finite optimum theta=\(\log2\), p2/3, Hsum4/3; one validation label1 or0. Smooth strictly convex training objective with invertible Hessian.
result: Sign formula and purported general conceptual derivation fail; empirical heuristic may survive. Major because the bridge is a stated principal contribution, not because every empirical claim collapses.

claim:
Section 3, page 4, presents equation (4), \[
 \min_{q,p,s}\int_0^{1}[p\dot q-H(q,p,s)]\,dt,\] as a variational description of the contact flow, followed by the reparameterization \(ds=\sqrt{H-H_V}\,dt\) and the geodesic problem (5). Appendix A.3, page 15, repeats the identification of the contact action with geodesic length. Section 5, page 6, invokes this correspondence to interpret (16)–(18) as uncertainty-aware geodesics and metric reshaping.
\(H=(q^{2}+p^{2})/2+s\), Eq7b. Initial state (0,0,1); t in [0,1]. Smooth contact trajectory \(q=p=0,s=\exp(-t)\). Fixed-endpoint variation delta \(s=t(1-t)\); positive \(s\) for small perturbation.
analysis:
Take the paper’s own (7b), \(H_B=(p^{2}+q^{2})/2+s\), with \(q(0)=p(0)=0\) and \(s(0)=1\). the displayed formula gives the valid smooth contact trajectory \(q(t)=p(t)=0\), \(s(t)=e^{-t}\). Fix even both endpoints of every variable, which is a more restrictive admissible variation than the unconstrained display. The perturbation \(s_\epsilon(t)=e^{-t}+\epsilon t(1-t)\) preserves these endpoints and remains positive for sufficiently small \(\epsilon\). Its first variation of the displayed formula is \[\left.\frac{dJ}{d\epsilon}\right|_{0}
 =-\int_0^1t(1-t)\,dt=-\frac16\ne0.\] Thus this contact trajectory is not even stationary for the stated functional. More generally, free variation of \(s\) imposes \(H_s=0\), in conflict with the very dissipative model \(H_s=1\) being advocated. There is also a direct incompatibility in the identification of \(s\): at \(t=0\) the true action derivative is \(\dot s=-1\), whereas the proposed reparameterization, with \(H_V=q^{2}/2\), gives \(ds/dt=\sqrt{1}=1\). Throughout this example the expression under the root is positive. The discrepancy is therefore not caused by a forbidden square root or a turning point.
result: An additional differential constraint \(\dot s=p\dot q-H\) and a terminal-action variational principle would change the admissible variations and hence define a different problem; it is not the unconstrained minimization written in (4). Using a separate length parameter would likewise remove the immediate same-variable contradiction but would require a fresh derivation of the claimed metric, parameter mapping and control equivalence. Appendix A does not supply these missing conditions: (29) is an implicit action expression followed by the same length identification. The Major impact is restricted to the central geometric justification for converting contact dynamics into the geodesic objectives (5), (16) and (18), a stated contribution of the method. It does not establish that the optimal-control objective (18) is unusable as a heuristic, or invalidate every possible geometric formulation of contact mechanics. Figure 4 was inspected: its trajectory illustration is consistent with a control modification but cannot establish the claimed variational equivalence. No general repair is verified here; a corrected constrained formulation and its claimed equivalence need a separate proof.

The contact solution is not stationary for Eq4; same \(s\) cannot be action and specified increasing length parameter. Invalidates central derivation supporting geodesic/metric-reshaping interpretation. Does not refute usability of heuristic control objective or all possible geometric reformulations.

 \Phi_{\rm kin}(q,p,s)=(q+\tau p,\ p,\ s+\tfrac12\tau p^{2}).\] At the stated test input, the printed and correct outputs are \((0.2,1,0.2)\) and \((0.2,1,0.1)\), respectively. analysis: Claim and assumptions. Appendix C.1, p. 16, assumes only that \(\Omega_+\) is convex with domain in the positive-measure cone, sets \(\Omega_1=\Omega_++\iota_{\mathcal P_1(Y)}\), and asserts, for every \(h\), \(\nabla\Omega_1^*(h)=\nabla\Omega_+^*(h-\tau_*)\). Its proof cites Danskin’s theorem without a uniqueness condition.

Complete check. Let \(Y=\{1,2\}\) and \(\Omega_+(p)=0\) on \(\mathbb R_+^{2}\) and \(+\infty\) elsewhere. This is a proper convex function whose domain is exactly the nonnegative-measure cone used with the simplex. Direct conjugacy gives \[\Omega_1^*(h)=\max(h_1,h_2),\qquad
 \Omega_+^*(z)=\begin{cases}0&z_1,z_2\leq0,\\+\infty&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\] The scalar minimum still exists: its feasible set is \(\tau\geq\max(h_1,h_2)\) and its optimizer is \(\tau_* =\max(h_1,h_2)\). At \(h=(0,0)\) it equals zero. But \(s\mapsto\Omega_1^*(s,0)=\max(s,0)\) has left derivative \(0\) and right derivative \(1\). Thus the asserted gradient does not exist. The independent finite-difference check at \(10^{-6}\) returns those same one-sided slopes; the displayed exact calculation is the proof. If “positive” is interpreted strictly, taking zero on the open positive orthant yields the same conjugates and the same failure at \(h=0\).

Counterevidence, correction and impact. This is a defect in the breadth of the lemma, assessed Minor. The paper’s central KL and quadratic generators are strictly convex; their relevant maximizing probability vector is unique, and the scalar calculations above support their formulas. The example does not refute Propositions 1–4 under those stronger conditions. A defensible local repair is to limit the gradient assertion to points where both conjugates are differentiable and a common maximizer exists; the gradients then equal that unique maximizer. This does not purport to repair every possible duality pathology allowed by the very broad first sentence of Lemma 1. No experimental consequence is inferred.
claim: For every \(h\), convex \(\Omega_+\) with domain in positive measures implies equality of the displayed gradients.
\(Y\)={1,2}. \(\Omega_+\) is zero on the positive/nonnegative cone and infinity elsewhere. \(h=(0,0)\).
result: The displayed gradients need not exist. Local overstatement; no demonstrated damage to core KL/sparsemax equivalence or published experiments.

analysis: Immediately before Theorem 4.1, p. 4, the paper says that a new DDPM can be constructed to realize (13). Yet the DDPM in (2) has Gaussian transitions, while (15) multiplies such a Gaussian by a generally nonquadratic reward factor. Normalization does not prove closure in that family.

Use the same one-step base chain but take the smooth bounded reward \[R_0(x)=\frac{2+\cos x}{3}\in[1/3,1].\] It satisfies positivity and finite normalization, and can itself be a valid auxiliary class probability with CG strength one. Direct Gaussian integration gives \[E_1(z)=\frac{2+e^{-(1-a)/2}\cos(\sqrt a z)}3,
 \quad \bar K_0(x\mid z)=\frac{R_0(x)\phi(x;\sqrt a z,1-a)}{E_1(z)}.\] For \(z=0\), the second derivative of its log density is \[\frac{d^{2}}{dx^{2}}\log\bar K_0(x\mid0)
 =-2+\frac{-2\cos x-1}{(2+\cos x)^{2}}.\] It equals \(-7/3\) at zero and \(-1\) at \(\pi\). Every nondegenerate Gaussian log density has constant second derivative. Thus (15) is a valid non-Gaussian kernel, even if a learned Gaussian variance is allowed. Independent quadrature gives \(E_1(0)=0.9262669276904681\) and kernel integral \(0.9999999999999998\), agreeing with the exact calculation.

Counterevidence, correction and impact. Theorem 4.1’s abstract transition and marginal formulas survive. The marginal score identity in (17) follows algebraically where differentiable, but inserting that score into a finite Gaussian update does not establish equality with these non-Gaussian kernels. A continuous-time diffusion limit is a distinct possibility requiring its own assumptions; it does not make the finite-step kernel Gaussian. Assessment: Major for the claimed exact DDPM realization. The defensible repaired statement is a Markov change-of-measure theorem with positive integrable reward, without Gaussian-transition closure. No repaired exact finite-step REG sampler is certified, and no benchmark effect is inferred.
claim: A new DDPM can be constructed to realize the scaled joint law.
Same one-step Gaussian base chain. \(R_0=(2+\cos  x)/3\) smooth positive bounded in [1/3,1]. Reward can be a valid CG classifier probability with strength1.
result: Valid transformed Markov kernel is non-Gaussian, contradicting exact finite Gaussian realization. Core exact-realization claim invalid, but no benchmark consequence established.

analysis: Section 3, pp. 3–4, argues that the endpoint target (5), \(\bar p_0\propto p_0R_0\), implicitly leaves every \(p_t\), \(t>0\), unchanged, and therefore declares the target itself invalid. That implication is absent from (5): specifying one marginal leaves the joint law unspecified. Indeed, marginalizing the paper’s own (13) gives exactly (5), as Section 4 explicitly observes. When \(E_t\) is nonconstant, other marginals change.

An explicit finite example removes any normalization ambiguity. Set \(T=1\), \(a=1/2\), \(X_1\sim N(0,1)\), and \(X_0\mid X_1=z\sim N(\sqrt a z,1-a)\); hence \(X_0\sim N(0,1)\). Take \(R_0(x)=e^{bx}\), \(b=1\). This is positive and integrable, with \(Z=e^{b^{2}/2}\). Completing squares gives \[\begin{aligned}
 \bar X_1&\sim N(\sqrt a b,1),\\
 \bar X_0\mid\bar X_1=z&\sim N(\sqrt a z+(1-a)b,1-a),\\
 \bar X_0&\sim N(b,1).\end{aligned}\] The last line is exactly \(p_0(x)e^{bx}/Z\). The new initial mean is \(1/\sqrt2\), the transition intercept is \(1/2\), and their combined endpoint mean is \(1\). Both joint scaling and terminal marginal scaling are satisfied; the latter never required an identity reward at \(t=1\).

Counterevidence and impact. Prescribing incompatible scaled marginals at every time can be inconsistent, and fixing a particular initial law and transition ansatz introduces additional restrictions. The example does not assert that a fixed original start with every original score/noising identity unchanged automatically realizes the target. It shows that those restrictions cannot be inferred from the terminal-marginal equation alone. Assessment: Major, because the claimed invalidity of marginal objectives is a central theoretical contribution. A precise correction is that joint tilting selects one path-space extension of a valid terminal target, whereas an arbitrary timewise score modification need not sample that target.
claim: Eq5 implicitly sets all Rt, \(t>0\), to identity and is therefore invalid.
result: Invalid inference from endpoint constraint; joint tilt is one valid extension of same endpoint target. Central claim that marginal objective is inherently invalid fails; no claim that naive guidance samples target.

analysis: With \(h=4096,s=2048,\alpha=0.99\), the displayed adjusted-speedup formula on page 15 evaluates to \(3.027292\), not \(2.95\). Its OCC overhead ratio is \(0.028206\), not \(5.6\%\).

The unadjusted ratio is \(3.115460\) and the stated DGE ratio is \(0.000918\), consistent with the rounded \(3.12\) and \(0.1\%\). These are arithmetic checks of the printed model, not hardware benchmarks. Moreover, the DGE operation applies to weight entries (equations (6), (22) and the inspected backward code), whereas its overhead is counted as \(96bsh\) activation-shaped elements. For the standard dense block counted in Table 5, the corresponding six weight matrices contain \(12h^{2}\) entries, giving \(96h^{2}\) scalar-operation units under the paper’s eight-operation assumption. This assumption itself treats nonlinear operations as equal-cost FLOPs. Clarify the counted objects, precision throughput baseline, quantile-sort and memory costs before interpreting the estimate as runtime. The paper explicitly excludes native FP4 measurements, which substantially limits the consequence of this issue.
claim: The adjusted-speedup substitutions and DGE operation count should equal the expressions evaluated at the stated parameters.
result: The displayed substitutions and operation count have the identified local numerical discrepancies; a corrected end-to-end speed measurement is not established here.

analysis: Appendix C.3, equation (28) and its following paragraph, infers equivalence from equal peak bounds. This does not establish equality of the gradient functions.

Let \(u=2x/\delta-1\), \(g_c(u)=\min\{k^{-1}|u|^{1/k-1},c\}\), and \(g_\epsilon(u)=k^{-1}(u^{2}+\epsilon^{2})^{(1/k-1)/2}\). Setting \(\epsilon=(kc)^{-k/(k-1)}\) makes both peaks equal \(c\). Nevertheless, at \(|u|=\epsilon\), \(g_c=c\) whereas \(g_\epsilon=c\,2^{(1/k-1)/2}\). For \(k=5,c=3\), these values are \(3\) and \(2.273575\). Their agreement at a single point cannot prove equivalence in a neighborhood. Both are bounded positive surrogate gradients, so the practical cap remains well defined. Equation (7) itself has an infinite derivative at the midpoint; it is continuous but not differentiable there. No convergence or superior gradient-accuracy guarantee follows merely from boundedness.
claim: The paper describes bounded smoothing and clipping as mathematically equivalent transformations. Their functions must therefore agree on the stated input domain.
result: Matching the peaks does not make clipping and smoothing equal in a neighborhood. Both can be bounded positive surrogate gradients without that claimed equivalence.

analysis: Appendix C.2, equations (18)–(22), describes its result as the true weight gradient, but omits derivatives through the weight-dependent absmax scale in equation (1).

Writing \(s=s(w)\) and \(F_i(w)=Q(sw_i)/s\), direct differentiation of a smooth surrogate gives \[dF_i=Q'(sw_i)\,dw_i+
 \left\{w_iQ'(sw_i)/s-Q(sw_i)/s^{2}\right\}ds.\] The second term couples a column through its maximum. For a positive, unique maximum \(w_1\) and E2M1 maximum 6, \(s=6/w_1\) and \(Q(6)=6\), so \(F_1=w_1\) exactly and its total derivative is 1. At \(k=5\), the paper’s interval surrogate has endpoint derivative \(1/k=0.2\); the frozen-scale formula instead gives 0.2. This is a counterexample to the unconditional chain-rule claim, not to using 0.2 as a chosen surrogate update. Explicitly stopping differentiation through \(s\) repairs the derivation’s intended scope. The acquired code uses a power-of-two scale, piecewise constant away from scale transitions, and a custom backward pass; this is relevant counterevidence against imputing a historical training error from the paper’s absmax formula.
claim: The derivative of the scaled objective must include the scale's dependence on the weight unless the analysis explicitly freezes that scale.
result: The derivative formula requires a frozen-scale interpretation; it does not equal the full weight derivative when the scale depends on the weight.

claim: The acquired Megatron training path must enable the residual-compensation operation before that path identifies the described compensated training recipe.
analysis: The acquired Azure/MS-AMP commit is `9746ea85289f8e6233646e73ace35f730d1245d5` (1 December 2025), later than the conference proceedings. Static inspection covered `msamp/operators/fp4_quantize/fp4_quantize.py` lines 1–186, its CUDA kernel lines 1–140, `msamp/megatron/layers.py` lines 1–218, and `msamp/common/tensor/meta.py` lines 37–56.

The CUDA lookup thresholds agree with Appendix A, including upward ties. The piecewise DGE derivative is capped at 3 and evaluated on saved scaled weights. The API correctly interprets the clamping parameters as empirical quantiles, resolving the ambiguity in equation (9), whose literal bounds \(1-\alpha,\alpha\) would otherwise clip negative activations incorrectly.

Needs Evidence: OCC reproduction path. The Megatron activation call (line 67) enables clipping but omits `residual_compensation`; the callee defaults that argument to false (line 114). The forward function then passes the quantized input to one FP8 GEMM and adds only bias (lines 108–116). Thus this inspected entry point discards the clipped residual and does not realize the sparse residual multiplication described in Section 3.2. The optional API can add a residual back before casting, but that is not selected here, and is not by itself the stated high-precision sparse GEMM. A paper-matched configuration/commit and compensation implementation are needed to connect this release to Tables 1–3. This is an observed release limitation; the historical runs may have used different code, and no effect on their scores is inferred.

Figures 3–6 were inspected as images. Figure 5 supports a small positive FP4 loss gap, with transient spikes, rather than exact equality. Table 2’s mean accuracy is sometimes higher under FP4; Table 3’s average perplexity is worse for 7B and 13B, so “comparable” is more defensible than uniform superiority. The ablations separate weight and activation mechanisms and vary \(k\), \(\alpha\), and quantization granularity. Their lack of run-level uncertainty and raw checkpoints prevents a significance or reproducibility conclusion. Figures 11–14 visibly support heterogeneous activation tails and channel outliers; they do not alone establish a distribution-wide optimal clipping quantile.
result: The acquired training path does not enable the residual compensation needed to identify the described recipe. Its relationship to the experiment-producing configuration remains unresolved.

analysis: Location and classification. `Model/CoRE.py`, functions `cross_align` and `cross_rec`, compared with Eqs. (8)–(12). Minor confirmed release/specification discrepancy; impact on original experiments is Needs Evidence.

The release constructs the intra-city reconstruction targets from projected query/key products, not the raw embedding Gram matrices specified in Eq. (10). Setting both linear projections and their biases to zero then makes all released targets and cycle products zero regardless of the embeddings. Its pairwise-distance default epsilon leaves only a tiny numerical floor (approximately \(4\times10^{-12}\) for two regions in each city). For \(Z^X=Z^Y=I_2\), the written Eq. (12) instead equals one at these zero projections. Thus the release permits a trivial projection collapse that does not correspond to the displayed objective. This shows an objective discrepancy, not that training actually converged there.

The release also omits the second relative matrix normalization described after Eq. (8), and computes a mean of squared row distances rather than a mean over all entries. Ignoring the numerical epsilon, the latter is a factor \(N_a\) for the manifold matrix and factors \(N_X,N_Y\) for the respective individual terms. With weights all set to one these differences are not a single harmless global rescaling of the whole objective. The constant one in the code’s distance-to-Gram transformation cancels when taking differences; it is not itself an error. The mobility loader globally normalizes trip counts, so the weighted reconstruction sum agrees with averaging over trips in Eq. (4), and no missing-normalization finding is assigned to that term. The source needs reconciliation with the reported loss definitions and actual run configuration before it can serve as a reproduction of the paper.
claim: Released losses change targets and relative weighting.
Current pinned release; standard pairwise epsilon accounted for.
result: Current implementation is not the displayed objective; historical empirical impact unresolved.

analysis: Location and classification. Eqs. (3)–(13), especially the alignment interpretation following Eq. (12) and the last paragraph of Section 3.4. Major for the central claim that optimizing these losses ensures directly compatible semantic coordinates.
Hold the source embeddings \(Z^X\), anchors \(A\), and linear query/key matrices fixed, and replace only \(Z^Y\) by \(-Z^Y\). Each objective term remains unchanged:
1. Intra-city dot products \(Z^Y(Z^Y)^\top\) do not change, so every destination probability and the mobility loss are identical.

2. The first relative matrix \(A_{\rm rel}^Y\) changes sign, under either the stated cosine similarities or Eq. (7)’s dot products. Row normalization preserves this sign change. The second Gram matrix \(A_{\rm rel}^Y(A_{\rm rel}^Y)^\top\) is identical, including its final normalization. Hence \(L^{\rm LMA}\) is unchanged for every common anchor realization.
3. Both cross-city attention matrices in Eq. (11) change sign. Their cycle products and both intra-city correlation targets in Eq. (10) are unchanged. Hence \(L^{\rm LIA}\) is unchanged.

Consequently Eq. (13) has exactly the same value for the two orientations, for any weights \(\alpha,\beta\). This is not a simultaneous global rotation, which a source predictor could absorb: the source coordinates and trained predictor stay fixed while the target reverses. No final nonnegative embedding constraint or nonnegative/softmax attention constraint appears in the stated equations. The actual PDF was checked to exclude an OCR omission. The two cities have separate encoders. A sign-reversed output is compatible with the final linear-valued attention aggregation; it is not excluded by an identified assumption.

For a concrete nonzero example take two regions per city, \(d=2\), \(Z^X=I_2\), and \(Z^Y=\pm I_2\). Use any anchors with nonzero rows and set \(W_q=W_k=2^{1/4}I_2\). Both alignment losses are zero in both orientations: cross-attention is \(\pm I_2\), its cycles are \(I_2\), and the anchor Gram matrices agree. The mobility losses agree for any given counts. With identity trip counts each city has \(L^{\rm RE}=\log(1+e^{-1})\simeq0.31326\). A source ridge regressor with intercept, regularization one and labels \((1,3)\) predicts \((1.5,2.5)\) on \(I_2\) and \((2.5,1.5)\) on \(-I_2\). Against the same target labels its MAE changes from 0.5 to 1.5. The script independently calculates the losses and solves the centered ridge system; it also verifies sign invariance on unequal-size random matrices.

This directly limits the claim that cycle consistency and manifold matching establish individual semantic alignment. Increasing the number of random anchors cannot break this exact symmetry. It does not show that all trained runs reverse orientation, nor does it refute the six reported city-transfer results. Optimization biases, city structure or additional undocumented implementation choices could favor useful orientations empirically. A repair needs an explicit orientation-identifying cross-city constraint/assumption, or a narrower empirical claim with an acknowledged identifiability limit. A sign-flip diagnostic on saved embeddings would help distinguish the objective from favorable optimization behavior. No such historical diagnostic or repaired method was run.
claim: Full objective does not identify relative semantic orientation.
Real-valued embeddings, linear unnormalized attention as written; no final positivity restriction; fixed source predictor.
result: Defeats general inference from optimized losses to compatible semantic coordinates, not reported empirical means.

analysis: Location and classification. Sections 2–3, Eqs. (1), (6)–(12), pp. 2–5; dependent zero and basis claims in Section 4 and Appendices C/F. Major: the purported vector structure and its derived zero-class interpretation are not established.

For an operation on equivalence classes, changing a representative must not change the result. Section 3 verifies familiar identities of functions but never verifies this prerequisite. Consider two unit-volume bins and normalized piecewise-constant densities, written as two-entry vectors: \[p=(0.7,0.3),\quad p'=(0.9,0.1),\quad q=(0.15,0.85),
 \qquad \tau=0.5.\] All three densities are nonnegative and integrate to one. Both \(p\) and \(p'\) classify just the first bin; moreover \(p'=2(p-\tau)+\tau\), precisely an allowed transformation in Eq. (1), with normalization constant one. Nevertheless the equal-mixture construction in Eq. (6) gives \[(p+q)/2=(0.425,0.575),\qquad (p'+q)/2=(0.525,0.475).\] At the same threshold \(0.5\), these classify opposite bins. Equivalently the unnormalized sums at threshold one classify opposite bins. Thus even restricting inputs to normalized genuine densities does not make the asserted class operation independent of the representative. The mixture identity in Appendix A is correct for specified component densities and equal mixing weights; it is not a well-defined union operation on their decision-equivalence classes.

The direct Eq. (11) failure is equally explicit at zero threshold. Let \(h=(1,-1)\), \(h'=2h\), and \(g=(-1.5,1.5)\). Then \([h]=[h']\), but \(h+g=(-0.5,0.5)\) and \(h'+g=(0.5,-0.5)\) induce opposite decisions. Signed functions are permitted by the valid-logit set \(S\) in Section 2; they can also be obtained by centering and scaling nonnegative densities and their thresholds. They are unavoidable if the claimed negative scalar multiplication is retained. There are no equality-boundary cases in these examples. More abstractly, at zero threshold the proposed scalar rule gives \(2[h]=[2h]=[h]\) for every such nontrivial decision class. In a real vector space subtraction would force \([h]=0\), contradicting the claimed distinct class-vectors.

Alternatives considered. Page 3 explicitly acknowledges that arbitrary representative logits cannot be merged. Passing to their equivalence sets does not remove the problem when addition is then defined through those same representatives. Picking a distinguished density would require additional information and a different construction, rather than prove the present quotient well-defined. Applying Boolean union/complement to already computed indicators is legitimate (the four rows of Table 1 were checked); it does not identify union with vector addition. In particular, union is idempotent whereas real-vector addition is not, except at zero.

Appendix F introduces threshold tuples and monotone transforms, but retains the same representative addition in Eq. (44). Strictly increasing transforms already include the rescaling counterexample. As literally written, allowing non-decreasing constant transforms also destroys decision preservation by collapsing both the logit and its threshold to the same constant. The appendix expressly calls its argument intuition and omits constraints; restricting these transforms would remove that latter degeneracy but would not repair the additive counterexample.

Dependent zero and basis interpretations. The ordinary zero function has integral zero, so normalization is undefined. A sequence \(\varepsilon r(x)\to0\) normalizes to any chosen probability density \(r\), not uniquely to a uniform one. Independently checking \(r=(0.8,0.2)\) at three positive \(\varepsilon\) values gives the same nonuniform normalized result. The constant-path choice in Eqs. (19)–(20) does give a uniform law on each fixed finite box. However, \(q_R=(2R)^{-1}\mathbf1_{[-R,R]}\) has total mass one and converges pointwise to zero, with \(q_R([-1,1])=1/R\to0\). It has no probability limit that is uniform on the whole real line. The same obstruction holds in higher dimensions. Section 4 itself labels the derivation an indication, and Appendix F also disclaims a formal proof; those qualifications must be preserved. They do not support the stronger discovery claim in the conclusion.

Appendix C’s independence assertion is also unsupported. In particular, Appendix F’s monotone decision equivalence gives \([x]=[x^{3}]\) at zero threshold, since cubing and its inverse preserve the threshold decisions. Even before quotienting, its ordered multivariate tensor coefficients are redundant: nonzero coefficients \(m_{12}=1\), \(m_{21}=-1\) give \(x^\top m x=0\) for every \(x\). The stored exact/finite checks include this cancellation. Symmetric multi-index coefficients and explicit approximation/domain conditions would be needed for a different polynomial parameterization; a learned quadratic separator remains usable without the claimed universal basis.

Consequence and repair scope. The proposed real vector space, its additive-identity distribution, and the associated basis theorem require replacement. A finite-domain noise classifier and ordinary Boolean operations remain coherent empirical constructions. This review verifies the counterexamples, not a replacement theory or a claim that noise training cannot help.
claim: Decision-equivalence addition is not well defined; derived vector-space claims fail.
Two unit-volume bins and normalized positive densities; threshold rescaling allowed by paper. Signed logits independently allowed by S.
result: Central real vector space, unique uniform additive-identity distribution and basis inference not established.

analysis: Location and classification. `MNIST_CIFAR/MNIST/repository_zero.py` and `MNIST_CIFAR/ZeroHelperFunctions/Curiosity.py`, especially lines 26–30 of the latter. Minor, restricted to the two-output cross-entropy variant in the inspected revision; the exact historical experiment route is unverified.

That variant trains two output logits for each unary model. The combiner selects the largest last-column raw logit across models, without subtracting the corresponding noise logit. Let two models output \(A=(0,2)\) and \(B=(0,1)\) for one input. The combiner selects \(A\). Adding 10 to both outputs of \(B\) gives \((10,11)\), so it selects \(B\), although every probability, cross-entropy loss and within-model prediction of \(B\) is unchanged. The independent calculation obtains the same \(B\) class probability \(0.7310586\) and loss \(0.3132617\) before and after the shift. Adding a common final-layer bias realizes this invariance for all inputs. Uniform noise in the loss does not fix this free offset.

Compare a log-odds margin or probabilities with explicit prior/noise calibration, and authenticate the executed configuration. This suggested local change removes the additive-offset ambiguity but does not prove general cross-model calibration. Crucially, the separately inspected `MNIST/repository.ipynb` specifies a single-output BCE variant, to which this two-logit invariance does not apply. Its configuration also differs from the current helper’s binary-branch selector, so execution provenance is needed. The grouped `JamesWeb.py` route uses softmax probabilities and masks a model’s noise-class win; it likewise is not subject to the raw-offset example. The finding therefore is not assigned indiscriminately to Figures 41–44 or their reported accuracies.
claim: Two-output CE repository variant compares arbitrary raw logit offsets.
Two-output CE variant, final common bias free; not one-output BCE.
result: Released CE combination is not invariant to individually equivalent classifiers; does not prove reported accuracies false.

analysis: Location and classification. Section 6, Eqs. (26)–(29), pp. 8–9. Minor algebraic error in density normalization.

With the paper’s definition \(p_n(u)=k\), substituting in Eq. (26) gives \(G=\log p_d-\log k\), not \(\log p_d-k\). Hence \(p_d=k e^G\), not \(e^{G+k}\). For \(p_d=0.4\) and \(k=0.25\), \(G=0.4700036\) gives the correct density 0.4, while the printed expression gives 2.0544407. One could instead define a new symbol \(k=\log p_n\), but that is not its definition in the text. The score identity is unchanged because the missing term is constant in \(u\).

More generally, the Bayes binary log-odds is \(\log p_d-\log p_n+\log(\pi_d/\pi_n)\) when the sampling priors differ. For equal priors and uniform noise on a finite box, the positive region is a density superlevel set \(p_d>1/V\); it is not automatically the full distributional support or an arbitrary future class’s complement. This does not contradict the paper’s conditional mode-seeking generation discussion, but does not establish exact recovery of a true manifold either.
claim: Noise-contrastive density formula substitutes k for \(\log(k)\).
k has explicit density meaning; equal priors as Eq26.
result: Absolute density normalization wrong, no demonstrated empirical score failure.

claim: Trainer fails to restore model training mode after epoch evaluation.
New model starts train mode and standard helper loop used; CIFAR architecture has mode-sensitive layers.
analysis: Location and classification. `MNIST_CIFAR/ZeroHelperFunctions/zeroTrainer.py`, lines 69–107, 127–159; `MNIST_CIFAR/Networks/networks.py`. Minor implementation issue, with unmeasured historical effect.

Each epoch invokes training followed by three evaluation routines. Those routines call `self.model.eval()`, but the training routine and surrounding loop never restore `self.model.train()`. Static syntax inspection finds evaluation calls at lines 107, 129 and 159 and no model-training-mode call. Consequently, after the first evaluation a newly constructed model stays in evaluation mode for subsequent optimization epochs. The CIFAR architectures contain both batch normalization and dropout, so dropout is disabled and running batch-normalization statistics cease to update. Gradients and optimizer updates still occur; this is not a claim that training stops.

The installed framework’s actual mode implementation was read and hashed. A separately created BatchNorm/Dropout probe confirms the behavior: the batch counter is 1 after the training forward, remains 1 after an evaluation-mode forward, and becomes 2 after explicitly restoring training mode. Restore the mode at the start of each training epoch and then compare affected runs. Both compared CIFAR models share the helper; the direction and magnitude of any benchmark effect cannot be inferred. The inspected notebook uses 100 epochs while the script and Figure 29 use 50, further limiting historical attribution. Pure linear/ReLU MNIST models do not acquire the same dropout/normalization consequence.
result: Later CIFAR epochs optimize with dropout disabled and frozen running BN statistics; benchmark magnitude unknown.

analysis: For cross-class channels, Appendix A.4 assigns \(t=\sqrt{b_{ij}/4}\) and \(s=-\sqrt{b_{ij}/4}\) at both channel indices \((K-1)i+j\) and \((K-1)j+i\). Consider \(K=2\) singleton classes and \[B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] This is a nonnegative symmetric block matrix as required by Definition A.4. The diagonal channel values vanish. Both cross-channel indices equal \(3\), and the displayed rule gives both nodes the same nonzero pair \((t_3,s_3)=(1/2,-1/2)\). Both features lie in \(T^{K^{2}}\). Nevertheless, \[f_1^\top Lf_2=\frac14-\frac14=0\ne1=b_{12}.\] All decoded probabilities are zero, whereas the claimed representation would have cross probability \(1-e^{-1}\). The cut-norm error in the block matrix is \(2/2^{2}=1/2\), despite starting from an exact block target.

This is not restricted to a particular value of the weak-regularity class-count bound. For any \(K\ge2\), a zero-diagonal target with nonzero off-diagonal blocks makes every assigned feature satisfy \(s_n=-t_n\), and hence makes the entire Lorentz Gram matrix zero. The independent \(K=4\) calculation with off-diagonal entries one gives cut error \(3/4\). Thus the failure remains for larger permitted class counts. The index map also collides, but correcting only the indexing does not correct the same-sign cancellation.

The original page image confirms the two negative signs; the adjacent bipartite example on p. 4, which uses opposite exclusive signs, provides clear counterevidence to interpreting this as a necessary limitation of IeClam. The error is in the printed construction, not in the cone’s expressive capacity.

The dimension and tolerance bookkeeping cannot be used literally either. Theorems 3.7–3.8 print a minus sign before \(\log(\epsilon/2)^{2}\). At \(\epsilon=1/2\), these expressions give \(K=-69.1852\) and \(C=2^{-28}\), neither a code dimension. A charitable reading is to square \(-\log(\epsilon/2)\) instead. Even then, A.4 requests only \(\|\widetilde A-B\|_\square\le\epsilon\) and subsequently adds \(\epsilon/2\), which yields at best \(3\epsilon/2\), not the stated \(\epsilon\). The strict bound also needs slack. These are not used as isolated typographical complaints: the displayed expressions do not establish the central quantitative guarantee.

This is Major under the claim-level standard. Theorem 3.8 is the proof supporting the paper’s probability-valued universality contribution. A repairable invalid construction remains an invalid core derivation. The counterexample does not disprove the existence of another encoding, and the benchmark results do not depend on implementing this proof construction.
claim: Write \(f=(t,s)\), \(L=\operatorname{diag}(I,-I)\), and \[T^C=\{(t,s): |s_c|\le t_c\text{ for all }c\}.\] The decoder \(p_{nm}=1-\exp(-f_n^\top Lf_m)\) is a probability on this cone because \(t_{nc}t_{mc}-s_{nc}s_{mc}\ge0\) coordinate by coordinate. Theorem 3.8 claims that every target graph can be approximated in the regularized log-cut distance by a cone-constrained code whose dimension depends only on the error tolerance.

The proof first approximates \(\widetilde A=-\log(1-(1-\delta)A)\) by a symmetric nonnegative block matrix \(B\), with block values \(b_{ij}\). The essential next assertion (p. 16) is that its prescribed features satisfy \(f_n^\top Lf_m=b_{k_nk_m}\). Without this equality the weak-regularity approximation does not transfer to the probability decoder.
