claim: Actualflow -1/16 vs claimed<=-1/8; discrete -31/512 alsofails. Independent realizabletwoexamplegreedywitness.

Twosingle-node graphs features(.5,0),(0,1),linearGCN. CanonicalK=GNTK=\(\operatorname{diag}(.25,1)\),tightuppergamma1. N1 trainfirstgraph y1,initial parameter \(\theta=0\),squaredloss,\(\tau=1\),\(\eta=1/4\).
analysis:
Use two one-node, edgeless graphs with features \(x_a=(1/2,0)\) and \(x_b=(0,1)\). A one-layer \(\kappa=1\) GCN is \(f_\theta(G)=x_G^\top\theta\). Choose its actual tangent kernel as the canonical kernel: \[K(G,G')=x_G^\top x_{G'},\qquad
 K_{\{G_a,G_b\}}=\begin{pmatrix}1/4&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] The kernel is strictly positive definite, with tight global upper bound \(\gamma=1\). Train on the one observation \((G_a,1)\), starting at \(\theta=0\), with squared loss, \(\tau=1\) and \(\eta=1/4\). The smoothness and step-size conditions hold; the tangent/canonical kernels agree throughout.

At time zero the actual flow gives \[\dot{\mathcal L}(0)=-\eta K(G_a,G_a)=-1/16,
 \qquad\hbox{whereas Eq.~\text{(eq:claimed)} requires }\dot{\mathcal L}(0)\leq-1/8.\] The inequality is false. Under a discrete-step reading, \(\theta_1=(1/8,0)\) and \(f_{\theta_1}(G_a)=1/16\), so \[\mathcal L_1-\mathcal L_0
 =\tfrac12(15/16)^{2}-\tfrac12=-31/512>-1/8,\] also contradicting the asserted reduction. This issue is independent of Problem 1.

Appendix \(B\), Eq. (44), p. 19, upper-bounds a positive quadratic form. Equation (46) substitutes that bound into a negatively weighted term, which reverses the valid inequality direction. Even the scalar case above suffices, without any ambiguity about entrywise versus positive-semidefinite matrix bounds.

For canonical-kernel gradient flow the valid identity is \[\dot{\mathcal L}=-\frac{\eta}{N^{2}}d^\top Kd,\qquad
 d_i=\partial_f\ell(f(G_i),y_i).\] If additionally \(K\succeq\mu I\), this implies \(\dot{\mathcal L}\leq-\eta\mu\|d\|_2^{2}/N^{2}\). This changed-assumption flow statement is verified algebraically; it is not a repair of the published finite-step theorem or a proof of improved teaching speed.

Section 4.3, p. 6, claims that gradient size can be increased by maximizing projection coefficients without computing kernel-section norms. In fact, \[\|d_i K(G_i,\cdot)\|_{\mathcal H}
 =|d_i|\sqrt{K(G_i,G_i)}.\] Consider the same linear graph family with \(x_1=(0.1,0)\), \(x_2=(0,1)\), targets \((2,1)\) and \(\theta_0=0\). The target is realizable by \(\theta^\star=(20,1)\). The largest-residual rule chooses graph 1, although its sample-gradient norm is \(0.2\), versus 1 for graph 2. For one selected example and \(\eta=0.1\), full empirical squared loss changes from 1.25 to 1.248001 if graph 1 is selected, or to 1.2025 if graph 2 is selected.

Thus coefficient ordering alone does not provide the claimed gradient-size justification. Equal kernel diagonals would repair the single-example norm ordering; multiple-example correlations and full-loss descent still require analysis. This does not assert that the heuristic must always choose an optimal step or cannot help empirically. Together with the false sufficient-reduction proposition, it undermines the core analytic justification, while leaving empirical time savings to separate evidence.
result: Upperbound substitutedin negativequadraticterm invalid; largerresidual neednotmean largergradient orlargerfulllossdrop. False central reduction guarantee; analytic justification forheuristic not valid as stated.

analysis: Appendix A.3, equations (14)–(24), pp. 16–17, claims to derive the time weight used by the training scheme in Section 4.3. Equation (15) is not equal to its purported rearrangement (16). The resulting condition \(\lambda/c_{\rm out}^{2}=1\) reverses the factor needed for a unit-coefficient normalized regression target.

A direct identity check avoids any interpretation of training dynamics. At \(t=1/2\), \(a=1\), \(b=16\), \(Z_1=1\), \(Z_0=0\) and \(F=0\), the printed coefficients give \[c_{\rm skip}=-\frac{30}{17},\qquad

claim: Algorithm2 samples the teacher-logit distribution using the field trained by Eq13.
Independent Gaussian endpoints Z0 \(N(0,16I)\), Z1 \(N(\mu,I)\), \(\mu=(1,-1)\). Perfect conditional-expectation vector field; exact flow.
analysis: Equations (11)–(13), p. 4, use \(Z_t=tZ_1+(1-t)Z_0\), Gaussian noise at \(t=0\), teacher logits at \(t=1\), and regression target \(Z_1-Z_0\). Algorithm 2, p. 5, instead initializes that noise at \(t_N=1\), integrates to decreasing times, and finishes with \(z\leftarrow z-(t_1-t_0)u_\phi(t_1,z,x)\). This does not sample the target specified by the training path.

Fix \(x\), take independent \(Z_0\sim N(0,16I)\) and \(Z_1\sim N(\mu,I)\), with \(\mu=(1,-1)\) in a two-logit example. Define \[S(t)=t^{2}+16(1-t)^{2}>0.\] The population minimizer of the conditional squared-velocity regression is \[v^*(t,z)=E[Z_1-Z_0\mid Z_t=z]
 =\mu+\frac{17t-16}{S(t)}(z-t\mu).\] The exact solution from an arbitrary time \(s\) is \[z(t)=t\mu+\sqrt{\frac{S(t)}{S(s)}}\,[z(s)-s\mu].\] Differentiation verifies the identity directly, since \(S'(t)=2(17t-16)\). Correct forward integration from \(s=0\) transports \(N(0,16I)\) to \(N(\mu,I)\). Starting \(N(0,16I)\) at \(s=1\), as printed, instead gives \[Z_\epsilon\sim N\!\left(
 [\epsilon-\sqrt{S(\epsilon)}]\mu,\;16S(\epsilon)I\right).\] For \(\epsilon=0.001\), the mean is approximately \(-3.995000125\,\mu\) and the covariance is \(255.488272I\). The desired mean and covariance are \(\mu\) and \(I\). This smooth, nonsingular example rules out an explanation based only on endpoint instability or numerical solver error. The effect is not an irrelevant common logit offset.

Core dependency and counterevidence. The training-to-sampling connection is necessary to the paper’s principal distribution-distillation method, so an invalid sampling derivation warrants Major even if easily repaired. However, `edfm.py:171--204` constructs increasing times from 0 to 1 and uses positive Euler/Heun increments. `models/flowmatching.py:35--40` trains the matching forward target. Thus the available sampler already has the correct direction; there is no evidence here that Algorithm 2’s defect generated the published scores. A corrected paper algorithm should follow that increasing-time convention, or explicitly transform both time and velocity for a reversed convention.
result: Backward source initialization gives mean -3.995000125mu and covariance255.488272I at \(\epsilon=0.001\), rather than target. Invalid training-to-sampling connection in core printed method.

claim: Released ProxyEnDD implements per-example teacher-precision regularization for the stated baseline.

Batch size above1 and unequal teacher precisions. Proper symmetric Dirichlet students and realizable teacher sample precisions1,9. Closed-form optima use zero epsilon and fixed unshifted precision solely to isolate broadcasting; finite configured epsilon does not restore paired coefficients.
analysis: The released EnDD baseline mixes teacher precision across minibatch examples. In `metrics/losses.py:219--231`, the entropy-like `prior_term` has shape \((B,)\), but division by `t_prec[:, None]` produces a \((B,B)\) matrix. The final mean therefore replaces a mean of matched example terms by a product of means. This is a demonstrated objective error, not merely a possible shape concern.

Write \(A_i\) for the student Dirichlet KL penalty, ignoring constants independent of student parameters, and \(\tau_i\) for the corresponding teacher precision. Holding the code’s unshifted precision convention fixed to isolate broadcasting, the intended and actual terms are respectively \[\frac1B\sum_i\frac{A_i}{\tau_i},
 \qquad
 \left(\frac1B\sum_iA_i\right)
 \left(\frac1B\sum_j\frac1{\tau_j}\right).\] For \(B=2\), take student Dirichlets \((2,2)\) and \((3,3)\), whose KL penalties to the uniform Dirichlet are approximately \(0.125092803\) and \(0.267864048\). With \(\tau=(1,9)\), the paired penalty is \(0.0774277373\), while broadcasting gives \(0.109154681\).

The error can change learned diversity even at an ideal optimum. Let both teacher means be \((1/2,1/2)\), with precisions 1 and 9. These values are realizable by symmetric teacher predictions \((q_\tau,1-q_\tau)\) and \((1-q_\tau,q_\tau)\), where \[q_\tau=\frac{1+\sqrt{1-e^{-1/\tau}}}{2}.\] Substitution into the released precision formula yields \(\tau\). For a per-example coefficient \(c\), the proxy objective \[E_Q[-\tfrac12\log q_1-\tfrac12\log q_2]
   +c\,D_{\rm KL}(Q\|\operatorname{Dir}(1,1))\] is minimized by \(\operatorname{Dir}(1+1/(2c),1+1/(2c))\). Correct unshifted pairing gives \((1.5,1.5)\) and \((5.5,5.5)\). Broadcasting makes both coefficients \((1+1/9)/2=5/9\), so both optima become \((1.9,1.9)\). The distinction in teacher uncertainty is lost. These closed-form values use the ideal zero-epsilon objective and the unshifted convention solely to isolate broadcasting. For \(K\) uniform teacher classes the same variational identity gives the unique optimum \(Q_c^*=\operatorname{Dir}((1+1/(Kc))\mathbf1)\): the objective equals \(cD_{\rm KL}(Q\Vert Q_c^*)\) plus a constant. At the configured \(K=10\), precisions 1 and 9 give symmetric concentrations 1.1 and 1.9 when paired, but 1.18 for both inputs after broadcasting. Repeating the two types 128 times gives batch size 256. Uniform means with either precision are realizable using the ten cyclic permutations of \((p,(1-p)/9,\ldots,(1-p)/9)\), each repeated three times: the precision formula gives \(\tau=4.5/\Delta(p)\) with \(\Delta(p)=\log(0.1)-[\log p+9\log((1-p)/9)]/10\), which ranges from zero to infinity for \(0.1<p<1\). The configured epsilon perturbs these closed-form numbers but leaves the erroneous shared coefficient and identical per-input objectives intact.

Reachability and counterevidence. The official README’s EnDD command invokes `kd_and_endd.py` with `config/distillation/endd_c10_frnrelu.yaml`; that configuration selects `ProxyEnDD`, ten classes, batch size 256, thirty teachers and offsets 1. Lines 211–215 of the driver call this loss. Sections 5.2–5.3 and Figures 1 and 3 (pp. 1,6–7) make teacher-diversity transfer and full-distribution Wasserstein fidelity central comparisons; Appendix B, equation (39), specifies the per-example teacher-precision objective. The witness destroys precisely the conditional uncertainty that this baseline should preserve. It therefore supports Major for the official released comparison/reproduction route. Batch size one or equal teacher precisions remove this particular cross-example error, but general configured batches need not meet those conditions. The historical commit, predictions and corrected comparisons are not supplied; the direction and magnitude of changes to the published figures remain Needs Evidence.

There are two related specification distinctions. First, equation (39) divides by the shifted teacher precision \(\sum_k\widehat\beta_k=\tau+K\,t_{\rm offset}\), whereas the code constructs shifted `t_alphas` but uses unshifted `t_prec`. Second, the statement that the shifted Dirichlet mean equals raw-logit softmax is false: for ten raw exponential logits \((9,1,\ldots,1)\), the shifted mean’s first probability is \(5/14\), while softmax gives \(1/2\). Nevertheless, removing the training offset at prediction can intentionally recover the original ensemble mean when \(\widehat\alpha=\beta+1\). This counterinterpretation prevents inferring an unfair baseline solely from the use of softmax. The broadcasting defect is independent of that convention.
result: \((B,)\)/(B,1) gives(B,B); paired penalty.0774277373 becomes.1091546808; different intended uncertainties collapse to common optimum; generalK optimum Dir((1+1/(Kc))*ones), giving \(K=10\) pairedalpha1.1/1.9 versus broadcast1.18 for both; repeating128 times matchesB256. Major for the pinned official baseline reproduction/comparison route: shared precision coefficient erases input-specific predictive uncertainty even at the ideal optimum, directly damaging the teacher-diversity and full-distribution fidelity role. Historical figures or corrected scores are not attributed.

claim: For a correctly classified source image \(x\), let \(g(d)\) be the radial distance to the first adversarial boundary along \(\hat d=d/\|d\|_2\). Eq9 computes decision-boundary curvature and supports curvature-sensitive bridge metric.

\(x=(.5,.5)\), two-pixel domain\([0,1]^{2}\). rho=.01*(23-\(\sqrt3\)*\(\sin(\theta)\)-22*\(\cos(\theta)\)); original class interior. smooth closed regular boundary; positive radii; all rays unique. exact unit outward \(N\)=(.5,\(\sqrt3/2\)), \(d=(1,0)\). \(a=-.015<0,b=.15>0\); genuine bridge88/525 in(0,1).
analysis: Appendix B.3, p. 13, Eq. (9), identifies the decision boundary’s curvature in the physical two-dimensional plane with \(b/(1+a^{2})^{3/2}\), where \(a=G'(0)<0\), \(b=G''(0)>0\). This is the graph-curvature formula for \((k,G(k))\), not for \(z(k)\).

Take a two-pixel image space \([0,1]^{2}\), source \(x=(1/2,1/2)\), and the smooth radial boundary about \(x\) \[\rho(\theta)=r[1-\sqrt3\sin\theta+v(1-\cos\theta)],
\qquad r=1/100,\quad v=22.\] Assign the original class to the interior and the adversarial class to the boundary and exterior. Its radial extrema are \(r(23\pm\sqrt{487})\), approximately \(0.00931924\) and \(0.450681\). Thus every radius is positive, the entire curve is inside the pixel square, and every ray from \(x\) has exactly one boundary intersection. The curve is smooth and regular because \(\rho^{2}+(\rho')^{2}>0\).

At \(\theta=0\), the current boundary point is \(p=x+r(1,0)\), with \(d=(1,0)\). Since \(\rho'(0)=-\sqrt3 r\), the actual outward unit normal is \[N=\frac{(\rho(0),-\rho'(0))}{\sqrt{\rho(0)^{2}+\rho'(0)^{2}}}=(1/2,\sqrt3/2).\] Consequently the paper’s exact interpolation gives \[
G(k)=r\left[23-\frac{22-(19/2)k}{\sqrt{1-k+k^{2}}}\right].\] Direct differentiation yields \(a=-3r/2=-0.015\) and \(b=15r=0.15\), satisfying the stated derivative signs. Solving \(G(k)=G(0)=r\) gives the nonzero bridge \[k_{\rm bridge}=\frac{88}{525}=0.167619\ldots\in(0,1).\] Squaring is legitimate because \(22-(19/2)k\) is positive throughout \([0,1]\); the other root is \(k=0\). Moreover \(G(k)<r\) between these roots. This example therefore also has the bridge required by the method, rather than exploiting a missing-ray or missing-bridge pathology.
result: If the intended object is the auxiliary graph \((k,G(k))\), Eq. (9) is valid for that graph. It then cannot be used as a derivation of the physical decision-boundary curvature. Page 3 identifies detecting varied boundary curvatures as the first contribution; pp. 5–6 use the bridge threshold to characterize narrow high-curvature regions and motivate the escape rule. The missing geometric correspondence therefore affects a central explanatory contribution and supports Major.

This witness tests the exact Eq. (9), not the separate higher-order-neglect step in Eq. (10). No assumption that its cubic remainder is negligible is used. The example does not show the attack fails or loses benchmark accuracy. The correct general plane-curve formula is \[\kappa=\frac{|\det(z',z'')|}{\|z'\|^{3}},\qquad
z'=G'u+Gu',\quad z''=G''u+2G'u'+Gu''.\] It restores the curvature calculation, but a full revised relation between this curvature and \(k_{\rm bridge}\) remains unproved. Even for graph curvature, an inverse proportionality inferred from \(-2a/k_{\rm bridge}\) requires controlling \(a\) across the comparison.
Invalid exact physical-curvature derivation. core geometric interpretation and curvature-driven escape rationale.

analysis: Even granting the intended, exactly reversible residual convention, the transformed supervised coupling need not minimize the SB objective with only endpoint marginals constrained.

Use a legitimate additive-noise degradation, \[X\sim N(0,4),\quad E\sim N(0,1),\quad X\perp E,\qquad
 Y=X+E,\qquad U=Y-X=E.\] Here \(U\) is the pseudo-image and the inverse \(X=Y-U\) is exact. The transformed endpoint marginals are \(N(0,1)\) and \(N(0,5)\), while their data coupling has covariance one.

Choose unit Brownian reference diffusion starting from \(N(0,1)\). This is Equation (15)’s schedule \(\sigma_t^{2}=t,\bar\sigma_t^{2}=1-t\). The reference endpoint covariance and alternative coupling covariances are \[\Sigma_R=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \Sigma_c=\begin{pmatrix}1&c\\c&5\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad |c|<\sqrt5.\] Every \(\pi_c=N(0,\Sigma_c)\) has the same prescribed marginals.

For the path law \(P_c\) obtained by mixing reference bridges with endpoint coupling \(\pi_c\), disintegration gives \[H(P_c\mid R)=H(\pi_c\mid R_{01})
 =\frac12\{5-2c-\log(5-c^{2})\}.\] The independent check independently derived this expression from the Gaussian trace and determinant formula and checked: \[\begin{array}{c|c}
 c& H(P_c\mid R)\\ \hline
 1\quad\hbox{(hashed data)}&0.8068528194\\
 3/2&0.4941995442\\
 c_\star=(\sqrt{21}-1)/2&0.4172447380
 \end{array}\] The supplied paired coupling is therefore strictly suboptimal. At \(c_\star\), the off-diagonal precision entry equals the reference’s value \(-1\); the density ratio factorizes as \(f(U)g(Y)\). The resulting path law is Markov. For any competing law with the same marginals, the expectation of \(\log f(U)+\log g(Y)\) is constant, so relative-entropy decomposition proves this law is the marginal SB optimum. The comparison is not an artifact of allowing a non-Markov optimum.
An unconditioned network need not reproduce the entire supplied bridge mixture. The corresponding ideal-predictor interpretation also fails to attain the marginal optimum in this example.

Equation (15) samples \[Z_t=(1-t)U+tY+\sqrt{t(1-t)}\,\xi,\qquad
 S(t):=\operatorname{Var}(Z_t)=1+t+3t^{2},\] with independent standard Gaussian \(\xi\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(U,Z_t)=1\). Thus the ideal endpoint predictor is \(\widehat U(z,t)=z/S(t)\). The one-dimensional Gaussian conditional mean and median coincide, so this result does not require inserting a square into the printed loss norm.

The continuum reverse Brownian-posterior update has drift \[b_{\rm rev}(t,z)=\frac{z-\widehat U(z,t)}t
 =\frac{1+3t}{S(t)}z.\] Starting at terminal variance five, its variance remains \(S(t)\): \(S'=2(1+3t)-1=1+6t\). Equivalently, its forward drift is \(3tz/S(t)\). The independent check verified both variance equations symbolically. At \(t=1/2\), this construction has variance \[\frac94=2.25,
 \qquad\hbox{whereas the SB optimum has}\qquad
 \frac{6+\sqrt{21}}4\simeq2.645644.\] Hence even exact prediction in the continuous-time limit gives a different interior marginal. If instead the model conditions on the LQ endpoint and preserves the supervised pairing, the preceding endpoint-KL comparison applies directly.

A paired restoration objective may intentionally preserve the data coupling rather than optimize over all marginal couplings. That is a meaningful alternative objective. The result here concerns the claimed identification with Equation (3), not usefulness of supervised restoration. Reversible preprocessing alone does not supply the missing optimal-coupling condition. Indeed, \(Y\mid U=u\sim N(u,4)\), so this residual hash does not even eliminate all one-source/multiple-target relations.

The conditional Gaussian formula in Equation (15) itself checks: for independent increment variances \(a,b>0\), the bridge mean is \((bU+aY)/(a+b)\) and variance is \(ab/(a+b)\). The invalid step is promoting correct conditional bridges and reversible hashing to the asserted global optimality guarantee. This is another Major issue tied directly to the core theoretical contribution. No complete repaired optimality theorem or experimental score failure is claimed.

analysis: The paper argues that a single HQ image with multiple LQ outcomes prevents a unified Schrödinger bridge (SB), invoking uniqueness of an SDE solution from an initial value. This argument motivates PHM as a correction guaranteeing feasible, optimal, reversible solutions (pages 1–2, 5, 9, and 16). The inference confuses a unique stochastic law with deterministic endpoint transport.

Consider the allowed reference process \[dX_t=dW_t,\qquad X_0\sim N(0,1),
 \quad X_0\ \hbox{independent of }W.\] Its marginals are \(p_t=N(0,1+t)\). Prescribe \(\nu_0=N(0,1)\) and \(\nu_1=N(0,2)\) in Equation (3). The reference law \(R\) is feasible and \[H(R\mid R)=0.\] Nonnegativity and the zero condition for relative entropy imply that \(P^\star=R\) is the unique optimum. Nevertheless, \[X_1\mid X_0=x\sim N(x,1).\] Every fixed starting value has a nondegenerate distribution of degraded endpoints. Thus a unique optimal SB coexists with exactly the one-to-many stochastic relation declared problematic.

All densities are smooth and positive, with finite second moments. The forward drift energy is zero. Under the backward-time convention, the reverse drift is \(x/(1+t)\), whose expected energy is \[\int_0^{1}\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{X_t^{2}}{(1+t)^{2}}\right]dt
 =\log2<\infty.\] An independent symbolic check verified \(\partial_t p_t=\tfrac12\partial_{xx}p_t\), the endpoint covariance, and this energy. This example avoids singular Dirac endpoint or infinite-energy objections.

If a law is already pinned to \(X_0=x,X_1=y\) almost surely, then \(P^{xy}=P\). Theorem 4.1 can be read as this valid conditional statement. Likewise, one already-pinned law cannot simultaneously have two different terminal Dirac marginals. Appendix C’s choice of a Dirac endpoint measure is consistent with that narrow reading.

It does not establish the application’s general infeasibility claim. In the example above, conditioning additionally on \(X_1=y\) produces a Brownian bridge with drift \((y-X_t)/(1-t)\). Different conditional drifts can belong to one valid unconditional Markov law. Pathwise uniqueness fixes the driving Wiener path as well as the initial state; it does not remove random terminal outcomes.

analysis: The printed variance numerator uses eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\) of \(\Sigma\) paired with coordinates \(\mu_i\), without specifying that the mean is expressed in the covariance eigenbasis.

For \(X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)\), the coordinate-invariant formulas are \[\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\|X\|_2^{2}&=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma+\|\mu\|_2^{2},\\
 \operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^{2})
 &=2\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{2})+4\mu^\top\Sigma\mu\\
 &=\sum_i\{2\lambda_i^{2}+4\lambda_i(U^\top\mu)_i^{2}\},
 \quad \Sigma=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i)U^\top .\end{aligned}\] These follow by expanding independent Gaussian coordinates after orthogonal rotation. The lemma instead prints \(\sum_i(2\lambda_i^{2}+4\lambda_i\mu_i^{2})\). For \[\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mu=(1,0),\] the actual variance is \(28\). Pairing the original mean coordinates with eigenvalues \(1,3\) gives \(24\), or \(32\) after reversing their order. An invariant variance cannot depend on that ordering.

Appendix B explicitly states the correct rotated mean \(U^\top\mu\) before later writing \(\mu_i\). This is decisive counterevidence: reading those later coordinates in the eigenbasis restores the moment calculation and Chebyshev argument. The supported defect is a local mathematical statement/notation omission, not a failure of Gaussian norm analysis or a demonstrated violation of the claimed probability bound for a particular threshold. Replacing the numerator by the invariant expression above is analytically verified. No empirical result was shown to depend on the erroneous coordinate reading.

analysis: In `NINCO/detection_methods.py`, `evaluate_Relative_Mahalanobis_norm`, lines 548–662, training normalization is conditional on missing class-statistic caches. A later, separately conditioned global fit can consequently use raw features while the class fit and test features are normalized.

Test features are normalized at lines 569–570. Lines 572–580 load `mean_norm.npy` and `prec_norm.npy`. Training normalization at line 585 lies inside the branch at line 583 that runs only if these class statistics are incomplete. Global caches are checked separately at lines 607–617; on a miss, lines 623–629 estimate their mean and covariance directly from the current training array.

This state occurs in the documented workflow. README line 100 recommends `–method all`. `NINCO/evaluate.py`, lines 28–37, places `Mahalanobis_norm` before `Relative_Mahalanobis_norm`; line 416 selects this list. The loop at line 244 passes the same stored raw training array (assigned at line 109) and per-model cache path (line 217) to the two functions at lines 274–287. The first function normalizes by local rebinding at `detection_methods.py`:453 and saves the class caches at lines 468–469. It does not modify the caller’s raw array in place. The relative call then skips training normalization and, if its global caches are absent, fits a raw global Gaussian under normalized-cache filenames.

Take 1,000 classes with three raw training features each. In 500 classes use \[A=\{(2,0),(0,2),(-2,0)\};\] in the other 500 use \[B=\{(2,0),(0,-2),(-2,0)\}.\] All 3,000 vectors are nonzero, every class is nonempty, and the construction respects the source’s hard-coded 1,000-class loop. It tests the finite-feature estimator, which is defined without requiring the empirical features to be exactly Gaussian.

After normalization, the two distinct class means are \[\mu_A=(0,1/3),\qquad \mu_B=(0,-1/3),\] and direct centered sums give \[C=\operatorname{diag}(2/3,2/9),\qquad
 g=0,\qquad G=\operatorname{diag}(2/3,1/3).\] The raw global covariance is \(G_{\rm raw}=4G\), with the same zero mean. All three covariance matrices are positive definite. Let \(u=(0,1)\) and \(v=(4/5,3/5)\); both already have unit norm. Exact arithmetic yields:
Quantity | \(u | v\)
Minimum normalized class distance | \(2 | 32/25\)
Correct normalized global distance | \(3 | 51/25\)
Raw-global distance at normalized test point | \(3/4 | 51/100\)
Correct relative score | \(1 | 19/25\)
Mixed-coordinate relative score | \(-5/4 | -77/100\)

Thus the correct method ranks \(u\) above \(v\), but the mixed fit ranks \(u\) below \(v\). The discrepancy is not a common additive offset or an increasing transformation that would leave ranking metrics unchanged. The independent check verified these fractions symbolically and separately fitted the covariance matrices from the explicit 3,000-row synthetic array. Neither computation called author code.

analysis: Assessment: Major; a central closed-form transport theorem is false on its own model space.

Assumption-valid certificate. Take the upper-half-plane metric \(g=(dx^{2}+dy^{2})/y^{2}\) and the semicircle of radius one centered at \((1,0)\). Set \[v=1+i,\qquad u=\frac85+\frac45i,\qquad h_v=(1,0).\] Both points lie strictly in the upper half-plane on this geodesic; all tangent coordinate vectors are admissible. The left endpoint is zero, so the paper’s translation parameter is \(a=0\). Inversion sends \[\widetilde v=-\frac12+\frac12i,\qquad
\widetilde u=-\frac12+\frac14i,\] which are on the same vertical line. Thus the vertical scaling ratio in Equation (16) is \(1/2\). Substitution gives \[P_{\rm paper}h_v=\frac12J_{\rm paper}(\widetilde u)
J_{\rm paper}(v)h_v=(2/5,-3/10).\] Its target metric norm squared is \[\frac{(2/5)^{2}+(3/10)^{2}}{(4/5)^{2}}=\frac{25}{64},\] although \(\|h_v\|_{g_v}^{2}=1\). This contradicts the isometry property used by Equation (17). It is not a mesh-approximation error.

Lemma 4.3 also wrongly identifies arbitrary complex Möbius transformations with hyperbolic isometries and states that \(1/z\) is a self-isometry of the upper half-plane. But \(1/i=-i\) is outside that domain. The usual real-coefficient fractional maps with positive determinant preserve it; \(-1/z\) and real translations used in the corrected construction are valid. Thus the intended strategy survives, while the printed group statement and matrix calculation do not.

Spherical scope check. Theorem 4.1, pp. 5–6, sets \(e_1=u\), \(e_2=(u\times v)/\|u\times v\|\), \(e_3=e_1\times e_2\). For \(0<\theta<\pi\), \(v=\cos\theta\,e_1-\sin\theta\,e_3\), not the plus-sign endpoint printed for its path. Moreover, \(h_v=a e_3+b e_2\in T_vS^{2}\) forces \(a=0\). Its advertised source representation therefore does not cover a generic tangent vector. We do not present an \(a\ne0\) vector violating that hypothesis as a theorem counterexample. A correct generic, non-antipodal formula is \[P_{v\to u}h=h-\frac{\langle h,u\rangle}{1+\langle u,v\rangle}(u+v),
\quad h\perp v.\] For \(u=(1,0,0)\), \(v=(1/2,\sqrt3/2,0)\), and \(h=(-\sqrt3/2,1/2,0)\) it returns \((0,1,0)\). Decomposing \(h\) into the geodesic tangent and fixed perpendicular direction proves the formula. These coordinate and endpoint issues need correction, but the decisive false theorem in this Problem is the all-assumptions hyperbolic certificate.

The released geometry matrices and spherical frames are precomputed and unavailable for inspection; the README describes a more explicit exponential-map embedding. Neither the wrong printed matrix nor the spherical convention is attributed to historical runs without that evidence.

\(M=\mathbb R^{2}\) with flatmetric. \(N=(0,\infty )\)xR with d\(X^{2}\)/\(X^{2}\)+\(dY^{2}\). phi(\(x\),y)=(\(\exp(x)\),y) global exact isometry. Evaluatex0/JacobianI.
analysis: Assessment: Major for an invalid derivation directly supporting the central transport construction; the lemma’s conclusion remains true.

Lemma 4.4 is the commutation principle used in Theorem 4.5. In its proof, Appendix A.4, steps (50)–(51) and (56)–(57) discard derivatives of coordinate Jacobians, leading to Equation (54): \[\Gamma^k_{ij}\partial_k\phi^m
=\partial_i\phi^l\,\partial_j\phi^k\,\widetilde\Gamma^m_{lk}.\] This transforms connection coefficients as if they were a tensor.

Take \(M=\mathbb R^{2}\) with \(dx^{2}+dy^{2}\) and \(N=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\) with \(dX^{2}/X^{2}+dY^{2}\). The global diffeomorphism \(\phi(x,y)=(e^x,y)\) is an exact isometry, because its pullback metric is \(dx^{2}+dy^{2}\). At \((x,y)=(0,0)\), its Jacobian is the identity, source Christoffel symbols vanish, and \(\widetilde\Gamma^X_{XX}=-1\). Equation (54), with \(i=j=x,m=X\), says \(0=-1\).

The correct identity includes the missing term: \[\Gamma^k_{ij}\partial_k\phi^m
=\partial_i\partial_j\phi^m+
\partial_i\phi^l\,\partial_j\phi^k\,\widetilde\Gamma^m_{lk}.\] Here the omitted Hessian is \(1\), giving \(0=1-1\). The correct connection transformation already appears in the paper’s Equation (40); its later elimination is invalid.
result: Eq54says0=-1; correct identity includes Hessian and gives 0=1-1. Major invalid written derivation directly supports the central fast-transport construction; not a false lemma or benchmark-refutation claim.

Lemma 4.4 is a valid geometric principle: isometries preserve the Levi–Civita connection and hence parallel fields with the pushed-forward initial value. The false printed proof step does not invalidate that principle, and the principle does not validate Problem 2's incorrect differentiation.

analysis: Assessment: Major; the quantity used to select the core geometric branch is not a valid intrinsic Gaussian-curvature expression as written.

Equation (1), p. 3, defines \[\widehat K_i=\frac12\sum_{j\in N(i)}
\frac{v_j-v_i}{\|v_i-v_j\|_2}\,\varphi_{ij}\cdot n_i.\] Visual inspection confirms that the denominator is the Euclidean norm, with subscript \(2\), not its square. Figure 2 defines \(\varphi\) as the arccosine of the dot product of adjacent unit face normals. Thus \(\varphi\) is unchanged by reversing all normals.

Complete finite check. Use the regular octahedron inscribed in the unit sphere. At \(v_i=(0,0,1)\) the four neighbors are \((\pm1,0,0),(0,\pm1,0)\), and the consistent outward vertex normal is \(n_i=(0,0,1)\). Adjacent outward face normals have dot product \(1/3\), so every edge has \(\varphi=\arccos(1/3)>0\). Every unit edge from \(v_i\) has normal component \(-1/\sqrt2\). Therefore \[\widehat K_i=-\sqrt2\arccos(1/3)\simeq-1.74083950.\] The intrinsic angle defect at that convex vertex is \(2\pi-4(\pi/3)=2\pi/3>0\), and the underlying unit sphere has positive Gaussian curvature. Reversing the orientation makes the printed estimate positive, even though intrinsic Gaussian curvature is orientation independent.

Uniformly scaling all coordinates by \(s>0\) leaves every unit edge, normal, and dihedral angle unchanged. Hence \(\widehat K_i\) stays fixed, whereas the underlying sphere has \(K=s^{-2}\), and an angle-defect estimator divided by area also scales as \(s^{-2}\). This is an exact invariance failure, rather than an assertion that a coarse-mesh estimator must equal smooth curvature exactly. With the paper’s \(\epsilon=10^{-3}\), the outward-oriented example is assigned the negative-curvature branch of Equation (12).

Counterevidence and consequence. The current README explicitly says Gaussian estimates and principal directions come from `libigl`; `CURVGT.py` loads precomputed curvature and branch masks. Their generating source is absent. It is therefore not established that the experiments used Equation (1). The Major finding is the invalid printed geometric quantity directly feeding the central construction. An angle-defect-over-area expression is a possible discrete replacement, but its exact area convention, convergence assumptions, and correspondence to the historical preprocessing were not verified. No complete pipeline repair is claimed.

analysis: Assessment: Major within the released core parameter-sharing implementation; historical benchmark impact is unbound.

In the pinned `CURVGT.py`, line 292 contains \[\texttt{x\_j*(cur\_tree\_mask+1)\%2 + pt\_ed2*cur\_tree\_mask}.\] The comment says a masked edge should use the identity. The negative-curvature branch selects this expression at lines 295–297, and repeated tensor broadcasts call it at lines 313–315, 326–334, and 389–391. Ordinary operator precedence applies the remainder to the scaled feature, not to the mask.

For a binary mask \(m\) and intended linear transport \(T\), the actual scalar-coordinate operation is \[R_m(x)=\bigl((m+1)x\bmod 2\bigr)+mT(x).\] At \(m=0\), \(R_0(-1/2)=3/2\) instead of \(-1/2\); it is neither the identity nor an odd linear map. At \(m=1\), even a positive \(x=1/4\) adds an unintended \(1/2\) to \(T(x)\). With \(T\) equal to the identity this gives \(3/4\) instead of \(1/4\). The latter example is not needed to assume that every actual edge has identity transport: the erroneous additive term occurs for any \(T\).

The precise binary-mask correction is \((1-m)x+mT(x)\), or applying remainder to the integer mask before multiplying \(x\). Its two cases are verified algebraically. This repairs only the mask selection, conditional on correct frames and \(T\); it is not a certified repair of the entire source. The defect directly breaks the claimed linear, inner-product-preserving parameter transport used throughout the core subtree mechanism. Actual activation frequency, stored tensors, and effects on published scores remain unknown, since those artifacts were not inspected and this commit is not bound to the experimental version.

analysis: Assessment: Major for the frozen release’s core \(H^{1}\) evaluation; historical table values remain unverified.

The source builds a padded vertex-to-face incidence array using \(-1\) at lines 95–99. Both `H1Criterion` definitions, lines 674–691 and 829–846, index the face field with this array and average all slots without masking the padding. In this indexing convention \(-1\) means the last face.

For a vertex with incidence row \([0,-1]\), let the valid face gradient be \((1,0,0)\) and the unrelated final face gradient be \((3,0,0)\). Such different gradients are realizable by piecewise affine scalar fields on separate mesh triangles. The computed average is \((2,0,0)\) instead of \((1,0,0)\); with unit mass the gradient contribution is \(4\) instead of \(1\). Altering a nonincident face changes this vertex’s loss. The batch offset also uses the number of vertices rather than the number of face rows, although \(G\) produces face gradients; their equality is not guaranteed on the meshes in Table 4.

A correct padded average sums only valid incident faces and divides by their count, and each batch must offset by the actual face count. These statements are verified as indexing/aggregation identities; complete execution on the excluded meshes was not performed. Counterevidence is important: the feature-construction path does mask its face averages, and the training loss is the separate \(L^{2}\) routine. The demonstrated evaluation defect does not, by itself, identify errors in the paper’s historical \(H^{1}\) values.

The dependency is a core evaluation path. Equations (22)–(23) and Table 1 report \(H^{1}\) alongside \(L^{2}\) for all three PDE benchmarks. In the frozen source, lines 744–750 aggregate this faulty \(H^{1}\) loss; lines 801–809 use it during training evaluation and after loading the selected model. The second evaluation path calls the same defective aggregation at line 870 and prints and returns it at lines 877–885. Thus the admissible aggregation counterexample changes an actual primary evaluation output, not merely an unused helper. This supports Major for the frozen implementation. The separate \(L^{2}\) training objective remains unaffected, and the absent historical run binding limits attribution to published scores rather than the severity of this demonstrated evaluation failure.

claim:
Let \(P\) be the joint law of the \(N\) surrogate parameters and let each marginal equal \(P_\Theta\). For loss \(h_z(\theta)=\ell(f(\theta;x),y)\), write \[L_P(z)=\mathbb E_{\theta\sim P_\Theta}h_z(\theta),\quad
 L_E(z)=N^{-1}\sum_i h_z(\theta_i),\quad
 R(E)=\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_z N^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i h_z(\theta_i).\] The empirical attack must maximize \(L_E\) over the same feasible region used to define the population optimum. Under that optimization assumption, \[{\rm TE}=L_P(z^*)-L_P(z)
 \le \Phi_1(E)+\Phi_2(E)\le2\sup_z|L_P(z)-L_E(z)|,\] where \(\Phi_1=\sup_z(L_P-L_E)\) and \(\Phi_2=\sup_z(L_E-L_P)\). The proof of Lemma 3.2 survives. For an approximate empirical maximizer, its optimization gap must be added; the review does not assume a finite-step attack solves the maximization exactly.

For fixed \((x,y)\) and finite second moment, \[\mathbb E_\theta(f_\theta(x)-y)^{2}
  =(\mathbb E_\theta f_\theta(x)-y)^{2}+\operatorname{Var}_\theta f_\theta(x).\] This directly verifies Theorem 4.1, including the empirical analogue. Independent exact arithmetic with predictions \(-1,2\) and label \(1\) gives \(5/2=1/4+9/4\). The identity alone does not prove that changing the selected ensemble monotonically improves target attack success: the distributions, optimum, and loss can change together.

Appendix C.4, Eq. (25), p. 26, inserts independent Rademacher signs into differences between two independent copies of a jointly dependent ensemble, obtaining \[\mathbb E_P\Phi_1(E)\le2\mathbb E_P R(E).\] Equation (28), p. 27, repeats this for \(\Phi_2\). Such coordinatewise swaps preserve an i.i.d. product law, but need not preserve a dependent joint law. Absolute continuity with respect to the product law does not supply swap invariance.

Take \(N=4\), a fair sign \(T\in\{-1,1\}\), and \(\theta_1=\cdots=\theta_4=T\). Set \(\mathcal X=\{-1,1\}\), \(y=1\), \(f_\theta(x)=\theta x\), and \(h_x(\theta)=(1-\theta x)/2\in[0,1]\). Each marginal is fair. The product law \(Q=P_\Theta^{\otimes4}\) assigns positive probability to every sign tuple, so \(P\ll Q\); indeed \(H_2(P\Vert Q)=8\).

Population loss equals \(1/2\) at either input. Every realized ensemble has one input with empirical loss zero and one with loss one. Therefore \(\Phi_1=\Phi_2=1/2\). If \(S=\sum_{i=1}^{4}\sigma_i\), exact enumeration gives \(\mathbb E|S|=3/2\) and \[R(E)=\frac{\mathbb E|S|}{2N}=\frac3{16},\qquad
 \mathbb E_P\Phi_1=\frac12>\frac38=2\mathbb E_P R(E).\] The ghost-sample supremum before sign insertion has expectation \(1/2\); after the independently signed insertion it is \(3/16\). Thus the disputed equality and its concluding bound actually fail under the theorem’s dependence and bounded-loss assumptions.

analysis: Supported impact: Major for a central complexity claim.

Lemma B.3 adds positive homogeneity, which sigmoid does not satisfy. Restricting Lemma 4.2 accordingly would remove the preceding counterexample, but does not justify the remaining proof operations. First, the two-layer calculation on p. 17 removes Rademacher cross terms after taking an input supremum. With \(N=2\), scalar hidden activations \(V_1(x)=\max(0,x_1)\) and \(V_2(x)=\max(0,x_2)\) on \(\|x\|_2\le1\), direct four-sign enumeration gives \[\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_x|\sigma_1V_1(x)+\sigma_2V_2(x)|
 =\frac{\sqrt2+1}{2}>1
 =\sup_x\sqrt{V_1(x)^{2}+V_2(x)^{2}}.\] Thus the printed cross-term elimination is false even with ReLU and common scalar output weights. Second, Lemma B.3 concerns one common matrix \(W\) across summands. The subsequent layer removal on p. 19 applies this logic to distinct matrices \(W_{i,j}\). A bound by the maximum matrix norm does not permit factoring different matrices out of a signed sum. For example \(v_1=v_2=1\), \(W_1=1\), \(W_2=-1\), and signs \((1,-1)\) give \(|\sum_i\sigma_iW_iv_i|=2\) but \(\max_i|W_i|\,|\sum_i\sigma_iv_i|=0\). Third, pp. 19–20 introduce a maximizer \(W^*_{i,1}\) inside the sign-dependent supremum and subsequently cancel cross terms as if that maximizer were independent of the signs. With scalar \(x=1\) and freely selected \(|w_i|\le1\), \(\sup_{w_1,\ldots,w_N}\sum_i\sigma_iw_i=N\), not a quantity of order \(\sqrt N\). If the intended ensemble is fixed, this extra supremum changes the object; if it is genuinely optimized, independence cannot be assumed.

The linear fixed-ensemble bound on p. 16 is valid; it does not make these nonlinear steps valid. No counterexample to the final bound restricted to positively homogeneous ReLU networks is asserted here. A sound ReLU-specific argument remains needed. Merely adding a missing activation adjective does not resolve the demonstrated proof defects. Lemma 4.2 directly supports the headline guidance about ensemble size and model complexity and its substitution into the transferability analysis. The explicit stated-assumption counterexample and invalid core proof therefore support Major. Published accuracy tables are not declared false, and no benchmark loss is required for this assessment.

analysis: Supported impact: Minor, confined to Theorem C.1’s noisy extension. On p. 21, Theorem C.1 keeps the definition \(L_P(x,y)=\mathbb E_\theta(f_\theta(x)-y)^{2}\) at fixed \((x,y)\), but replaces \(\mathbb E_\theta(g(x)-y)^{2}\) by the label-noise variance \(\eta^{2}\). Averaging over model parameters does not average over the realized noise. For a single input, let \(g=1/2\) and every model predict \(1/2\). Let \(y=1\) with probability \(3/4\) and \(y=-1\) with probability \(1/4\), independently of the model. Then \(\rho=y-g\) has mean zero, variance \(3/4\), and is independent of the constant input. At the valid point \(y=1\), the actual risk is \(1/4\), whereas Eq. (14) gives \(3/4\). The variance identity is restored by explicitly averaging over noise as well. Theorem 4.1 uses the noiseless specialization and independently has the valid fixed-label proof above. This generalization error therefore does not invalidate the main decomposition; it supports a localized Minor finding, based on dependency rather than appendix location.
result: Model averaging cannot average fixed realized noise.

claim:
The paper seeks particle diversity while retaining low loss and low sharpness in Bayesian parameter-efficient fine-tuning. On p. 4, its joint loss for \(K\) particles is \[
 \ell(\theta_{1:K};x,y)
 =\frac1K\sum_{i=1}^K l(\theta_i;x,y)
   +\alpha l_{\rm div}(\theta_{1:K};x,y),
 \qquad \alpha>0.\] Let \(f^i_{-y}\) contain the prediction probabilities after deleting the true-label coordinate, and let \[
 F=\left[\frac{f^1_{-y}}{\|f^1_{-y}\|},\ldots,
          \frac{f^K_{-y}}{\|f^K_{-y}\|}\right]
 \in\mathbb R^{(C-1)\times K}.\] Section 4.3, p. 5, defines \(l_{\rm div}=\det(F^\top F)\). Page 6 identifies this with squared spanned volume and states the intention to maximize that volume, while retaining the positive sign in the minimized objective.

The statistical development uses an independent joint distribution \(Q^K\), with \(Q\) subsequently represented as \(K^{-1}\sum_i\mathcal N(\mu_i,\sigma^2I)\) and prior \(P=\mathcal N(0,I)\). Corollary 4.3 supplies the Gaussian complexity term used to motivate the practical objective. These are central links between the proposed mechanism and its formal justification.
Corollary4.3 Gaussian complexity substitution.
\(Q\) mixture N(\(\mu_i\),\(\sigma^{2}\)I), P N(0,I); \(d=1\), allmeans0,\(\sigma=0.1\).
analysis: Assessment: Major. Corollary 4.3 and its p. 18 proof use a false Gaussian KL expression in a central generalization-bound derivation.

Convexity in the first argument gives the valid mixture inequality \[\mathrm{KL}\left(\frac1K\sum_i\mathcal N(\mu_i,\sigma^2I)
       \,\middle\Vert\,\mathcal N(0,I)\right)
 \le\frac1K\sum_i
   \mathrm{KL}(\mathcal N(\mu_i,\sigma^2I)\Vert\mathcal N(0,I)).\] The proof then replaces the right side by \[
 \frac1{2K}\sum_i(\|\mu_i\|^{2}+d\sigma-d\log\sigma).\] For standard deviation \(\sigma>0\), direct expectation of the Gaussian log-density ratio instead gives \[
 \frac1{2K}\sum_i
 \bigl(\|\mu_i\|^{2}+d(\sigma^{2}-1-2\log\sigma)\bigr).\] The paper’s covariance notation and reparameterization \(\theta_i=\mu_i+\sigma\epsilon_i\) both identify \(\sigma\) as a standard deviation; interpreting it as a variance would not reproduce the displayed formula either.

Take \(d=1\), all \(\mu_i=0\), and the practical value \(\sigma=0.1\). Coincident mixture means are not excluded by the stated family, and the mixture is then exactly \(\mathcal N(0,0.01)\), so the mixture inequality is equality. Its actual KL is \[\tfrac12(0.01-1-2\log0.1)=1.8075850930.\] The printed substitution gives \(\tfrac12(0.1-\log0.1)=1.2012925465\), an underestimate of \(0.6062925465\). Thus the substituted expression is neither the asserted equality nor a valid upper bound in this case. This checks the Gaussian substitution itself; it does not purport to construct an entire statistical experiment violating every possible version of the final bound.

Conditional on the preceding theorem and its hypotheses, replacing the Gaussian term would produce the complexity contribution \[L\sqrt{\frac{\sum_i\|\mu_i\|^{2}+
       Kd(\sigma^{2}-1-2\log\sigma)+2\log(1/\delta)}{4N}}.\] The full PAC-Bayesian/DRO argument is not certified by this local correction. In particular, uniformity requirements, the loss bound, and the relationship between iid mixture draws and one draw from each component deserve separate checking.

The practical fixed-\(\sigma\) setting makes the erroneous part a constant with respect to the means, so this error alone need not alter their gradients or measured accuracy. It nevertheless invalidates the displayed derivation of a central formal bound. That supports Major under the requested standard without asserting that the final statistical inequality is false in every setting.
result: TrueKL1.80758509 > printed1.20129255. Core displayed bound derivation unsupported; not universal theorem falsity.

analysis: Assessment: Major. For binary classification, the normalized non-target construction cannot supply the claimed particle-diversity pressure, including for the reported Camelyon task.

For \(C=2\), every non-target vector is a positive scalar \(a_i\). Its normalization is \(a_i/|a_i|=1\). Therefore \[F=[1,\ldots,1],\qquad F^\top F=\mathbf1_K\mathbf1_K^\top.\] For \(K>1\), the printed determinant is identically zero, independent of all particle predictions. More generally, the printed determinant vanishes whenever \(K>C-1\), because the Gram matrix lacks full rank.

The release’s jitter does not restore a binary prediction signal. For a hard-label binary example, \[\det(\mathbf1_K\mathbf1_K^\top+\varepsilon I)
 =\varepsilon^{K-1}(K+\varepsilon).\] This is positive but constant. At \(K=4\), \(\varepsilon=10^{-7}\), its negative logarithm is \(46.9679925668\), with zero prediction derivative in exact arithmetic. This conclusion concerns mathematical signal, not floating-point residuals.

Page 7 states that the Bayesian methods use four particles. The staged `src/data.py`, lines 103–108, assigns two classes to `patch_camelyon`, and `configs/dro/patch_camelyon.yaml`, line 27, sets four particles. Camelyon appears in the main comparisons and diversity ablations. The counterexample is therefore tied to an actual low-class-count setting of the core mechanism, rather than an unrelated unsupported application.

The source masks coordinates using the target tensor. The exact code corroboration above uses hard labels, matching the mathematical definition of removing the ground-truth label. Soft-label masking conventions require separate care and are not used to claim an executed training result.
result: Robustness regularization, supervised loss, ensembling and other training differences may still improve Camelyon accuracy. The calculation does not falsify the reported score. Nor does it prove that all multiclass settings lack a diversity signal: regularized Gram objectives can vary in higher-dimensional cases.

The supported Major finding is the absence of the claimed explicit interaction signal in a reported application of the principal mechanism. Fixing the sign in Problem 1 alone does not fix it. A rank-aware diversity construction, a different representation, or a stated restricted domain would be needed. No replacement method or its empirical behavior is verified here.

analysis: The plotting implementation scales the random mean shift by \(1-\alpha\) instead of \(|\alpha|\).

In the released notebook `c2-figures-2-3-imperfect-info.ipynb`, source cell 4, both the bias and shift band widths are set to \((1-\alpha)\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta)}\). But for fixed true parameters the random shift is \(D=\alpha\widehat\theta-|\alpha|p_0\), whereas the random bias is \(B=(1-\alpha)\widehat\theta-(1-|\alpha|)p_0\). Therefore \[\operatorname{sd}(D)=|\alpha|\operatorname{sd}(\widehat\theta),
 \qquad
 \operatorname{sd}(B)=|1-\alpha|\operatorname{sd}(\widehat\theta).\] The released shift width is too large by \(7/3\) for the plotted \(\alpha=0.3\), and by \(7/2\) for \(\alpha=-0.4\), at nondegenerate points. Figure 2 and the page 5 discussion interpret the shaded bands as one-standard-deviation ranges; they are not 95% confidence intervals. The published image was inspected and is consistent in appearance with the released scaling, but no original plotting arrays or hash-bound generation receipt was available. The lemma assumes the original corruption conditions and \(0<h_t\le\tau\), and asserts \[\sum_t\|g_t-C_{h_t}\widetilde g_t\|\le2k\max(\tau,G).\] Choose \(d=1\), \(T=4\), \(G=k=1\), \(h_t=\tau=1/4\), losses \(\ell_t(w)=w\), and \[(g_1,g_2,g_3,g_4)=(1,1,1,1),\qquad

 \text{asserted upper bound}=2.\] The last line of the proof invokes the budget for \(\|g_t-C_{h_t}\widetilde g_t\|\) although the assumption bounds \(\|g_t-\widetilde g_t\|\). Uncorrupted rounds can acquire clipping error.

 \le \sum_t(G-h_t)_+ +2k\max(G,\tau).\] Indeed, insert \(C_{h_t}g_t\) by the triangle inequality. analysis: Assessment: Major. Appendix A.1, p. 12, defines \(G\) with positive expected log-policy, log-prior and log-transition terms. Both prose and Algorithm 1 then prescribe gradient descent: \[\theta^{k+1}=\theta^k-\eta_k\nabla_\theta G(\theta,\theta^k).\] Appendix A.2, p. 13, correctly specifies the M-step target as \(\arg\max_\theta G(\theta,\theta^k)\). These directions conflict.

For \(g=\nabla_\theta G(\theta^k,\theta^k)\ne0\) and sufficiently small positive \(\eta\), \[G(\theta^k-\eta g,\theta^k)
=G(\theta^k,\theta^k)-\eta\|g\|^{2}+O(\eta^{2}).\] The printed step therefore decreases the maximization target. Even generalized EM seeks an increase rather than necessarily an exact maximizer; the sign does not implement that weaker requirement either.

Use the exact posterior in Problem Problem 1 (#prob:forward), so this finding is independent of its erroneous E-step. The paper includes \(p(z_1)\) among the learned parameters. Holding the remaining model components fixed, parameterize \(p(z_1=A)=\sigma(\theta)\), where \(\sigma\) is logistic. For posterior \(q_A=3/4\), the varying part of \(G\) is \[G(\theta)=\tfrac34\log\sigma(\theta)
+\tfrac14\log(1-\sigma(\theta)).\] At \(\theta=0\), \(G(0)=-\log2\) and \(G'(0)=1/4\). The exact maximizer is \(\theta=\log3\). Parent independent arithmetic gives:
\(\eta | G(-\eta/4)\), printed descent | \(G(+\eta/4)\), ascent

Every descent value is below \(-0.6931471806\), while ascent increases it. The small-step example avoids dependence on an excessive learning rate. The block calculation is one valid optimization subproblem, and the preceding differential argument supplies the general sign conclusion. Actual values and source bindings are in .

analysis: Assessment: Major. Appendix A.2, p. 14, defines \(\alpha_{t,z}=p(s_{1:t},a_{1:t},z_t=z\mid\widehat\theta)\) but initializes \(\alpha_{1,z}=p(z_1=z\mid\widehat\theta)\). The recursion starts with the current action likelihood at \(t=2\). The stated terminal likelihood is \(\sum_z\alpha_{T,z}\), and the terminal posterior uses \(\beta_{T,z}=1\).

By the displayed formula, the required initialization is \[
\alpha_{1,z}=p(s_1)p(z_1=z)\pi_z(a_1\mid s_1^L).\] A common initial-state factor can be dropped from normalized mode posteriors if handled consistently, but a mode-dependent action probability cannot. The example below sets \(p(s_1)=1\), eliminating that possible distraction.

Use three states \(S=\{o,u,v\}\), two actions \(A=\{a,b\}\), two modes \(\{A,B\}\), history length \(L=1\), discount \(\gamma=0.95\), and entropy temperature one. The initial state is \(o\), and the initial modes have probability \(1/2\) each. From \(o\), action \(a\) reaches \(u\) deterministically and action \(b\) reaches \(v\). Both \(u\) and \(v\) are absorbing under either action. The hidden-mode kernel is the identity at every state.

This kernel is a valid state-independent special case of the stated state-conditioned model; no strict-positivity or irreducibility premise is imposed in the paper. It also makes the mode-specific policy optimal for the full process, removing any separate question about anticipated future mode changes.

Set \[d=\frac{1-\gamma}{\gamma}\log3,
\qquad
r_A(o,u,v)=(0,d,0),\qquad
r_B(o,u,v)=(0,0,d).\] Rewards are bounded, real and state-only. At an absorbing state \(s\), entropy-regularized optimal value is \[V_z(s)=\frac{r_z(s)+\log2}{1-\gamma}.\] At \(o\), the difference between the two mode-A action values is \(\gamma d/(1-\gamma)=\log3\), with the opposite sign in mode B. The Boltzmann policy therefore has \[\pi_A(a\mid o)=\tfrac34,\qquad
\pi_B(a\mid o)=\tfrac14,\] and each action at \(u\) or \(v\) has probability \(1/2\) in either mode. These emissions are derived from the paper’s soft-policy construction, rather than assigned arbitrarily.

The independent parent script constructs the soft values and action probabilities and checks their Bellman residuals. The reported maximum residual is zero at the used floating precision, below \(10^{-12}\); the auxiliary calculation independently confirms the construction.

Observe \(\xi=((o,a),(u,a))\). The environment transition factor is one. Exact joint weights are \[\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &z_2=A&z_2=B\\ \hline
z_1=A&3/16&0\\
z_1=B&0&1/16
\end{array}\] and hence \[p(\xi)=\tfrac14,\qquad
p(z_2\mid\xi)=(\tfrac34,\tfrac14).\] The printed initialization gives \(\alpha_1=(1/2,1/2)\). Even applying the subsequent recurrence correctly gives \[\alpha_2=(1/4,1/4),\qquad
p_{\rm printed}(\xi)=\tfrac12,\qquad
p_{\rm printed}(z_2\mid\xi)=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12).\] Thus the sequence likelihood doubles and the terminal mode-A posterior differs by \(1/4\). This calculation uses only the unambiguous terminal condition; it does not depend on the separate problematic backward boundary expression on the same page.

With the displayed formula, \(\alpha_1=(3/8,1/8)\) and \(\alpha_2=(3/16,1/16)\), restoring the enumerated likelihood and posterior exactly. These fractions are independently evaluated with exact rational arithmetic in the independent output cited above.

The E-step posterior weights determine reward fitting, hidden-mode transition fitting, and the inferred behavioral segmentation in main Eqs. (1)–(4) and Appendix A.1 Eqs. (5)–(7). The printed recurrence therefore fails at a central inference step for an allowed model. This supports Major even though the omission is short and a correct intended factorization is available elsewhere.

A reinterpretation of \(\alpha_1\) as a pre-emission message would require the recursion to multiply the first action before proceeding; the printed formulas do not do that. The joint on p. 13 is internal counterevidence about intended correctness, not a validation of the conflicting boundary formula.

The inspected release is correct on this point: `gw5/swirl/swirl_func.py`, lines 171–182, initializes log-forward values as `log(pi0) + log_likes[0]`. Lines 184–200 use the next emission in the backward scan; lines 202–224 construct normalized marginals and wire the E-step. Analogous first-emission terms occur in the inspected labyrinth and spontaneous-behavior routes. No released or historical run is claimed to omit the first action.

A consistent backward recursion from the displayed formula is \[\beta_{t,z}
=P(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t)
 \sum_{z'}P_z(z'\mid z,s_t)
 \pi_{z'}(a_{t+1}\mid s_{t+1}^L)\beta_{t+1,z'},
\qquad \beta_{T,z}=1.\] The printed p. 14 expression instead uses current-action and shifted state-conditioning indices, with a separate self-referential first-boundary line. Correcting all boundaries and indices to the joint resolves the specification. The forward correction is verified exactly on the finite case; no empirical performance repair or complete implementation rerun is certified.

result: The surrounding formulas evidently intend the signed convention \(z_-=\min(z,0)\). That alternative explains the error and is strong counterevidence against treating the theorem statements as false. The original rendered pages confirm that the conflict is not text extraction.

A global convention swap alone is insufficient to verify every proof line. On p. 19 the final contradiction uses equal positive expectations for \(G_-\) and \(G_+\); signed negative parts instead have opposite expectations. With the nonnegative convention each mean is \(1/\sqrt{2\pi}\), not the printed \(\sqrt{2/\pi}\). A valid local replacement is to square the asserted zero random variable on the disjoint loss-type events, yielding \[0=\tfrac12\{\mathbb P(\Omega_\nearrow)+\mathbb P(\Omega_\searrow)\}>0,\] a contradiction. These local repairs restore the inspected algebra; they are not a certification of a completely revised proof.

Printed p*: \(\mathbb E[p_*^{2}]\)=.5, E Gp=0, squared distance=1.5 vs phi=.5; cone fails with probability.25; constraint=.7071>0 at \(\delta=2\). Invalid derivation in both sides of Theorem3.4, the core dependency for Theorem2.7; finite theorem2.6 projection also affected.
claim: Exact half-normal moments plus independent 60-node Gauss-Hermite diagnostic and original-page visual checks.
Balanced null logistic with independent \(U\),\(G\) standard normal and independent \(Y\)=±1. Strict convex C1, integrability, noncoercivity, both Ass2.4=.5 and b=\(D\)=1 verified.
analysis: The paper explicitly defines \(z_-=\max(-z,0)\) on p. 3. Lemma A.1, p. 9, requires \(tU+p\leq0\) on \(\Omega_\nearrow\), but defines \(p(t)=-tU+(G+tU)_-\) there. It asserts cone membership, \(\varphi(t)=\mathbb E[(G-p(t))^{2}]\), and at the optimizer \(\mathbb E[p_*^{2}]=\mathbb E[Gp_*]\). These assertions are incompatible with the stated convention.

Let \(U,G\) be independent standard normals and let \(Y\) be an independent balanced sign. Use \[\ell_y(u)=\log(1+e^{-yu}),\qquad
\Omega_\nearrow=\{Y=-1\},\quad\Omega_\searrow=\{Y=1\}.\] Each loss is \(C^{1}\), strictly convex and nonconstant. Its infimum is zero and its Gaussian-input expectation is finite, since \(\ell_y(u)\leq\log2+|u|\). There are no coercive losses, so the probability requirement is satisfied. The two positive expectations in Assumption 2.4 each equal \(1/2\): independence gives one half of the second moment of \(U\). The growth condition holds with \(b=1,D(Y)=1\), using \(\log(1+e^u)\geq u\) and \(\log(1+e^{-u})\geq-u\). Both required moments of \(D\) are finite. This is an allowed single-index model with a constant response link, not a noiseless separable exception.

Symmetry and independence give \(\varphi(t)=(1+t^{2})/2\), so \(t_*=0,\delta_\infty=2\). The printed candidate is \[p_*=G_-I_{\{Y=-1\}}+G_+I_{\{Y=1\}}.\] On \(\{Y=-1,G<0\}\), of probability \(1/4\), it is positive where the cone requires it to be nonpositive. Exact half-normal moments give \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[p_*^{2}]&=\tfrac12,&
\mathbb E[Gp_*]&=\tfrac12(-\tfrac12)+\tfrac12(\tfrac12)=0,\\
\mathbb E[(G-p_*)^{2}]&=\tfrac32\ne\varphi(0)=\tfrac12,&
\mathcal G(p_*)&=1/\sqrt2>0.\end{aligned}\] Thus the asserted direction is infeasible even at the allowed boundary \(\delta=\delta_\infty=2\). An independently written 60-node Gauss–Hermite calculation in `check.py`/`calc.json` confirms respectively \(0.5,\ 2.03\cdot10^{-17},\ 1.5\). The analytical identities, rather than quadrature accuracy, establish the contradiction.

The proof of Lemma A.1 on p. 10 also uses \(z_-^{2}=z_-z\), which is false for the defined nonnegative negative part. The finite-dimensional projection on p. 13 repeats the same sign. Lemma E.1, pp. 18–19, uses the false moment identity to certify the nonexistence direction’s feasibility in the displayed formula. Its claimed bound on the ray loss fails too: at \(Y=-1,G=-1\), \(\ell_{-1}(p_*)=\log(1+e)=1.313262>\ell_{-1}(0)=0.693147\). The strict inequality persists on a positive-probability set.

For the existence branch, Lemma E.2, p. 20, forms \(\widetilde v=-aU+(aU+v)_-\) on increasing losses and asserts \((a,\widetilde v)\in C\). With \(a=0,v=G,\delta=3\), the input is feasible because \(\mathcal G(G)=1-\sqrt{3/2}=-0.224745<0\). Its expected loss is at most \(\log2+\sqrt{2/\pi}<2\), so it lies in an allowed sublevel set. Yet the constructed \(\widetilde v\) again violates the cone on \(\{Y=-1,G<0\}\). The projection inequality (25), followed by (26)–(27) on p. 21, therefore lacks its asserted premise. These steps support both sides of Theorem 3.4 and hence the nonlinear system’s phase transition in Theorem 2.7; the finite-dimensional proof of Theorem 2.6 also uses the projection. This is a consequential invalid core derivation, even though it has an evident local repair.

claim: Each one-sided tail is bounded by \(\exp(-2t^{2}/\text{sum centered MGF proxies squared})\). Independent bounded real input; G globally 1-Lipschitz; centered MGF proxy exactly 1/2.
analysis: Source claim: Theorem C.2, p. 17, defines ||X||_psi2 as the smallest a satisfying E exp(beta X)<=exp(beta^2 a^2/2), then claims each one-sided tail of a 1-Lipschitz function G of independent inputs is at most exp(-2t^2/S), where S=sum_j||X_j-E X_j||_psi2^2. The proof of C.1 explicitly applies this formula in Eq. (2), p. 18.

Complete counterexample: choose T=1, G(x)=x, X~Bernoulli(1/2), and t=1/2. G is globally 1-Lipschitz on R, independence is automatic, X is even bounded in [0,1], and E X=1/2. The centered MGF is cosh(beta/2)<=exp(beta^2/8), so the proxy is at most 1/2. Comparing second derivatives at beta=0 forces its square to be at least Var(X)=1/4; hence the minimum proxy is exactly 1/2.

\[\Pr\{X\ge1\}=\frac12,\qquad \exp\!\left[-\frac{2(1/2)^{2}}{(1/2)^{2}}\right]=e^{-2}=0.1353352832<\frac12.\] The lower tail at X<=0 gives the same contradiction. This is an analytic finite-distribution refutation, not a simulation. Replacing >= by > would not save the statement: take t just below 1/2. The issue is not an alternative convention for a norm because the paper supplies its exact MGF definition.

The cited primary reference, Kontorovich (2014), uses the subgaussian diameter of the symmetrized distance epsilon|X-X’| and a different exponential constant. Its Theorem 1, physical p. 4, does not state C.2’s substitution of the centered-input proxy. The relevant source PDF and hash are retained.

The advertised C.1 width also fails on the intended admissible-domain reading. Take n=m=1; one task containing the only skill; h=max and g=f=identity; decision ability X1~Bernoulli(mu),0<=mu<=1; action ability X2=1 deterministically. The noise family can be written X1=mu+sigma(B_mu-mu) with fixed sigma=1, B_mu~Bernoulli(mu); sigma2=0. All values lie in [0,1], the abilities are constant across difficulty, the decision family is stochastically increasing, and the two subskill draws are independent. Then Err=1-X1, L=1, Err_avg=1-mu, MinDer=1, and MaxDisp=1/4 over this family. Hoeffding’s centered MGF bound gives proxy squared at most 1/4 for every Bernoulli(mu), and equality holds at mu=1/2; hence the supremum is exactly 1/4.

\[\tau=\frac9{10},\quad\theta=\frac25,\quad\mu_c=\frac1{10},\quad\gamma=\frac12\sqrt{\log(5/2)}=0.4786153810.\] At mu=7/12=0.5833333, mu>=\(\mu_c\)+gamma=0.5786153810, but actual P=Pr(X1=1)=7/12<3/5=1-theta. Thus the upper guarantee fails. A second lower-branch example is recorded in the calculation JSON. If one insists on an unrestricted nonnegative parameter domain, the source must first define valid profiles there; that domain ambiguity does not rescue C.2 and is not concealed in this C.1 example.

Impact: this invalidates a substantial derivation of the central general-noise phase-transition guarantee and undermines downstream claims that use its unmodified constants. It does not by itself refute every bounded-uniform special case, the existence of threshold phenomena, or the observed simulations. In particular, in the positive-width, nondegenerate case, the main bounded-uniform statement can use ordinary bounded differences: each coordinate range is at most sigma_l, giving a valid tail bound with denominator \(L^{2}\) n(sigma1^2+sigma2^2); its stated width then has sufficient slack. The general-noise extension needs a distinct repair.

analysis: Source claim: Appendix C.2, pp. 20-21, considers the mean-zero scaled-uniform polynomial ability profile 1-s^beta and mean error aggregation. The printed formula has absolute-value bars: it claims |d Err_avg/d beta1|=(beta1/(2n))sum_j s_j1^(beta1-1). The objection is to this magnitude, not to a lost sign in text extraction. The paper then uses it to claim a zero derivative at beta1=0 and a lower bound (1/(4n))sum_j \(s_{j1}\) on beta1 in [1/2,2].
Because the noise has mean zero for every parameter value, the correct expectation and derivative, for interior difficulties 0<s_jl<1, are:

\[\mathrm{Err}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac1{2n}\sum_j(s_{j1}^{\beta_1}+s_{j2}^{\beta_2}),\qquad\left|\frac{\partial\mathrm{Err}_{\mathrm{avg}}}{\partial\beta_1}\right|=\frac1{2n}\sum_j s_{j1}^{\beta_1}\log(1/s_{j1}).\] The source expression is the derivative of s^beta with respect to s, rather than beta. A complete numerical check uses n=1,s11=0.9,beta1=1, any fixed interior s12 and fixed beta2, and any permitted scaled-uniform noise level, for example sigma=0.1. These profiles remain in [0,1]; all aggregators are averages and independent noises can be used. The actual derivative magnitude is 0.9 log(1/0.9)/2=0.0474122320. The printed magnitude is 1/2, and the claimed interval lower bound is 0.9/4=0.225, which is greater than the actual magnitude.

On the full local interval beta1 in [1/2,2], the true minimum in this example is 0.9^2 log(1/0.9)/2=. The magnitude of the right derivative at beta1=0 is log(1/0.9)/2=0.0526802578, not zero. For an unrestricted beta1>=0 the infimum is nevertheless zero as beta1 tends to infinity, so the global infinite-width conclusion can survive for a different reason.

analysis: Source claim: p. 6, ’Illustration with linear ability profiles’, states that opposite ability gaps of order sigma sqrt(log(1/theta)/n) imply P12-P_l>=1-2theta for both original workers. \[P_1=P_2=P_{12}=1,\qquad P_{12}-P_1=P_{12}-P_2=0<1-2\theta=0.8.\] The margins can be checked without guessing the hidden asymptotic constant. analysis: Source claim and location. Section 3.5, p.5, Eq.(9)–(10), defines a samplewise adaptive weight and states that it preserves the forward-KL limiting behavior as \(\alpha\)\(\to\)0. This supports the multi-divergence explanation in Section 3.1 and the interpretation of the ablation in Section 5.3. The printed new normalization contains no additive pseudo-Huber constant. Write w=w_DMD w\(\alpha\) and retain the common DMD weight exactly.

\[w_\alpha=\alpha\frac{\|s_q-s_p\|}{\|s_q-s_{m_\alpha}\|},\qquad
\gamma^w=\mathbb E_q\!\left[J_\theta g\, w_{\mathrm{DMD}}w_\alpha\frac{s_q-s_{m_\alpha}}{\alpha}\right].\]

Complete check. For 0<\(\alpha\)<1, positive p,q and \(\Delta\)\(\ne\)0, the valid mixture-score identity from Proposition A.2 gives \(s_q\)\(-\)\(s_m\)\(\alpha\)=D\(\alpha\)\(\Delta\) with D\(\alpha\)>0. Homogeneity of the norm then gives w\(\alpha=\alpha\)/D\(\alpha\). Substitution yields the following pointwise identity, before any expectation or limit.

\[w_\alpha\,\frac{s_q-s_{m_\alpha}}{\alpha}=\Delta,\qquad
\gamma^w=\mathbb E_q[J_\theta g\,w_{\mathrm{DMD}}\Delta]\quad(0<\alpha<1).\]

This is the same DMD-weighted reverse-KL direction as at \(\alpha\)=1. Before the new normalizer, the forward limit is (p/q)\(\Delta\): its density ratio changes the generated-data expectation to a real-data expectation. The new normalizer removes precisely that factor. Calling the update weighted does not preserve the missing \(\alpha\) dependence.

Implementation check. At pinned [R2], main/sjsd/sjsd_guidance.py:263–276 computes \[R=\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{mean}((p_\alpha-p_0)^{2})}
                   {\operatorname{mean}((p_1-p_0)^{2}+10^{-6})}},
 \qquad \mathrm{grad}=\frac{p_\alpha-p_0}{A R},
 \qquad A=\operatorname{mean}|p_1|.\] Exact mixture denoisers imply p\(\alpha\)\(-\)p0=D\(\alpha\)(p1\(-\)p0). Hence D\(\alpha\) cancels even with this stabilizer: the remaining factor depends on the reference difference, not \(\alpha\). The current implementation therefore does not rescue the claimed limit [E2].

Supported impact: Major. The failure directly affects the asserted divergence geometry of a central practical update. It leaves the unweighted derivation intact. Alpha can still affect learned-score approximation, amortization and the optional GAN regularizer. The finding does not assert that the whole algorithm, its finite training trajectories or its empirical ablation are \(\alpha\)-independent.

Parameters and assumptions. Use two dimensions, \(\sigma\)=1, p0=\(\tfrac12\)\(\delta\)_(1,0)+\(\tfrac12\)\(\delta\)_(\(-\)1,0), and g\(\theta\)(z)=\(\theta\) at \(\theta\)=(2,1). The latent may be standard normal and ignored. The noised laws are a two-Gaussian mixture p and q=N((2,1),I), both smooth, strictly positive and finite-moment. \(\mathbb E_q\)[\(\partial\)\(\theta\) log q]=0. Only their noised scores are used; the unnoised point masses do not enter the density differentiation.

\[f_p(y)=(\tanh y_1,0),\quad
\Delta(y)=(2-\tanh y_1,1),\quad
w_{\mathrm{DMD}}=\frac1{\|(2,1)-f_p(y)\|_1}=\frac1{3-\tanh y_1}.\]

The second coordinate of \(\Delta\) is one, so the score-difference norms never vanish. The DMD weight lies strictly between 1/4 and 1/2, so all weighted expectations exist. Let u(y)=((2\(-\)tanh y)/(3\(-\)tanh y), 1/(3\(-\)tanh y)). The actual weighted update for every interior \(\alpha\) is E_[N(2,1)]u. analysis: Source claim and dependency. Corollary 4.1, p.6, fixes \(\alpha\) and noise and states that a minimizer of Eq.(14) recovers both the fake score and log(p/q). The following text interprets this as density-ratio learning; Eq.(15) uses the factors separately, and Section 4.2 uses the ratio in a generator regularizer. Appendix A establishes only the combined mixture-score optimum. Existence of one correct factorization does not identify all minimizers.

Interior counterexample. Let p0=N(0,1), q0=N(1,1), \(\sigma\)=1 and \(\alpha\)=1/2. A generator is g\(\mu\)(z)=\(\mu\)+z with standard-normal z, at \(\mu\)=1. Then p=N(0,2), q=N(1,2), and m=(p+q)/2. All densities are positive and smooth, moments and DSM risks are finite, and the usual differentiation and score-mean conditions hold. Choose the following smooth, wrong learned factors.

\[\ell_\psi(y)=0,\quad D_\psi=\tfrac12,\quad
s_{\mathrm{fake}}(y)=2s_m(y)-s_p(y),\quad
s_{\mathrm{exp}}=\tfrac12s_p+\tfrac12s_{\mathrm{fake}}=s_m.\]

The DSM conditional-mean decomposition is a constant plus E_m||s_exp\(-\)\(s_m||{}^{2}\). Thus this pair attains the global minimum of Eq.(14), not merely a stationary point. It is also a legitimate fake density score, not an arbitrary nonintegrable vector field. With c=e^(1/2), h=N(2,2), one has q\({}^{2}\)/p=c h and

\[r(y)=\frac{p(y)+2q(y)+c h(y)}{3+c},\qquad
\nabla\log r=\nabla\log(m^{2}/p)=2s_m-s_p.\]

The mixture weights are positive and sum to one. Moreover r is the \(\sigma\)=1 convolution of the same weighted mixture of N(0,1), N(1,1), N(2,1). Even requiring a normalized density score obtained under the same noising process does not exclude the construction. The regression theorem states no architectural or additional identifying constraint that forbids these function-space factors.

Both claimed conclusions fail: the true log ratio is 1/4\(-\)y/2, not zero; at y=0, \(s_q\)=0.5 while \(s_{\rm fake}\)=0.437823499114. The replay verifies the density normalization and exact combined-score identity, with numerical score residual below 8.89\(\times\)10^\(-\)16 [E1]. The scientific defect is the invalid inference from mixture-score identification to separate component identification.

Generator consequence. Let D*=p/(p+q). For the location parameter \(\mu\), the Jacobian is one and \(\Delta=s_q\)\(-\)\(s_p\)=1/2. The correct divergence gradient is \(\mathbb E_q\)[D*]. At the wrong global Eq.(14) minimizer above, Eq.(15) uses D\(\psi\)=1/2 and \(s_{\rm fake}\) separately, producing 1\(-\)\(\mathbb E_q\)[D*].

\[\gamma_{\rm true}=2\mathbb E_q[D^*\Delta]=\mathbb E_q[D^*],
\qquad \gamma_{\rm wrong}=\mathbb E_q[(D_\psi/\alpha)(s_{\rm fake}-s_p)]
=1-\mathbb E_q[D^*].\]
Check | Result
Correct divergence gradient | 0.44406083715653066
Eq.(15) at wrong global DSM minimizer | 0.5559391628434693

Thus even exact estimation of the combined mixture score does not suffice for the proposed separate-factor gradient. Major is supported by a false central identification guarantee and its direct methodological dependency. The fact that the correct pair is also a minimizer is important counterevidence to a stronger allegation of impossible learning, but does not establish the corollary’s identification claim.

Practical counterevidence. The paper trains across \(\alpha\) and emphasizes mass at \(\alpha\)=0. More decisively, the released SMD trainer sums a separate fake-only DSM loss with real/fake interpolated losses (main/sjsd_dist/train_sjsd_dist.py:376–379). Its interpolation detaches component predictions while training the gate [R2,E2]. This richer objective is not identical to the fixed-\(\alpha\) premise. The counterexample is not an empirical failure of that implementation.

A precise restricted replacement is available. Assume exact realizability and simultaneous attainment of a joint objective with positive weight on \(\alpha\)=0 and at least one interior \(\alpha\). The \(\alpha\)=0 term forces \(s_{\rm fake}=s_q\) almost everywhere. The interior term then forces (D\(\psi\)\(-\)D*)(\(s_p\)\(-\)\(s_q\))=0. Therefore the log ratio is identified wherever \(s_p\)\(\ne\)\(s_q\). This is an analytic statement about exact minima, not a finite-training convergence guarantee.

The nondegeneracy condition matters. If p=q, choosing \(s_{\rm fake}=s_p\) gives the correct mixture score for every \(\alpha\) and any ratio head, so the objective cannot force \(\ell\)=0. The score-based generator gradient is nevertheless zero. Appendix D.3 explicitly assumes accurate component scores and is consistent with this limitation; it is not a proof of the original simultaneous-identification claim.
