Complete instance. Set d=1, let target contexts be i.i.d. Uniform[0,1], let the source covariate density be gP(x)=1/2+x, and draw source prices independently and uniformly on [0,1]. Source triplets are i.i.d. with deterministic revenue YP=pP. Target revenue is also deterministically Yt=pt. Thus f(x,p)=p in both domains and the optimal price is one.

Every operative condition is satisfied. The source density integrates to one, lies between 1/2 and 3/2, and differs from \(Q_X\), giving genuine covariate shift. \(P_X\)(B) >= (1/2)QX(B) on every ball, so the exact nonnegative transfer exponent is gamma=0 with \(c_\gamma\)=1/2. Independent uniform source prices give kappa=1 exactly. Uniform target mass obeys r <= \(Q_X\)(BX(x,r)) <= 2r, so cQ=1,CQ=2. The revenue is bounded and Lipschitz with CLip=1. Set CI=1 and Cr=2; then Cr^4 \(c_\gamma\) cQ=8, exactly the tuning requirement.

Correct result. The first price remains Uniform[0,1] for every possible source dataset and every nP. Its expected regret is integral from zero to one of (1-p) dp = 1/2. All later regret terms are nonnegative. Therefore total expected regret is at least 1/2, independently of the source sample size.

Contradiction with the stated bound. Take integer m>=10, \(n_Q\)=m and nP=\(m^{8}\). All constants above stay fixed and the prescribed radius is positive and less than 1/2. The claimed bound is C m[log(m+\(m^{8}\))/(m+\(m^{8}\))]^(1/4), asymptotic to C(8 log m)^(1/4)/m, which tends to zero. No allowed fixed C can dominate the first-round loss. This growing-target sequence avoids relying on a fixed-horizon asymptotic reading.

Proof dependency. Appendix B.1, Eq.(16), pp.13-14, uses the optimistic index-maximizing property of the initially selected ball. Algorithm 1 then replaces that ball by a child centered on the already selected context/price. Eqs.(20)-(21) and the source-rich counting step charge regret to the small final-child radius as though it retained the same argmax property. If the symbol means the original root, it may have no parent and cannot receive the child’s radius bound; if it means the final child, it was not chosen by that argmax. The distinction is essential to the claimed transfer benefit.

claim: \(p_X\ge c_\gamma*\widetilde r^\gamma*q_X\) everywhere =>exact inf exponent0 for every fixed hard instance; claimedgamma>0 not attained as exact value.
analysis: Source claim. Appendix C Step 2, p.25, claims that the distributions constructed in Eqs.(68)-(69), p.23, have transfer exponent equal to the prescribed gamma and hence belong to the class used in Theorem 4.4. Definition 2.3, p.3, defines the exponent by an infimum over all admissible positive constants. [R1, R4]

Complete check of that inference. Write a=\(c_\gamma\) rtilde^gamma, which is strictly positive for any fixed constructed instance with finite gamma and positive rtilde. On each inner covariate box the source density is a times the target density; outside the outer boxes the two densities agree; in the remaining regions the target density is zero. Therefore \(p_X\)(x) >= a \(q_X\)(x) pointwise everywhere, and \(P_X\)(B) >= a \(Q_X\)(B) for every measurable ball B. Exponent zero is admissible with constant a. Nonnegative exponents then imply that the infimum in Definition 2.3 is exactly zero.

For example, with prescribed gamma=1, \(c_\gamma\)=1 and rtilde=1/32, the constructed density ratio on the target’s inner support is 1/32, and outside the boxes it is one. The correct exact exponent is zero, while the proof asserts one. This is a countercheck of the construction’s membership claim, not an admissible instance used to falsify the final lower rate.

Alternative interpretation. In transfer-learning bounds it is often useful to index a class by any exponent satisfying a fixed-constant mass inequality, rather than by the smallest exponent. On that larger admissible-exponent interpretation, the construction may satisfy the intended inequality with the advertised fixed \(c_\gamma\). But that is different from the literal infimum definition, and the proof explicitly claims equality. The fact that a depends on the horizon does not prevent exponent zero for each fixed distribution; it does explain why a uniform fixed-constant class is a different object.

Dependency and judgment. Under the paper’s literal exact-exponent class, the proposed hard instances with gamma>0 do not establish the claimed minimax lower bound for that class. This is a substantial invalid membership step in the core optimality derivation and supports Major with that precise interpretation. Recasting the model as an admissible-exponent class removes this specific objection, but the separate information-bound failure below remains. No complete corrected lower theorem or replacement exact-exponent construction is verified.
\[p_X(x)\ge a\,q_X(x)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad P_X(B)\ge a\,Q_X(B),\qquad a=c_\gamma\widetilde r^\gamma>0,\qquad \gamma_{\inf}=0.\]

claim: r1/32,kappa0,nP1000; one fixed policy chooses uniquelyempty source price bin. Under everycenter law EOu/nQ>=1-31*\((30/31)^{1000}\)>.9999999999998, whileown-lawboundrequires1/16.
analysis: Source claim. Appendix C Step 3.2, p.27, Eq.(79), uses a counting argument to choose a price-bin index u visited at most 2nQ/L times in expectation for many alternatives, where L=floor(1/rtilde). It then sets the common bump center ptilde to that bin and defines the source price density in Eq.(70). The resulting visit bound is used in the target KL calculation, Eq.(82), and ultimately in the matching lower-bound rate. [R1, R4]

Invalid inference. A pigeonhole argument is valid under a fixed collection of probability laws. Here the laws of the adaptive action counts already depend on the bump center through both the reward function and the source-price distribution. After selecting u, redefining the center changes those laws. The preceding average over bins does not supply a self-consistent low-visit center.

A concrete fixed-policy witness makes the failure explicit. Set rtilde=1/32, L=32, kappa=0 and nP=1000. In the candidate family whose center is bin u, Eq.(70) gives zero source-price probability to that bin and equal probability 1/31 to each of the other 31 bins. Use one policy for every possible u and every sign vector: count all source prices in the 32 bins; choose the center of the uniquely empty bin, breaking multiple-empty ties by a fixed rule; then use that price on every target round. The policy uses only observed source data and is admissible.

With probability at least 1-31(30/31)^1000, every nonempty bin has appeared in the source data. On this event the policy identifies the true empty bin u. Thus, for every candidate u and every sign vector, its expected count in the subsequently declared bump bin is at least [1-31(30/31)^1000]nQ. This exceeds 0.9999999999998 \(n_Q\), whereas Eq.(79) requires at most nQ/16. There is no candidate center satisfying the needed inference for this fixed policy.

Assumption and scope checks. Kappa=0 is explicitly allowed. Source prices are independent of source contexts and signs, and source triplets remain independent across time. The witness works with the paper’s covariate construction at gamma=0,\(c_\gamma\)=1/2: the inner density ratio is 1/2, the outside ratio is one, and positive shell mass gives genuine covariate shift. Its exact exponent is zero, so the witness does not rely on Problem 2. Rewards can be the paper’s bounded Lipschitz Bernoulli bump family. It refutes the selection/count inference at this construction step; it is not asserted to refute the minimax lower theorem itself.

Impact and repair. The extra small-bin visitation factor is used to obtain the target information budget and hence the claimed continuous-price minimax exponent. Replacing the argument requires a valid fixed-reference change-of-measure or another hard family; neither is supplied by the displayed pigeonhole step. This substantial invalid derivation supports Major. The abstract possibility of the same minimax rate, and the target-only lower-rate claim with a different proof, remain open within this inspection. No full repair is certified.

analysis:

The following counterexample proves failure, rather than merely identifying a missing proof step. Set \[\mathcal X=\mathbb R,\quad X\sim{\rm Uniform}[0,1],\quad Y=1,\quad
s(x,1)=x,\quad n=1,\quad\alpha=\tfrac12,\quad m=2,\quad\delta=\tfrac18.\] All draws are independent. The domain is closed and convex, the score is continuous and 1-Lipschitz, and the conformal rank is valid. Then \(q_\alpha=X_{\rm cal}\). Condition on \[q_\alpha\in(0.499,0.501),\] an event of calibration probability \(0.002>0\). A positive-probability set of failing calibrations suffices to refute the theorem’s almost-sure qualifier.

Define \(h(x,\epsilon)=x+g(\epsilon)\), where \(g\) is the continuous piecewise-linear interpolant of \[(0,0),\quad(0.26,0.26),\quad(0.27,-0.27),\quad(0.48,0.48),\] and \(g(\epsilon)=0.48\) for \(\epsilon\ge0.48\). The cone \(|g|\le\epsilon\) is convex, so all segments obey the attack budget. The attack is fixed independently of every sample and of \(q_\alpha\).

Here \(\delta'=1/16\). The binomial-inversion formulas in Eqs. (14)–(15) give a lower endpoint \(L_2=1/4\) when both restrictive indicators succeed, an upper endpoint \(U_0=3/4\) when both conservative indicators fail, and a lower endpoint \[L_1=1-\sqrt{15}/4=0.03175416\ldots\] when exactly one restrictive indicator succeeds. For the two evaluation inputs, consider these three disjoint events:
1. Both are below \(0.239\). At \(\epsilon=0.26\) both restrictive indicators succeed, but \(\gamma_h=q_\alpha-0.26\in(0.239,0.241)<L_2\).
2. Both are above \(0.771\). At \(\epsilon=0.27\) both conservative indicators fail, but \(\gamma_h=q_\alpha+0.27\in(0.769,0.771)>U_0\).
3. One is below \(0.019\) and the other above \(0.241\). At \(\epsilon=0.48\) exactly one restrictive indicator succeeds, but \(\gamma_h=q_\alpha-0.48\in(0.019,0.021)<L_1\).

The first and third events are disjoint because the latter has an input above \(0.241\); the second is disjoint from both because each has a small input. Their total probability is \[0.239^{2}+0.229^{2}+2(0.019)(0.759)
=\frac{34601}{250000}=0.138404>\delta=0.125.\] Thus, for every calibration in the stated interval, the claimed simultaneous event fails with probability exceeding its permitted risk. analysis: Section 4.2, p. 7, claims that calibration on the underlined score \(\underline s_{\rm lip\text{-}rcp}\) of Eq. (19) yields the same result as robust inference by quantile translation equivariance. Actual visual inspection confirms the underline. Equation (19), p. 6, defines this as \(s-K\epsilon\), where \(K=L_nL_s\).

Translation equivariance instead gives \[q_{\rm lower}=q_\alpha-K\epsilon.\] Ordinary inference with that threshold tests \(s\le q_\alpha-K\epsilon\). Robust inference tests \[s-K\epsilon\le q_\alpha
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad s\le q_\alpha+K\epsilon.\] These are opposite shifts. The equivalent calibration uses the upper score \(\overline s=s+K\epsilon\).

For a complete probabilistic witness, retain \(\mathcal X=\mathbb R\), \(X\sim{\rm Uniform}[0,1]\), \(Y=1\), \(s=x\) and independent draws, now with \(n=9\), \(\alpha=0.1\), \(K=1\) and \(\epsilon=0.1\). Its marginal coverage is \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(M-0.2)_+]
&=\frac9{10}-0.2+\frac{0.2^{10}}{10}\\
&=0.70000001024<0.9.\end{aligned}\] This integrates the density \(9u^{8}\) of \(M\); it is also verified with exact fractions. Robust inference, or calibration on the upper score, includes iff \(X\le M\) and has coverage \(0.9\).

analysis: Objective 4.1 (p. 4) optimizes \(\operatorname{cov}_{\beta}(\Lambda_\pi)\) for the expected feature matrix of one trajectory. Proposition A.1 (pp. 15–16) instead proves that an adaptive sequence of \(n_\beta\) episodes visits each supported terminal feature once, then concludes that the terminal-feature probabilities are \(1/n_\beta\). The latter does not follow for the last episode, nor for each individual episode, without specifying how the output episode is selected.

Consider a deterministic one-step MDP with two actions leading to terminal features \(e_1,e_2\), zero nonterminal features, a fixed initial state, and behavior probabilities \((0.9,0.1)\). This satisfies the formal assumptions with \(n_\beta=2\), \(0<\epsilon<0.1\), and finite actions. Initially either terminal gives maximal coverage, so the conditioned first-episode distribution is still \((0.9,0.1)\). In episode two the policy chooses the previously unvisited terminal, giving marginal probabilities \((0.1,0.9)\), not \((1/2,1/2)\). For \(\lambda=0.01\), the one-episode objective is \[f(p)=\left((p+\lambda)^{-1}+(1-p+\lambda)^{-1}\right)^{-1},
 \qquad f(0.9)=0.098137\ldots< f(1/2)=0.255.\] This refutes the individual-episode interpretation of the final probability statement. It does not refute the cumulative-coverage induction: both features are visited exactly once. A uniformly sampled episode from the two-episode interaction has the optimal distribution. More generally, specify the output as the uniform mixture of the \(n_\beta\) episode policies, including their induced histories, or define the objective using normalized cumulative occupancy. Then the proof’s conclusion follows by linearity and the convexity of \(x\mapsto1/(x+\lambda)\). The phrase “after playing for \(n_\beta\) episodes” plausibly intends precisely this interpretation, so the established finding is a Minor output-policy specification ambiguity. The example does not refute the intended cumulative-coverage guarantee, and the original per-episode optimality interpretation is not certified. The main informal proposition also replaces zero nonterminal features by a common extra coordinate; its fixed contribution does not disturb the balancing argument.

The internal induction was checked under its stated deterministic, finite-action, positive-support assumptions: before the last round an unvisited supported terminal exists, its conditioning event has positive probability, and an action with no supported continuation to such a terminal has conditional mass zero. The notation \(w^{\pi_\beta}(s)\) is defined for terminal visitation but later applied to intermediate states; a time-indexed reachability probability would avoid this additional local notational defect.
result: Exact two-terminal example: episode marginals (.9,.1) and (.1,.9); each has coverage .098137..., whereas uniform mixture .255. analysis: Rating: Major. Locations: p. 6, Theorem 4.4, Eqs. (24)–(31); p. 13, Theorem A.2, Eqs. (43)–(50) and recurrence (59); p. 14, Eqs. (65)–(68).

Use the two-dimensional, four-bit max–min floor/clamp quantizer of Eqs. (19)–(22). For a nonconstant vector \(u\), set \(m=\min u\), \(M=\max u\), \(s=(M-m)/15\), \(z=\lfloor-m/s\rfloor\), and \[Q(u)_i=s\{\operatorname{clamp}(\lfloor u_i/s\rfloor+z,0,15)-z\}.\] Define \(Q(u)=u\) for constant vectors, including zero. This supplies the zero-range case left undefined by the scale formula and satisfies the abstract theorem’s requirement \(Q(0)=0\).

Take \(A=[1,0]:\mathbb R^{2}\to\mathbb R\), whose spectral and Frobenius norms both equal one, and \[x=(-6.999,8.001),\quad Q(x)=(-6,8),\quad
 \|x\|^{2}=113.002002,\quad
 |A(x-Q(x))|^{2}=0.998001.\] The scale is one and zero point six. All decimal inputs here are exact terminating rationals.

For (R1), take \(T=3\), \(a_3=0\), \(a_2=x\), \(a_1=2x\), and evaluate \(t=1\). Both increments are \(x\), giving \(\widetilde o_1=-12\) and \(o_1=-13.998\). Therefore \[\|o_1-\widetilde o_1\|^{2}=3.992004
 >3c\|x\|^{2}=3.39006006.\] This strictly violates Eq. (30)/(49).

For (R2), take \(T=4\), \(a_4=a_3=a_2=0\) and \(a_1=x\). All earlier updates are zero; the final compensated output is \(AQ(x)=-6\). Therefore \[\|o_1-\widehat o_1\|^{2}=0.998001
 >(2c)^{2}\|x\|^{2}=0.0452008008.\] This strictly violates Eq. (31)/(50).

An exact-Fraction computation and a separate implementation agree on all values and assertions. These sequences can be independent degenerate random variables, so the pre-theorem independence sentence does not exclude them. No unbiased quantization, random error cancellation, nonzero initialization or diffusion-specific input restriction appears among the theorem’s hypotheses. The norm-one projection removes matrix-norm ambiguity. The bandwidth corollary gives a sufficient generic bound, not an additional restriction excluding a quantizer whose stronger global bound has been proved directly.

The proof’s Eq. (67) also prints a plus sign before a quantized term where the residual requires a minus sign. Correcting that sign alone does not repair the reversed geometric weights. These replacement bounds are reviewer derivations, not claimed author corrections.

Both core quantitative inequalities and their derivation are invalid. This merits Major without requiring a benchmark score reduction or difficulty of repair. The corrected recurrences preserve a substantial part of the method’s qualitative rationale. No conclusion is drawn that all generated images fail, that reported quality scores are false, or that compensation cannot be useful. The paper itself notes that nonlinear feedback in a full diffusion network goes beyond this fixed-operator model.

analysis: Rating: Minor, release-scoped. Locations: Section 5.1, p. 7; Appendix D.2, p. 17; README lines 61–85; `scripts/sample_diffusion_ddim.py:145,620`; `scripts/sample_diffusion_ldm.py:421,551`; `qdiff/quant_layer.py:134--208,307--347`.

The paper distinguishes channel-wise activation LCQ from tensor-wise LTQ and says the main activation scale uses each channel’s minimum and maximum. The pinned entry points pass `args.act_tensor` directly to `channel_wise`; the flag is false by default and described as enabling tensor-wise activation quantization. The documented CIFAR and LSUN dynamic commands omit it.

For an activation of shape \(N\times C\times H\times W\), the quantizer’s true branch reduces all three trailing dimensions and reshapes the remaining scales to \((N,1,1,1)\). The false branch takes extrema over the entire input and produces one scalar. The wrapper sends conventional convolution activations, possibly split along channels, without moving the channel axis to dimension zero. Thus neither route creates the advertised \(C\)-axis scales: for \((N,C,H,W)=(2,3,1,1)\) the scale shape is \((2,1,1,1)\) or scalar, not \((1,3,1,1)\).

Preserving axis zero is appropriate for output-channel weight tensors, and per-example quantization can reasonably be called tensor-wise. The defect concerns the described activation channel axis and default reproduction commands, not terminology alone. Stable Diffusion’s deliberately tensor-wise setting is also not refuted.

This static discrepancy prevents equating the pinned documented route with the stated LCQ configuration. Historical experimental impact remains Needs Evidence because exact experiment commits/configurations and logs were not supplied. A repair should make the activation channel axis explicit and align defaults and flag meanings. No author-code or patched-code run was performed.

analysis: Severity: Minor; a supported reproduction discrepancy with unmeasured historical effect. Section 4.2, page 5, says that test images are resized and then center-cropped to \(224\times224\). analysis: Location and classification. Appendix C Algorithm 1 versus `maskgen.py`:67–100. Minor confirmed release/specification discrepancy; applicability to the reported runs is Needs Evidence.

Algorithm 1 forms a backward softmax using the backward temperature. In the released function, the lines constructing that softmax are commented out; a hook instead multiplies the gradient at the forward logits by \(\tau_f/\tau_b\). Freeze the temperatures by taking the permitted adaptation rate zero, let \(l=(1,-1)\), \(g=(0,0)\), \(\tau_f=1\), and \(\tau_b=3\). If \(J(p)=\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top\), the source then yields \(J(p_f)/\tau_b\), where \(p_f=\operatorname{softmax}(l/\tau_f)\), whereas Algorithm 1 yields \(J(p_b)/\tau_b\). Their first diagonal entries are approximately 0.0350 and 0.0747. Scaling the forward Jacobian cannot generally substitute the differently shaped backward softmax Jacobian. The independent calculation verifies the discrepancy; it does not execute autograd or the author program. With equal temperatures the two coincide, which limits the affected scope.

There is also a noise-scaling difference. The source uses \((l+g)/\tau_f\), so its hard argmax is unchanged by any positive forward temperature for fixed \(l,g\). The paper uses \(l/\tau_f+g\). For \(l=(1,-1)\), \(g=(-0.4,0.4)\), the latter changes its chosen index between temperatures 1 and 3, while the source does not. These strict comparisons persist in a neighborhood of the noise values. The reference implementation therefore cannot be assumed to validate the written two-temperature algorithm. A repair needs one specified estimator and a matching forward/backward implementation, followed by new gradient and empirical checks. No such author-code repair was run.

analysis: Location and classification. Section 2.2, Eqs. (3)–(5), and Appendix B.1, Eqs. (19)–(21), pp. 4 and 13–14. Major: a central derivation of the optimization objective is invalid.

The identity \(I(X;X^m\mid Y)=\mathbb E_{X,Y}D_{\rm KL}(p(X^m\mid X,Y)\Vert p(X^m\mid Y))\) is valid. It does not permit replacing \(X^m=X\odot M\) by \(M\). The map from \(M\) to \(X^m\) depends on the very random variable \(X\) whose information is being measured; it is not a fixed invertible transformation of one variable. Equality of conditional distributions cannot be obtained by merely renaming the argument.

Take a length-two univariate sequence \(X=(Y,Z)\) where \(Y,Z\) are independent uniform signs, and let the black-box classifier read the first coordinate. All quantities are finite and discrete, so no differential-entropy singularity is involved. Two admissible fixed masks give
\(M | I(X;X^m\mid Y) | I(X;M\mid Y) | I(X;Y\mid X^m)\)

Both masks preserve the classifier’s predictions exactly, so the semantic JS constraint in Appendix B.1 cannot remove this counterexample. The full mask retains one bit of independent nuisance information; the mask itself is constant and conveys none. With the reported prior \(r=1/2\), both deterministic mask laws have the same finite prior penalty \(2\log 2\), so the proposed mask penalty does not distinguish their different nuisance retention.

The same mismatch can be exhibited with strictly interior mask probabilities. Compare masks independent of \(X\) with retention probabilities \((3/4,1/4)\) and \((3/4,3/4)\) under prior \(r=1/2\). Both have mask penalty \(2[(3/4)\log(3/2)+(1/4)\log(1/2)]\), while their retained nuisance information is respectively \(1/4\) and \(3/4\) bit, by the erasure channel on \(Z\). The first-coordinate mask distribution is identical, so the expected semantic penalty for a classifier of that coordinate is also identical. This pair has equal semantic penalty, rather than the perfect fidelity of the deterministic pair.

The issue is not confined to deterministic endpoints. If both mask entries are independent Bernoulli\((1/2)\) variables independent of \(X\), then \(p(M\mid X)=q(M)\) and \(L_{\rm mask}=0\), while \(I(X;X^m\mid Y)=1/2\) bit. The nonzero signs make an erased coordinate distinguishable from an observed coordinate. The independent script enumerates all 16 equally likely joint outcomes to verify these values. This second case isolates the regularizer; unlike the fixed-mask pair, it is not claimed to satisfy perfect semantic fidelity.

A valid variational identity would instead be \[\mathbb E D_{\rm KL}(p(M\mid X,Y)\Vert q(M\mid Y))
=I(X;M\mid Y)+\mathbb E_YD_{\rm KL}(p(M\mid Y)\Vert q(M\mid Y)).\] It concerns the mask, not the retained values. An actual derivation for the criterion must keep \(X^m\) in the conditional distribution, or add and justify assumptions linking its information to the mask. An alternative honest repair is to call \(L_{\rm mask}\) a mask-prior regularizer and withdraw the asserted derivation/equivalence. Sparsity and fidelity penalties may still improve the practical model, but empirical usefulness does not restore the missing identity. No complete replacement guarantee is verified here.
claim: Information in retained signal cannot be replaced by information in mask.
Admissible finite length-two inputs, binary masks and well-defined entropies; semantic condition explicitly checked for fixed masks.
result: Invalidates core theoretical derivation, not empirical performance by itself.

analysis: The discussion following equation (8), page 5, attributes instability near \(u=0\) to normalized weights and their gradients vanishing. As an explanation of the displayed operator, that behavior is incorrect in general.
result: There is a null derivative in the radial direction, and a downstream loss may annihilate other derivative directions. Neither fact implies vanishing normalized weights or a vanishing full Jacobian near zero. At \(v=0\), equation (8) is undefined. An implementation using \(\max(\|v\|,\varepsilon)\) can make the output approach zero within the floor region, but its local derivative is then \(\operatorname{diag}(b)/\varepsilon\), again generally nonzero. The inspected `normalize_weights` function calls `F.normalize`; it does not establish the claimed general mechanism.

A defensible replacement is that exact normalization removes radial information, is undefined at zero, and can have large transverse sensitivity near zero. In contrast, \[R_{\mathrm{scale}}(0,b)=b,\qquad
 D_uR_{\mathrm{scale}}=\operatorname{diag}(b).\] These identities support a local conditioning distinction. They do not prove globally stable optimization or measured improvements. Equation (9) and the reported empirical gains are not refuted. The assessment is Minor: this is a local mathematical explanation error, and no logical dependence of the core performance conclusion on the erroneous vanishing argument has been established.

Output=(1,0), norm1; Jacobian \(\operatorname{diag}(0,1/r)\), transverse derivative diverges as \(r\)→0. Local mechanism error. Eq.(9) and empirical performance are not refuted; no core performance dependency demonstrated.

claim:

 \] The normalized expression requires \(u\odot b\ne0\). Grouping requires divisibility of the input width by the group count; it imposes no additional restriction that changes the following per-column calculation. Periodic activations occur downstream.

The latent code is sampled from an encoder posterior and mapped to INR parameters by the HD. analysis: The arrays in `experiments/image_metrics.py` accumulate all observations seen so far, but the entire cumulative dataframe is appended after every batch. The saved rows therefore do not form a once-per-example evaluation dataset.

Metric accumulation occurs at lines 85–92; prefix FID calculation and broadcasting at lines 94–102; dataframe construction and `to_csv(..., mode=’a’)` at lines 105–108 in the pinned snapshot [code]. The defect matters when a run has at least two nonempty batches and its CSV is interpreted as an ordinary table of evaluation observations.

For \(B\) equal-size batches of \(b\) examples, the file receives \(b,2b,\ldots,Bb\) rows, totaling \[b\sum_{i=1}^B i=\frac{bB(B+1)}2\] instead of \(bB\). An observation from batch \(j\) appears \(B-j+1\) times. With two one-example batches whose PSNR values are \(10\) and \(30\) dB, the written rows are \(10,10,30\); their mean is \(50/3\) dB instead of \(20\) dB.

FID is recomputed on each cumulative prefix and broadcast over that prefix’s rows. For illustrative prefix FIDs \(5\) and \(3\), the file contains \(5,3,3\); its mean is \(11/3\), whereas the final full-set statistic is \(3\). Averaging prefix FIDs does not produce a full-set FID. These numbers are synthetic serialization inputs, not measured LDMI activations. The independent diagnostic records them without importing or executing repository code.
result: The in-memory arrays accumulate each observation once. The final progress-bar PSNR and FID can therefore be correct despite duplicated serialized rows. The final appended block also contains every PSNR once together with the final FID, so a reader deliberately selecting that block can recover a valid summary. Neither the paper nor the inspected files establishes that Tables 1–4 were computed by averaging the entire CSV.

For a fresh evaluation file, a precise correction is to write the completed PSNR array once after the loop and store the final global FID separately as a summary scalar. Alternatively, per-prefix records must be explicitly labeled and cannot be interpreted as independent observations. analysis: Source claim: Appendix E.2, p. 23, theoretical runtime item 1(a), states that for fixed ambient dimension the alpha complex has a number of simplices linear in the number of points. This is distinct from the preceding empirical observation that Figure 11 appears linear on two particular data families. The unconditional combinatorial statement is false already in dimension three.
\[P_i=(i,0,0),\quad Q_j=(0,j,1),\quad 0\le i,j<m,\qquad N=2m.\]

For every adjacent pair on each line, the four points \(P_i\), P(i+1), \(Q_j\), Q(j+1) form a tetrahedron of nonzero determinant -1. Set x=i+1/2, y=j+1/2 and z=(\(x^{2}-y^{2}\)+1)/2. Their circumsphere has center (x,y,z) and squared radius 1/4+y^2+z^2.

Hence all (m-1)\(^{2}\) such tetrahedra are strict Delaunay cells, and the full alpha filtration eventually includes them. The size is at least quadratic in N, despite dimension three being fixed. Strict inequalities allow small generic perturbations; the argument does not require an ambiguous cospherical triangulation. The reviewer replay checks exact instances m=3,5,10, while the formulas establish the entire family.

analysis: Source claim: Theorem C.1(v), p. 18 extends the sphere support result to any contractible union M of (n+1)-simplices whose boundary n-simplices satisfy the empty-circumsphere condition. Its proof, p. 19 infers that a contractible M has boundary homotopy equivalent to an n-sphere, then transfers the support argument. Contractibility alone does not supply either that boundary topology or the common filling scale used for spheres.

Take n=1. In local coordinates define five points and let M be the union of the two filled triangles OAB and OCD. Translation of this entire configuration will be used on the next page to satisfy even the theorem’s opening sphere premises.
Point | Local Euclidean coordinates

M is star-shaped about O and hence contractible. Its boundary is two triangular circles meeting at O; all five points are boundary points. Both filled triangles have strict empty circumdisks and are Delaunay cells. Every one of their six boundary edges is strictly Gabriel relative to the whole local point cloud: no other point is in or on its diameter disk. Exact squared-distance tests are saved; the smallest Gabriel margin is 1/2.
Event | Alpha radius
Small triangle fills | 1/sqrt(3)
Large triangle boundary edges appear | 3/2
Large triangle fills | sqrt(3)
Any cross edge between nonshared triangle vertices | At least sqrt(13)/2 > sqrt(3)

Throughout the large persistent class’s lifetime (3/2, sqrt(3)), the local complex is therefore a filled small triangle joined at O to an unfilled large circle. Any interpolation gamma in (0,1), including the default 0.3, selects a scale within this same interval. These are actual alpha-filtration events, not an arbitrary abstract complex substituted for the paper’s geometry.

An interpretation concern must be addressed: C.1 begins with random samples S on a unit sphere and allows arbitrary extra points at distance at least 2 from S. The five-point configuration alone is not such a sphere sample. To avoid relying on whether ’more generally’ cancels the opening premise, retain that premise explicitly.

Let S consist of three independent uniform points on the unit circle centered at the origin. Translate the five local points and M by T=(100,0), and define X=S union (T+{O,A,B,C,D}). The external points are fixed independently of the random sample. Every translated point has norm at least 97, so its distance from every point of S is at least 96, far exceeding the required 2.

All relevant local Delaunay circumdisks and Gabriel disks lie strictly to the right of x=95; thus no point of S enters them. Every simplex joining the two components has circumradius at least 48, since it contains an edge of length at least 96. Consequently the local alpha complex and all previous strict inequalities remain unchanged through radius sqrt(3). Almost surely, the three noncollinear sphere samples form a filled triangle at radius 1; this separate component contributes no first homology during the large class’s lifetime.

Even if one additionally imports the Gabriel condition for S itself, there is a positive-probability event on which it holds. Require one sample in each arc of angular radius pi/24 centered at 0, 2pi/3 and 4pi/3. This has probability 6(1/24)^3=1/2304. Consecutive angular gaps are between 105 and 135 degrees, making the triangle acute, hence its edges strictly Gabriel. The failure below persists throughout that event, so it cannot be dismissed as a measure-zero special configuration.

M is a contractible subset of the Delaunay triangles of this full X and meets every explicitly imposed boundary condition. Thus the embedded example also covers inheritance of the initial sampling/separation premises. A further restriction that M must use only vertices of S would exclude it, but that restriction is not stated in the universal ’any contractible subset M’ clause and would narrow the claimed extension.

Evidence: math_audit_embedded_replay.py/results.json proves the uniform bounds and checks an illustrative exact matrix realization. The probability argument uses the full arc event, not a claim that one fixed equilateral sample has positive probability. The earlier local example and its narrower-scope notes remain preserved.

Use edge order OA, OB, AB, OC, OD, CD. Let \(c_s\)=(1,-1,1,0,0,0) and \(c_l\)=(0,0,0,1,-1,1). The oriented boundary of M is g=\(c_s\)+cl. Both are real cycles, so no finite-field lifting failure is involved. During the entire interval above, the local curl space is spanned by \(c_s\), the boundary of the filled small triangle.
\[P_{\rm curl}g=c_s,\qquad P_{\rm harm}g=c_l,\qquad F(O,A,B,C,D)=(1/2,0,0,1,1).\]

The first homology is one-dimensional at this scale; every nonzero representative of the surviving class has the same normalized harmonic support. There is no basis-selection ambiguity. Under the printed coface weights, the three small edges have W=1/4 and the large edges W=1. The transformed input is 2cs+\(c_l\) and the weighted curl direction 2cs; projection again gives cl. The released inverse-first-power weights also remove the small component.

Thus the stated support is all five points of M, whereas the calculated support is only {O,C,D}; all sphere-component values are zero. A and B are boundary vertices, so replacing ’points contained in M’ by ’boundary points’ does not fix this example. The standard algorithm appropriately discards an already-filled component, contradicting the overbroad guarantee rather than the Hodge machinery.

Dependency: Section 3, p. 6 and the conclusion, p. 9 invoke C.1 as theoretical support for recovering point-level topological structure. Part (v) is the step extending that guarantee beyond the common-scale sphere setting. Its invalid boundary inference and missing filtration-scale control yield a demonstrably false support conclusion. Major is supported for this core theoretical extension, independently of whether the empirical clustering scores survive.

Counterevidence: the inspected C.1(i)-(iv) sphere proof retains a common filling radius 1, boundary births below 1 and separation from mixed simplices. Those conditions avoid this failure. Contractibility alone, or a change in boundary wording, is insufficient for the arbitrary-contractible extension.

analysis: Assessment: Major for the core released implementation; historical experimental attribution Needs Evidence. Section 3 and Figure 3, p. 3, motivate sparse loss and gradient computation through selected base-model weights while retaining dense LoRA branches. The pinned `sparselora/modules/linear.py`, lines 19–22 and 30–40, instead performs activation gather and output scatter inside `torch.no_grad()` blocks. This removes the selected base path from reverse-mode differentiation.

The source path is not an unreachable utility. In `registry.py`, lines 33–47, a PEFT base projection is assigned `out_scatter` or `in_gather`. The API replaces eligible linear modules at `api.py`, lines 101–123. The attention module passes selected indices to those projections at `llama.py`, lines 71–88 and 104–108. In `linear.py`, lines 51–71, the patched adapter forward adds the base result to the dense LoRA result.

The finding assumes an enabled sparse layer with a nonempty proper subset of channels, a frozen base weight, and an input that depends on an upstream trainable adapter. These are ordinary fine-tuning circumstances. The selected index set can be held fixed locally; no derivative of a top-\(k\) decision is required.

For `out_scatter`, the selected matrix multiplication is initially differentiable with respect to its input. The subsequent `scatter_add` is evaluated under `no_grad`, so the assembled output loses that graph. For `in_gather`, the input gather itself is detached. Multiplication by a frozen base weight cannot restore the missing dependency. PyTorch’s primary documentation confirms that computations inside this context are excluded from the reverse-mode graph even when inputs require gradients. Neither gather nor scatter-add is a factory-function exception.

Let an upstream scalar adapter parameter produce \(x(\theta)=(\theta,0)^\top\). Take frozen \(W=\operatorname{diag}(2,3)\) and retain channel 0. The intended selected base computation produces \(y=(2\theta,0)^\top\), with \[L(\theta)=\tfrac12\|y\|^{2}=2\theta^{2},\qquad
 \left.\frac{dL}{d\theta}\right|_{\theta=1}=4.\] A fixed-index scatter or gather must preserve this derivative. Treating the selected result as detached gives contribution zero instead. An independent rational-arithmetic central difference at \(\theta=1\), with step \(10^{-6}\), is exactly \(4\). No author function was imported or executed, and this is not represented as a PyTorch runtime test.

The same reasoning applies if residual or LoRA branches are present: those branches can still carry gradients, but the selected frozen-base contribution is missing. Freezing a weight eliminates its own parameter update; it does not eliminate the Jacobian needed to train parameters preceding that weight.
claim: Location: Section3/Figure3 p.3; modules/linear.py19-22,30-40; registry.py33-47; api.py101-123.
Paraphrase: Sparse selected-weight loss and gradient computation with dense adapters.

Pinned release a2fd69de93b1168080346ec113c99501f0bb58b1. Enabled sparse PEFT base projection; proper channel subset. Frozen base weight; input depends on upstream trainable parameter. Indices fixed locally; no derivative through top-\(k\) required.
result: Keeping LoRA dense does permit learning, and dense tokens and other paths remain active. Thus this finding does not show that training completely stops, that all gradients vanish, or that any printed benchmark number is false. Deliberately using a stop-gradient approximation is another possible algorithm, but it is not the selected-weight backpropagation described in the paper and requires explicit characterization.

The acquired release is pinned, but no historical training commit or raw run log ties these exact lines to the reported experiments. That part of the conclusion is Needs Evidence. The release-level defect is nevertheless material: it changes the optimization mechanism and may reduce backward work beyond channel sparsification. It therefore affects both algorithmic fidelity and the interpretation of a speed measurement made with this implementation. Major is supported for the core implementation without requiring an observed accuracy loss.

The scoped correction is to leave mask prediction or index selection outside autograd if desired while retaining differentiable activation gather/scatter operations. This restores the selected base Jacobian. No source was modified, no repaired training run was performed, and neither corrected accuracy nor corrected speed is claimed.

Release omits selected frozen-base contributions to upstream gradients. Major released implementation defect; historical accuracy and speed effects remain Needs Evidence, not demonstrated benchmark damage.

C full Frobenius ball radius \(r>0\). \(M=N\) scalar response. \(p>n\). \(\mu\)>0.
analysis: Section 4.1, p.4, defines the sparse-case neighborhood as the full Frobenius ball \(C=\{B:\|B-A^*\|_F\le r\}\) and Assumption 2 demands, for all \(A,B\in C\), a positive \(\mu\) such that \[L(B)\ge L(A)+\langle\nabla L(A),B-A\rangle+\tfrac\mu2\|B-A\|_F^2.\] The following text asserts that the curvature conditions can be proved with high probability. For scalar responses (\(M=N\), explicitly allowed in Section 3.1), vectorize the coefficient to \(p\) coordinates and write the design as \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\). If \(p>n\), choose a nonzero \(h\in\ker Z\). For any \(r>0\) choose \(0<t<r/\|h\|\). Taking \(A=A^*\), \(B=A^*+th\) gives \(L(B)=L(A)\) and \(\langle\nabla L(A),th\rangle=0\), while the final term is strictly positive. The assumed inequality is impossible.

This holds for every underdetermined design, including every realization of independent standard Gaussian entries satisfying Assumption 4 with population covariance \(I\). Increasing signal size to satisfy the minimum-signal assumption does not change the kernel. The script also checks \(Z=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) and \(h=(-1,-1,1)^\top\), for which \(Zh=0\) and at \(\mu=1/2\) the unsatisfied quadratic term is \(3/4\) before rescaling.

Interpretation and impact. This does not refute Theorem 5 as an implication conditional on Assumption 2: in the stated regime its antecedent is unavailable. It does invalidate the advertised application of that full-ball hypothesis to high-dimensional scalar regression with \(p>n\). This is Major for that core scope claim. A sparsity-restricted cone or a tolerance-bearing curvature inequality could be suitable, but would require changed assumptions, an argument that the error lies in the admissible set, and a new proof. The actual full-ball definition cannot be replaced silently. Overdetermined designs and other restricted formulations remain possible.

claim: \(F\) and the displayed \(F\)-perp decompose general error/gradient inner products.

analysis: Section 4.2.2, p.5, defines \(F=\{W:\operatorname{col}(W)\subseteq U,\operatorname{row}(W)\subseteq V\}\) and labels the space with both column and row spaces perpendicular to \(U,V\) as \(F^\perp\). Its projections are written \[P_F(W)=UU^\top WVV^\top,\qquad P_N(W)=(I-UU^\top)W(I-VV^\top).\] Both displayed maps are genuine orthogonal projections, but their ranges do not exhaust the matrix space. The first equality after (23) in Lemma 14, p.25, nevertheless decomposes an arbitrary inner product using only these two projections. Equation (35), p.27, repeats this decomposition in the deterministic error bound; pp.34–35 use it to identify the oracle estimator with the penalized estimator.

Complete algebraic check. Let the true unfolding be \(A^*=\operatorname{diag}(4,0)\), hence \(U=V=e_1\), and set \[W=e_1e_2^\top=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.\] This is a legitimate two-mode tensor/matrix; no high-order restriction excludes it. Then \(P_FW=P_NW=0\) while \(W\ne0\). With the other inner-product factor also \(W\), the unprojected product is \(\langle W,W\rangle_F=1\), whereas the asserted two-term decomposition gives zero. This refutes the universal algebraic identity used by the proof, not merely a bound’s constant. It is independent of distributional, curvature and signal-strength assumptions: those assumptions do not imply vanishing cross components of arbitrary gradients or estimation errors. Indeed, \(A^*+\epsilon W\) remains rank one for every \(\epsilon\), so a low-rank restriction alone does not eliminate this direction.

Correct identity and limits of repair. With \(P=UU^\top\) and \(Q=VV^\top\), the full identity is \[W=PWQ+PW(I-Q)+(I-P)WQ+(I-P)W(I-Q).\] The true complement of \(F\) has projector \(W-PWQ\). Alternatively, the tangent-space projector is \(PW+WQ-PWQ\), whose complement is the paper’s \(P_N\). Substituting that tangent space changes dimension, rank and projected-noise bounds; it does not by itself prove the stated oracle rate. The example does not claim to instantiate every assumption of Theorem 6 as a stochastic counterexample. It is a decisive counterexample to a universal proof identity on which that theorem’s derivation depends.

Impact. Major for the central low-rank oracle argument. The abstract and Theorem 6 rely on this derivation, and Appendix B.5 refers back to it for slice-wise low rank. The sparse case does not use the same matrix decomposition and is not refuted by this calculation. Evidence: `check_output.json`, `projection`; source pp.5,25,27,34–35.
result: Original Frobenius product 1, projected decomposition 0. Invalid central low-rank oracle proof; not a claimed full stochastic counterexample.

The appendix assumes \(0\le i<N\), \(0\le j<F\), \(x=iF+j\), and positive closeness thresholds. It defines spatial support by \(|i_1-i_2|<a_1\), but the flattened expression omits the absolute value. \left|\left\lfloor x_1/F\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor x_2/F\right\rfloor\right|<a_1.\]

For the temporal support, the modulo condition \(|x_1\bmod F-x_2\bmod F|<a_2\) is correct. With the same \(N,F\), \(a_2=1\), and \((x_1,x_2)=(0,4)\), the modulo difference is zero but every allowed \(k\) gives a magnitude of at least four. |(x_1-x_2)-F\Delta i|<a_2.\end{aligned}\] This follows by substitution of \(x_r=i_rF+j_r\). Alternatively, retain the modulo expression and describe slash bands with their frame-boundary truncations. Consider independent candidates, each correct with probability \(p=0.1\), with all correct candidates of identical reasoning quality. All correct candidates share one correct final answer and all incorrect candidates one wrong final answer. Each candidate receives 50 independent binary checks, approving a correct candidate with probability \(0.7\) and an incorrect one with probability \(0.6\). These laws do not change with \(k\). Retain the maximum score within each final-answer group, then select the higher-scoring group, breaking a tied maximum uniformly between groups. This is the no-comparison selection rule in the inspected `create_verifications_minimal.py`, lines 633–684; selection uses no answer key.

The scaling plots omit tie-breaking and subsample one primary pool of 200 candidates and 50 checks per candidate; the 20 subsampling seeds are not 20 independent original experiments. Final-answer correctness and correctness of intermediate reasoning are different targets, explicitly separated in the paper.

Section 2.2 (p. 3), supported by Figures 2–3 (pp. 4, 6), conditions accuracy on at least one correct candidate. It presents this as isolating the burden of discriminating among more candidates after accounting for the increased chance of finding a correct answer. The ensuing increase is taken to demonstrate that the larger pool contains higher-quality correct responses, where quality means rigor or freedom from reasoning flaws. This is one of the three principal explanatory factors introduced on p. 3 and contributes to the abstract’s interpretation of scalability.

The condition fixes existence of a correct candidate, not their number or the opportunities for a fixed stochastic verifier to assign a high score. Thus the reported conditional trend does not distinguish improved objective response quality from repeated chances to verify equally good responses.

The abstract’s partial attribution is cautious, but the more specific isolation and demonstration language in Section 2.2 requires evidence that this control does not supply. No direct candidate-quality measurement or analysis fixing the number of correct candidates was located in the inspected release or relevant appendix.

analysis: For \(k=5\), \(S=2\), \(n=1\) and \(\epsilon_c=1/4\), the claimed condition holds, but a valid masked convolution has expected gradient cosine \(4096/15625=0.262144>1/4\). The failure affects the core data-independent guarantee and supports Major impact.

Use a single-channel \(103\times103\) input, a \(5\times5\) kernel, stride two, zero padding of width zero (valid convolution), and weights all equal to one. There are \(50\times50\) output locations. At each forward pass choose one of the 25 offsets \((a,b)\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}^{2}\) uniformly and independently of the preceding pass; apply that same one-point mask across all spatial positions. Thus \(n=1<S^{2}=4\), and \(n\le S^{2}\epsilon_c=1\). This is a shared-weight convolution of the form in Definition 1. There is no circular padding, asymptotic image limit or nonuniform mask sampling.

Let the scalar logit be the sum of all convolution outputs, with a second logit zero. Evaluate cross-entropy for class zero of the zero-logit class at the all-zero input. Its derivative with respect to the summed logit is \(1/2\). Consequently, apart from this common positive scalar, the input gradient for mask \((a,b)\) is the indicator of \[G_{a,b}=\{(2i+a,2j+b):0\le i,j<50\}.\] Each set has 2500 distinct entries, so both gradient norms are nonzero and the cosine for a mask pair is exactly \(|G_{a,b}\cap G_{c,d}|/2500\). This supplies a legitimate classifier loss, not merely an artificial unnormalized dot product.

Appendix A.1, p. 13, Eq. (20), obtains the stricter expression \[n\le \frac{k^{2}(\epsilon_c-1)}{\lfloor k/S\rfloor^{2}}+S^2.\] It then relaxes it to \(n\le S^{2}\epsilon_c\) in Eq. (21). For the example, the former right-hand side is \(-11/16\) and the latter is one. A weaker necessary restriction on \(n\) does not retain a sufficient guarantee obtained from the earlier worst-case inequality. The proof therefore cannot justify using every point in the enlarged interval as safe. The exact convolution calculation demonstrates that this is a real failure of the asserted sufficiency, not just an unproved implication.
claim: DCS samples a binary mask with \(n\) retained points in a \(k\times k\) convolutional boundary, with stride \(S\). Equations (6)–(8), p. 4, relate the input-gradient cosine similarity of two independently sampled paths to the retained points. Lemma 1 gives \(n\le S^{2}\epsilon_c\), and the surrounding text says this guarantees small expected gradient similarity. The combined interval in Eq. (12) is subsequently used as a guarantee governing the robustness/natural-accuracy trade-off. The counterexample below concerns this sufficiency claim, with uniformly sampled, spatially shared convolution masks.
\(n\le S^{2}\) \(\epsilon_c\) guarantees expected gradient cosine <=\(\epsilon_c\).

Uniform independent shared convolution masks. \(k=5\),S2,\(n=1\),\(\epsilon_c=1/4\). Valid \(103\times103\) single-channel convolution, all weights1. Nonzero cross-entropy input gradients at zero input.
result: If Lemma 1 is interpreted only as a necessary upper restriction, the counterexample does not refute that one-way reading. The main text, however, explicitly uses it to guarantee small similarity and Eq. (12) to guarantee the trade-off. That interpretation is what fails. The public `MaskedConv2d` in `model/randpos_resnet.py`, lines 321–359, multiplies one weight tensor by a mask and calls `conv2d`; the mask is spatially shared. Lines 685–733 also form a spatial mask and tile it across channels. This supports the shared-mask interpretation used here. Some released calls choose three points rather than one; the universal lemma and Table 5 explicitly include \(n=1\), so the counterexample is not a claim to reproduce the default experiment. If a different formulation independently resamples a separate mask at every spatial location, it would be a different stochastic operator requiring its own proof; no such independence assumption repairs the published shared-convolution guarantee.

The method’s introductory contribution and Section 4 explicitly rely on this bound to claim data-independent control of gradient similarity. This is a central theoretical dependency even though the empirical method may remain useful. Figures 3–4 and the grid-search heatmaps in Figure 6 are finite observations and do not establish the universal claim. The counterexample does not show a drop in CIFAR or ImageNet robustness, and it is not an attack on the trained networks. No general corrected bound is claimed: keeping an intermediate inequality is not sufficient until the earlier probability and gradient decompositions are also verified.
Sufficiency claim false for shared masks; necessary-only interpretation distinguished. Invalid data-independent core guarantee; experiment failure not claimed.

analysis:
Section 2.3 (p. 4) defines \(B\) image pairs, one normalized vector \(u_i\) and \(v_i\) from each image, and \(B^{2}-B\) cross-view negatives. Algorithm 1 forms a \(B\times B\) similarity matrix and applies cross-entropy in both directions. Its row loss is \[
 \ell_i=-\tau s(u_i,v_i)+\log\sum_{k=1}^{B}\exp\{\tau s(u_i,v_k)\},\] with the positive term included in the denominator. Equation (3), however, sums to \(2B\) while retaining a lower-branch vector \(y_k^L\), and excludes \(k=i\). There are only \(B\) such lower-branch vectors. With the pair ordering used in Algorithm 1, \(k=i\) is the positive rather than the anchor’s self-comparison.

These differences affect the calculation. For \(B=2\), let \(u_1=v_1=e_1\) and \(u_2=v_2=e_2\), choose the paper’s \(\kappa=64\) and an admissible positive scale \(\tau=1\). Both vectors have unit norm. The positive and negative similarities are \(1\) and \(1/130\). Equation [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) gives \[\ell_i=\log(1+e^{-129/130})=0.3153363.\] Merely changing the upper limit to \(B\) while retaining the exclusion gives \(-129/130=-0.9923077\), a different objective; if the scale grows, this latter expression tends to \(-\infty\) rather than zero. The expression with the original upper limit is undefined under branch-local indexing.

A charitable global-index interpretation would concatenate both branches and exclude the anchor itself. That produces an ordinary all-view contrastive objective, but also introduces same-branch negatives absent from Algorithm 1. It requires changing the vector notation and still does not describe the supplied \(B\times B\) computation. The frozen `models_mae.py`, lines 167–189, agrees with Algorithm 1 and includes the diagonal positives. The supported correction is Equation [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) and its transpose average. This is a Minor formula defect: the paper itself contains the coherent intended algorithm, and no loss error in the historical experiments is established.
claim: The displayed denominator should define the same contrastive objective as the implemented cross-view normalizer. \(B\) normalized vectors per branch; positive pairs share index; kappa64, \(\tau=1\) admissible.
result: The displayed denominator does not describe the coherent cross-view algorithm and released computation. This is a formula discrepancy rather than an established historical implementation loss error.

claim: The frozen public recipe should identify the training model and operative settings used for the reported result. Frozen commit; ordinary PatchEmbed trainability; constructor/launcher path inspected statically.
analysis: The paper specifies a fixed Xavier-initialized patch projection (Section 2.1, p. 2), a trainable scale in the loss (p. 4), and \(\kappa=64\) by default (p. 5). In the frozen `models_mae.py`, lines 26–68 and 162–164, the default is \(\kappa=1/64\) and the temperature is the ordinary scalar \(0.07\). Similarities use the same rational formula as Equation (2), followed by division by that scalar. The pre-training constructor in `main_pretrain.py`, line 157, passes no concentration override, and the argument parser exposes none.

This is not a harmless reciprocal notation for \(\kappa\): the formula multiplies by the stored value in both sources. For orthogonal vectors, \[s_{64}(0)=1/130=0.0076923,\qquad
 s_{1/64}(0)=32/65=0.4923077.\] At \(c=.5\) the values are \(0.0227273\) and \(0.7441860\). Their relation is not a single global rescaling or additive shift that a softmax temperature could absorb. The fixed reciprocal temperature could represent the numerical value \(\tau=1/.07\), but it does not implement training of \(\tau\).

The projection weights are initialized and then used directly in the forward path; only the positional embedding is explicitly frozen. The pre-training optimizer receives the model’s ordinary trainable parameters, with no projection exclusion or detachment. Under the ordinary `timm.PatchEmbed` behavior, the projection therefore remains trainable. This contradicts the fixed-projection recipe; it does not assert that its resulting gradients are nonzero on every input.

There is a separate immediate recipe inconsistency: `PRETRAIN.md` passes `mae_vit_large_patch16`, while the frozen model namespace defines the `sae_vit_large_patch16` family. The entry point indexes that namespace directly, so the documented name cannot resolve if execution reaches model construction. This conclusion is static; the launcher was not run. The appendix also lists a ViT-L pre-training batch of 2,400 (Table 10, p. 16), whereas the main-text default is 2,048.

These are Minor release and specification defects with unresolved historical provenance. An exact benchmark configuration, including the concentration, scale parameterization, projection freeze and actual batch layout, is needed to choose a faithful repair. Simply replacing defaults here would not establish reproduction of 85.8% accuracy.
result: The frozen defaults do not identify the reported recipe. The experiment-producing settings and model correspondence remain unresolved.

claim: Effective optimizer batch size should not be identified with the contrastive negative pool without the corresponding per-forward or cross-rank construction. Local loss matrix bxb; no feature gather; accumulation A and devices R.
analysis: The discussion around Table 3 (p. 6) attributes batch-size gains to a larger negative pool. `PRETRAIN.md` recommends gradient accumulation to retain an effective batch size when memory or GPU count is reduced. The entry point calculates this size as \(bAR\), where \(b\) is the per-device microbatch, \(A\) is the accumulation count and \(R\) is the number of devices.

The release’s loss, however, constructs similarities only from the current local input. No cross-device feature gathering appears in this path. `engine_pretrain.py`, lines 45–60, computes the loss separately for each microbatch, divides by \(A\), and accumulates its gradients. Distributed gradient synchronization and later scalar logging do not add feature vectors to a loss denominator. Each anchor therefore has \(b-1\) negative candidates, not \(bAR-1\).

The distinction is exact, not merely a potential optimization difference. In the two-image example of Problem 1, processing both images together gives loss \(0.3153363\). Processing two singleton microbatches with \(A=2\) gives zero in each: the sole class has probability one. Its gradient is identically zero. For a nonstationary comparison, keep \(u_1=e_1,u_2=e_2,v_2=e_2\) and set \(v_1=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\) at \(\theta=.3\). The full symmetric loss is \(0.4477130\), with central-difference derivative \(0.2866228\) in \(\theta\) (step \(10^{-6}\)); the accumulated singleton derivative remains exactly zero. All vectors are normalized and both procedures have optimizer effective batch two.

Accumulation still increases the number of images contributing to an optimizer step, so that conventional meaning of effective batch is valid. It cannot be used to infer an equivalent contrastive pool. Nor is a local-negative objective intrinsically invalid. The documented recommendation does not explicitly promise an identical negative pool. Moreover, varying the local microbatch at fixed accumulation and device counts would enlarge both the effective batch and the local pool, a reading compatible with the Table 3 explanation. The available evidence therefore establishes a scope clarification, not a demonstrated batch-semantics error or a falsification of Table 3. An assertion that the historical runs held the pool fixed while attributing gains to a larger pool would need additional run configuration evidence. Faithful comparisons must report both microbatch/pool size and optimizer batch size; a changed global-pool implementation would require feature aggregation with appropriate gradients and its own validation.
result: Optimizer accumulation and the per-forward contrastive pool are different quantities. The effective batch alone does not identify the negatives used in the objective.

analysis: Propositions 4.2–4.3 and their proofs do not establish the special-case relationships invoked to support the central expressiveness comparison.

The proof reaches the polynomial Eq. (16) by removing the nonlinear functions. That changes the architecture instead of identifying parameters of the displayed formula. Every finite instance of the displayed formula is real analytic and satisfies \[|h(t)|\leq\sum_{k=1}^{K}|\alpha_k|\sum_{m=0}^{M}(|a_{km}|+|b_{km}|),\quad t\in\mathbb R.\] It cannot equal the admissible nonconstant polynomial \(p(\lambda)=\lambda\) on \([0,2]\): equality on an open interval would extend to all real arguments by analytic uniqueness, contradicting boundedness. The continuation argument tests agreement inside the graph-spectrum interval; it does not assume that graph eigenvalues lie outside it.

The proof of Proposition 4.3 uses \(a_0\lambda=R\sin(\lambda+\phi)\) in Eqs. (19)–(20). Set \(a_0=1\) and take the three-node path: \[A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix},
\quad D=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,1),\quad
L=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1/\sqrt2&0\\-1/\sqrt2&1&-1/\sqrt2\\0&-1/\sqrt2&1\end{pmatrix}.\] The graph is undirected, binary, and has no zero degree. Its characteristic polynomial is \((1-t)((1-t)^{2}-1)\), giving normalized-Laplacian eigenvalues \(\{0,1,2\}\). All graph assumptions used by the paper are satisfied.

Write the proposed replacement as \(g(\lambda)=a\sin\lambda+b\cos\lambda\). Matching \(0\) gives \(b=0\); matching \(1\) gives \(a=1/\sin1\). At \(2\) the replacement yields \[g(2)=\frac{\sin2}{\sin1}=2\cos1=1.08060461173628\neq2.\] The contradiction therefore holds on a legal finite spectrum, not only on a continuous interval.

The text also calls this replacement approximate. Even under that interpretation, a single shifted sinusoid cannot attain arbitrary precision: every such \(g\) satisfies \(g(2)-2\cos1\,g(1)+g(0)=0\). Setting \(e_j=g(j)-j\) gives \[\max_{j=0,1,2}|e_j|\geq\frac{2-2\cos1}{2+2\cos1}
=\tan^{2}(1/2)=0.298446410409525.\] This bound diagnoses Eq. (19) only. It does not constrain the full multi-harmonic GrokFormer.
claim: For \(K=1\), the real trigonometric polynomials contain constants, form an algebra, and separate points on \([0,2]\): distinct points in an interval shorter than \(2\pi\) cannot share both sine and cosine. Their uniform closure is therefore \(C([0,2])\). Thus Proposition 4.4’s approximation conclusion can hold when \(M\) depends on the target and tolerance, even though its proof unnecessarily assumes additional differentiability. No fixed-\(M\) guarantee follows. Also, \[h(PLP^\top)=Ph(L)P^\top\] for a permutation \(P\). Equal eigenvalues receive equal responses, so eigenbasis signs and rotations within repeated eigenspaces cancel. This verifies the stated scalar convolution, not every truncated implementation.

Page 5 states that polynomial and Specformer filters are simplified variants of the proposed filter, using these special cases to support greater universality and flexibility. The theoretical comparison is an explicit contribution on p. 2. Appendix C, pp. 18–19, Eqs. (13) and (15)–(23), supplies the derivations. This is a core theoretical dependency, irrespective of whether benchmark scores survive.
finite K,\(M\) and finite coefficients. undirected binary graph; positive degrees; normalized spectrum [0,2]. \(a_0=1\) in Eq19.
result: Approximation with increasing \(M\) and interpolation on a particular finite spectrum remain possible. Interpreting a simplified variant as replacement of basis functions by the identity describes a modified architecture, not the claimed exact inclusion. In addition, the Specformer proof restricts attention to the identity and compares logarithmically spaced real frequencies \(\epsilon/10000^{i/M}\) with integer frequencies without a mapping. The restricted calculation cannot establish the unrestricted family’s inclusion.

The demonstrated invalid core derivation supports Major. It does not establish that the method is ineffective or experimentally inferior. The density statement in Section 2 is a supported replacement approximation claim, but it does not repair the original comparative containment theorem. Evidence: original-page rendering `s19.png`, independent `check.py`/`check.json`, and `theory_notes.json`.
Core comparison proof invalid; exact polynomial inclusion on interval false. Core theoretical containment claim; no empirical score loss inferred.

analysis: Lemma 3.1 (page 6), repeated as Lemma D.6 (page 18), states that Algorithm 3 uses at most \(2\lceil\log_2 T\rceil\) rounds. The two counters in the page 14 pseudocode permit more rounds, even with constant bounded rewards and no exploration.

Let \(T=2^L\) with \(L\geq2\), and define \[h=2^{-(L-1)},\qquad q=h-2^{-2L}.\] Give the target arm constant reward zero and its only competitor constant reward \(q\). Both are valid \([0,1]\)-bounded i.i.d. distributions. Consider a call after the competitor has been sampled once, with target empirical mean zero and competitor empirical mean \(q\). Such a state is reachable from zero initial estimates in Algorithm 1: list the competitor first, complete its first search and first-phase block, and then search for the target. For \(T=65536\) the relevant first-phase block is much shorter than the horizon. The principal rewards may be identically zero. All later empirical means stay constant.

The first \(L-1\) midpoint bids are \(1/2,1/4,\ldots,h\). Each is strictly above \(q\), so each selects the target. The midpoint counter is then \(C_1=L-1\) and the stored upper offer is \(h\). The next \(L\) midpoint bids are \[h(1-2^{-j}),\qquad j=1,\ldots,L.\] They are all strictly below \(q\), since even the largest equals \(h-2^{-(2L-1)}<h-2^{-2L}=q\). Each therefore fails and triggers an asymmetric check at bid \(h\), which strictly succeeds. The algorithm does not test its \(C_1\) stopping condition on those failed midpoint rounds. It returns at line 17 when the successful-check counter reaches \(C_2=L\). The total is exactly \[
 (L-1)+2L=3L-1>2L.\] No tie-breaking convention is needed. The independently written exact rational diagnostic, with \(L=16\), recorded 47 offer rounds against the stated limit of 32. Its entire bid/action transcript is retained in `verification/0176/check_results.json`.
claim: Location: PDF p6 Lemma3.1, p18 LemmaD.6, p14 Algorithm3.

\(T=2^L\); finite witnessT=65536,\(L=16\). Two bounded iid constant-reward arms: target0, competitor \(q\)=\(2^{-(L-1)}\)-\(2^{-2L}\). Competitor has previously been sampled, target empirical mean0; reachable from Algorithm1 zero initialization by listing competitor first. result: This example does not establish an error in the returned incentive bound: the returned offer is \(h+2/T\), with overpayment \(2/T+2^{-2L}\). Its runtime also remains \(O(\log T)\). The issue is therefore Minor: the precise round bound and the duration argument in Lemma D.6 are false, but a change of the constant does not by itself refute the asymptotic regret orders. The source proof’s proposed worst case, in which every midpoint fails, misses the initial successful midpoint rounds accumulated before the repeated checks. No new universal sharp bound is asserted in this report.

claim: Lemma G.6 asserts, conditional on the event \(\mathcal E\) defined on page 42, that every target offer in every phase strictly exceeds the target’s minimum incentive. Its base case is phase 1, when the offer is \(2d+T^{-1}\) for all target arms. The page 42 notation then identifies intended target rounds \(\mathcal T^E_{m,a}\) with actual arm rounds \(\mathcal T_{m,a}\). Algorithm 7, Equation (45), and Lemmas G.7–G.10 use the resulting sample allocation and design matrices. The proof of Theorem 5.1 on pages 43–44 expressly invokes Lemma G.6 in its regret decomposition and sample counts.

\(d=1\); \(T=65536\); \(\delta =1/T\). \(A={+1,-1}, s*=-1, \nu *=0\), initial estimate0; all in unit ball and A spans R. Agent greedily maximizes ordinary least-squares estimate plus incentive. First agent noise is equiprobable Rademacher ±1; all later noises and all principal noises0; these are conditionally1-subgaussian. Phase1 uses exact G-design rho(+1)=rho(-1)=1/2 and targets+1 first. Probability1/2 branch has initial noise-1; \(\mathcal E\) holds throughout subsequent path. Algorithm8 initial-width2 requires the intended dyadic extension \(i=-1\) (\(z=1/4\)), absent from its stated natural-number indices; under that reading it immediately breaks at \(\epsilon_0=1\) before any observations. Literal nonnegative indexing leaves initialization undefined.
analysis: The proof of Lemma G.6 (page 46) uses \(\pi_a^\star\leq\max_b\|\widehat s_t\|\|b-a\|\leq 2d\) to conclude that the capped offer strictly exceeds the minimum incentive. The corresponding norm claim also appears in the explanation of Algorithm 8 on page 9. The stated OLS model does not imply \(\|\widehat s_t\|\leq d\).

Set \[
 d=1,\quad \mathcal A=\{+1,-1\},\quad
 s^\star=-1,\quad \nu^\star=0,\quad
 \widehat s_1=0,\quad T=65536,\quad \delta=T^{-1}.\] Both arms and both parameters satisfy the unit-ball restrictions, and the arms span \(\mathbb R\). Let the first agent noise be a Rademacher random variable, taking \(+1\) and \(-1\) with probability \(1/2\) each, and let every later agent noise and every principal noise be zero. The first noise is conditionally 1-subgaussian because \(\mathbb E e^{\lambda\eta}=\cosh\lambda\leq e^{\lambda^{2}/2}\); the later zero noises also meet the condition. The linear model permits this time-dependent noise sequence. There is no exploratory behavior.

Choose the phase-1 design \(\rho_1(+1)=\rho_1(-1)=1/2\) and list the \(+1\) arm first in Algorithm 7’s target loop. Its design matrix is \(G=1\), and \(\max_a a^{2}/G=1\); thus it is even an exact optimal design and certainly satisfies the stated 2-approximation requirement. Its phase-1 block has at least two rounds. There is an initial-index ambiguity in Algorithm8: it defines \(z_i\) for \(i\in\mathbb N\), but its initial unit ball has width2 in the normalized direction. Thus line3 has no admissible nonnegative index. Under the natural intended dyadic extension to \(i=-1\), one has \(z_{-1}=1/4\) and, with \(\epsilon_0=1\), line4’s threshold is \(4/\|a_1-a_2\|=2\). The algorithm therefore breaks before any incentive or observation and returns \(c_1\in[-1,1]\). For the variant \(\{1,-1/4\}\) below the threshold is \(16/5\), so the same immediate return holds. The execution witness uses this explicit intended reading; the literal natural-number indexing instead leaves the initial search undefined. It does not silently assume that a nonempty search has already occurred.

For every such permitted output, the \(33\epsilon_0\) term with \(\epsilon_0=1\) makes Algorithm7’s first-phase offer equal to the cap. The subsequent false norm bound and target rejection are independent of which \(c_1\in[-1,1]\) is returned.

Initially, the incentive \(2+T^{-1}\) makes the agent choose \(+1\). On the event \(\{\eta^A(1)=-1\}\), of probability \(1/2\), its first reward is \(-2\). After that observation, \[U=1,\qquad \widehat s=1^{-1}(1)(-2)=-2.\] At the next intended \(+1\) round, the displayed formula yields \[\pi^\star_{+1}=(-2)(-1-1)=4.\] The actual offer is \(2+T^{-1}<4\). Equivalently, the two scores are \[\widehat s(+1)+2+T^{-1}=T^{-1},
 \qquad \widehat s(-1)=2.\] The agent strictly prefers \(-1\), so arbitrary tie-breaking is immaterial. The claimed inequality \(\pi_{+1}>\pi^\star_{+1}\) is false.

This is not merely an example outside the good event. After any \(n\geq1\) observations on the specified branch, all arms have squared value one and all later noises vanish. Therefore \[
 U_n=n,\qquad
 \widehat s_n=s^\star-\frac1n,\qquad
 |a(\widehat s_n-s^\star)|=\frac1n
 \quad(a\in\mathcal A).\] Writing \(L_0=\log(4KT/\delta)\) with \(K=2\), we have \[\frac1n \leq \sqrt{\frac{2L_0}{n}}\qquad(n\geq1).\] Thus the path satisfies even the conventional confidence radius using the squared Mahalanobis norm. The event displayed on page 42 uses a norm under the square root; its radius is no smaller on this example. The agent part of \(\mathcal E\) holds at every later time, including all times after phase 1 to which that event applies. All principal observations and the principal estimate are zero, so the principal part holds exactly. Consequently \(\mathcal E\) holds on the probability-\(1/2\) branch that violates Lemma G.6.

For the two symmetric arms, a wrong sign happens to preserve the scalar Gram increment. This coincidence does not rescue the target-selection lemma. Replace the arm set by \(\{1,-1/4\}\) and retain all other parameters, the half-half design, and the same first noise. Now \[G=\frac{17}{32},\qquad
 \max_a\frac{a^{2}}{G}=\frac{32}{17}<2,\] so this remains an admissible design. After the first reward, \(\widehat s=-2\) and the minimum incentive for target \(1\) is \(5/2\), again larger than \(2+T^{-1}\). The agent selects \(-1/4\); its actual Gram increment is \(1/16\), whereas the prescribed target allocation uses \(1\). For every continuation, \(U\geq1\) and \(\widehat s-s^\star=-1/U\), so \(|a|/U\leq |a|\sqrt{2L_0/U}\) proves that the confidence event remains satisfied. Principal observations remain zero. This variant directly invalidates identifying the designed and actual sample allocations.
result: The norm restriction in the model is on the true parameter and the initial estimate, not on every later OLS estimate. Interpreting the agent as using projected OLS would change the specified behavior. analysis: Lemma 3.1, page 6, claims that the number of draft sequences whose target tokenization starts with a fixed token of length \(m\) is \(2^{m-1}\). Its Appendix G proof counts partitions whose concatenation equals the token exactly. Those are different events.

Let the alphabet be \(\{a,b\}\), the complete draft vocabulary up to length two be \[D_2=\{a,b,aa,ab,ba,bb\},\qquad T=\{a,b\}.\] Both expressibility conditions in Algorithm 3 hold. Stop after one draft token, which also satisfies the suggested semantic stopping rule because the first target character is then irrevocably determined. For target token \(t=a\) of length \(m=1\), the qualifying stopped sequences are \((a),(aa),(ab)\). There are three, whereas the lemma gives \(2^{0}=1\). The single exact reconstruction is only \((a)\). If the lemma’s sequences have no stopping or length restriction at all, infinitely many continuations qualify, so its finite equality still cannot hold.

This discrepancy remains even after giving the paper the favorable interpretation that only first-token-determining stopped paths count. The two omitted paths cross the target token boundary in one draft token; they cannot be represented by cutting the target string into internal segments. Appendix C, pages 14–15, explicitly counts ways to reconstruct a target string exactly, and its plotted “Hello” tree displays precisely these exact partitions. Such a tree is not in general the whole proposal event in Theorem 3.2.

Use the same six-token vocabulary with uniform draft probabilities, and target \(p(a)=4/5\), \(p(b)=1/5\). The true first-token proposal is \[\psi(a)=q(a)+q(aa)+q(ab)=1/2,\qquad\psi(b)=1/2.\] Exact-string reconstruction masses would instead be \(\widetilde\psi(a)=\widetilde\psi(b)=1/6\), whose sum is only \(1/3\). If these incomplete masses are substituted for \(\psi\) in Algorithm 3, both possible target candidates are always accepted because \(p(a),p(b)>1/6\). The output law is then \((1/2,1/2)\), not \((4/5,1/5)\). Using the true \(\psi\) gives accepted mass \((1/2,1/5)\), rejection mass \(3/10\) placed on \(a\), and the exact target law. The independent script verifies all quantities using rational arithmetic.

This does not disprove Theorem 3.2 read with the correct first-token proposal distribution. It shows why the exact reconstruction calculation described as computing that distribution cannot generally be substituted into the theorem. No SLRS implementation was run, and no claim is made that the benchmarked SLEM or TLI uses this incomplete mass.
claim: Enumerate all6 stopped paths and exact rational acceptance/output law.

Complete draft vocabulary \(D_2\) over a,b; target character vocabulary. Stop after1 token, also first-token-determined stopping. Uniform draft; target4/5,1/5. Operative assumptions: Alphabet {a,b}; complete \(D_2\) has every nonempty string of length <=2; target vocabulary contains single characters. Both T-to-D* and D*-to-T* expressibility conditions hold. Use a valid S1 that stops after one draft token; the first target character is also already fixed under every continuation. Uniform q is strictly positive on \(D_2\); target \(p=(4/5,1/5)\).

claim: Exact \(p=q=(1,0)\) boundary.

\(p\)=q normalized on a common vocabulary. The source also says non-trivial; whether this already excludes Dirac distributions is not separately formalized.
