The Dirac example satisfies unequal probabilities but may fail the independent non-trivial assumption; it cannot be presented as an unconditional theorem counterexample.
analysis: Theorem 3.1, pages 5 and 21, assumes a non-trivial distribution and states that there are unequal token probabilities. Unequal probabilities alone permit \(p=q=(1,0)\), for which both acceptance rates are one. However, non-trivial may independently exclude this point mass; the example therefore does not establish failure under every stated assumption.

The proof correctly computes \(\alpha_{\rm EM}=\sum_t p(t)^{2}\) and \(\alpha_{\rm SD}=1\) when \(q=p\). Strict inequality holds exactly when \(p\) is not concentrated at a single token. Having at least two positive-probability tokens is the appropriate condition; unequal probabilities are neither sufficient in the presence of zeros nor necessary (a nondegenerate uniform distribution also gives strict inequality). If “non-trivial” was intended independently to mean non-Dirac, the result is sound and the displayed explanation should simply be clarified. The assessment is Needs Evidence for the interpretation of the condition, with a scope clarification rather than a demonstrated substantive error. Under the non-Dirac reading the strict comparison and its proof are valid.

For Theorem 4.1, let \(Z=\sum_{t\in T\cap D}q(t)>0\). On the intersection, \(q_2(t)=q(t)/Z\geq q(t)\), so termwise monotonicity of \(\min\{p(t),\cdot\}\) proves \(\alpha_2\geq\alpha_1\). Outside it, the relevant common accepted mass is zero. In an independent four-symbol example with \[p=(.2,.5,.3,0),\qquad q=(.1,.1,0,.8),\] intersection mass is \(.2\) and acceptance rises from \(.2\) to \(.7\) after normalization. The lossless rejection identity still returns \(p\). The zero-intersection case discussed in the text needs an explicit autoregressive fallback because the formula defining \(q_2\) is then undefined; it cannot literally run a zero-denominator normalization. These conditions do not undermine the positive-mass theorem.
result: Unequal probabilities alone allow equality, but the Dirac example may violate non-triviality. The strict theorem is valid under the natural non-Dirac reading. No substantive theorem defect established under the non-Dirac reading; clarify the condition only.

analysis: Rating: Major. Locations: Algorithm 5, p. 6, lines 4–6; Algorithm 6, p. 8, calls in lines 4 and 8 and cutoff tests in lines 5 and 9; Lemma G.1 termination argument, p. 36; Theorems 4.1–4.2 and Algorithm 11, pp. 6 and 37–39.

UPDATE filters candidates at threshold \(\tau\). While its pool is empty, it replaces \(\tau\) by \((1-\epsilon)\tau\) and searches for elements with marginal at least \(\tau\). It has no \(\tau_{\min}\) input or internal cutoff. Its caller tests whether \(\tau<\tau_{\min}\) only after UPDATE returns.

For Theorem 4.1 take \(n=8\), \(k=2\), \(\ell=2\), \(\epsilon=1/10\) and \[f(S)=\mathbf1\{x\in S\}\] for a distinguished element \(x\). This is normalized, nonnegative and modular, with \(M=f(O)=1\) and \(\tau_{\min}=\epsilon M/k=1/20\). Both initial pools become \(\{x\}\) at threshold one. Their sizes are below \(2\ell\), so Algorithm 6 uses its sequential branch. The first solution selects \(x\), and line 13 removes it from all other pools. The next solution calls UPDATE on the restricted ground set excluding selected elements.

Every remaining marginal is zero. After \(r\) threshold reductions, \[\tau_r=(9/10)^r>0\] for every finite integer \(r\ge0\). No remaining element passes the threshold. UPDATE never returns, and the caller’s cutoff test cannot be reached. The threshold crosses \(1/20\) after 29 reductions, which is irrelevant to the unmodified inner loop. This is an exact-arithmetic nontermination proof, not an inference from a timeout. Eventual floating-point underflow is neither specified nor a proof of the claimed oracle-model complexity.

The proof on p. 36 counts only logarithmically many threshold levels by asserting deactivation below \(\tau_{\min}\). That deactivation is implemented in the caller and cannot interrupt the inner loop as written. Therefore both termination and finite adaptivity/query claims for the printed algorithms fail on admissible inputs.
The pinned source contains an internal guard. In `src/algs/algs_pig.cpp:505–540`, `Pig::update` receives `tau_min` and uses
> while (\(\tau\) > margeGains[0].gain && \(\tau > \tau_{\min}\))

before returning to its caller. The independent check read these bytes directly. This prevents the demonstrated infinite loop in that release on the present instance, whose restricted ground set is nonempty. It does not establish the historical provenance of the experimental checkout or certify the entire implementation.

Passing \(\tau_{\min}\) to the pseudocode UPDATE and returning once it falls below the cutoff repairs this local nontermination and enables the existing caller to retire the solution. Full proof and implementation repair verification remains separate. Major reflects invalid central termination and complexity guarantees, not difficulty of repair or demonstrated benchmark degradation.
claim: PIG/PItG return in finite stated adaptive/query complexity.
Singleton modular objective; legal \(n=8\),\(k=2\),\(\ell=2\),\(\epsilon=1/10\) and main \(n=20000\),\(k=1000\),\(\ell=20\),\(\epsilon=1/10\).
result: Remaining marginals0 imply UPDATE never returns; caller cutoff unreachable. False termination/query/adaptivity claims for central published algorithm.

analysis: Rating: Major. Locations: Algorithm 2 and Theorem 3.1, p. 4; Claim 3.1 and Lemma 3.2, p. 5; proof of Lemma 3.2, p. 15, Eq. (8); final theorem analysis, p. 19.

Algorithm 2 initializes \(G=\varnothing\), \(V=U\), and \(m=\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor\). For each of \(\ell\) outer rounds, it starts \(\ell\) solutions \(A_l=G\). It selects \(m\) elements for each solution by greedy marginal maximization over the shared \(V\), deleting each selected element from \(V\). It retains a random \(A_l\) as the new \(G\). There is no reset of \(V\) inside the outer loop.

Theorem 3.1 claims \[\mathbb E f(G)\ge(1/e-\epsilon)f(O),
 \qquad
 \ell\ge\frac{2}{e\epsilon},\quad
 k\ge\frac{2(e\ell-2)}{e\epsilon-2/\ell},
 \quad \ell=O(\epsilon^{-1}).\] Theorem hypotheses allow modular objectives, since these are nonnegative submodular functions and the monotone subclass is not excluded.

Take \(\epsilon=1/10\), \(\ell=10\), \(k=1000\), \(m=100\) and \(|U|=10000\). Let \(H\subset U\) contain 1000 elements and set \[f(S)=|S\cap H|.\] All other elements, including the added dummy elements, have weight zero. This objective is normalized, nonnegative and modular. Its optimum is \(f(O)=1000\). The parameter bounds hold: \[10>7.3575888234=\frac{2}{e\epsilon},\qquad
 1000>701.1960288238=\frac{2(e\ell-2)}{e\epsilon-2/\ell}.\] There are enough ordinary zero-weight elements to complete all selections, so the example does not depend on whether dummy elements are included in \(V\) at initialization.

In round one the \(\ell m=1000\) selections exhaust all of \(H\): every useful element has marginal one and every other element has marginal zero. Each candidate solution receives exactly 100 useful elements. Whichever candidate is selected, \(f(G_1)=100\). The other 900 useful elements were deleted from \(V\) and are never restored. All later additions have zero marginal value. Therefore every random branch returns value 100, and \[\mathbb E f(G)=100<(1/e-0.1)1000=267.8794411714\ldots.\] The parent’s independent finite calculation reproduces the ten-round value sequence \((100,\ldots,100)\). The all-branch assertion follows from the invariant that all candidate values are equal in every round, rather than from an incomplete enumeration of random runs.

At round two, partition the 900 remaining optimal elements into ten sets \(O_l\) of size 90. This meets Claim 3.1’s requirements: newly selected zero-weight elements do not intersect \(O\). Yet \[\Delta(A_l\mid G_1)=0,\qquad
 \Delta(O_l\mid A_l)=90,\] contradicting Lemma 3.2’s first inequality. The proof’s p. 15 assertion that an optimal element outside the current solution sets remains in the candidate pool is false for elements discarded in an earlier round.

Resetting \(V\) to \(U\setminus G\) at the beginning of each round is a plausible intended correction. It fixes this example and the exhibited availability failure. It is absent from the visually inspected pseudocode, however, and the complete corrected proof has not been certified. The parallel implementation’s repeated `parallel_tg` calls reconstruct candidate sets from the current \(G\); hence this serial counterexample is not evidence that the released parallel experiments made the same permanent deletion.

The demonstrated theorem-to-algorithm mismatch is central and supports Major even though the apparent specification repair is short. It does not establish a lower bound against the intended reset algorithm or falsify empirical objective values.

Nonnegative modular f(S)=|S intersect \(H\)|; n10000,\(k=1000\),\(\ell=10\),\(\epsilon=1/10\); all theorem conditions checked.
result: Every branch returns100 <267.879441; Lemma3.2 would require0>=90. Demonstrated false guarantee for core simplified algorithm as printed.

analysis: Source claim and exact location. Section 4.2, p. 7, states that federated learning ensures data privacy and security because raw data stay local and only model updates, such as gradients, are shared. The healthcare example then infers compliance with privacy regulations from training without sharing raw patient data. No secure-aggregation protocol, formal privacy guarantee, update-observation restriction or noise mechanism is specified for this claim [S1].

Suspect inference. Raw-data locality is a statement about where records are stored and directly transmitted. Confidentiality is a statement about what another party can learn from the released messages. A gradient can encode the record even though the record itself is never transmitted. The premise therefore does not entail the stated guarantee.

Definitions and assumptions. Consider a client training a linear predictor f(x)=\(w^\top\) x+b on one record (x,y), using squared loss L=0.5(f(x)-y)\(^{2}\). Let the coordinating server observe the client gradient with respect to both w and b. This is an ordinary gradient-sharing instance of the broad setting described in the paper; the source imposes no minimum local batch size and no mechanism concealing individual updates. The raw record remains on the client.

\[r=w^\top x+b-y,\qquad g_w=rx,\qquad g_b=r,\qquad x=\frac{g_w}{g_b}\ \ (g_b\ne0).\] Complete finite example. Take x=(2,3), y=1, w=(0,0) and b=0. Then r=-1, so the shared messages are \(g_w\)=(-2,-3) and \(g_b\)=-1. Dividing the vector by the scalar recovers x=(2,3) exactly. The original claim’s premises hold: data are local, only a model gradient is shared, and the learning computation is valid. Nevertheless, the server learns the complete input. If the client instead transmits a one-step SGD model update with a common nonzero learning rate, the ratio of the weight and bias updates yields the same x.

The derivative identities prove the general one-record result whenever r is nonzero; the finite computation checks the stated parameters. This reviewer-owned calculation is not an execution of author code or a reproduction of the attack algorithm in [S3]. The source claim supplies no privacy metric or threat model under which the revealed input could still be regarded as protected.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. FL can reduce direct centralized collection of raw records, and a properly protected protocol can offer specific privacy properties. Neither point rescues a guarantee based solely on localization. Section 6, p. 9, calls for attention to privacy and security, and the p. 10 Impact Statement recognizes risks, but neither introduces a protection mechanism that excludes this example. The example does not claim that every FL system leaks every record, or that a specific hospital deployment uses this vulnerable configuration.

Calibrated judgment: Minor retained. The error removes the automatic privacy/security assurance and the resulting healthcare compliance inference. Its bounded role follows from the actual dependency structure: Section4.1, p.6, defines Scaling Out through specialized variants and connecting interfaces; Section4.2 offers FL alongside parameter-efficient adaptation, conditional control and coordination protocols. Neither specialization nor interoperation is derived from the false confidentiality premise. The error is an application-enabling assurance on one route, rather than a derivation or necessary generalization establishing the scaling axes. The saved example satisfies the stated data-locality and update-sharing conditions; later privacy cautions do not exclude it. Collaboration without centralizing raw records survives as an architectural capability, not a guarantee about released messages. This remains a known-issue reproduction attributed to Zhu, Liu and Han [S3].
claim: Local raw data and shared updates ensure privacy/security and regulatory compliance.
One-record client gradient, known model, visible individual gradient/update, no added protection stipulated; raw record remains local.
result: Minor retained because the error concerns an application-enabling assurance on one branch of the architecture, rather than a derivation or necessary generalization establishing the proposed scaling axes. The automatic privacy/security assurance and resulting compliance inference must be withdrawn.

Federated learning can avoid centralizing raw data, but confidentiality and security depend on the adversary model, which updates are visible, and the protections applied to those updates. Regulatory compliance cannot be concluded from FL alone.

analysis: Source claim and location. Case study 2, p. 6 right column, describes the permission to use COMPAS in sentencing largely through the existence of other reasons for the decision. After reproducing five cautions, p. 7 right column says the court has full discretion whether and how to take the list into account. Section 5, p. 8, summarizes the opposing position as permitting biased systems with a warning label. On p. 7 left column, the accompanying trade-secret discussion says courts have no information about the system whatsoever. These passages together imply a materially weaker set of safeguards and a more complete information vacuum than the primary opinion describes.

Decisive check. The official State v. Loomis opinion, 2016 WI 68, filed July 13, 2016 [S2], paragraph 98 says risk scores may not determine incarceration or sentence severity, and may not be the determinative factor in deciding whether an offender can be safely and effectively supervised in the community. Paragraph 99 requires the court to explain independent factors supporting the sentence. Paragraph 100 requires the written advisement and then separately lists the cautions. Thus, independent sentencing reasons and warning labels are not the entire rule. The prohibitions are express conditions of the permission described in paragraphs 8 and 120.

The information claim is also too absolute. Paragraphs 51-56 distinguish unavailable factor weights and risk-calculation details from information that is available: the defendant’s report, underlying questions and answers, criminal-history inputs, and portions of the practitioner’s guide. The majority reasons that the defendant can challenge relevant underlying information. Whether this is enough is open to the paper’s criticism, but it is not an absence of all information.

Alternative reading and counterevidence. Paragraph 71 gives sentencing courts discretion in assessing a risk tool’s accuracy, and the decision does not prescribe a numerical weight for each caution. The paper can reasonably question whether judges actually avoid cognitive bias or whether the safeguards work. Justice Abrahamson’s concurrence, paragraphs 132-135, expressly records the court’s limited understanding of COMPAS and calls for stronger on-record reasoning; this supports the paper’s concern. These points do not erase the majority’s substantive restrictions or convert partial disclosure into no disclosure. The review therefore does not assert that the court eliminated all discretion, that the warnings are empirically effective, or that the author’s normative disagreement is erroneous.

Bounded consequence and verified correction. Replace the blanket account with this statement: Loomis permitted consideration of COMPAS subject to substantive restrictions, independent sentencing reasons and written cautions, while leaving the internal weighting algorithm undisclosed and some input and report information available. The sufficiency and practical effectiveness of those protections can then be criticized explicitly. Each clause is supported by the cited paragraphs. This repairs the factual summary; it does not validate COMPAS, establish absence of bias, or resolve the policy disagreement. The incorrect 2018 date in the paper is not counted as a separate substantive issue.

Evidence: source_pages/source_p6.png and source_p7.png visually confirm the paper’s wording; sources/0034/conceptual_loomis_2016.pdf preserves the official opinion. The check is primary-source contradiction with a specified alternative reading, not a numerical counterexample or an empirical causal result.

The false warning-only/total-information-vacuum account strengthens one case illustration. Its correction still leaves the internal scoring mechanism undisclosed; available inputs permit some challenges without establishing sufficient model-level explanation. Section6, p.8, makes the proposed assessment conditional on technically supported notice and a fair opportunity to contest, and the separately checked K.W. notice/contestation evidence does not depend on Loomis. Thus the source correction alters the claimed extent of one case’s deficit without defeating those independent premises. This bounded factual role, rather than survival of a broad agenda, supports Minor. It does not validate the broadest incompatibility language, establish safeguard efficacy, or certify COMPAS safety or fairness.
claim: Permission to use COMPAS summarized through other reasons and caution labels; unqualified full-discretion phrasing; courts described as having no system information whatsoever.
Claims evaluated as an account of this historical decision, not as an empirical assertion that safeguards always work.
result: Minor retained for a bounded factual characterization that changes the claimed extent of this case's procedural deficit. The corrected source leaves identified access limitations relevant to the explanation-to-contestation argument, and independent K.W. premises remain. This is not a validation of the paper's broadest incompatibility language.

analysis: The submitted vector is \(H_{\mathrm{sub}}(X)=(X_1,1-X_1)\). It can take only the values \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\), each of which determines \(X_1\) but conveys no information about the independent label \(Y=X_2\).

Conditioned on either attainable submitted vector, \(Y\) is still a fair bit. Consequently, for every deterministic map \(e\) of the submitted predictions, \(\Pr(e(H_{\mathrm{sub}}(X))=Y\mid H_{\mathrm{sub}}(X))=1/2\). Averaging over the two vectors gives population accuracy \(1/2\). Randomized maps are mixtures of deterministic maps and have the same accuracy.

Each submitted predictor also has accuracy \(1/2\). Thus even the best prediction-only ensemble gains zero over the submitted models: \(\sup_e\Pr(e(H_{\mathrm{sub}}(X))=Y)=1/2\). The exact four-point calculation enumerates all \(16\) binary maps on the four possible binary prediction pairs and gives the same result; only two pairs occur in this distribution.

However, \(g(X)=X_2\) is an equally simple permitted predictor using a coordinate already available to every competitor, and \(\Pr(g(X)=Y)=1\). Ensemble saturation within the submitted family therefore coexists with a strictly better permitted, unsubmitted predictor. It cannot by itself bound performance over the larger permitted class.
claim: Section 8 infers near-maximal attainable signal within competition constraints from little or no improvement when ensembling submitted predictions. Test that implication under a common population-accuracy objective and the same input access and simple-model budget for every competitor.

Let \(X_1,X_2\) be independent Bernoulli\((1/2)\) variables and \(Y=X_2\), so the four input pairs each have probability \(1/4\). Both coordinates are available. The permitted class contains one-coordinate binary rules using either coordinate. The submitted predictors are \(h_1(X)=X_1\) and \(h_2(X)=1-X_1\); an ensemble receives only their prediction vector at test time.
result: The demonstrated failure concerns the implication used to answer the deadline opportunity-cost objection. It does not measure a missed gain in an actual competition. The reported experience of small ensemble gains can remain accurate, and the proposed contemporaneous-comparison and contamination-control mechanisms do not require exhaustive search of all permitted models.

source_report_paragraphs.text: A submitted-prediction ensemble is any rule whose test-time information is the vector of submitted predictions. The permitted hypothesis class may contain methods absent from that vector. Population accuracy is the objective in the diagnostic example. Its probabilities are known exactly, so the calculation has no sampling error or numerical tolerance. The example tests an implication in the argument; it is not a reconstruction of an actual Kaggle competition.

Source and suspect step. Section 8, PDF p.9, left column, second paragraph, answers the objection that deadlines may exclude valuable work. It moves from the authors’ experience of little or no ensemble improvement to the conclusion that competitions extract nearly maximal signal within their constraints [S1]. The empirical observation may be accurate. The unsupported step is treating performance within the submitted prediction family as a bound on the larger permitted family.

Complete construction. Let X1 and X2 be independent Bernoulli(1/2) variables and let Y=X2. Both input coordinates are available to every competitor. Permit one-coordinate binary rules using either coordinate with the same simple model and input-access budget. The submitted rules are h1(X)=X1 and h2(X)=1-X1. The permitted but unsubmitted rule is g(X)=X2. There is no data leakage, access advantage, or more expensive model in g.
\[\begin{gathered}\Pr(X_1=a,X_2=b)=\tfrac14,\quad a,b\in\{0,1\},\qquad Y=X_2,\\ H_{\rm sub}(X)=(X_1,1-X_1),\qquad g(X)=X_2.\end{gathered}\]
Input (X1, X2) | Y | Submitted vector (h1,h2) | g

For either attainable prediction vector, the conditional label remains a fair bit. Thus every deterministic ensemble e(H_sub), including a combination learned from separate labeled data, has population accuracy 1/2. This is true even for an oracle selecting the best such map. Randomized rules are mixtures of deterministic rules and retain accuracy 1/2. Adding any number of submitted models whose joint predictions depend only on X1 leaves the same information limitation.

\[\begin{gathered}\sup_e \Pr(e(H_{\rm sub}(X))=Y)=\tfrac12=\max_i\Pr(h_i(X)=Y),\\ \Delta_{\rm ensemble}=0,\qquad \Pr(g(X)=Y)=1.\end{gathered}\] Finite verification. independent_check.py evaluates the four support points with exact rational arithmetic and enumerates all 16 binary lookup maps on the four possible binary prediction pairs. Only two pairs occur in this distribution, but checking all 16 maps covers every deterministic combination. Every map scores 1/2, both submitted models score 1/2, and g scores 1. All assertions passed under Python 3.13.5, with actual process exit code 0. The saved results are in verification/0035/independent_check_results.json.

Original-condition check. The paragraph supplies no formal model-class or search-coverage assumption. The example preserves its premises of available submissions, no improvement through aggregation, a common evaluation metric, and fixed competition constraints. It shows that those premises alone cannot imply nearly optimal attainable performance. It does not claim the actual competitions use this distribution, that entrants miss an obvious coordinate, or that their unsubmitted improvement is 50 percentage points.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. Diverse teams may provide useful practical evidence of broad search. That evidence still needs a connection to unexplored permitted methods. An ensemble that additionally accesses X2 and learns g has introduced a new information source and hypothesis; its success would not follow from earlier prediction-only saturation. The authors’ experiential observation remains unrefuted. Krogh and Vedelsby’s established ensemble analysis [S3] supplies related context about shared errors and prediction disagreement; its squared-loss identity is not used as a proof of this binary-accuracy example.

Calibrated dependency and judgment: Minor retained. Section8, p.9, uses the near-maximality inference to answer the objection that a deadline excludes valuable submissions. Because time bounds are part of the definition on p.1, this is a substantive failed rebuttal. However, Section1.1, p.2, locates the gold-standard rationale in anti-cheating practices and renewable tasks. Sections6.1-6.2, pp.7-8, describe contemporaneous comparisons and guarded/prospective test data; Section7, p.8, explicitly treats evaluations as point-in-time results. No method, metric, contamination-control mechanism or downstream recommendation is derived from exhaustive signal extraction. The demonstrated damage is consequently bounded to the unsupported reassurance about excluded approaches. This is a dependency-based Minor judgment, not one based on paper type, section placement, ease of repair or the general usefulness of competitions.

analysis: Source claim. Appendix C, p. 24, interprets GSM8K ID7876 as a high-difficulty/low-guessing item whose properties arise from complex multistep calculation. The item specifies a 900-watt air conditioner and a reduction in runtime BY five hours per day for 30 days, but prints 81 as the answer.

\[E_{\rm saved}=0.9\,{\rm kW}\times5\,{\rm h/day}\times30\,{\rm day}=135\,{\rm kWh}.\qquad81=0.9(8-5)30.\] The printed value is the remaining energy use under the stated wording; it would be energy saved if runtime were reduced TO five hours. The source also confuses power and energy units. Hence this item is not clean evidence that low guessing/high estimated difficulty is caused by calculation complexity. analysis: Source claim and dependency. Page 3, Section 2.1 and page 18, Eq. (1) define the 3PL model. Page 7, Section 3.2 then assigns each candidate item information \(\alpha^{2}\) p(1-p) and selects its maximizer. That is an operational selection prescription, not merely a background mention: it is the mechanism used to explain why adaptive evaluation can use fewer informative items. Section 3.2 does not restrict this prescription to c=0. Appendix Eq. (4), p. 19, explicitly uses the probabilities defined in Eq. (1).

\[\begin{aligned}s&=\sigma(\alpha(\theta-\beta)), & p&=c+(1-c)s,\\p'&=\frac{\alpha(p-c)(1-p)}{1-c},\\ I(\theta)&=\frac{(p')^{2}}{p(1-p)}=\frac{\alpha^{2}(p-c)^{2}(1-p)}{(1-c)^2p}.\end{aligned}\] Complete derivation. For y in {0,1}, the derivative of y log p + (1-y) log(1-p) is (y-p)p’/[p(1-p)]. Its squared expectation equals (p’)^2/[p(1-p)] because the Bernoulli variance is p(1-p). Differentiating the stated 3PL probability yields the displayed expression. The main-text simplification follows for c=0; it does not hold for general c.

Counterexample. Take two distinct candidate items with theta=0, alpha_A=alpha_B=1, beta_A=beta_B=log(2), c_A=1/4, and c_B=1/10. Thus s_A=s_B=1/3. Both discriminations are strictly positive, both guessing probabilities are strictly between zero and one, all parameters are finite, and the paper permits item-specific guessing parameters. All operative conditions are satisfied.
Quantity | Item A | Item B
Success probability p | 1/2 | 2/5
Derivative p’ | 1/6 | 1/5
Main-text information | 1/4 = 0.25 | 6/25 = 0.24
Correct Fisher information | 1/9 = 0.111111... | 1/6 = 0.166666...

The main prescription selects A; the correct maximum-information rule selects B. A supplies only two-thirds of B’s Fisher information in this example. This is an analytic identity failure with an exact finite witness, independently replayed using rational arithmetic. It does not purport to prove a particular change in aggregate benchmark rankings.

Alternative reading and repair. Interpreting Section 3.2 as an unstated 2PL illustration makes its formula correct, but that restriction is absent and excludes the nonzero guessing factors emphasized elsewhere. Appendix B, p. 20, Eq. (5) already states the correct general expression. Replacing the main expression with Eq. (5), or explicitly restricting that passage to c=0, repairs exactly this selection identity. The corrected identity has been analytically checked; experiment-level implementation and results have not been repaired or reproduced. Ease of this correction does not remove the demonstrated damage to the core prescription. Evidence: E1, E2, E3.

analysis: Assessment: Major; invalid accounting of the core adaptation mechanism.

Appendix F and Listing 2 (p. 29) specify a final hidden width of 512; the M head outputs \(rd=8\cdot4096=32768\) values. For the narrower value projection, this branch truncates the output after evaluating the head.
Claim 1.  Under this stated architecture and operation convention, the dense output heads alone require \(4{,}294{,}967{,}296\) FLOPs.

Proof. A dense map from 512 features to 32768 outputs requires \(2\cdot512\cdot32768\) FLOPs per vector in this convention. Applying it to 128 vectors gives \[C_{\rm heads}=2\cdot128\cdot512\cdot(4096\cdot8)
=4{,}294{,}967{,}296.\] In contrast, direct integer evaluation gives \(C_{\rm printed}=5{,}373{,}952\). Therefore \(C_{\rm heads}/C_{\rm printed}=799.2195\ldots\). A complete network cannot cost less than its evaluated dense heads. This discrepancy does not depend on costs of activation functions or normalization. ◻

For the published backbone, count the task projection once, mixer and first residual block for 64 layer/module vectors, and the subsequent A/B-dependent blocks for 128 vectors. The resulting dense-matrix count is \[\begin{aligned}
C_{\rm M}&=131{,}072+33{,}554{,}432+33{,}554{,}432\\
&\quad+83{,}886{,}080+4{,}294{,}967{,}296
=4{,}446{,}093{,}312.\nonumber\end{aligned}\] These terms correspond respectively to the task projection, mixer plus first residual block, second residual block, final hidden block, and output heads. The reviewer-written integer calculation and exact output are in `independent_check.py` and `check_results.json` within this paper’s verification directory.

analysis: Assessment: Minor; incorrect literal interpretation, without a demonstrated operator failure.

Consider three coarse vertices \(a,b,c\), with nonnegative symmetric adjacency \[A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\0&0&2\\1&2&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
S_H=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] These integer weights are consistent with prior aggregation of one and two original edges. Every vertex is assigned to exactly one nonempty cluster, \(P=\{a,b\}\) and \(Q=\{c\}\). Set all attention logits to zero, achievable by a zero attention vector. There are two actual directed edges per ordered cluster pair, so each has weight \(1/2\) under the stated actual-edge normalization. Eq. (12) yields \[A_{\rm new}=\begin{pmatrix}0&3/2\\3/2&0\end{pmatrix}.\] At \(h=1\), the support graph has exactly one shortest path from \(P\) to \(Q\), but \(T_1(P,Q)=3/2\). A fractional value is not the number of ordinary paths, even under a parallel-edge counting interpretation. This example also avoids the normalization-domain ambiguity discussed below, since all pairs across \(P,Q\) are actual edges.

For a weighted matrix the exact identity is \[(A^h)_{ij}=\sum_{v_0=i,\ v_h=j}\prod_{t=0}^{h-1}A_{v_t v_{t+1}},\] where the sum runs over length-\(h\) walks. At the shortest support distance, it is a sum of products along shortest paths. This gives the correct weighted-connectivity interpretation and reduces to ordinary counting when all participating weights are one. It can still provide a useful message-passing strength. Thus the witness refutes the literal count assertion on the paper’s weighted domain, not the usefulness or computability of its operator. Reading the prose as an informal weighted path-strength description supplies a natural clarification; no benchmark change is inferred. The rational calculation is preserved in `check_results.json`.
claim: Section 3.3, p. 6, states that \((A^{(l)})^h(i,j)\) represents the number of \(h\)-step walk paths and that the nonzero strengths in \(T_h^{(l)}\), Eq. (15), reflect the number of shortest paths. This is correct for a binary adjacency matrix. The same architecture is expressly applied to weighted coarsened graphs, whose entries are sums or attention-weighted averages of connectivity strengths.
Nonnegative symmetric weighted adjacency from graph coarsening. Hard partition of all three vertices into two nonempty clusters. Zero logits, actual-edge normalization, \(h=1\).
result: Literal count interpretation false; correct value is weighted product-sum. Interpretation of edge strengths. No invalid support mask, operator failure or benchmark damage.

analysis:
The abstract, contribution 1 on page 2, Section 3.2 on pages 4–5, and Appendix A.2 claim recovery of the previous global model’s statistics. Equation (15) requires \[\mu_k=N_k^{-1}\sum_i f(\omega,x_{ki}),\qquad
 v_k=N_k^{-1}\sum_i(f(\omega,x_{ki})-\mu_k)^{2} .\] However, `HybridBatchNorm.forward` first computes raw `curr_mean` and `curr_var`, then forms hybrid `mean` and `var`, and adds those hybrid quantities to the collection buffers. These are not the required raw moments.

Specifically, writing \(a=\operatorname{sigmoid}(\alpha)\), the collected quantities in the first batch after clearing are \[m_k=(1-a)\mu_{\rm old}+a\mu_{b,k},\qquad
 u_k=(1-a)v_{\rm old}+av_{b,k}.\] In `Client.buffer_update`, the network is in training mode, the buffers are cleared, and the forward call enters this branch. The main driver calls this function before local SGD, then passes its outputs to `Sever.aggregate_only_buffer`. The server applies the pooled formula to \(m_k,u_k\), not to \(\mu_{b,k},v_{b,k}\).

The release does perform a separate collection pass before SGD, and its server includes the correct between-client term. These are positive design elements. They do not repair incorrect inputs to the pooled identity. The finding materially contradicts the exact-statistics component of the method as publicly implemented, and its use during evaluation makes it more than an unused helper defect. The historical code used for Tables 1–8 is not established; this review does not infer lost accuracy or fabricated results.

The collection function additionally stops after the first unshuffled batch of at most 64 examples. Section 5 discusses random subsampling of 128 images, while Equation (7) uses the whole local dataset. The server weights by the collected counts rather than the supplied full-client weights. Those differences require a precise sampling/estimand specification. They are unnecessary for the counterexample above, which uses every example.

analysis: Appendix A.1, Equation (14), page 13, replaces the absolute value of a sum of feature differences by the sum of their absolute values using an equality sign. Only a triangle inequality holds in general. The following prose asserts that greater data-distribution differences imply greater statistical offset; the calculation does not establish that assertion.

For an explicit one-step model consistent with the setup, take \(f(w,x)=w\), equal client sizes, \(w_0=0\), learning rate 1, and losses \[L_1(w)=\tfrac12(w-1)^{2},\qquad L_2(w)=\tfrac12(w+1)^2.\] The local weights are \(1,-1\), their global average is 0, and the aggregated local feature mean equals the global feature mean. Thus the left side in the disputed step is 0, while the average absolute discrepancy is 1. Scaling the targets to \(\pm c\) increases the local discrepancy without changing the mean offset. Heterogeneity can cause a mismatch, but cancellation prevents the claimed universal conclusion. Replace the equality by an upper bound and qualify the prose. This repairs a supporting motivation argument; it does not refute the valid pooled-moment identity.

For clarity, that identity follows directly by writing \(z_{ki}-\bar z=(z_{ki}-\bar z_k)+(\bar z_k-\bar z)\), summing the square, and using \(\sum_i(z_{ki}-\bar z_k)=0\): \[\sum_{k,i}(z_{ki}-\bar z)^{2}
 =\sum_kN_k\{v_k+(\bar z_k-\bar z)^{2}\}.\] An independent unequal-group example verifies it numerically. In the rendered Equation (16), the between-client term \(N_k(\bar z_k-\bar z)^{2}\) is outside the inner sum over \(i\), inside the brackets of the outer sum over \(k\). It is not multiplied by \(N_k\) a second time. The first displayed variance line places an indexed \(N_k\) before the sum over \(k\); placing it inside that sum resolves this local notation issue, and the subsequent grouped expansion gives the valid pooled identity above. Exact equality to the finite-data sample statistic should be distinguished from unbiasedness for a superpopulation, which additionally requires a specified sampling model.

analysis: Equations (5)–(7), page 4, require two adjacent-score drops strictly below the target. No assumption guarantees enough below-target candidates, and no fallback is stated. For scores \(3,2,1\) with target score 1, the eligible subset is empty and the top-two operation is undefined.

The pinned implementation introduces an additional separation condition. In `data/fashionIQ.py`, `FashionIQDataset.rerank_score`, and the corresponding CIRR method, it searches for two drop indices whose separation exceeds `consecutive_threshold`; the FashionIQ configuration sets that threshold to 1. For a target score 10 and below-target scores \(9,7,1\), the only drop indices are 0 and 1, so no pair is accepted. The endpoint variables are assigned only inside the successful branch, but used afterward. On the first query this leaves them undefined; later queries can retain preceding values. This conclusion follows from static control flow, not from executing the release.

The failure is not limited to tails too short to supply a valid pair. Take target score \(0.95\) and below-target scores \[(0.9,\,0.8,\,0.6,\,0.3,\,-0.1).\] These strictly ordered scores lie in \([-1,1]\) and are realizable as dot products between a unit query \(e_1\) and unit candidates \((s,\sqrt{1-s^{2}})\). Their successive differences are \((-0.1,-0.2,-0.3,-0.4)\), with ascending sort indices \((3,2,1,0)\). Lines 231–244 compare only adjacent entries of this sorted index list: \((3,2),(2,1),(1,0)\). Each pair has separation one, so the strict \(>1\) condition always fails. Yet original drop indices 0 and 3 form a valid separated pair. Line 248 then uses endpoints that were never assigned for this query. This exact scalar construction is recorded in `check_results.json`; no author function was executed.

Arbitrarily long tails have the same behavior: choose \(s_j=b-\delta j(j+1)/2\) with sufficiently small \(\delta>0\). The scores remain within the valid interval while drop magnitudes increase strictly, so neighboring sorted drop indices remain one apart. Corpus size alone therefore does not supply a completeness guarantee.

The training driver calls this selector at `train_qure.py`, lines 37–40, when configured reranking is active. Query-specific hard-negative selection is a core contribution, and the released search can fail to complete that update or reuse another query’s endpoints despite admissible available choices. This supports Major for the pinned implementation. The pairwise loss identity remains valid; historical occurrence, experiment commit and score effects remain unknown. Define a complete endpoint search or explicit fallback, reset per-query state, and specify short-tail and tie policies. No implementation repair or empirical rerun is certified.

analysis: Location and claim. Definition 4.1, Eq. (4), p. 5, describes a camera moving horizontally around the object at fixed elevation and uses \[x_\alpha=(x-W/2)\cos\alpha+W/2-z\sin\alpha,\qquad y_\alpha=y.\] The same page defines \(z\) as distance from the camera center to the object. The depth prior is converted by multiplication, \(Z_{\rm absolute}=rZ_{\rm relative}\). This equation supplies the point correspondences used by TTM and the rectification loss.

Decisive check. Consider a visible point marker at the orbit’s look-at pivot, two level cameras looking at that pivot, common principal point \(W/2=100\), and camera distance \(D=4\). Choose compatible length and image units with local scale one. The marker lies on both optical axes, so its horizontal coordinate is 100 in both views, under either centered perspective projection or an orthographic camera. Its camera-centered depth/range is \(z=D\). For \(\alpha=\pi/6\), Eq. (4) gives \[x_\alpha=100-4\sin(\pi/6)=98.\] This example stays within the fixed-elevation circular setting; it requires neither unrestricted poses nor occlusion.

Dependency and interpretation. Rotation about the object pivot needs a coordinate measured relative to that pivot. The equation rotates camera-centered depth without the translation that changes the rotation origin. Setting the pivot’s depth to zero repairs this example but changes the stated convention. Multiplication by a scale factor alone cannot generally provide the missing offset. These coordinates select the neighboring feature block, making this a core correspondence issue.

analysis: Location and claim. Proposition 4.2, Eq. (5), p. 5, claims stability and convergence of \(T_\alpha(\widehat x_0)\) to \(T_\alpha(x_0)\). Decisive check. The declared operator is \(T_\alpha:V\to V\), with \(V=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{2},\mathbb R)\). At \(\alpha=0\), \(T_0\) is the identity. Let \(x_0=\phi\), \(\widehat x_0=1.1\phi\), and \(\|\phi\|_2=1\), with \(\phi\) smooth and compactly supported. Use the same constant-depth scene for both images; a constant depth estimator is continuous and has bounded derivative zero. Coordinate displacement is zero, whereas \[\|T_0(\widehat x_0)-T_0(x_0)\|_2^{2}=0.01.\] The first inequality of Eq. (15) requires \(0.01\leq0\). Varying scene appearance with fixed depth suffices; inaccurate depth is not needed.

Scope of the refutation. This disproves the proof step. It does not disprove the conclusion for \(T_0\), whose identity action is Lipschitz. Interpreting \(T_\alpha\) as a coordinate map alone changes the declared image/feature operator. Coordinate displacement can satisfy a conditional estimate \[\|u_\alpha(\widehat x_0)-u_\alpha(x_0)\|
 \leq r|\sin\alpha|L_{\mathcal H}\|\widehat x_0-x_0\|\] when the depth estimator \(\mathcal H\) is Lipschitz. A feature-resampling estimate additionally needs appearance differences, spatial regularity, warp distortion, and visibility control. These terms cannot be removed by bounding coordinates.

Core dependency and repair. The invalid step bridges diffusion prediction error to TTM feature stability. The algorithm also freezes first-stage depth, while the proof compares depth estimates of changing predicted images. A corrected theorem must specify the fixed depth map, operator and norm, and residual depth bias. The training-loss/KL discussion around Eq. (19) does not itself provide a per-instance inference error bound. Appendix E and Fig. 12 give favorable tested trajectories but cannot validate the false inequality. Additional regularity may support a revised conclusion; no global impossibility is asserted.

analysis: Location and claim. Theorem 4.4, Eq. (13), p. 7, claims that the gradient error from omitting the UNet Jacobian tends to zero as \(t\to0\), justifying Eq. (14). Appendix B.3, pp. 14–15, treats the relevant gradient factors as bounded and argues that the predicted-noise Jacobian vanishes. Neither independence from the data nor a uniform dual-anchor loss-gradient bound follows from the formulation.

Construction using the specified loss. Put \(\sigma=\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\), \(\alpha_t=1-\sigma^{2}\), and take the fixed linear predictor \(\epsilon_\theta(z,t)=z\). Its Jacobian is the bounded identity. At the current spatial point choose predicted clean feature \(u=(h,0)\), \(h=\sigma>0\), by setting \[z_t=\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}h}{1-\sigma}(1,0).\] This satisfies Eq. (6) exactly. In each adjacent \(3\times3\) block put seven copies of \(e_1=(1,0)\) and two of \(e_2=(0,1)\), placing the latter away from all four corners. Both adjacent blocks are identical. The negative anchor is therefore \(e_1\), and the positive anchor is \(u\). Choose \(m^+=m^-=1/2\), the setting in Appendix C.1. All cosine similarities are defined for every \(\sigma>0\).

The exact chain factor is \((1-\sigma)/\sqrt{\alpha_t}\); omission uses \(1/\sqrt{\alpha_t}\). The \(y\)-component of their gradient difference therefore tends to \[-\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}g_y
 \longrightarrow c(A-B)
 \approx0.0402565818\neq0.\] An independent centered finite difference agrees with the analytic \(g_y\) at \(h=0.01\): \(-4.47184791807\) versus \(-4.47184791824\). For \(\sigma=10^{-2},10^{-3},10^{-4},10^{-5}\), the error components are approximately \(0.0447207,0.0407028,0.0403012,0.0402610\). These verify the construction; they are not model evaluation results.

Assumptions and scope. The example uses the unregularized cosine and local gradient map defined in Eqs. (7)–(11). The current anchor approaches zero but is never zero at a positive noise level. A uniform positive lower bound on limiting anchor norms, explicit cosine regularization, or detached fusion weights changes the assumptions or gradient. None is specified in the theorem, and no acquired code settles the implementation. This is an explicit failure under a missing mathematical condition, not a claim that typical latent trajectories must realize it. The construction is a functional counterexample under the printed assumptions. It has not been shown to constitute a complete sampling trajectory of a particular trained denoiser. A trajectory-restricted guarantee requires explicit control of the loss gradient along that trajectory.

Counterevidence and consequence. Figures 10–11, p. 18, show small errors and similar results with/without the Jacobian in tested configurations. Those observations remain relevant, as do Table 2’s speed improvements. The theorem does not establish unconditional negligible correction error. Its one-step limit also does not control accumulated trajectory error or finite early denoising steps. This is Major because the invalid general justification directly supports the central acceleration; observed empirical score loss is not required for that classification.

analysis: Location and claim. After Definition 4.3, p. 6, \(M\circ T\) is called a group homomorphism. Appendix B.4, Proposition B.2, Eq. (29), p. 15, asserts for all \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2\in\mathbb R\) \[(M T_{\alpha_1})(M T_{\alpha_2})=M T_{\alpha_1+\alpha_2}.\] The p. 16 proof removes a copy of \(M\) because \(T\) acts on coordinates and \(M\) on features.

Decisive check with the actual weights. Set \(\alpha_1=\alpha_2=0\); the claim requires \(M^{2}=M\). On a large enough image interior, use scalar positive features \(Z(x,y)=1+x^{2}+y^{2}\), or this scalar times a common nonzero feature direction. Extend the field positively with a decaying tail if an \(L^{2}\) domain is required. Anchor similarities are constant across each block: \(C^+=1\), \(C^-=0\). Eq. (7) gives \(W_v=1/9\), regardless of the mixture coefficients summing to one. This remains true after fusion.

Thus \(M\) is ordinary \(3\times3\) averaging. At the origin, \[(MZ)(0,0)=\frac73,\qquad (M^2Z)(0,0)=\frac{11}3.\] These unequal exact values disprove Eq. (29), without inaccurate warping or numerical approximation.

Dependency and repair. Coordinate/feature separation does not imply idempotence; even commutativity leaves \(M^{2}\), not \(M\). This algebra explicitly justifies the adjacent operator underlying the core loss and its composition across views. The ordinary rotation-group identity for full 3D coordinates is not disputed. One may remove the homomorphism claim and retain a heuristic local loss, or prove a different statement under explicit projection/idempotence and equivariance conditions on a specified space. Generic dual-anchor averaging lacks those conditions. Empirical consistency improvements can coexist with the false algebraic claim.

analysis: Location and intended behavior. Section 3.1, pp. 5–6, defines temporal states from preceding states/actions and describes cached keys and values across consecutive training fragments. In the pinned source, `nnet/modules/emerald/tssm.py`, both `forward_obs` (lines 341–363) and `forward` (lines 459–481) apply the episode-separation mask only inside \[\texttt{if is\_firsts.any():}\] where `is_firsts` contains current-fragment flags. The separate argument `is_firsts_hidden` can contain a reset inside the cached context. The ordinary causal/context mask does not encode episode identity.

Reachable condition. Suppose all current flags are zero, while cached flags are \((0,1)\): one old-episode value followed by the first value of the new episode. With a context limit of 64, both cached positions remain visible to the next one-step query. The guard is false, so the release uses the key mask \[(1,1,1),\] although the episode-separation helper would produce \[(0,1,1).\] This situation can occur in online collection after an environment reset. The main model’s `env_step` retains the attention cache, resets the other state fields, constructs cached reset flags, and passes them to TSSM. When no environment has a reset in the current call, the guard skips those flags. The replay buffer also concatenates successive episodes across sequence fragments, so a reset may lie in a prior cached fragment.

Decisive consequence. Choose an attention head with equal logits and value components \((2,0,0)\). Such logits are obtainable by zero query and positional-score contributions. The released mask gives output component \(2/3\), whereas correct episode isolation gives zero. With the full default cache, take 63 old-episode entries followed by the new episode’s initial entry, put the value 2 in one old entry and zero elsewhere, and use equal logits. The next query gives \(2/65\) rather than zero, so the same failure occurs with the default 64-entry cache. Thus a previous episode can influence the current representation even with identical observations/actions in the current episode. This is a mathematical attention/control-flow check written by the reviewer; the author implementation was not executed.

Counterevidence and boundary. The guard works when a current reset is present. Moreover, `imagine` applies the episode mask whenever cached flags are supplied (lines 251–255), and `play` starts each evaluation episode with a fresh state/cache. These paths limit the finding and rule out a claim that every evaluated episode necessarily has cross-episode memory. A fully empty cache also avoids the issue. The source is not bound to the historical five-seed experiments.

Impact and repair. The defect affects episode isolation in released world-model learning/collection and can create a train/evaluation state-distribution difference. Apply the episode-separation mask whenever current or cached reset information is present; keep resetting current states/actions conditional on current resets. Alternatively, explicitly discard prior-episode cache entries per environment. Check a reset at the end of one fragment followed by a fragment with no reset. The supported impact is a localized episode-isolation defect in the inspected release. The direct evaluation path starts each episode with a fresh state, and the release has not been bound to the historical experiments. The available evidence establishes a boundary-condition defect but does not establish material harm to the core scientific conclusions; the supported assessment is Minor, with historical experimental attribution remaining Needs Evidence. No repair was applied to the author’s source.

analysis: Locations. Eqs. (2)–(3) and (6), pp. 6–7; Section 3.2, p. 7; Tables 6 and 10, pp. 15 and 17. The corresponding release locations are `nnet/models/emerald.py`, default configuration and `WorldModel.forward`, and `nnet/modules/emerald/decoder_network.py`.

Loss difference with a nontrivial gradient consequence. Eq. (2) states a KL masked-prediction objective and Eq. (6) adds it without an explicit extra coefficient. The release averages KL over masked positions, multiplies by 32, clips that quantity from below at one free nat, and applies weight \(0.5\). Dynamics/representation KL terms also use a free-nat threshold. For equal per-token divergences \(\kappa\), the released masked contribution reduces to \[L_{\rm mask}^{\rm release}=\frac12\max(1,32\kappa).\] Let \(q\) be uniform on 32 categories, and let \(p_x\) assign probability \(x/16\) to each of its first 16 categories and \((1-x)/16\) to each remaining category. Then \[\kappa(x)=\tfrac12\log\frac{1/2}{x}
           +\tfrac12\log\frac{1/2}{1-x}.\] At \(x=0.6\), \(\kappa=0.0204109973\), \(32\kappa=0.6531519123<1\), and \(\kappa'(x)=5/12\neq0\), whereas the released clipped contribution has derivative zero. A centered finite-difference calculation confirms the flat released loss. Thus the missing operation is not merely an additive constant or notation change. Free-nat regularization can be a reasonable design choice; the issue is the unbound specification, not proof that regularization is intrinsically wrong.

Imagination workload. Section 3.2 says that flattening all batch/time positions produces \(B^{\rm img}=BT\). With Table 10’s \(B=16,T=64\), this means 1,024 starting trajectories. The release defaults to `img_stride=4` and selects time indices \(0,4,\ldots,60\) when constructing `detached_posts` and their caches. It therefore starts \(16\cdot16=256\) trajectories. Both use horizon 15, but their sample count per update differs by a factor of four. This matters when reproducing training throughput and the actor/critic data volume.

Decoder channel count. Table 6 projects temporal hidden state to \(4\times4\times256\) before concatenation with 1,024 latent channels, giving 1,280 channels. The released main model passes `dim_cnn=32` to `DecoderNetwork`; its hidden projection outputs 32 channels and its concatenation has 1,056 channels. This is a concrete version difference, not a claim of a tensor-shape crash: the released projection is internally dimensioned for 1,056.

Interpretation, counterevidence, and repair. The README explicitly describes twenty-seed results from the public repository, while the paper reports five-seed aggregates. Later changes could explain these differences. No historical configuration was acquired, so the findings do not establish which objective, workload, or decoder produced the paper’s numbers. The public results retain strong performance. Supply a historical commit/configuration or a documented release-to-paper change record; state the mask reduction, free-nat clipping, loss weights, imagination stride, and actual channel widths. This is a Minor reproducibility/specification issue for the available version pairing; historical experimental attribution remains Needs Evidence.

analysis:
For \(y_c>0\), multiplying the displayed formula by \(y_c\) gives \[
 \sum_w \frac{f_w}{h_{c,w}}x_{c,w}\leq y_cT .\] Both \(y_c\) and \(T\) are decision variables in the direct minimization. Their product is bilinear. Treating \(y_c\) as integer rather than continuous does not make the displayed expression linear. An auxiliary-variable construction or an equivalent discrete reformulation is required, but none is specified in the paper. Thus the formulation as printed is not a MILP. This conclusion does not assert that the underlying scheduling problem cannot have a MILP representation.

The inactive case is separate. Activation coupling gives \(x_{c,w}=0\) when \(y_c=0\), but the left-hand side of the displayed formula then contains \(0/0\), which is undefined. One feasible configuration being unused is part of the intended search, rather than an exceptional input excluded by the paper. Defining an inactive configuration’s load to be zero is sensible, but that definition or an equivalent constraint must be supplied.

Finally, the displayed formula cannot by itself replace the makespan constraint. Consider one GPU type, one feasible single-GPU configuration, and one workload. Set its availability, hourly price, budget, GPU memory, and model memory requirement all to \(1\). The single GPU is connected to itself, so all resource filters are met. Let \[f=100,\quad h=1\ {\rm request/s},\quad x=1,\quad y=1,
 \quad \widehat T=1\ {\rm s}.\] Assignment, integrality, activation, budget, memory, and availability constraints are all satisfied. The displayed shortened test returns \(x/h=1\leq1\), whereas the required load is \(xf/(yh)=100\) seconds. The discrepancy is exactly the missing request-count factor; the example uses no zero denominator or fractional request. Omitting \(y_c\) can likewise remove the benefit of activating multiple copies. The finite fixture is saved in `initial_checks.json`; the derivation is exact.

A correct aggregate feasibility formulation for a fixed candidate \(\widehat T\geq0\) replaces the displayed formula by \[
 \sum_w \frac{f_w}{h_{c,w}}x_{c,w}\leq \widehat T\,y_c .\] This is linear because \(\widehat T\) is constant. At \(y_c=0\), activation coupling forces all corresponding assignments to zero and the displayed formula is well-defined. With an exact feasibility oracle, a genuinely feasible upper bound, and a valid lower bound, monotonicity in \(\widehat T\) gives ordinary binary-search certification. A heuristic’s failure to find a schedule is not automatically a proof of infeasibility.

The direct minimization also has an exact MILP repair under the stated divisible-load model. Let \(K_c\) be any finite upper bound on the copies of configuration \(c\) from GPU availability. Introduce potential replicas \(r=1,\ldots,K_c\), binary variables \(z_{c,r}\), and fractions \(u_{c,r,w}\geq0\). Minimize \(T\) subject to \[\begin{aligned}
 &\sum_{c,r}u_{c,r,w}=1,\qquad u_{c,r,w}\leq z_{c,r},\\
 &\sum_w \frac{f_w}{h_{c,w}}u_{c,r,w}\leq T
       &&\text{for every }(c,r),\\
 &\sum_{c,r}o_cz_{c,r}\leq B,\qquad
   \sum_{c,r}d_n(c)z_{c,r}\leq a_n,\qquad T\geq0 .\end{aligned}\] Every constraint is linear. Given a valid aggregate schedule with \(y_c>0\), activate \(y_c\) replicas and set \(u_{c,r,w}=x_{c,w}/y_c\) on each: their loads equal the aggregate per-copy load. Conversely, summing replica assignments gives \(x_{c,w}\) and \(y_c=\sum_rz_{c,r}\); summing their load bounds yields the displayed formula. Thus the two models have the same feasible makespans once inactive configurations are defined correctly. The proof extends by adding the model index. This repair establishes mathematical equivalence only; it does not verify runtime, numerical conditioning, workload prediction, or equivalence to the unpublished implementation.

The invalid classification and incomplete feasibility specification concern the central scheduling derivation, not a peripheral equation. They prevent a reader from reconstructing the advertised direct MILP and interpreting its comparison with binary search in Figure 9 without additional information. The supported severity is Major. The basis is the invalid core formulation and its dependency in the multi-model and solver-efficiency claims. No whole-paper failure, empirical score decrease, or difficult repair is required for that assessment. The GPU benchmarking observations can remain valid, and no numerical experiment is declared false on this evidence.
claim:
Section 4.3, p. 7, labels equations (1)–(7) a mixed-integer linear program and describes a solver that converges to an optimal fractional assignment. Its equation (3) is \[
 \sum_w\frac{x_{c,w}f_w}{y_ch_{c,w}}\leq T
 \quad\text{for all }c ,\] while equation (7) explicitly permits \(y_c=0,1,2,\ldots\). Appendix E, pp. 15–16, repeats this quotient in the multi-model formulation. Appendix F, p. 16, then displays the binary-search load test \[
 \sum_w\frac{x_{c,w}}{h_{c,w}}\leq \widehat T ,\] and its multi-model analogue. The source PDF itself contains these expressions; they are not extraction artifacts.

positive throughput h. nonnegative request counts. divisible workload fractions summing to 1. integer nonnegative replica count. feasible memory/connectivity-filtered configuration. price budget and GPU availability constraints.
result: Appendix F also says that the candidate must satisfy all constraints in Section 4.3. If this phrase includes the original makespan constraint at fixed \(T=\widehat T\), the full test rejects the example above; the shortened expression is then an incorrect or redundant description rather than evidence that the actual oracle accepted the example. This alternative is important. The report does not infer the implementation from that displayed expression.

Likewise, a competent implementation could have expanded replica counts, linearized bounded products, used a nonlinear solver, or used a correct fixed-\(T\) feasibility problem. These possibilities preserve the overall systems idea. No implementation snapshot or solver model was available to determine which occurred. The printed formulation nevertheless does not specify the claimed direct MILP, and Appendix E inherits the same problem. Appendix F’s approximate knapsack feasibility check supplies no stated false-positive/false-negative guarantee, so its approximation cannot be assumed to preserve a certified binary-search bracket.

Displayed model not a MILP. Literal shortened feasibility expression is invalid; this does not identify the actually executed solver. Invalid core mathematical formulation supports Major; no assertion of whole-paper collapse or measured benchmark loss.

analysis: Appendix L, pp. 18–19, uses Table 6 to support the statement that estimation errors range from \(4\%\) to \(7\%\), followed by a claim that the estimates suffice for selecting optimal configurations. Using the displayed measured throughput \(a\) as reference, the usual relative error is \[e=100\,\frac{|\widehat a-a|}{a}.\] For the seven rows in their published order, exact arithmetic on the displayed values gives \[(7.143,\ 6.818,\ 4.762,\ 9.524,\ 4.762,\ 5.556,\ 8.333)\%.\] In particular, the L40 \((2,4)\) row is \(a=0.42\), \(\widehat a=0.46\) requests/s, hence \(e=9.524\%\). Using the estimate in the denominator instead gives \(8.696\%\), also above \(7\%\). The H100+A100 row gives \(8.333\%\) or \(7.692\%\), respectively. Therefore neither common denominator reproduces the asserted range from the published table.
claim: Appendix L p19 says estimation errors range from 4%to 7%, citing Table6 p18.

result: The table rounds throughput to two decimals and does not state the denominator used for the quoted range. Unrounded measurements or a different metric could explain some difference. The check therefore establishes an inconsistency between the displayed evidence and the reported range, not the true raw-measurement error distribution. Whether the profiler preserves the optimum over the full configuration search requires rank-sensitive validation beyond this seven-row example; the present calculation does not supply that validation.

analysis: Proposition 1.  For every dataset satisfying the preceding conditions, the input-independent prediction \(\widehat Y_i=\mathcal Y\) for every \(i\) attains \(\operatorname{HIT}_k=1\) for every applicable mapping \(G_k\). The result also holds if samples with unmapped reference labels are omitted, provided at least one sample remains.

Proof. Let \(i\) be any retained sample. Since \(y_i\in\mathcal Y\), pointwise mapping gives \(G_k(y_i)\in G_k(\mathcal Y)\). Substituting \(\widehat Y_i=\mathcal Y\) into the indicator in the displayed formula therefore gives one. This holds separately for each retained sample and each wheel, so averaging over samples or wheels preserves one. If the mapping discards some labels, apply the same argument to every sample whose reference has a retained mapped value. No input feature is used. ◻

A finite witness makes all parameters explicit. Take \(\mathcal Y=\{\mathrm{happy},\mathrm{sad},\mathrm{angry},\mathrm{neutral}\}\), four arbitrary inputs, and reference sequence listing those four labels once each. With the identity mapping, a constant four-label prediction gets four hits and score \(1\), exactly the score of four correctly selected singleton predictions. The constant predictor makes no decision about which emotion occurs in which sample. Mapping happy to positive, sad and angry to negative, and retaining neutral changes none of these hits. Removing neutral from both mapped reference and prediction sets leaves three retained hits out of three, again one. The independent check script verifies these and further illustrative mappings. They illustrate a general proof, not a claim to have executed the authors’ wheel files.

The current released metric corroborates the admissible operation. In |my_affectgpt/evaluation/wheel.py|, |func_map_label_to_synonym| maps labels independently; |calculate_openset_onehot_hitrate| maps each reference and prediction and adds the size of their intersection. A single retained reference maps to one label, so that intersection is exactly the indicator above. The function additionally computes a specificity-sensitive auxiliary score, but |evaluation-scoreonly.py| discards it for the basic-emotion primary score. The existence of that auxiliary calculation does not alter Eq. (13) or the Table 2 primary metric.

More generally, for \(\widehat Y_i\subseteq\widehat Y'_i\), pointwise mapping preserves inclusion, and thus \(\operatorname{HIT}_k(\widehat Y')\geq\operatorname{HIT}_k(\widehat Y)\). Adding labels can never hurt the basic score, including when added labels contain no information about the input. This identifies the precise failure: the metric rewards coverage of the reference but does not identify selective recognition.

This issue is Major because the benchmark is a named core contribution, and four of its nine primary components can attain their best possible value without using the input. It directly weakens the basic-emotion comparisons and their contribution to the headline mean. This is material harm to the interpretation of a core evaluation, rather than a demand to refute all empirical gains.

The weighting is concrete. The four basic columns contribute \(4/9\) of the unweighted mean. As a metric stress calculation only, replacing the four full-modality AffectGPT basic scores by their all-label optimum and holding its other five scores fixed changes the mean from \(74.7689\) to \(88.8211\), a \(14.0522\) point increase. This is not a simulated model, an actual improvement, or an estimate of historical bias: it quantifies how the aggregator responds to an input-independent optimum in those columns. No benchmark-score loss, whole-paper collapse or difficult repair is required for this severity.

For the claim of selecting one basic label, require a single prediction \(\widehat y_i\) from the fixed basic vocabulary and score whether it equals the reference (or use the same explicitly documented canonical grouping on both). Then the displayed formula reduces to accuracy on that chosen label space. The constant all-label output is no longer admissible. This restores the specific distinction tested by the counterexample, but does not establish completeness of fine-grained annotations or validate all free-form reasoning.

A complementary open-description task can retain coverage as a named diagnostic and use exhaustively annotated reference sets, or an independently specified human evaluation, for additional-label correctness. The report does not assert that a new automatic precision penalty against the original single-label references is ground truth. The proposed singleton restriction is analytically checked; its effect on the actual rankings remains untested.
claim: The conditions relevant to the check are precisely those in the metric: \(\mathcal Y\) is finite; every reference label belongs to it; prediction sets may contain multiple labels; and the same label mapping is applied to prediction and reference. There is no cardinality limit, wrong-label penalty or exclusivity constraint in the displayed formula. The argument operates on the extracted sets supplied to the metric. It does not assume that a particular language-model extraction prompt will always convert an arbitrary caption into a specified set.

Finite reference vocabulary Y. Every ground-truth \(y_i\) belongs to Y. Variable-cardinality predicted sets with no exclusivity/cardinality constraint. Same pointwise grouping \(G_k\) applied to both reference and prediction. For omitted-unmapped implementation, at least one reference remains; result evaluated on retained subset. result: The authors explicitly disclose the missing penalty in the paragraph following Eq. (13), p. 7. Let \(s_{de}\) be the score of checkpoint \(e\) on dataset \(d\). This routine reports \[

analysis: Consider this original implementation:
Predict precisely these three signatures:

Code:
def f() -> str: ...
def h(x: int) -> int: ...
def g() -> int: ...

All functions are present; all parameters and returns use ordinary explicit primitive types; there is no `Any`, missing file, syntax error, external dependency, overload, dynamic dispatch, or untyped body. Thus neither missing predictions nor gradual-typing escape hatches explain the discrepancy. This is a counterexample to the metric’s interpretation, not a claimed member of the curated 50-repository dataset.

The predicted stub is internally type-correct. Applying its signatures to the original bodies instead changes only the return annotation of `f`. The literal return value \(1\) is an `int`, contradicting the predicted `str`; moreover `h(f())` supplies a declared `str` to a required `int` argument. The latter is an `arg-type` error, explicitly included in Appendix C.2.

An independently written fixture was checked with the already installed Mypy 1.14.1 and Python 3.13.5. The original implementation produced zero errors; the predicted stub produced zero errors; the reannotated implementation produced two errors, `return-value` and `arg-type`. This is an actual finite diagnostic on new reviewer-written programs, not execution of the authors’ evaluator. The paper reports Mypy 1.11.1/Python 3.12, so this run is not claimed to reproduce that environment. The structural argument does not depend on a version-specific diagnostic: the predicted stub contains none of the original return or call expressions.
claim:
For two base types the paper defines a Jaccard similarity of supported attribute sets after excluding common `object` operations. Ordered generic arguments are averaged positionwise and normalized by the larger arity; union members use a maximum-weight matching, again normalized by the larger cardinality. The root and argument contributions are averaged. These operations yield scores in \([0,1]\) when the base score does, handle unequal arities as specified, and are symmetric. The published example \[S(\mathrm{List[int]},\mathrm{Sequence[float]})
 =\tfrac12(0.7+0.6)=0.65\] is arithmetically correct. A partial-match score is a similarity heuristic, not a proof of type substitutability; this distinction alone is not counted as a defect.

The supplementary Tables 9–17 contain 50 rows per model, with 47 finite TypeCheck entries. Recomputed TypeCheck means include \(366.0213\) for GPT-4o, \(127.1277\) for Claude-3.5-Sonnet, and \(214.6170\) for DeepSeek-V3; these agree with Table 2 at its printed precision. The corresponding TypeSim means are \(0.80448\), \(0.78762\), and \(0.79468\). This is a check of published arithmetic, not a replication of the measurements. The three unavailable checker runs are disclosed in Table 6, rather than silently treated as zero.

Section 4.2 (p. 5) motivates TypeCheck using inconsistencies such as a predicted return type being incompatible with its uses, and interprets counted errors as obstacles to practical use. Section 6.2 (p. 7) compares model error counts with the original repository average of \(141.8\) and interprets a lower count as stronger consistency. The abstract and conclusion make repository-wide consistency a central contribution.

The released dataflow is decisive. `run.py` mounts the prediction directory. The Docker entry point invokes |scripts/evaluation.py| with that directory. Its `evaluate` function calls |get_repo_similarity(original_repo,prediction_directory)|. In `repo_similarity.py`, the original and prediction directories are passed separately to |get_type_dict_from_repo|. In `helpers.py`, that function copies each input program’s own files to a temporary directory and calls Mypy’s builder. No step inserts predicted signatures into the original function bodies or recreates their call sites. The predictions requested on pp. 7 and 14 are `.pyi` stub files. Ordinary stub files contain signatures but elide implementation logic [mypy].

Consequently the procedure compares \[E(P_{\mathrm{original}})\quad\hbox{with}\quad
 E(S_{\mathrm{predicted}}),\] where \(E\) is the selected error count and \(S\) is a stub program. To evaluate compatibility of predicted types with the original uses, the required object is instead \[E\!\left(P_{\mathrm{original}}[
       \text{predicted annotations}]\right).\] These quantities need not agree even for complete, syntactically valid predictions.

Complete syntactically valid predicted stub signatures. Explicit ordinary primitive types, no Any. Original function implementations and call sites fixed. Separate original/prediction checker inputs, as in released dataflow.
result: Stub checking can detect genuine inconsistencies in declarations, inheritance, and imports. It is useful for interface validation. The paper also reports missing rates, which provide information beyond the raw error count. These facts do not make the stub-only count a test of implementation compatibility: the counterexample has complete signatures and no missing files.

A separate possibility is that historical prediction folders contained transformed implementations in addition to stubs. No supplied raw prediction artifacts establish that, and the released pipeline does not perform such transformation. The report therefore does not assert that every published model score was generated by this commit, or that any ranking reverses. It establishes that the described/released evaluation does not support the broad interpretation placed on TypeCheck, and that the direct model-versus-original comparison changes the set of checked program obligations.

Assessment: Major. Repository-level consistency is a principal benchmark contribution and a central empirical conclusion. Losing the original usage constraints materially affects that measurement, even if TypeSim and the qualitative need for better type inference remain useful. A defensible repair is to apply predictions to a fixed implementation/caller corpus and count the same checks for every model, reporting parse/annotation failures separately. That repair design is logically targeted; its effects on the published benchmark require a fresh evaluation and are not verified here.

Correct implementation zero errors, predicted .pyi zero errors, reannotated unchanged implementation two errors: return-value and arg-type. The latter is in the paper's counted categories. Stubs remove the offending expressions.
