analysis: Consider a one-step finite MDP. Its initial state has three actions, each deterministically gives reward one and terminates. Fix \(\gamma=0.9\); its value is immaterial after termination. Let \(\pi_0,\pi_1,\pi_2\) be the deterministic policies choosing the respective actions. All policies are implementable, and each has return \(J(\pi_i)=1=J(\pi^\star)\).

Give the parent strategy masses \[p=(0.98,0.01,0.01).\] Let a more restrictive child require choosing either action one or action two. Its support is the proper subset \(\{\pi_1,\pi_2\}\). Condition the parent on that subset: \[q(\pi_1)=q(\pi_2)=\frac{0.01}{0.02}=\frac12.\] Both distributions are normalized, have finite Shannon entropy, and refer to policies in the same MDP. The refinement only removes a permitted policy. It preserves every remaining policy’s optimal value and implementability. Thus no loss of value, infeasibility, unknown dynamics, continuous density, or infinite support explains the example.

With natural logarithms, \[\begin{aligned}
 H(p)&=-0.98\log0.98-2(0.01\log0.01)
       =0.1119020569\ldots,\\
 H(q)&=-2\left(\tfrac12\log\tfrac12\right)
       =\log2=0.6931471806\ldots.\end{aligned}\] The support shrinks from three policies to two, but entropy increases by approximately \(0.5812451\) nats. Choose \(H_{\max}=0.2\), \(\tau=0.005\), and \(v_{\min}=0.1\). The parent satisfies the entropy budget; the child violates it. Every retained policy lies above the probability threshold and has value one, so both the relative and additive near-optimality requirements hold. Feasibility is one for both strategies, and the child-to-parent optimal-value ratio is one. All the operative value and feasibility conditions therefore survive while the claimed specificity implication fails.

The independent arithmetic check reproduces these numbers in |independent_checks_output.json|. More generally, \(H(p)=h(0.02)+0.02\log2\) here, whereas entropy conditional on the rare two-policy subset is \(\log2\). Conditioning can increase uncertainty for a particular selected branch, even though the average conditional entropy obeys a different inequality.
claim: The paper proposes choosing a distribution \(\delta_\Pi\) over policies before low-level reinforcement learning. Its Strategy Problem trades off specificity, represented by entropy, and retention of a near-optimal policy. The implementation builds a natural-language strategy tree using an LLM, estimates each node’s value and feasibility, and converts a chosen strategy into a distilled state score used for reward shaping. Experiments compare strategy-guided and baseline PPO/EDE agents in original and modified Crafter.

For a discrete prior with policy masses \(p_i\), write \[H(p)=-\sum_i p_i\log p_i,\qquad
 S_\tau=\{\pi_i:p_i\geq\tau\}.\] The appendix explicitly restricts its entropy argument to finite or countable policy collections. It assumes that a near-optimal policy belongs to \(S_\tau\), that candidate policies can be executed, and that episodes are independently sampled from the same initial-state distribution. These are substantive requirements. A natural-language node and a neural policy learner do not automatically provide an enumerable thresholded policy set or the required distribution.

Section 4.1, p. 5, constrains children to increasingly specific policy subsets. Section 4.3 then asserts \[H(\delta_{h_{i,j}})<H(\delta_{h_i})\] as a consequence of the tree’s design. Appendix B.2.1, p. 19, repeats that narrowing subgoals implicitly drives entropy down and explains that neither entropy nor the threshold \(H_{\max}\) is numerically checked. This is the proposed connection between the implementable tree construction and the formal specificity objective.

Support inclusion alone does not imply that Shannon entropy decreases. This remains false under the natural, favorable interpretation that a child distribution is exactly its parent’s conditional distribution on the retained policies, rather than an arbitrarily reweighted new distribution.

One-step finite MDP, three deterministic actions/policies, each reward1 and then termination, \(\gamma=0.9\). Parent masses(.98,.01,.01); child is exact parent conditional distribution on policies1,2. Proper subset support, normalized finite distributions, all policies implementable. \(H_{\max}=0.2\), \(\tau=0.005\), \(v_{\min}=0.1\); both relative and additive near-optimality requirements satisfied.
result: If every node were explicitly uniform on its finite support, strict support reduction would imply \(H=\log|\operatorname{supp}|\) decreases. An explicit entropy-contraction constraint would also suffice by assumption. Neither condition is imposed on the paper’s general strategy distributions or implemented by its language prompts. A verbal goal that is more concrete specifies no probability weights.

The assertion may be read as an intended design objective rather than a proven property. Under that reading, the formal inequality should be replaced by a heuristic hypothesis and should not be presented as guaranteed by hierarchy. Appendix B.2.1’s acknowledgment that entropy is not computed is important counterevidence to any claim that the implementation certifies the Strategy Problem; it does not make the displayed implication mathematically true.

The issue is Major. Specificity is one of the two defining quantities of the Strategy Problem, and automatic entropy reduction is the stated reason that the strategy tree addresses it without calculating entropy. The counterexample invalidates that central derivation. It does not invalidate the conditional PAC theorem or demonstrate that the recorded Crafter improvements disappear. Those surviving results do not remove the direct dependency of the formal-to-algorithm connection on the false implication.
Parent H=0.1119020568909309<=0.2; child H=0.6931471805599453>0.2. Support shrinks3to2 but entropy rises0.5812451236690144. Value and feasibility are unchanged.

analysis:
Appendix B.2, p. 18, selects a leaf using its root-relative feasibility and value. For a path \((h_0,h_1,\ldots,h_m)\), the displayed formulas give \[
 Q(h_m)=\prod_{j=1}^m
         f(h_j\mid h_{j-1})\,V(h_j\mid h_{j-1}).\] This discounts a locally promising subgoal when its ancestors retain little feasibility or value.
In the pinned `strategist/tree.py`, lines 57–83, |find_most_promising_leaf| performs a depth-first search and computes only

Code:
return node["feasibility"] * node["value"]

at each leaf or sequential node. The recursive return passes this score upward unchanged. No ancestor product is accumulated. Both strategy-tree refinement and default final selection call this method in `strategist_agent.py`. The prompts define value relative to the parent, so the omitted factors cannot generally be absorbed into the stored value.

The supplied `runs/crafter-mod-farm-easy_gpt-4o/tree.json` provides a decisive non-synthetic example. Treat sequential nodes as terminal candidates, exactly as the released selector does. Root feasibility and value both equal one. Each relevant field is a finite number in \([0,1]\). Applying the two explicitly specified arithmetic rules to the same JSON gives:
Candidate | Leaf-only score | Root-path score
Survival plan, node 11 | \(0.5200 | 0.3276\)

For example, the survival plan has local \(f=0.6\) and \(V=0.866666\ldots\), giving \(0.52\). Its parent has \(f=0.9\) and \(V=0.7\), so the paper’s score is \(0.9(0.7)(0.52)=0.3276\). Direct hunting is a root child with score \(0.7(0.6)=0.42\).

The released selection arithmetic therefore chooses survival (node 11); the stated root-relative rule chooses hunting (node 2). Both maxima are strict, so neither tie handling nor floating-point rounding explains the difference. The independent script reads only JSON data and computes both formulas; it does not import or execute `Tree`.

The issue is Major for the released automatic selection implementation. The ranking rule directly determines which strategy branch is refined or chosen for reward shaping, a central algorithmic decision. The actual supplied tree demonstrates a different chosen strategy, not merely a numerically different unused field. The paper’s intended algorithm and its release therefore disagree at a core step.

Multiplying the local factors along each root-to-candidate path restores the displayed formula for a fixed tree and declared parent-relative attributes; the calculation above verifies that specific repair. A log-domain implementation could avoid underflow. This repair does not validate LLM estimates, establish the historical experiment commit, or predict revised learning curves. Those would require separate provenance and experiments.

analysis: Let \(s_{t+1}\) be the state just reached by a training step. The collector saves its observation. The callback then resets the same underlying environment and completes evaluation trajectories, leaving its state at \(s_{\rm eval}\). The next training action is chosen using the saved observation of \(s_{t+1}\) but applied to \(s_{\rm eval}\).

An independent four-state deterministic fixture makes the inconsistency explicit. Let the sole action implement \(T(s)=(s+1)\bmod4\). Suppose training has just observed \(0\to1\). An evaluation segment resets to zero and stops at state three. The cached training observation remains one. The next actual transition is \(3\to0\), while the learner can record it as \(1\to0\); the valid transition from one is \(1\to2\). Thus the recorded transition has probability zero under the stated transition kernel. A real environment that forbids stepping after an episode ends can instead raise an error. The exact symptom depends on its wrapper, but the uncoordinated mutation remains.
This fixture checks the object-sharing mechanism only. It is not a Crafter simulation, and no author callback or training loop was run.

It assumes that a near-optimal policy belongs to \(S_\tau\), that candidate policies can be executed, and that episodes are independently sampled from the same initial-state distribution. These are substantive requirements. A natural-language node and a neural policy learner do not automatically provide an enumerable thresholded policy set or the required distribution.

analysis:
Suppose, as in the ordinary reading of a single fixed test split and sample accuracy, that the evaluated test set is the same for every method, and that easy and hard partition this set. Let \(n_E,n_H>0\) be the category sizes, and let \(c_{m,E},c_{m,H}\) be a method’s numbers of correct answers. Write \[p=\frac{n_E}{n_E+n_H}.\] The exact percentages must then satisfy \[\begin{aligned}
 E_m&=100\,c_{m,E}/n_E, &
 H_m&=100\,c_{m,H}/n_H,\\
 O_m&=100\,(c_{m,E}+c_{m,H})/(n_E+n_H)
     =pE_m+(1-p)H_m.                     \end{aligned}\] The same \(p\) is required for all methods, regardless of model size, training procedure, answer quality, or stochastic generation.

The finding is assessed as Major for the reported RAG evidence: Table 7 directly supports the central demonstration that a shared graph-conditioned model can outperform specialized and long-context competitors across task families. A comparison that cannot be reconciled with its disclosed evaluation population cannot currently carry that inference in its stated numerical form. This is a core evidence defect; a reversal of the empirical ranking or failure of every other task is not required to recognize it.

The precise corrective requirement is to supply the test example IDs, difficulty labels, generated answers, correctness rule, and aggregation procedure, then recompute all relevant columns on the declared common population or disclose and justify a different estimand. The necessary identity the displayed formula is a verified validation condition for common-test micro-accuracy. It is not a replacement set of experimental results. No numerical repair is adopted or asserted verified. Which entries or protocols need correction, and whether the headline advantage survives, remain Needs Evidence.
claim: Section 5, p. 7, identifies accuracy as the RAG metric. Appendix A.5, pp. 16–17, describes LongBench v2 as 503 multiple-choice questions divided into easy and hard categories, and states an \(8{:}1{:}1\) train/validation/test split. Table 7, p. 8, gives overall, easy, and hard results for seven methods. Its caption and Section 5.1 use these results to claim that GWM with 2k context outperforms long-context baselines and that GWM-E is superior to GWM-T on this task.

The original p. 8 image was inspected. The following are printed percentages, not values inferred from a chart: \[\begin{array}{c|rrr}
 & O & E & H\\ \hline
 \mathrm{BM25}&27.45&41.18&20.59\\
 \mathrm{GWM\text{-}T}&29.40&35.71&21.74\\
 \mathrm{GWM\text{-}E}&33.32&39.16&29.52
\end{array}\] The arXiv v1 HTML also contains these values; no correction is supplied by that version check.

Interpret the reported quantity as ordinary sample accuracy on one common fixed test set. Its easy and hard questions form a partition with positive sizes \(n_E,n_H\), and the same partition is used by every method. Each two-decimal printed percentage may differ from its unrounded value by at most \(0.005\) percentage points. The check allows that rounding interval and does not assume an undisclosed exact test-set size.
result: Several explanations are logically possible, and the check does not identify which occurred.

First, some table entries may be transcription or aggregation errors. That would require corrected entries, but the arithmetic alone cannot identify them. Second, rows may use different test subsets. This can explain different implied difficulty proportions, but then their overall accuracies are not measurements on the common fixed test population implied by the comparison.

Third, the authors may have used an undisclosed macro-average over task categories, with different aggregation weights for overall and difficulty-specific results. Such an estimand need not obey the displayed formula; it must be defined before these columns can be interpreted. Fourth, the values may average repeated experiments over changing random splits. In that case \[\overline O
 =\overline H+\overline{p(E-H)}\] need not equal \(\overline H+\overline p(\overline E-\overline H)\), because split composition and performance can covary. Repeated stochastic predictions on the same fixed split, by contrast, preserve the displayed formula after averaging and do not resolve the contradiction.

The paper’s inspected methods, appendix, and released files do not provide a macro-aggregation definition, changing-split protocol, per-row test IDs, or prediction records that resolve these alternatives. Therefore the established result is an incompatibility between the numerical table and the ordinary single-split accuracy protocol that is disclosed. The review does not conclude that the data were fabricated, that a particular model’s result is false, or that a corrected comparison must reverse the ranking.

Analytic partition identity plus independently authored exact rational arithmetic; original PDF Table 7 pixels actually viewed. For \(p\)=n_easy/(n_easy+n_hard), \(O_m=p*E_m\)+(1-\(p\))*\(H_m\) for every method on a common test set. Rounding bound: |(O-H)-\(p\)(E-H)|<=0.01 percentage points. Intervals. Bm25: 0.33268576979116077. Intervals. Bm25: 0.33365711510441964. Intervals. Gwm-t: 0.5476020042949177. Intervals. Gwm-t: 0.5490336435218325. Intervals. Gwm-e: 0.39315352697095435. Intervals. Gwm-e: 0.39522821576763484. The intervals are disjoint; the published table cannot be reconciled under the disclosed common-test sample-accuracy interpretation. All seven rows were checked. Checks completed: counterevidence. Checks completed: severity. Relevant frozen source passages/static source, existing actual check output and independent analytic integration; no author-code execution. For a common fixed test partition, overall accuracy is \(p\) times easy plus (1-\(p\)) times hard. The checked rounding intervals for the printed rows have no common \(p\), including disjoint BM25 and GWM-T intervals. Alternative undisclosed weighting or changing subsets remain explicit limitations. Major concerns internally inconsistent core RAG evidence, without a fabrication or ranking-reversal claim.

analysis: The abstract links the released GWM repository, and its README supplies dataset preparation and training instructions. This finding concerns only commit |4b9fe29f7e8fb2e7a6162956d86f8eaeffc2516b|. The source manifest records the repository tree as complete at acquisition; this is not a case in which the review excluded the missing internal modules.

The package initializer |gwm_e/model/__init__.py|, lines 1–3, imports |language_model.llaga_llama|, |language_model.llaga_mpt|, and |language_model.llaga_opt|. None of the corresponding Python modules or package initializers exists in the acquired tree. The language-model directory contains `gwm_llama.py` instead. Under ordinary Python import semantics, importing this package cannot load the three nonexistent relative modules merely by installing third-party dependencies.

Renaming the first import alone would not establish a working repair. In `gwm_llama.py`, line 27 imports `GWMMetaModel` and `GWMMetaForCausalLM`, but line 35 names the undefined base `GWMMMetaModel`, and line 42 names `LlagaMetaForCausalLM`. Further class references retain other names from the earlier implementation. These are reached during module/class construction, before an experiment can run.
A separate, conclusive control-flow defect occurs in |gwm_e/train/train.py|. The dataset constructor’s loop starts at line 663:

The `else` begins at line 702 and raises at line 703. Static AST inspection confirms that this is the for-loop’s `else` block, not an `if`-branch, and that the loop contains no `break`. Therefore, if all loop iterations finish normally, the constructor unconditionally raises. An exception inside an iteration also prevents successful construction. The subsequent assignment to |self.pretrained_embs| and sample-loading code is located after the unconditional raise within that block. This proof is independent of data content and does not require loading model weights or executing author code.
claim: The linked released code provides an implementation and training path for the described GWM.

Fix the inspected complete repository tree at commit `4b9fe29f7e8fb2e7a6162956d86f8eaeffc2516b`, with no excluded internal files. Use ordinary Python relative-import, class-definition, and `for`–`else` semantics. The claim concerns whether the documented package and dataset-construction path can complete under those semantics; no historical experiment snapshot is assumed to be identical.
result: The repository acknowledges that it builds on LLaGA and LLaVA. That explains the naming context but does not make absent relative modules available in the pinned GWM package. A private working tree or a different experiment commit may have contained the intended implementations; the reviewed manifest expressly does not bind this release to the published experimental run. The missing dataset download target in the README and absence of evaluation artifacts further limit reproduction, but are not used to infer a numerical defect in the paper.

This is a supported Minor released-artifact finding. It prevents a reader from following the supplied training path as released. The present evidence does not show that these failing source bytes generated the paper’s tables, that the graph operator itself is mathematically invalid, or that reported performance is lower. Its supported dependency is the usability of the released implementation, rather than a demonstrated failure of a core scientific conclusion; the severity remains Minor even within a report whose separate empirical-evidence finding is Major.

A complete repair would require an internally consistent model package and a corrected, tested dataset constructor. Several independent failures are present, so a one-line rename or indentation change is not certified as sufficient. No author files were modified, no proposed patch was executed, and no repair is marked verified.

All three relative llaga_* modules imported by model/__init__.py are absent; the directory instead contains gwm_llama.py. gwm_llama.py imports GWMMetaModel/GWMMetaForCausalLM but names undefined GWMMMetaModel and LlagaMetaForCausalLM bases. Dataset loop at line663 has a for-else whose first statement is unconditional raise ValueError at 703. No break exists in the loop subtree. Normal loop completion raises; an iteration exception also prevents successful construction. Sample-population statements after the raise are unreachable in that block. Source reads, existence checks, and AST parsing only. Checks completed: counterevidence. Checks completed: severity. Relevant frozen source passages/static source, existing actual check output and independent analytic integration; no author-code execution. Pinned module paths and undefined class names were statically checked, as was the dataset loop's for-else raise with no break. These are concrete release usability defects. Historical experiment execution is not tied to this snapshot, so the report correctly retains Minor and does not claim an end-to-end repair.

analysis: Appendix B.2, p. 17, defines positive clusters as co-clusters containing both generated and dataset sequences and negative clusters as co-clusters containing only generated sequences. It defines PCD and NCD as their respective counts divided by the total number of sequences. Tables 5 and 6, pp. 26–27, report a reference row with \(\mathrm{PCD}=0.990\) and \(\mathrm{NCD}=0.304\). Table 5 reports \(0.214\) and \(0.945\) for flow matching.

Complete check. Let \(G\) be the number of generated sequence instances and let \(P,N\) count the two kinds of clusters in the same clustering. Each counted cluster contains at least one generated instance, and clusters are disjoint. Thus \(P+N\leq G\). If the common denominator \(M\) is the number of generated instances, or the number of all generated-plus-reference instances, then \(M\geq G\), and \[\mathrm{PCD}+\mathrm{NCD}=\frac{P+N}{M}\leq 1.\] This argument does not require any monotonicity property of the clustering algorithm or an assumption that two thresholded clusterings are nested. The printed sums are \(1.294\) and \(1.159\). Even allowing independent rounding errors of \(0.0005\) in both entries, the sums are at least \(1.293\) and \(1.158\). They cannot represent the stated common-denominator quantities. ◻

Counterevidence and bounded impact. Separately normalized conditional densities, a transposed row, or an unstated denominator could explain the numbers, but each would require a corrected definition or table. The available repository lacks the co-clustering evaluation driver and underlying cluster counts, so the review does not choose replacement numbers. The contradiction prevents literal quantitative interpretation of these particular reference/ablation entries; it does not establish that the headline pLDDT or FD comparisons are wrong.

There is a separate, direct cross-table conflict in the ESMc-300M result: Table 3 and its discussion on p. 6 report \(\mathrm{CD}_{0.5}=0.963\), while Table 7 on p. 29 reports \(0.863\) for the corresponding AFDBv4-90 comparison. The difference is \(0.100\), not rounding. Both values remain below ESM2-650M’s \(0.986\), so the direction of that local comparison survives. The record must identify which value and run are authoritative. Likewise, the RFDiffusion unique success rate is described as \(0.06\) on pp. 8 and 36 but appears as \(0.07\), with an external-analysis footnote, in Table 13; either is below DiMA’s reported \(0.10\). These are Minor reporting defects, with exact corrections unverified. Source-image anchors are listed in Appendix 6 (#app:evidence).
claim: PCD/NCD count disjoint positive/negative co-clusters divided by a common total sequence count; repeated tables represent the same encoder comparison.

Every counted cluster contains a generated sequence and clusters are disjoint. The written denominator is common total generated or generated-plus-reference sequences. Three-decimal table rounding bounded by 0.0005 per entry.
result: Printed definitions and values cannot all be correct as written; replacement values unresolved. Local metric interpretation/reporting defect, not a demonstrated reversal of central comparative conclusions.

analysis: The CHEAP shorten-two component is evaluated in Sections 3.4.2 and E.6. In the pinned release, `src/encoders/cheap.py`, lines 74–86, first compresses the batch maximum length by two, then clips each uncompressed sequence length to that already compressed maximum before halving it again.

Complete check. Take the valid interface inputs \(\texttt{lens}=[254]\), \(\texttt{max\_sequence\_len}=254\), and \(\texttt{shorten\_factor}=2\). The allocated latent width is \(\lceil254/2\rceil=127\), but the per-sequence mask receives only \[\left\lceil\frac{\min(254,127)}2\right\rceil=64\] active positions, rather than 127. The decoding path at lines 70–71 explicitly truncates the sequence to twice the mask sum, so the output has at most 128 residues, not the requested 254. The length sampler returns raw sequence lengths and supplies no prior factor-two conversion. This calculation depends only on the explicit mask and output-slice arithmetic, not on the external CHEAP decoder’s behavior.

Counterevidence and impact. The supplied default and supported pretrained configuration use shorten-one, where this particular branch is inactive. No historical shorten-two configuration or generated-length records bind this code to the corresponding paper results. The supported judgment is therefore Minor for the optional released path, with historical impact unresolved. A precise repair is to clamp each raw length to the raw maximum before applying the single compression: \(m_i=\lceil\min(\ell_i,L_{\max})/2\rceil\), bounded by the allocated compressed width. For odd lengths the decoder must also retain the requested raw length if exact truncation is intended. This restores the mask count; it does not validate external decoder integration or old experiments.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Clamp each raw length to raw maximum then compress once, \(m_i\)=\(\left\lceil \min(\ell_i,L_{\max})/2\right\rceil\), bounded by latentwidth; retain original rawlength for exact odd-length output trimming.

Optional shorten_factor2 branch; valid lens[254],max_sequence_len254. Length sampler returns raw sequence length; output slice is governed by 2*mask.sum.

analysis: The method’s coordinate normalization and token reconstruction are described on pp. 3–4. The release’s documented decoder-training route calls `src/preprocessing/train_decoder.py`. In its `loss_step`, line 26 denormalizes the latent, then line 29 calls `batch_get_logits`. The ESM2 implementation, `src/encoders/esm2.py`, lines 89–95, denormalizes again. In contrast, `batch_decode`, lines 74–86, used by generation, denormalizes once. The training entry point enables the normalizer.

Core dependency. Figure 1, p. 2, identifies the decoder as one of the method’s three core components; the token-reconstruction paragraph, p. 3, describes its finetuning, and Table 5, p. 26, includes the finetuning ablation. The release’s `src/configs/config.yaml`, lines 3–4, selects ESM2 with the transformer decoder. `src/configs/decoder/transformer.yaml`, line 13, configures three new layers. `src/encoders/esm2.py`, lines 37–47, constructs this decoder and loads its checkpoint when present; `src/encoders/transformer_decoder.py`, lines 16–17, constructs the transformer and output projection from configuration. The documented Stage 2 command in `README.md`, lines 128–142, trains that decoder through the affected route. Finally, `src/diffusion/base_trainer.py`, lines 492–532, sends generated normalized latents through `pred_logits` and `batch_decode`, using the single inverse map. The discrepancy therefore crosses the default learned decoder’s training, validation, and deployment boundary.

Complete check. For one nondegenerate coordinate let the stored mean and standard deviation be \(\mu\) and \(s>0\), with \(s\geq 10^{-5}\) so the small-variance guard is inactive. Put \[N(x)=(x-\mu)/s,\qquad D(z)=sz+\mu.\] Training therefore presents \(D(D(z_t))\) to the decoder; generation presents \(D(z)\). Their difference at the same normalized input is \[D(D(z))-D(z)=s(s-1)z+s\mu.
 \] Equality for every \(z\) requires \(s=1,\mu=0\). The discrepancy also occurs in the noiseless decoder-validation branch, which bypasses corruption but not either denormalization.

For a valid finite interface example, take equally frequent raw encodings \(-1\) and \(3\). Their population mean is \(1\), variance \(4\), and normalized encodings are \(-1,+1\). The decoder’s training inputs are \(-1,7\), whereas the generation inputs are \(-1,3\). A two-class decoder with logits \(0,u-5\) correctly classifies targets \(0,1\) at the training inputs but assigns both generation inputs to class \(0\). Scaling both logits’ difference makes the training classification arbitrarily confident without repairing the inference mismatch. This establishes that fitting the double-transformed training inputs need not make the single-transformed inference path correct. It is an illustrative interface counterexample, not a claim that ESM2 produces these embeddings or that the released optimizer learns this classifier.

Counterevidence, repair, and impact. The discrepancy vanishes for identity statistics, at particular fixed points, or for a decoder insensitive to the transformed directions. The README also permits skipping decoder training with the pretrained `lm_head` (line 132); that alternative does not establish correctness of the default newly trained transformer path. Other encoders or historically different code are outside this finding’s demonstrated dependency. Actual normalization tensors and trained decoder weights are absent, so the example cannot estimate historical accuracy loss. A model might tolerate some mismatch. These possibilities bound the affected configurations and numerical impact; they do not make the default training and deployment interfaces equal.

Removing the outer denormalization from `loss_step`, while retaining the existing denormalization inside `batch_get_logits`, restores the single map \(D(z_t)\) algebraically for every admitted \(\mu,s,z_t\). This is an interface repair only: it does not validate old checkpoints or prove the paper’s reported finetuning improvement without retraining/evaluation. The supported assessment is Major for the pinned release’s default ESM2/transformer decoder-training route under nonidentity statistics. A core learned component is optimized and validated on a different latent-to-token interface from the one used in generation; the finite example proves that successful fitting and noiseless validation need not transfer through that interface. Quantitative historical effects and the paper’s reported finetuning gain remain Needs Evidence. The scope is this demonstrated core training/deployment inconsistency, without a claim that every encoder, checkpoint, or published protein-generation result fails.
claim: The decoder is a core DiMA component; advertised token reconstruction fine-tunes it for decoding generated normalized embeddings through the same inverse-normalization interface.

Default ESM2/transformer decoder configuration and documented Stage 2 training route with normalizer enabled. Stored mean mu and positive std s>=1e-5; for nonidentity statistics D(\(D(z)\)) differs generically from \(D(z)\). Finite interface counterexample is admissible algebra, not actual ESM embeddings, a measured learned decoder, or a recovered historical experiment.
result: A core learned decoder is trained and validated on D(\(D(z)\)) but deployed on \(D(z)\); the valid finite example proves that fitting/validation success does not generally transfer through the mismatched interface. Major for the pinned default ESM2/transformer learned-decoder route under nonidentity normalization: the advertised core component's training/validation contract is inconsistent with generation. This does not require a measured benchmark loss or whole-model collapse. Historical finetuning gains, magnitude of score effects and other configurations remain Needs Evidence.

claim: pLDDT evaluated over generated samples; released helper calculates each prediction then returns sequence-keyed dictionary.
Duplicate strings occur within a rank and not all unique sequence scores are equal. Counterexample uses deterministic admissible scores90 and 30; no actual folding-model values are asserted.
analysis: The inspected release’s `src/metrics/plddt.py`, lines 31–40, stores a predicted score under the protein-sequence string: \(\texttt{result[protein] = score}\). The active caller in `src/metrics/metric.py`, lines 24–27, averages that dictionary’s values. Repeated occurrences on one rank overwrite their earlier entries.

Complete check. Assume a deterministic quality score \(q(u)\in[0,100]\) for each distinct sequence \(u\), and let \(m_u\) be its multiplicity among generated draws. The ordinary mean over draws is \[\bar q_{\rm draws}=\frac{\sum_u m_uq(u)}{\sum_u m_u},
 \qquad
 \bar q_{\rm unique}=\frac{1}{|\{u:m_u>0\}|}\sum_{u:m_u>0}q(u).\] The code computes the second quantity within each rank. Take four valid score-bearing draws \(A,A,A,B\), with hypothetical scores \(q(A)=90\), \(q(B)=30\). Then the generated-draw mean is \(75\), while the one-rank dictionary mean is \(60\). This example uses admissible score values, assumes no score stochasticity, and executes no folding model. If split into equally sized rank lists \((A,A)\) and \((A,B)\), the equal average of rank-local unique means is \((90+60)/2=75\). Thus even with equal shard lengths, the implemented result can depend on the partition. The independently authored finite calculation reproduces these values.

Counterevidence and impact. Quality of distinct outputs is a legitimate estimand when explicitly defined, especially alongside a diversity measure. It is not the same as average quality per generated attempt. A dictionary may also serve as a computation cache, but the final average must then restore each key’s multiplicity if the target is the draw mean. When all predictions are distinct, the present implementation agrees with the draw mean on equal-sized shards. The paper explicitly discusses duplicate generation in some baselines, so this distinction is relevant to comparative evaluation; it does not prove that this release evaluated those historical baselines, or establish the direction of any historical ranking change.

This is a Minor released-evaluator defect in its correspondence to the stated sample evaluation. Its effect on published core comparisons is Needs Evidence. A precise local repair is to retain a score per sample index, or cache by sequence while averaging with occurrence counts, and reduce sums/counts across ranks. Algebra verifies that this restores the intended finite-sample mean. No corrected protein score is claimed.

The same file averages PDB atom B-factors, whereas p. 16 describes residue averaging. These agree if residue weights are equal or appropriate aggregation is used; otherwise atom counts weight residues differently. The exact dependency/PDB convention was not independently run here, so that additional correspondence remains unresolved. A separate unequal-shard indexing issue exists when sample count is not divisible by world size, but the default counts 512/2,048 are divisible by the usual configured multi-GPU counts; it is not used to infer damage to reported runs.
result: Source computes distinct-sequence mean per rank, not ordinary generated-draw mean. Released-evaluator semantics correction; historical central quality/ranking effect Needs Evidence.

analysis: Figure 6’s stated kernel sum is incompatible with the diagonal contribution of the defined RBF kernel.

Appendix D, p. 15, motivates the square-root normalizer by describing the sum of kernel entries as linear in subset size. It cites a linear-fit \(R^{2}=0.9766\) and Figure 6. In the actual rendered graph, the horizontal axis runs from \(350\) to \(700\) samples, while the ordinate labeled Kernel Entry Sum has observed values approximately \(55\)–\(165\). No axis multiplier or rescaling is displayed [paper, p. 15].

For any finite RBF bandwidth and finite embeddings, \[
K_{ii}=1,\quad K_{ij}>0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
T_n:=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}K_{ij}
=n+\sum_{i\ne j}K_{ij}\ge n.\] Every plotted value is below the corresponding \(n\). In particular, a value near \(55\) at \(n=350\) cannot be the full sum. This argument needs no assumptions about membership, training, unit normalization, or a particular bandwidth choice.

A scaled sum, a square root, or an off-diagonal-only quantity could explain the graph. Figure 2 explicitly zeroes its diagonal for visualization, so a similar convention is a plausible alternative; Figure 6 does not disclose it. None of these interpretations equals the full raw sum in the displayed formula. The plot alone cannot identify the correct replacement label.

For IID embeddings from a fixed distribution and a fixed kernel, \[
\mathbb E[T_n]=n+n(n-1)\mu,\qquad
\mu=\mathbb E[k(Z_1,Z_2)]>0.\] This calculation is not asserted unchanged when the bandwidth is re-estimated from each subset. It shows why a finite linear fit does not by itself establish a scaling law. As an independent illustration, fitting a line to the exactly quadratic values \(n^{2}\) at \(n=350,400,\ldots,700\) gives \[\widehat T_n=1050n-262500,\qquad R^{2}=\frac{441}{445}
=0.991011235955,\] which exceeds the reported fit despite being exactly quadratic. The case \(K_{ij}=1\) is realized by equal unit embeddings at any fixed positive bandwidth; the illustration is not a reconstruction of the authors’ plotted data.
Assessment: Minor. The displayed quantity cannot support Appendix D’s stated account of the raw sum. This does not establish incorrect score computation or changed fixed-size benchmark correlations.

The paper claims mitigation of size effects, not exact size invariance. Indeed, for fixed embedding maps and common bandwidth, replacing every row by \(m\) copies multiplies the numerator by \(m^{2}\) and \(E\) by \(m\), so \(S_{\rm replicated}=mS\). The normalizer reduces this replication scaling from quadratic to linear; non-invariance alone is not a separate broken promise. Unequal-size cross-benchmark comparisons still need an appropriate scope or calibration.
claim:
Let \(Z,Z'\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\) be the pre- and post-fine-tuning embeddings, with unit-norm rows. Define \[
u_{ij}=\left\lVert Z_i-Z_j\right\rVert^{2},\quad
v_{ij}=\left\lVert Z_i'-Z_j'\right\rVert^{2},\quad
K^\gamma_{ij}=e^{-\gamma u_{ij}},\quad
E_\gamma=\left(\sum_{i,j}K^\gamma_{ij}\right)^{1/2},\] for finite \(\gamma>0\). The paper’s actual Eq. (5), p. 4, is \[
S_\gamma(Z,Z')
=-\frac{1}{E_\gamma}
  \sum_{i,j}\left|K^\gamma_{ij}
       \log\frac{K^\gamma_{ij}}{K^{\prime\gamma}_{ij}}\right|
=-\frac{\gamma}{E_\gamma}
  \sum_{i,j}e^{-\gamma u_{ij}}\left|v_{ij}-u_{ij}\right|.\] The second equality follows exactly from \(\log(e^{-\gamma u}/e^{-\gamma v})=\gamma(v-u)\). It verifies the common-bandwidth expansions in the paper’s Eqs. (4) and (6).

Take two two-sample, two-dimensional configurations, \(A\) and \(B\). The first point is \(e_1=(1,0)\) before and after tuning in both. The second points are \[\begin{aligned}
z_{A,2}&=(-1/4,\sqrt{15}/4),&
z'_{A,2}&=(-3/4,\sqrt7/4),\\
z_{B,2}&=(3/4,\sqrt7/4),&
z'_{B,2}&=(3/5,4/5).\end{aligned}\] Every row has norm one: the relevant sums of squared coordinates are \(1/16+15/16\), \(9/16+7/16\), and \(9/25+16/25\). Since \(\left\lVert e_1-z\right\rVert^{2}=2-2z_1\) for a unit vector \(z\), \[(u_A,v_A,\delta_A)=(5/2,7/2,1),\qquad
(u_B,v_B,\delta_B)=(1/2,4/5,3/10),\] where \(\delta=\left|v-u\right|\). Thus all changes are positive, not contractions or cancellation artifacts. The two-point RBF matrices have diagonal one and positive off-diagonal entries; their eigenvalues are \(1\pm e^{-\gamma u}>0\). Both normalizers are positive.

The diagonal contributions to the displayed formula vanish, while the two off-diagonal contributions coincide. Therefore \[
S_\gamma(u,\delta)
=-\frac{2\gamma e^{-\gamma u}\delta}
        {\sqrt{2+2e^{-\gamma u}}}.\] Substitution gives the following values, independently checked to 30-digit working precision:
\(\gamma | S_\gamma(A) | S_\gamma(B)\) | Ordering

The order reverses between two bandwidths explicitly tested in Table 3. All exponentials are ordinary finite positive values; numerical underflow is irrelevant. Replicating each embedding type \(m\) times multiplies both scores by \(m\) and preserves the reversal, so the phenomenon is not tied to \(n=2\). The replication claim concerns the scoring functional at fixed embeddings, not a claim that retraining on duplicated data leaves a model unchanged.

analysis: Equation (4)’s condition \(f>0\) alone neither ensures differentiability nor gives the claimed identity for a discrete gradient. This is a local mathematical overstatement, assessed Minor; no central algorithmic failure is established.

Consider the single connected square object \([-2,2]^{2}\) with Euclidean boundary distance \[S(x,y)=2-\max(|x|,|y|),\qquad f(x,y)=\tfrac12S(x,y)\] on its interior. Its maximum distance is \(D=2\). At its center \(f(0,0)=1>0\), so the printed condition is satisfied, but the gradient does not exist: along the \(x\) axis the left and right derivatives are \(+1/2\) and \(-1/2\). If “gradient” instead means the common central difference on unit-spaced pixels, the two components at the center are both zero, so the reciprocal norm is undefined/infinite, not two. Forward differences both equal \(-1/2\), giving \(1/\|\nabla_+f\|=\sqrt2\), again not two. The samples are also obtained exactly from the nearest boundary pixels of this square; no learned-field error is required. The independent script uses rational arithmetic for these samples and separately checks the valid regular point \((1,0)\), where the gradient is \((-1/2,0)\) and the reciprocal equals two.

The identity is valid in the continuum at points where the signed distance is differentiable and has gradient norm one, with a positive fixed normalization constant and the same spatial metric. In a neighborhood with a unique smooth nearest-boundary projection, this follows by differentiating the Euclidean distance. Stating this restricted identity, then describing finite-difference and learned-field updates as approximations, repairs the mathematical assertion. It does not prove convergence, safe step sizes, or accuracy of the trained network. The square example does not show that the border pixel actually selected by every proposal lies on its medial ridge.

Appendix A.3, p. 14, explicitly replaces pointwise gradients with foreground/background averages and changes the step size, with at most 50 iterations. The public `object_reasoning.py`, lines 140–174, computes image gradients, adds numerical stabilizers to averages and reciprocals, and uses weighted reciprocal averages. Lines 441–471 apply the stopping rule, expansion/contraction adjustment, coordinate rescaling and image bounds. Thus the actual released algorithm is not the singular pointwise rule alone. These provisions are relevant counterevidence against inferring a catastrophic implementation failure from Eq. (4). No benchmark damage has been demonstrated, and the empirical contribution may survive this correction.
result: No derivative at center; central gradient zero, forward reciprocal norm \(\sqrt2\) instead of 2. Local universal wording/derivation overstatement; no demonstrated failure of averaged heuristic or empirical contribution.
claim: Eq4 recovers maximum signed distance at any positive foreground pixel.
Single square object. Exact Euclidean signed distance. Positive foreground pixel at center; normalization \(D=2\).

analysis: Assessment: Major. The paper presents Eq. (8) as the formula driving training. For ordinary nonzero real embeddings, cosine lies in \([-1,1]\), whereas the positive logarithmic term requires a positive argument. Neither normalization nor the model description imposes the needed positivity constraint.

Choose unit vectors \[z=(1,0),\qquad
y^+=(-1/2,\sqrt3/2),\qquad
y^-=(1/2,\sqrt3/2).\] Their cosine scores are \(-1/2\) and \(1/2\). The positive term in the displayed formula is \(\log(-1/2)\), which is not real. The vectors are nonzero and normalized. They can be embedded in a larger feature space by zero padding, or repeated across modality blocks without changing the cosine. Distinct item identities need not have injective embeddings.

The release provides no countervailing positivity condition. In `model.py`, final affine representation layers are applied to the modality outputs before concatenation, lines 255–267. `trainer.py`, lines 183–194, applies the corresponding affine maps to target-item features. The auxiliary inspection also traced the layer definitions and LayerNorm operations: neither restricts cosine scores to \((0,1)\). The shared-token architecture therefore does not supply the missing assumption.

Let \(\sigma(c)=1/(1+e^{-c})\). Retain the printed negative sign and insert a sigmoid link in the displayed formula. The resulting unweighted criterion is \[
L_{\rm unw}=-\frac{
 \sum_{k\in K_{\rm gt}}\log\sigma(c_k)
 +\sum_{k\in K_n}\log(1-\sigma(c_k))}{P+N}.\] The pinned source instead implements \[
L_{\rm src}=-\frac{
 (N/P)\sum_{k\in K_{\rm gt}}\log\sigma(c_k)
 +\sum_{k\in K_n}\log(1-\sigma(c_k))}{P+N}.\] In `trainer.py`, lines 213–232, the cosine scores are mapped through sigmoids; the positive sum is divided by the positive count and multiplied by the configured negative count before the overall average. The independent check inspected this full calculation. The default negative count is \(N=100\), recorded in `parameters.py`, lines 69–73. A sequence with \(P=2\) positives is permitted by the multi-answer task.

Parent calculation outputs in corroborate the derivative bound and give \[\begin{array}{c|rr}
c& L_{\rm unw}&L_{\rm src}\\ \hline
-1&0.3328695307&1.5946307598\\
0&0.6931471806&1.3591121187\\
1&1.2936538444&1.5946307598
\end{array}\] The exact derivatives, rather than this three-point table, establish the minima. The independent auxiliary output is ; its unweighted comparison likewise assumes the conventional negative sign.
claim: Section 3.4, PDF p.6, defines \(\cos\)(z_output,\(y^k\)) as ordinary cosine similarity. Eq.(8) has the conventional NEGATIVE prefactor -1/|K_gt union K_n|. It omits a sigmoid, another probability conversion, a positivity restriction and positive-class reweighting, and is stated to drive training. The minus is visible in the reliable PyMuPDF recovery rendering of the same original page.

Nonzero real output and item vectors, the domain needed for ordinary cosine similarity; no nonnegativity condition is imposed. A positive-item set and negative-item set with disjoint item identities; distinct items may have coinciding learned embeddings because no injectivity condition is imposed. For the source comparison \(P=|K_{\rm gt}\)|>0 and \(N\)=|K_n|; the default \(N=100\) is explicit in parameters.py line72, and \(P=2\) is allowed by the multi-label task. For the unweighted-versus-source minimizer comparison, retain the printed conventional negative sign and insert a sigmoid probability link; this comparator repairs the cosine-domain defect but not the released class weighting.
result: The release’s sigmoid makes its objective finite for the exhibited scores. This review does not infer that training the released code necessarily produces NaNs. Nor is a benchmark decline established. If \(P=N\), the weighting factor happens to be one; the stated task does not require that equality. Treating \(\cos\) as an implicit sigmoid score would contradict the explicit definition and would still leave the missing reweighting unresolved.

The finding concerns the mathematical rule used to train the central recommender, not a peripheral typographical claim. The domain failure and non-equivalent optimization criterion demonstrate an invalid core method specification, supporting Major under the required calibration even if a short correction is possible. The proposed token architecture and empirical comparisons may still be useful and correct under the actual implemented loss.

A source-aligned correction is the displayed formula, for nonzero embeddings and \(P,N>0\). It is finite on the cosine domain and matches the statically inspected per-sequence weighting. This verifies algebraic correspondence only. It does not identify the historical training objective or certify a retrained model. If unweighted BCE was intended, the code and historical provenance instead require reconciliation. The earlier missing-minus allegation is withdrawn: it arose from a missing glyph in the initial source rendering. The domain counterexample and weighted-objective comparison do not depend on that allegation.

This concerns the operative mathematical definition used to train the proposed recommender, not a peripheral prose claim: the displayed objective fails on its allowed domain and does not identify the source's training criterion even after the charitable sigmoid-link repair. On the user's core-contribution calibration, recommend Major for this central method-definition defect, while explicitly preserving the empirical and architectural conclusions not refuted by it. No empirical benchmark score reduction is established or required for the mathematical discrepancy. analysis: Source claim and location. Section 5.3, p. 7, states that in the infinite-ID-data limit the posterior over model parameters collapses, and uses this to argue that epistemic uncertainty cannot retain an OOD signal. Section 6, p. 9, extends the decreasing-usefulness interpretation. This statement needs identification conditions on parameters that affect the OOD inputs. It is not a consequence of increasing ID sample size alone [S1, E1].

Assumption-satisfying example. Consider a two-class logistic network p(Y=1|x,theta)=sigmoid(theta1*x1+theta2*x2), with independent proper priors theta_j in {-log 3,+log 3}, each equally likely. ID inputs are (1,0) and (-1,0), with labels generated by the specified model. The likelihood of any ID dataset is independent of theta2, so its posterior remains exactly its prior at every sample size, even if theta1 is learned perfectly. At the OOD input x=(0,1), the two possible predictive probabilities remain 1/4 and 3/4.

\[p(Y=1\mid x=(0,1),D)=\frac12,\qquad I(Y;\theta\mid x=(0,1),D)=1-h_2(1/4)=0.1887218755\ \mathrm{bits}.\] Here h2 is binary entropy in bits. The positive mutual information persists for every finite n and in the infinite-data limit because the ID likelihood contains no theta2 term. The independent checker evaluates the exact posterior symmetry and entropy, and the reasoning establishes the all-n statement.

Continuous proper-prior check. The same failure occurs with independent theta1 and theta2 uniformly distributed on [-log 3, log 3], so it does not rely on a discrete interpretation of the parameter integral. ID inputs (1,0) and (-1,0), each with positive probability, have model-generated labels. For every ID dataset, the likelihood contains only theta1; posterior(theta2|D) therefore equals its proper uniform prior exactly. At x=(0,1), symmetry gives predictive probability 1/2, while epistemic mutual information is 1 minus the prior expectation of h2(sigmoid(theta2)). Half the prior mass has |theta2| at least log(3)/2, providing the positive bound below.

\[I(Y;\theta\mid (0,1),D)\geq \frac{1-h_2(\sqrt{3}/(1+\sqrt{3}))}{2}>0,\] The bound is approximately 0.0262143336 bits and is independent of ID sample size. Strict positivity is analytic: binary entropy is strictly less than one away from probability 1/2. This establishes failure of unrestricted collapse, not any real-data AUROC or guaranteed detection success.

Alternative interpretation and impact. For an identifiable finite-parameter model with posterior consistency and continuous predictions at the query point, posterior concentration can make predictive epistemic uncertainty vanish. That restricted rationale is defensible. It does not yield a general monotonic AUROC claim, and it does not apply when ID observations leave OOD-relevant directions unidentified. The displayed finite last-layer Laplace experiment is not refuted by this example.

Judgment: Major for the invalid unrestricted derivation. Section 5.3 uses posterior collapse to explain a fundamental mismatch with OOD detection; Section 6 carries that argument into its data-size deterioration claim and guidance on Bayesian/ensemble methods when ID data are abundant. This is a direct dependency of a core technical argument, not an isolated observation. Survival of the finite Laplace scores or the broad position does not downgrade this separate error. Repair: state identification and posterior-concentration conditions for every OOD-relevant parameter direction, retain the finite experiment within its actual scope, and withdraw the unconditional data-size inference. A conditional concentration statement alone also does not prove a universal monotone AUROC trend. No universally reliable epistemic OOD detector is claimed.
claim: Let h be a fixed feature representation, P the ID feature distribution, Q the OOD feature distribution, and s(h) an OOD score, with larger values indicating OOD. For independent H_P~P and H_Q~Q, AUROC(s)=Pr[s(H_Q)>s(H_P)]+0.5 Pr[s(H_Q)=s(H_P)]. This is a pairwise ranking measure, not directly a fraction of individually unclassifiable images.
Model: \(\operatorname{sigmoid}(\theta_1\cdot x_1+\theta_2\cdot x_2)\).
result: Invalid unrestricted collapse premise supports the core epistemic-uncertainty rationale in Section 5.3 and the data-size/method guidance in Section 6. Finite Laplace results survive but do not reduce this claim-level severity.

analysis: Source claim and location. Section 4.1, p. 4, first describes an oracle as a binary linear classifier trained to distinguish ID and OOD features, then treats 1 minus its AUROC as irreducible error that no feature-based method can reduce. Figure 2, p. 5, uses that interpretation in its error decomposition. Section 5.6, p. 9, uses the same argument for a greater-than -5% irreducible residual in the large DINOv2 representation. The released implementation explicitly constructs torch.nn.Linear(feature_dim,2), ood_score.py line 92 [S1-S3, E1-E3].

Suspect step. Let A_all be the supremum of AUROC over all permitted feature-based scores, and A_lin the best affine-score AUROC. Set inclusion gives the inequality below. An observed finite-trained oracle is no better a universal ceiling. The direction needed for the paper’s universal residual floor is not justified.

\[A_{\mathrm{all}}\ge A_{\mathrm{lin}},\qquad 1-A_{\mathrm{all}}\le 1-A_{\mathrm{lin}}.\] Complete counterexample. Set h(x)=x in one dimension. ID features take -1 and +1 with equal probability; OOD features take -2 and +2 with equal probability. The two ID classes are their signs, so a supervised linear classifier using this same representation classifies the ID labels perfectly. All four support points are distinct; no overlap or feature ambiguity is present. No assumption in the oracle argument requires continuous features or excludes these distributions.

For s(h)=w h+b with w>0, the OOD point +2 beats both ID points and -2 beats neither: two wins among four equally likely pairs, so AUROC=1/2. For w<0 the ordering reverses and again gives two wins. For w=0 every pair ties and AUROC=1/2. The two-class linear-softmax oracle has the same ordering. Yet s(h)=|h| or \(h^{2}\) ranks both OOD points above both ID points, giving AUROC=1. This proves the claim for every affine score, rather than only for the finite coefficients checked by the independent script.

It shows that failure of a linear discriminator does not establish such equality. Nor does it establish zero Bayes error for the actual ImageNet-derived feature distributions.

analysis: Theorem 3.1, PDF p. 4 and repeated p. 13, assumes initial safety solely as \(b_j(x(0))\ge0\) for every \(j\). This does not suffice for its high-order invariance conclusion. Even granting an exact, sign-corrected QP head, the enforced inequality can hold while the system leaves that set immediately.

Use two independent double integrators: \[\dot q_j=v_j,\quad \dot v_j=u_j,\quad b_j=q_j,\qquad j=1,2.\] Set \(m=2\), all penalties equal to one, \(\alpha_{j,i}(r)=r\), \(H=I_2\), \(F=0\), and constant observations. The relative degree is two; the coefficients are smooth and the exact QP feedback is locally Lipschitz. The shared first-order barrier functions and constraints become \[\psi_{j,1}=v_j+q_j,\qquad
 u_j+2v_j+q_j\ge0,\qquad
 u_j=\max(0,-2v_j-q_j).\] The QP is always feasible. Let the initial state be \[
 (q_1,v_1,q_2,v_2)(0)=(0,-1,1,0).\] Both \(b_j(0)\ge0\), as required by the printed theorem.

For \(0<t<1\), the actual QP-controlled solution is \[
 q_1=-te^{-t},\qquad v_1=(t-1)e^{-t},\qquad
 u_1=(2-t)e^{-t},\qquad (q_2,v_2,u_2)=(1,0,0).\] Differentiation verifies both differential equations. Moreover \(u_1>0\) and \(u_1+2v_1+q_1=0\), so the displayed formula is the unique pointwise QP minimum, not an arbitrary feasible control. Nevertheless \(q_1(t)<0\) immediately. Two identical heads and their convex mixture produce the same trajectory.

The obstruction is already visible at the boundary: \[\psi_{1,1}(0)=-1,\qquad
 \psi_{1,1}(t)=-e^{-t}<0,\qquad
 \dot\psi_{1,1}(t)=e^{-t}>0.\] Appendix B, PDF p. 14, claims that \(b_j(x(0))\ge0\) allows initialization with \(\dot\psi_{j,m-1}(x(0))\ge0\), then invokes Nagumo to conclude \(\psi_{j,m-1}\ge0\). The displayed trajectory already has that positive derivative. A positive derivative cannot establish membership of a set from an initial point outside it.

No finite lower-order penalty can correct this boundary initialization: every zero-passing \(\alpha\) gives \(v_1(0)+p_1\alpha(q_1(0))=-1\). The outward velocity also makes \(\dot q_1(0)=-1\), independently of any finite acceleration. Thus this is not a poor choice of a tunable finite initialization that the stated theorem can always repair.
result:
A conventional higher-order barrier result restricted to \[\psi_{j,i}(x(0))\ge0\quad
 \text{for every }j\text{ and }i=0,\ldots,m-1\] excludes this witness. Importing that condition changes the theorem’s explicit \(b\)-only hypothesis; the paper’s own initialization argument attempts, unsuccessfully, to bridge the difference. This report does not refute a correctly restricted HOCBF theorem.

For the constant, unit-linear, second-order setting above, the correction is directly verifiable. The QP ensures \(\dot\psi_{j,1}+\psi_{j,1}\ge0\). If \(\psi_{j,1}(0)\ge0\), integrating factors yield \(\psi_{j,1}(t)\ge e^{-t}\psi_{j,1}(0)\ge0\). Then \(\dot q_j+q_j=\psi_{j,1}\ge0\) implies \(q_j(t)\ge e^{-t}q_j(0)\ge0\). This proves safety on the corrected initial domain for this setting and for convex mixtures sharing these constraints. It does not certify arbitrary observation resets, varying penalties, or all of the paper’s merging claims.

The supported impact is Major, independently of Problem 1: an invalid inference is needed by the central safety theorem. This does not invalidate the measured success of the reported trajectories or safety guarantees on a properly restricted initial domain. Experimental trajectories alone cannot prove the theorem’s broader quantifier.

claim:
The system is \(\dot x=f(x)+g(x)u\), with locally Lipschitz \(f,g\). For each safety specification \(b_j\), the paper defines \[\psi_{j,0}=b_j,\qquad
 \psi_{j,i}=\dot\psi_{j,i-1}+p_i\alpha_{j,i}(\psi_{j,i-1}),
 \quad 1\le i<m.\] The lower-order penalties \(p_i\ge0\) are shared among heads; \(\alpha_{j,i}\) are strictly increasing and pass through zero. Each head minimizes a strictly convex quadratic objective with positive-definite \(H\), subject to \[
 L_f\psi_{j,m-1}+L_g\psi_{j,m-1}u_k+
 p_{m,k}\alpha_{j,m}(\psi_{j,m-1})\ge0.\] The final control is \(u=\sum_k w_ku_k\), where \(w_k\ge0\) and \(\sum_k w_k=1\).

When the same \(\psi_{j,m-1}\) and Lie derivatives are shared, summing the displayed formula with these weights is valid: \[L_f\psi_{j,m-1}+L_g\psi_{j,m-1}u+
 \Big(\sum_k w_kp_{m,k}\Big)\alpha_{j,m}(\psi_{j,m-1})\ge0.\] This algebra is not refuted below. The issues concern whether the printed explicit head actually solves its QP, and whether the stated initial domain permits the subsequent invariance conclusion.

The counterexamples use precisely two specifications, singleton partitions \(S_1=\{1\}\) and \(S_2=\{2\}\), constant observations and parameters, and two identical heads with \(w_1=w_2=1/2\). Thus soft-min aggregation, switching of selected constraints, observation noise, discretization, heterogeneous heads, and singular Gram matrices do not explain either failure.
Initial \(b_j\)>=0 alone suffices for safety of ABNet for all later times.

analysis: Appendix A, PDF p. 12, equations (14)–(15), use \(\max(\cdot,0)\) in gate formulas whose sign must be nonpositive. For a nonsingular feasible QP these formulas can produce an infeasible control. This invalidates the printed explicit solution used in equation (4) and its exact-QP safety justification.

Equations (8)–(13) define \[g_i=-L_g\psi_{i,m-1},\quad
 h_i=L_f\psi_{i,m-1}+p_m\alpha_{i,m}(\psi_{i,m-1}),\quad
 \widehat u=-H^{-1}F,\] \[\widehat g_i=H^{-1}g_i,\qquad
 \widehat h_i=h_i-g_i^\top\widehat u,\qquad
 G_{ij}=\widehat g_i^\top H\widehat g_j.\] The transformed problem minimizes \(v^\top Hv\) subject to \(\langle\widehat g_i,v\rangle_H\le\widehat h_i\), and the displayed solution is \(v=\lambda_1\widehat g_1+\lambda_2\widehat g_2\). The main text, PDF p. 3, explicitly specifies \(\lambda_i\le0\). The first gate branch tests \(G_{21}\max(\widehat h_2,0)-G_{22}\widehat h_1<0\); the second tests \(G_{12}\max(\widehat h_1,0)-G_{11}\widehat h_2<0\). In the second branch the printed gates are \(\lambda_1=\max(\widehat h_1,0)/G_{11}\) and \(\lambda_2=0\). These conventions rule out rescuing the formula by changing the meaning of the inequalities.

The new explicit head in equation (4) depends on these gates. Appendix B, PDF p. 13, then explicitly invokes its claimed identity with the exact QP solution to conclude that each head satisfies the safety constraints. This is a direct dependency of the core safety argument.

Let \[\dot x=(-1,0)^\top+u,\quad
 b_1(x)=x_1,\quad b_2(x)=x_2,\quad
 x(0)=(1/4,1)^\top.\] Take \(m=1\), \(\alpha(r)=r\), \(p_{m,k}=1\), \(H=I_2\), and \(F=0\). All coefficients are smooth, the initial state is strictly safe, and the two relative degrees are one. The head QP is \[
 \min_u \tfrac12(u_1^{2}+u_2^{2})
 \quad\text{subject to}\quad
 u_1\ge1-x_1,\quad u_2\ge-x_2.\] It is feasible everywhere and has a unique solution. At the stated initial state, \[\widehat g_1=-e_1,\quad\widehat g_2=-e_2,\quad
 G=I_2,\quad \widehat h=(-3/4,1)^\top,\quad\widehat u=0.\] The first branch test equals \(3/4<0\), which is false; the second equals \(-1<0\), which is true. The printed formula consequently gives \[\lambda_1=\max(-3/4,0)=0,\quad\lambda_2=0,\quad u=(0,0).\] The first constraint residual is \(-3/4\), so this is not a QP solution. The actual minimizer is \((3/4,0)\) with gates \((-3/4,0)\).

The same printed branch persists along \(x_2(t)=1\), \(x_1(t)=1/4-t\). It therefore crosses the safety boundary at \(t=1/4\) and is negative immediately afterward. In contrast, the actual QP feedback has \(u_1=1-x_1\), so its trajectory is \(x_1(t)=e^{-t}/4>0\), \(x_2(t)=1\). The witness isolates the gate error without higher-order initialization complications.

It gives the correct control in the displayed formula. This is actual implementation counterevidence: the finding does not establish that the available implementation or original experiments used the wrong sign.

Replacing the printed positive truncations by negative truncations repairs this witness and agrees with the required multiplier sign. A complete solver certification would additionally require a full KKT analysis and explicit treatment of dependent constraints and zero denominators; it is not supplied by this one example or by static code inspection.

analysis: The background’s universal global statement about the matrix exponential is false, including on the rotation group actually used by the method. Assessment: Minor.

Take the matrix Lie group \(\mathrm{SO}(2)\) and its Lie algebra \[\mathfrak{so}(2)=\{\theta J:\theta\in\mathbb R\},
 \qquad J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] This is exactly the real skew-symmetric rotation setting, with no additional regularity or learning assumptions. Since \(J^{2}=-I\), expansion of the absolutely convergent exponential series gives \[\exp(\theta J)=I\cos\theta+J\sin\theta.\] The distinct Lie algebra elements \(0\) and \(2\pi J\) therefore both map to \(I\). The map is not injective and hence cannot be a global bijection or diffeomorphism. The independent numerical calculation reproduced this identity to a maximum entrywise residual of \(4.44\times10^{-16}\), but the series calculation is the decisive exact argument; floating-point equality is not being substituted for proof.
claim: Section 3.1, PDF page 4, describes, in paraphrase, the matrix exponential as a smooth bijection from the Lie algebra to every Lie group and calls it a diffeomorphism. No neighborhood restriction is attached to this global assertion. The later phrase about \(U,V\) being close accompanies Equation (1), not a restriction of the exponential’s domain or codomain. The original page image was inspected to rule out an extraction artifact.
Matrix Lie group. Lie algebra real matrix subspace. No local neighborhood restriction stated.
result: A valid local statement is that the exponential maps a sufficiently small neighborhood of \(0\) diffeomorphically onto a neighborhood of the identity. In the planar case this is explicit: restricting \(\theta\) to \((-\pi,\pi)\) gives a smooth inverse angle on the rotation group with the rotation by \(\pi\) removed. This is not a global coordinate system for the full group. A half-open interval that covers every planar rotation still has a discontinuous inverse at the cut and is not the full vector-space Lie algebra.

The construction in Section 4 only evaluates the smooth forward exponential. It neither computes a global logarithm nor relies on distinct skew parameters producing distinct rotations. The static code agrees with this forward-only use. Consequently the false background assertion is a supported local mathematical defect, but no dependency that invalidates the central learned rotation method, its empirical comparisons, or its optimization has been established. The repair is to state local invertibility and retain the globally smooth forward map. It does not require changing the encoder, and it has not been adopted by the authors on any source checked here.
Global injectivity fails, hence global diffeomorphism fails. Supported local mathematical defect; no central dependency on global inverse established.

Independent derivation. Let Y and P be centered random variables with unit variance, finite second moments and correlation rho. For a linear calibrated predictor aP, the mean squared error is the following quadratic. Its derivative vanishes at a = rho, and its second derivative is 2, so this is the unique minimum.

\[\mathbb{E}(Y-aP)^{2}=1-2a\rho+a^{2},\qquad a^*=\rho,\qquad R^2_{\rm calibrated}=1-(1-\rho^{2})=\rho^2.\] Thus even in this favorable, fully specified calibration example, rho = 0.91 gives R-squared = 0.8281, not 0.91. More generally, a forecast’s out-of-sample R-squared also depends on its scale, offset, comparison baseline and evaluation set. This calculation is an illustration of the invalid inference, not a reanalysis of the source data. In particular, 82.81% must not be substituted as an empirical predictive-variance result: the source’s 0.91 is disattenuated and is not the correlation of a supplied calibrated prediction vector.

Calibration is a substantive distinction here: Hewitt’s PDF p. 8 reports systematic overestimation of effect magnitudes and evaluates a rescaling correction. This does not invalidate the reported association; it shows why association and numerical prediction accuracy should be separately identified. [S2]

Primary-source check for Centaur. Binz et al., arXiv:2410.20268v1, PDF p. 12 Eq. (1), defines a normalized log-likelihood metric relative to uniform guessing. PDF p. 4 names it pseudo-R-squared and describes a participant-level training/test split. The source’s 160-experiment dataset should not be interpreted as 160 unseen experiments. [S3]

\[R^2_{\rm pseudo}=1-\frac{\log p_{\rm model}(D)}{\log p_{\rm guess}(D)}.\] Complete metric-distinction example. Take independent Bernoulli responses with success probability p = 0.9. Let the model assign probability 0.9 to success on every trial and the guessing baseline assign 0.5. Both are valid probability distributions, all likelihoods are nonzero, and expected log likelihoods are finite. On a per-observation expected-log-likelihood basis:

\[H(p)=-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p),\quad R^2_{\rm pseudo}=1-\frac{H(0.9)}{\log 2}=0.5310044064\ldots\] The same model’s conditional-mean prediction is the constant 0.9. Its squared-error risk is 0.9(0.1) = 0.09, exactly Var(Y). Therefore its variance-based predictive R-squared relative to the mean baseline is zero. The positive pseudo-R-squared arises from improving over uniform probabilities; it does not mean 53.1% of response variance is explained. This is a population calculation illustrating metric non-equivalence, not an estimate from Centaur’s experiments.

Counterevidence and severity. A charitable reading treats ’variation’ as informal language for statistical correspondence. Section 4.5.2 even explicitly mentions correlation, and the appendix supplies the correct r notation. Those qualifications make a central-invalidity claim unwarranted, but they do not make a numerical percentage-of-variation interpretation correct. The error concerns how supporting evidence is communicated; the high reported association and the motivation to investigate simulation remain. Judgment: Minor.
claim: Correlation and likelihood-based fit are mislabeled as explained variation.
result: Overstates/interprets supporting metrics; prospective central thesis intact.

analysis: Theorem 3.1 (p. 3) and Theorem K.1 (p. 22) assume that two tasks have distinct input-output distributions and require different optimal parameter configurations (K.2). They also assume that at least one layer has expected gradients that cannot be related by any real scalar multiplier (K.3). The conclusion is that some layer has different norms of these expected gradients.

\[\exists l^*: \left\|\mathbb E_{T_A}[
abla_{W_{l^*}}\mathcal L]ight\|_2
e\left\|\mathbb E_{T_B}[
abla_{W_{l^*}}\mathcal L]ight\|_2.\] The printed formulas and Definition K.4 use the norm of an expected gradient, not the expectation of individual gradient norms. The decisive pages were inspected as images to avoid a formula-extraction error. Both task expectations are evaluated at a common parameter checkpoint, consistent with the shared pretrained-model proxy in Eq. (3). The statement supplies no convergence condition, optimizer constraint, or temporal quantifier that would force a norm inequality.

Use one fixed image-and-text instruction input and three possible next tokens. Task A has probabilities q_A=(1/2,1/3,1/6); task B has q_B=(1/3,1/2,1/6). These can be realized as six-example datasets with token counts (3,2,1) and (2,3,1). Both distributions have full support and are distinct. With logits w in \(R^{3}\), the ordinary expected token cross-entropy is:

\[F_q(w)=\log\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^3e^{w_j}\right)-q^\top w,\qquad \nabla F_q(w)=\operatorname{softmax}(w)-q.\] Each risk has finite minimizers w=log(q)+c*1. The optimal predictive distribution is uniquely q. Because q_A differs from q_B, no single parameter configuration can achieve both predictive optima on the same input. K.2 is therefore satisfied; uniqueness of every redundant neural parameter is not required.

\[g_A=\left(-\frac16,0,\frac16\right),\quad g_B=\left(0,-\frac16,\frac16\right),\quad \|g_A\|_2^{2}=\|g_B\|_2^{2}=\frac1{18}.\] No scalar multiple of \(g_B\) equals \(g_A\): their first components already rule this out. Thus K.3 holds. Nevertheless, the two norms both equal sqrt(2)/6. This is a counterexample to the asserted implication, rather than merely a missing justification for it.

To realize the example within the claimed model class, use a bias-free residual transformer with one active feed-forward output projection P. On the fixed instruction, choose its hidden activation u=e1 with unit norm, and a fixed affine readout that subtracts the residual base and maps the active coordinates to logits w=P u. At P=0, the expected gradient of P is g_q u^T; its flattened L2 norm is exactly ||g_q||. Earlier feed-forward gradients vanish because their path contains P=0.

Other attention branches can have both value and output factors zero. Other feed-forward branches can have both factors zero with an activation satisfying phi(0)=0; use bias-free branches or fixed biases. They are identity residual blocks with zero parameter gradients at this checkpoint. A fixed zero visual-to-predictive projector makes the visual transformer’s gradients zero. The theorem contains no requirement that every modality have nonzero influence for every task. Extra inactive dimensions and blocks can be added without changing the example.

Hence the active layer has equal nonzero gradient norms and non-collinear expected gradients, while every other transformer layer has equal zero norms. There is no layer with the claimed inequality. Setting P u=log(q_A) or log(q_B) realizes the respective finite optima while leaving the other blocks unchanged. The witness is a formal admissible model, not a claim about the actual InternVL2 weights used in the experiments.

Sequential presentation does not exclude this checkpoint. With fixed features and only P trained, choose 0<eta<1 and let w_pre solve w_pre=eta(softmax(w_pre)-q_A). The map is a contraction because the softmax Jacobian has operator norm at most 1. A finite fixed point exists, and one legitimate task-A gradient step maps w_pre exactly to zero, where task B may begin. The source imposes no requirement that task A be fully optimized first.

The proof on p. 23 first places equal-norm, non-collinear gradients on the same sphere in Eq. (26). That geometry is consistent with all preceding assumptions. It then asserts that equal norms would require reconciling incompatible updates and would violate sequential training. No mathematical condition supplies this purported contradiction.

\[g_A^\top g_B=\frac1{36}>0,\qquad \cos(g_A,g_B)=\frac12,\qquad D_{-g_A}F_B(0)=-\frac1{36}<0.\] The example also shows that non-collinearity does not imply opposing updates. A sufficiently small descent step for either task reduces both losses locally. Independent reviewer arithmetic gives the following values for a task-A step with eta=0.1:
Risk | Before step | After task-A step

The supported impact is the failure of the stated formal foundation for task-specific gradient-magnitude discrepancies. The paper prominently uses this theorem in Section 3.1 and its contribution list to motivate nonuniform allocation. Appendix location or an easy wording edit does not reduce that demonstrated mathematical impact. The empirical sensitivity heatmap and successful benchmark comparisons can still be observations even though this universal theorem is false.

A valid weaker conclusion is that some expected gradient vectors differ; that follows directly from K.3. It does not prove different magnitudes, different layer rankings, or optimal parameter allocation. Even a common positive rescaling of every layer’s gradient norm between tasks preserves all rankings.
claim: At least one transformer layer must have different norms of the two task-expected gradients. Distinct distributions and disjoint optimum sets satisfy K.2; no real scalar maps \(g_B\) to \(g_A\), satisfying K.3.
result: Refutes the claimed formal foundation for task-dependent gradient-magnitude discrepancies and the asserted theoretical allocation motivation. Does not refute measured sensitivity patterns, benchmark scores or all practical uses.
