claim: Appendix A p.15 states equal trainable parameters for a fair comparison, justified by rank 4 on all baseline locations versus rank 8 with allocation budget ratio 0.5. The check uses the stated attention/output targets, ranks 4 and 8, 24-layer LLM and vision components, respective model matrix shapes, and the published task-1 Figure 6 selection. This is a test of the published design rationale, not a reconstruction of historical checkpoints.
analysis: Appendix A (p. 15) states equal trainable parameter counts, justified by rank 4 on all baseline layers versus rank 8 on half the method’s allocation locations. Eqs. (5), (14) and (15) actually constrain counts of experts/layers. A LoRA adapter on a d_out by d_in matrix has r(d_in+d_out) trainable weights, so selecting half the locations does not in general select half the parameter cost.
Target weight | LoRA parameter cost at rank r
LLM fused qkv: 2048 to 4096 | 6144 r
LLM attention output: 2048 to 2048 | 4096 r
Vision qkv: 1024 to 3072 | 4096 r
Vision attention output: 1024 to 1024 | 2048 r

These dimensions follow the stated InternVL2-2B model and its pinned official configuration: the LLM has 16 query heads and 8 key/value heads, and the vision attention uses ordinary qkv projection. With the paper’s attention-only target description, rank 4 over all 24 LLM and 24 vision blocks gives 1,572,864 LoRA weights.

The published Figure 6 was visually checked and independently sampled at its exact two fill colors. Every task row contains 48 selected attention/output subslots. For task 1, the LLM has 21 first-subslot and 15 second-subslot selections; vision has 11 and 1. Regardless of which subslot is assigned to qkv versus output within each modality, rank 8 yields between 1,638,400 and 1,900,544 weights. This is 4.17% to 20.83% above the stated attention-only baseline. The counts are reproducible from the archived source figure; they are not measured checkpoint tensors.

Thus the published count-based explanation does not establish the claimed equality, and its illustrated task-1 allocation is inconsistent with that equality under the stated target matrices. The public allocator likewise budgets by score-row count and enforces a 25% minimum vision share rather than weighting actual parameter costs. However, the released baseline wrapper also includes feed-forward target modules when no architecture filter is supplied, unlike the manuscript’s attention-only description. This prevents treating the preceding theoretical counts as verified counts of the original experimental runs.

The demonstrated failure of this equality rationale is Major because Appendix A uses it to justify the fairness of the central parameter-constrained comparison. This conclusion does not require an empirical ranking reversal or a claim that the released source produced the original experiments. Actual matched-run counts remain Needs Evidence: supply per-task architecture files and tensor counts for every baseline, distinguishing new trainable adapters, frozen accumulated adapters and auxiliary autoencoders. A cost-constrained allocation can use sum_j I_j r_j(d_in,j+d_out,j)<=B. If that changes the selected architecture, its performance requires a new comparison. Table 11 already reports O-LoRA at nominal 2x and 4x budgets still below D-MoLE; that preserves relevant performance counterevidence, but does not make the published equality calculation valid.
result: Severity boundary: Major applies to the demonstrated invalid equality rationale and its core comparison dependency. It does not assert a false score, an executed unfair run, or that budget differences explain the observed advantage. Not established: Actual original checkpoint counts, whether the executed comparison favored D-MoLE, or its effect on rankings.

analysis:
Appendix A.1, p. 13, claims for unit \(X,Y\) and full-rank maps on the shared semantic subspace that \[|\langle M_QX,M_KY\rangle|
 \le \|M_Q^\top M_K\|\,|\langle X,Y\rangle|.\] This is false under the stated assumptions.

Take the two-dimensional shared semantic subspace and \[M_Q=I_2,\quad
 M_K=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
 X=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 Y=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}.\] Both transformations are full rank, are different as allowed, and operate on exactly the same subspace. Both input vectors are unit. The left side equals \(1\) and the right side equals \(0\), since \(\langle X,Y\rangle=0\). Equal subspaces and equal effective ranks therefore do not imply the proposed preservation of input inner products. The correct general inequality is \[|\langle M_QX,M_KY\rangle|
 \le\|M_Q^\top M_K\|\,\|X\|\,\|Y\|.\] It does not infer high original semantic alignment from a large transformed attention product. A stronger condition such as \(M_Q^\top M_K\) being a scalar multiple of the identity would be sufficient for the disputed form, but is not among the assumptions.

This finding is Major: pp. 3–4 explicitly rely on this analysis to connect attention-defined groups with high-level semantic similarity, which is the motivation for oracle-space routing. The counterexample invalidates that mathematical justification. It does not show that empirical attention groups are useless, and the later semantic-distribution assumptions can still be posited independently. The valid spectral bound is a verified algebraic replacement, but not a repair of the claimed semantic implication.
claim: Attention inner products preserve original semantic inner products through stated bound.

Use the shared two-dimensional semantic subspace with unit vectors \(X=(1,0)^\top\) and \(Y=(0,1)^\top\), and choose \[M_Q=I_2,\qquad M_K=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Both maps are full rank, act on exactly the same subspace, and are distinct as the assumptions permit.
result: Claimed bound false even with exactly identical query/key subspaces. Invalidates the stated mathematical attention-to-semantic-similarity justification central to group construction.

paragraphs: Require \(K\)>\(\sqrt{(1/n-1/m)/2}\) for the fixed-threshold asymptotic Gaussian comparison, and add/prove routing boundary/center conditions.

analysis: Lemma 5, pp. 14–15, asserts that \(\|Y\|+m<K\|Z\|\) has probability tending to one as dimension increases for any fixed \(m>0,K>0\) and \(n<m\). Its stated Gaussian construction admits an exact zero-probability counterexample.

Let \(n=1\), \(m=2\), \(K=1/4\), and let \(x_1,x_2\) be independent \(N(0,I_d)\) vectors for any \(d\). Select the singleton subset \(S\) uniformly from \(\{1\}\) and \(\{2\}\), exactly as required. In the paper’s notation, \[Z=x_1-x_2,\qquad
 Y=\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}-x_S=
 \begin{cases}-Z/2,&S=\{1\},\\ Z/2,&S=\{2\}.\end{cases}\] Hence \(\|Y\|=\|Z\|/2\) identically. The claimed event becomes \[\frac12\|Z\|+2<\frac14\|Z\|,\] which is impossible, including when \(Z=0\). Its probability is zero for every dimension, not asymptotically one. The example satisfies isotropic Gaussianity, independence of the \(x_i\), random subset selection, positive fixed constants and \(n<m\).

The proof’s comparison of \(\mathbb E\|Y\|^{2}\) with \(\mathbb E\|Z\|^{2}\) cannot justify an arbitrary factor \(K\). In addition, its variance calculation assumes independence of the two squared norms, although here one is exactly one quarter of the other. The claimed Chebyshev conclusion therefore cannot repair the counterexample.

The passage from a smaller continuous displacement to fewer discrete assignments is an approximation on pp. 3, 5 and 14, not a proved error bound. The explicit routing model permits the following check. Let \(H=\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb R^d\), let \(s_1,s_2\) be independent uniform variables on \([1,2]\), and let \(u_1,u_2\) be independent \(N(0,I_d)\), independent of the semantic variables. These satisfy Assumptions 1–4 with semantic center \(1.5\) and radius \(0.5\). Take \(W_Q=P\), \(W_K=2P\), where \(P\) projects onto the semantic coordinate. The two tokens belong to one thresholded group with \(\epsilon=0.01\): even including self-attention, the second token’s attention to the first is at least \(1/(1+e^{4})>0.01\).

A raw top-one gate with rows \(P\) and zero assigns both tokens to expert 1. For oracle routing, the permitted nearest-center rule with centers \(c_\pm=(1.5,\pm a,0,\ldots,0)\), \(a>0\), assigns by the sign of the first identity coordinate. The growing means are \(z_1=t_1\) and \(z_2=(t_1+t_2)/2\). If \(X=u_{1,1}\) and \(Y=u_{2,1}\), the oracle changes expert precisely when \(X\) and \(X+Y\) have opposite signs. Rotational symmetry of \((X,Y)\) gives probability \(1/4\), independently of \(d\). Thus token CSD is zero for the pair, while oracle CSD is one with probability \(1/4\).

This does not set the raw router to a globally constant dense model: negative-semantic groups elsewhere use its other expert. Nor does it claim these centers were observed in a trained run. It shows that the explicit distribution and nearest-centroid assumptions do not supply the claimed routing guarantee; a further restriction connecting learned centers, semantic directions and boundary margins would be needed. The appendix’s informal cluster-density approximation does not provide such a bound. The independent 100,000-pair sign diagnostic gave \(0.24843\), consistent with the exact \(1/4\); the proof does not depend on this simulation.

This is Major: a demonstrated false lemma is used directly in the core theorem, and its claimed discrete-routing consequence needs additional control. Averaging independent noise can still reduce variance, and actual learned centers may be favorable. Those facts neither establish the stated universal high-dimensional result nor refute the reported empirical improvements. The threshold condition above is a partial lemma repair, not a verified replacement for the full CSD theorem.
claim: Lemma5 and its use to prove Theorem1's high-dimensional locality guarantee.

Let \(n=1\), \(m=2\), \(K=1/4\), and take independent \(x_1,x_2\sim N(0,I_d)\) for any identity dimension \(d\). Choose the singleton subset \(S\) uniformly from \(\{1\}\) and \(\{2\}\), as prescribed. These choices satisfy \(n<m\), positive fixed constants, isotropic Gaussianity, and the stated sampling rule.
result: Event probability0 for every d. Additional explicit Assumptions1-4/nearest-centroid construction gives token pair CSD0 and oracle swap probability1/4 at every d. False lemma directly supports core Theorem1; full CSD guarantee unestablished.

analysis: Claim and scope. Theorem 2, p. 4, and Appendix A.3, p. 13, assert that alignment in the sense of Eq. (2) implies I(\(Z_\alpha\);N_alpha)=I(Z_beta;N_beta)=0. Equation (2), p. 2, permits general kernel functions. The theorem is a necessary-condition claim; this review does not reverse it into a sufficiency claim.

Use independent fair signs S,A,B, inputs (S,A) and (S,B), common essence S, and independent nuisances A,B. Set \(Z_\alpha\)=(S,A)/sqrt(2), Z_beta=(S,B)/sqrt(2). Both representations are deterministic functions of their own inputs, unit norm, sufficient for S, and preserve one bit of their respective nuisance. The essence and nuisance assumptions verified in Problem 1 also hold in this sign-valued construction.
\[k(z,z')=l(z,z')=z_1z'_1,\qquad K=L=\tfrac12 ss^\top,\qquad {\rm CKA}(K,L)=1.\]

This is a valid positive-semidefinite kernel with nonzero centered Gram norm whenever both signs occur. Nevertheless, I(\(Z_\alpha\);N_alpha)=I(Z_beta;N_beta)=1 bit. The Gram equality holds for arbitrary repetitions of the full support and in the population limit. It is not the finite-sample exception already acknowledged by the appendix.

Proof failure. Appendix A.3 infers a deterministic surjection from \(Z_\alpha\) to Z_beta when nuisance information is present. Here H(Z_beta|\(Z_\alpha\))=H(B)=1 bit, so no such function exists. It also assumes that the kernel distinguishes the relevant unequal representations, which a permitted projection kernel need not do.

Counterevidence and exact impact. The actual release uses full-feature linear CKA. In this same example its CKA equals 1/2, so the counterexample does not refute those measured values or the narrower empirical association. The supported Major judgment concerns the central stated theoretical guarantee and its proof under the kernel generality allowed by Eq. (2). Perfect similarity under a kernel cannot certify removal of information that kernel ignores.
result: Inputs: Xa=(S,A),Xb=(S,B), independent fair signs. Representations: \(Z_a=(S,A)/\sqrt2,Z_b=(S,B)/\sqrt2\). Kernel: k(z,z')=\(z_1\)*z1', valid PSD. Cka: 1. Nuisance mi bits each: 1. Full feature linear cka: 1/2. actual released default is full-feature linear CKA. this example does not refute those measured CKA values.

The counterexample does not establish failure for every restricted kernel/representation coupling. The inspected full-feature linear choice and empirical trends survive this particular counterexample.
claim: Perfect CKA under permitted kernels does not imply zero nuisance information.

paragraphs: 1/tauprime=1/tau+\(2\beta\) yields exact intended negative-loss identity up to \(2\beta\).

analysis: Location: Appendix B, p. 15, Eqs. (34)-(40). The appendix differentiates a variant whose positive-pair numerator uses tau’ and whose denominator uses tau, then claims a sample-dependent effective temperature gap. The printed positive-log signs already disagree with minimization and the displayed gradients. Even after correcting those signs to the intended negative log loss, the positive-pair derivative in Eq. (38) is wrong.

\[D=\sum_k e^{s_{ik}/\tau},\qquad L'_i=-s_{ii}/\tau'+\log D,\qquad
\frac{\partial L'_i}{\partial s_{ii}}=-\frac1{\tau'}+\frac{e^{s_{ii}/\tau}}{\tau D}.\]

The denominator’s positive-pair term differentiates at tau, not tau’. The printed Eq. (38) instead places tau’ in both the prefactor and the numerator exponential of this correction. At \(s_{ii}\)=0.2, one negative similarity s_ij=0.1, tau=0.5 and tau’=0.25, the correct derivative is -2.9003320054; Eq. (38) gives -0.7189762528. These cosine similarities are feasible for unit vectors, for example an anchor e1 and two vectors having first coordinates 0.2 and 0.1.
An exact calculation is simpler than Eq. (40). For unit-norm vectors, the squared-distance penalty is proportional to 2 beta(1-\(s_{ii}\)). Therefore:

\[\begin{aligned}
L_i&=-s_{ii}/\tau+\log D+2\beta(1-s_{ii}),\\
\frac1{\tau'}&=\frac1{\tau}+2\beta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L_i=L'_i+2\beta .
\end{aligned}\]

The equivalence uses a constant coefficient mapping for fixed beta and tau; it does not yield the appendix’s claimed sample-dependent adaptive gap. Symbolic differentiation and simplification in regularizer_replay.py verify the derivative and the zero residual of this identity.

Impact and limits. This invalidates the appendix’s particular adaptive-temperature derivation, a bounded secondary explanation. It does not refute the observed learned-temperature trajectories in Section 5.3 or the regularizer’s implementation. The repaired algebra concerns this numerator/denominator variant only; it is not an empirical explanation or a verified dynamical model of information homeostasis.
result: Sii: 0.2. Sij: 0.1. Tau: 0.5. Tauprime: 0.25. Correct derivative: -2.900332005375044. Printed derivative: -0.7189762528256864.

claim: Cross-modal KL does not upper-bound unconditional input information.
analysis: Claim and location. Section 4.2, p. 4, Eq. (17), and Appendix A.5, p. 14, Eqs. (25)-(29), state that I(\(Z_\alpha\);\(X_\alpha\)) is upper-bounded by the average KL divergence between the paired modality-conditional representation laws. This bound is then converted into the squared-distance regularizer in Eq. (18), and used in the claimed information-bottleneck objective and loss, Eqs. (19)-(20).
\[I(Z_\alpha;X_\alpha)\ \leq\ {\mathbb E}_{X_\alpha,X_\beta}D_{\rm KL}\!\left(p(z\mid X_\alpha)\,\|\,q(z\mid X_\beta)\right)\quad\hbox{(claimed).}\]

Complete counterexample. Let S,A,B be independent fair bits. Take \(X_\alpha\)=(S,A), \(X_\beta\)=(S,B), essence Y=S, and nuisances N_alpha=A, N_beta=B. Each encoder outputs the shared bit through the same binary symmetric channel: P(Z=S|S)=9/10 and P(Z!=S|S)=1/10. The two encoder draws can be conditionally independent.

All operative assumptions hold. The inputs are conditionally independent given S; Y is determined by either input, so both essence Markov chains hold. Each nuisance is independent of Y and determined by its own input. In bits, H(\(X_\alpha\))=H(\(X_\beta\))=2 and H(Y)=H(N_alpha)=H(N_beta)=1, verifying Definition 2’s entropy identity. The encoders are stochastic functions of their own inputs and all their output probabilities are positive.
\[\mathbb E D_{\rm KL}(p\|q)=0,\qquad I(Z_\alpha;X_\alpha)=\log 2+\tfrac9{10}\log\tfrac9{10}+\tfrac1{10}\log\tfrac1{10}=0.3680642072>0.\]
The conditional laws coincide on every positive input pair, making KL zero, while Z still encodes S. The claimed inequality is therefore false, independently of any numerical approximation.

Gaussian restriction does not rescue it. Let S instead be a fair sign, retain independent nuisance bits, and use N(S,1) as both encoders’ conditional law. Their means agree for every positive pair, so both KL and the proposed squared-distance term are zero. Yet I(Z;S)>0 because N(-1,1) and N(1,1) are distinct. Reviewer-owned quadrature gives approximately 0.3368308203 nats; strict positivity follows analytically from non-independence.

Invalid step. Appendix A.5 treats the remainder after inserting q(z|\(X_\beta\)) as a nonnegative KL term in Eq. (28). The averaging measure still depends on the same z being integrated inside the alleged KL. The stated expression is not the nonnegative KL decomposition needed for Eq. (29). Marginal input information cannot be discarded merely because paired conditional encoders agree.

Correct identity. Under the local-encoder Markov relation \(Z_\alpha - X_\alpha - X_\beta\), let p(z|\(X_\beta\)) be the conditional distribution induced by the alpha encoder. Directly add and subtract its log density:

\[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E D_{\rm KL}(p(z\mid X_\alpha)\|q(z\mid X_\beta))
&=I(Z_\alpha;X_\alpha\mid X_\beta)\\
&\quad+\mathbb E_{X_\beta}D_{\rm KL}(p(z\mid X_\beta)\|q(z\mid X_\beta)).
\end{aligned}\]

Thus the computable cross-modal KL upper-bounds conditional input information, not total input information. Equivalently, total information is bounded by that KL plus I(\(Z_\alpha\);\(X_\beta\)). In the counterexample, conditional information is zero while the shared-information term is positive, exactly accounting for the discrepancy.
\[I(Z_\alpha;X_\alpha)\leq \mathbb E D_{\rm KL}(p\|q)+I(Z_\alpha;X_\beta).\]

Impact. Equation (17) is the stated theoretical bridge from input compression to the proposed distance penalty. Its failure invalidates that bridge and the claimed exact substitution into the ordinary IB objective. This is central derivation damage even if the same agreement regularizer improves practical alignment or captioning.

What a correction does and does not establish. Conditional-information regularization can give a defensible alternative motivation. With exact information quantities, I(Z;\(X_\beta\))-beta I(Z;\(X_\alpha|X_\beta\)) equals (1+beta)I(Z;\(X_\beta\))-beta I(Z;\(X_\alpha\)). It changes the coefficient relationship and does not restore the printed Eq. (17). Replacing information terms with InfoNCE lower bounds is also a surrogate optimization, not exact equality of the objectives or their minimizers.

Appendix A.6 survives: equal spherical covariance yields KL = ||mu_alpha-mu_beta||^2/(2 sigma^2). The error occurs before that valid Gaussian algebra. The analytic conditional identity is verified; no corrected training run, performance claim or author-adopted repair is asserted.
result: Inputs: Xa=(S,A),Xb=(S,B); independent fair bits S,A,B. Essence: S. Nuisances: A. Nuisances: B. Encoders: identical BSC(0.1) conditional laws on S. Expected kl: 0. Mi nats: 0.3680642071684971. Gaussian variant: same N(S,1) posterior, zero KL but positive MI. Gaussian KL-to-MSE formula correct. Agreement loss remains well-defined. Empirical scores not disproved.

claim: Definition1 does not imply the minimal sufficient statistic premise of Lemma1.
analysis: Source: Definition 1 and Lemma 1, p. 3; Appendix A.1, p. 13. The definition supplies two Markov chains, while the proof immediately treats the essence as a minimal sufficient statistic and infers a bijection. Those Markov chains alone do not supply that premise.

Counterexample. Let independent fair signs S,A,B define \(X_\alpha\)=(S,A), \(X_\beta\)=(S,B). Both Y=S and Y’=\(X_\beta\) satisfy \(X_\beta\) - Y - \(X_\alpha\) and Y - \(X_\beta - X_\alpha\). For Y, this follows from independent nuisances and the fact S is known from \(X_\beta\). For Y’=\(X_\beta\), both conditional-independence statements are immediate. Yet Y has two states and Y’ four, with H(Y’|Y)=1 bit; no bijection on their supports exists.

Even the displayed nuisance constraints can be met: for Y=S choose A,B; for Y’=\(X_\beta\), both input entropies and H(Y’) are two bits, so constant nuisances meet Definition 2’s displayed identities. The latter interpretation shows why the formal definition does not capture the intended common-information meaning.

Alternative reading and calibrated impact. The surrounding prose calls essence the common part, and Appendix A.1 clearly intends a minimal sufficient statistic. That stronger intended definition is not supplied by the two displayed Markov chains. The supported judgment is Major: Section 3.1 explicitly identifies the unique essence-induced input partition as the learning target, treats the essence as unique thereafter, and Section 3.2 uses Lemma 1 to claim that all ideal representations create the same partition. The verified nonbijective essences invalidate this formal uniqueness guarantee within the paper’s central information-theoretic formulation. The finite-discrete repair below and the survival of Theorem 1 and Appendix A.4 do not establish the original lemma under Definition 1.

Precise finite-discrete repair. Add H(Y|\(X_\alpha\))=0 for each candidate essence. Equation (5) then forces H(Y|\(X_\beta\))=0. Given Eq. (4), any other deterministic variable shared by both conditionally independent inputs must be constant conditional on Y; hence it is a function of Y. Apply the same reasoning in reverse to obtain a bijection on the supports. This repairs the lemma in the stated finite-discrete setting; no unrestricted continuous-variable repair is asserted.

Checked statements that survive. Theorem 1 follows directly by selecting the identity task T=Y in its premise about all deterministic tasks. Its proof’s unnecessary Markov-chain sentence can be replaced by T - Y - \(Z_\alpha\), without changing the conclusion. Appendix A.4’s equality I(\(Z_\alpha\);Y)=I(\(Z_\alpha\);\(X_\beta\)) follows from the two stated Markov chains and local encoder conditional independence. Neither result is refuted by the uniqueness example.
result: Y: S. Yprime: (S,B)=Xb. H yprime given y bits: 1. Surrounding common-part/minimal-sufficient-statistic intention is stronger than the displayed definition. The finite-discrete deterministic-essence repair is valid within its stated scope. Theorem 1 and Appendix A.4 remain valid under their own stated/local encoder assumptions. No empirical-score claim is disproved by this uniqueness counterexample.

result: Theorem B.3 says its coefficient equations must hold for equivalence, which can be read as a necessary-condition statement. The defect is the subsequent use of those marginal conditions to identify the reverse conditional, not merely that wording.

A separate dependent coupling can validate the deterministic transition. Let one shared \(E\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\) generate \[z_n=\sqrt{a_n}z_0+\sqrt{1-a_n}(\gamma\rho+E)\] at every timestep, with the deterministic construction’s constant \(\gamma\). Each marginal remains exactly equation the displayed formula. Eliminating \(E\) gives \[z_{n-1}=\iota_nz_n+\zeta_nz_0.\] This is an exact marginal-preserving construction. It abandons the conditional independence of Theorem 5.2. The inspected passages do not distinguish such a new joint from the independent-noise joint before identifying their conditionals. Independently sampled training marginals and a different sampling joint can coexist, but their probabilities must be distinguished.

(1-a_(n-1)) I > 0 versus 0 for the same conditional; cross-covariance 0 versus \(\sqrt{(1-a_{n-1})(1-a_n)}\) I. Invalid derivation directly supplies core CDM sampler and ELBO argument. Empirical performance not refuted.
analysis: The independent-noise posterior and the deterministic reverse kernel cannot be the same conditional law.

Conditional-variance contradiction. Choose any internal timestep \(1<n<N_r\) with \(0<a_n<a_{n-1}<1\), and condition on any actual admissible pair \(z_0,z_c\). The residual definition is then automatically satisfied; no special output of the learned compressor is required. The stipulated independent standard Gaussian noises give \[\operatorname{Var}(z_{n-1}\mid z_n,z_0,z_c)
 =(1-a_{n-1})I\succ0.\] The proposed conditional kernel with the paper’s default \(\eta=0\) gives the variance \(0\) for the identical conditioning information. A nondegenerate Gaussian cannot equal a point mass. Equivalently, the independent-noise joint has \[\operatorname{Cov}(z_{n-1},z_n\mid z_0,z_c)=0,\] whereas generating the pair with the proposed deterministic kernel gives \[\operatorname{Cov}(z_{n-1},z_n\mid z_0,z_c)
 =\iota_n(1-a_n)I
 =\sqrt{(1-a_{n-1})(1-a_n)}I\ne0.\] Every condition used here is the one in the paper’s own construction. The contradiction holds for every nondegenerate internal pair of its schedule, rather than requiring a specially chosen schedule. ◻

The independent exact arithmetic in supplies an illustrative scalar calculation: \(a_{n-1}=16/25\), \(a_n=9/25\), \(\iota_n=3/4\), \(\zeta_n=7/20\). The two conditional variances are \(9/25\) and \(0\); the two cross-covariances are \(0\) and \(12/25\), while the marginal variance \(\iota_n^{2}(1-a_n)=9/25\) still matches. This illustration is not asserted to be a particular Stable Diffusion timestep pair. The general proof above covers the stipulated schedule.

The assessment is Major: the invalid identification supplies the core CDM reverse derivation and is reused by the ELBO argument. If the stated independent conditional is compared with a zero-variance model kernel, the KL divergence is infinite, not the displayed finite squared-error surrogate. A positive-variance model or a separately defined joint would require its own derivation.

The shared-noise construction above restores exactly the deterministic marginal-preserving transition. It is a partial mathematical repair, not a verification of the complete stochastic construction, ELBO, learned loss, or experiments. The finding does not show that the sampler is unusable or that the reported images and compression gains disappear.

Definition 5.1 and equation (11), p. 6, specify the forward marginals.  \iota_n=\sqrt{\frac{1-a_{n-1}}{1-a_n}},
 \qquad
 \zeta_n=\sqrt{a_{n-1}}-\iota_n\sqrt{a_n},
 \qquad

Equation (2), p. 4, defines total rate as \(R=R_c+R_{z_c}\). Section 4.2, p. 5, and Appendix A.3, p. 13, describe index coding as an efficient way to transmit text conditioning; Figure 16, p. 15, compares its bit costs with zlib. The paper does not itself state that semantic bits are omitted.

In the pinned release, `nn_indices.py`, lines 22–49, constructs a per-input character histogram, sorted alphabet, and cumulative distribution from a decimal representation of token indices. Lines 52–66 pass numeric symbols and the CDF to the arithmetic encoder, then return `encoded_bytes`, `cdf`, and `unique_chars`. Lines 68–76 require all three objects for decoding. In `inference_res.py`, lines 82–105, the decoder reuses the encoder’s CDF and alphabet in memory, while lines 100–101 charge only \(\operatorname{len}(\texttt{encoded\_data})\times8\). The analogous path occurs in `inference_res_pfo.py`, lines 93–116. These are static source observations, not executed reproduction results.
Pinned 2026-05-07 release. Codec accepted CPU integer index inputs [333] and [444]. Alphabet/CDF constructed per input. Charged payload contains arithmetic bytes only.
analysis: The pinned implementation’s counted text payload is insufficient to reconstruct its encoded token indices without caption-dependent side information.

Consider valid single-index inputs \([333]\) and \([444]\) to the helper on CPU. Both indices lie within the CLIP vocabulary’s integer range. Their decimal strings are `333` and `444`; both have length three, a one-symbol alphabet, CDF \([0,1]\), and numeric symbol sequence \([0,0,0]\). Thus the numerical arguments delivered to the arithmetic encoder are identical, while the alphabets required for reconstruction are respectively \(\{\texttt{3}\}\) and \(\{\texttt{4}\}\). The encoded payload cannot distinguish the two inputs. The exact independent check records these CDFs and sequences without importing Torch, torchac, or author code.

This is an injectivity failure for the payload considered alone, not a claim about a particular byte count returned by torchac. The caption-dependent alphabet is essential in this witness. General inputs also require agreement on the probability model and sequence length. They could be serialized, made fixed and shared, or reconstructed by an explicitly synchronized model; the inspected path does not charge or establish any such mechanism.
result: In-process decoding can succeed because the missing objects are passed directly from the encoder. That does not make them available to a separate decoder at the reported payload length. Conversely, the inspected release is a 2026 commit, and no evidence binds it to the 2025 numerical experiments. The paper’s actual total-rate definition includes text bits.

The supported assessment is Minor for the release-level implementation defect; the magnitude and historical provenance of any error in the paper’s core rate comparisons are Needs Evidence. A larger severity for the historical results would require the actual experiment-generating code, complete serialized streams, and rate–distortion data. No additional-bit estimate or corrected BD-rate is invented. A valid repair must implement and count a complete decoding protocol, then recompute the affected rates; that repair has not been performed.
The counted payload alone is non-injective; required side information is passed in memory and uncharged. Supported release defect; magnitude and effect on published RD comparisons Needs Evidence.

claim: Independent quartiles, arithmetic mean and circular mean.
Six valid roll indices 1,1,1,359,359,359, ordinary IQR filter, decode index minus180.
analysis: In `r01/inference.py`, lines 26–47, `get_3angle_infer_aug` combines six crop predictions. Azimuth uses circular averaging; rotation uses the ordinary IQR-filtered mean defined in `r01/utils.py`, lines 104–119, before subtracting \(180^\circ\).

Take six valid 360-bin rotation predictions \[(1,1,1,359,359,359).\] Every value is in the decoder’s domain. The quartiles are 1 and 359; all six survive the stated \(1.5\,\mathrm{IQR}\) filter. Their mean is 180, hence the returned roll is \(0^\circ\). The individual decoded rolls are instead \(-179^\circ\) and \(179^\circ\): all lie within one degree of the same physical angle at \(180^\circ\). Circular averaging returns that angle, so the implemented rule can create a \(180^\circ\) error from individually accurate predictions. The independent calculation is retained in `calc.json`; `code.json` binds the exact source members and lines.

A circular mean, with a declared rule for a zero resultant, repairs this boundary example; it does not guarantee robust aggregation for arbitrary multimodal predictions. The plain inference function performs no such averaging, and `app.py`, line 60, disables augmentation by default. No evidence binds this optional path to the paper’s benchmark scores. The supported consequence is a released optional-feature failure.

claim: Central tracking evaluations use root mean square aligned position error.

Pinned commit d462a5917eb9dc9d4079bd4d642a91486626a250. Rigid position alignment with correspondences; valid full-rank eight-position trajectories. Default Replica config enables final evaluation; historical table binding unknown.
analysis: The tracking metric is specified as root mean square absolute trajectory error on p. 5 and in Tables 1, 4–6, 10–11, 13, 15 and 20. In `utils/eval_helpers.py`, lines 29–63 align estimated and ground-truth positions and form per-position Euclidean errors. Lines 66–83 return their arithmetic mean; lines 544–550 call the result `ate_rmse` and report it as ATE RMSE.

For aligned errors \(e_i=\|R\hat t_i+t-t_i^{\rm GT}\|_2\), these quantities are \[M=\frac1n\sum_i e_i,\qquad Q=\sqrt{\frac1n\sum_i e_i^{2}}.\] They satisfy \(M\le Q\), with equality exactly when all magnitudes agree. The prior square root constructs each Euclidean distance; it does not make the subsequent arithmetic mean an RMSE.

Take all eight ground-truth positions \(g=(x,y,z)\in\{-1,1\}^{3}\), in metres, and estimates \[\hat g_A=g+0.01yz(1+x)e_1,\qquad
 \hat g_B=g+0.012yz e_1,\qquad e_1=(1,0,0).\] Both error fields have zero mean and zero cross moment with \(g\). The centered cross-covariance is \(8I_3\), positive definite and full rank. Identity is the unique optimal rigid rotation and translation is zero. The construction therefore does not exploit degenerate alignment. A has four zero errors and four errors of \(2\) cm; B has eight errors of \(1.2\) cm:
Trajectory | Returned mean (cm) | Correct RMSE (cm)

The ranking reverses. Imposing a common first-pose convention by subtracting each trajectory’s first center adds only translations removed by alignment. A Independently authored SVD calculation verifies both conventions, covariance and residuals; a mathematical auxiliary independently verified the construction.

This is an active path: `src/vtgaussian_slam.py` imports the evaluator at line 28, invokes it for saved evaluation around lines 1389–1396, and for final evaluation around lines 2880–2886. The released Replica configuration enables the latter through `use_wandb=True`. Tracking accuracy is a core contribution, so a mathematically different statistic capable of reversing its ordering supports Major without requiring a demonstrated benchmark-score loss. However, historical trajectories, logs and code-to-table bindings are absent. No particular published score correction is established.

Compute \(\sqrt{\operatorname{mean}(e_i^{2})}\) after alignment, preserve frame correspondence and regenerate affected tables from original runs. Correct arithmetic is verified on the witness, but no author-code patch or experiment was run. A similar square-root-before-mean expression occurs in the released depth RMSE calculation; the paper’s reconstruction tables explicitly use depth L1, so that naming defect does not itself invalidate those tables.

analysis: Section 5.1, Eq.(10)-(11), p.4, and Appendix A.4, pp.14-15, require the top-c eigenvectors of G. analysis: On physical page 24, the weighted increment integral is bounded by \(C(d^{2\gamma+1}+|x|^{4\gamma+2})^{1/2}h^{2}\). The square root cannot hold uniformly in \(x\) under the stated assumptions.

Take the one-dimensional Ornstein–Uhlenbeck potential \(U(x)=x^{2}/2\) and use the admissible polynomial upper-growth exponent \(\gamma=2\). This smooth potential satisfies dissipativity, the one-sided condition, log-Sobolev, and the required third-derivative bound (its third derivative vanishes). For deterministic \(X_0=x>0\), \[\mathbb E|X_s-x|^{2}=x^{2}(e^{-s}-1)^{2}+1-e^{-2s}.\] Since \((1+x^{2}+X_s^{2})^{2}\ge x^{4}\), the left side of (169), with \(t=0\), is at least \[x^{4}\{x^{2} A(h)+B(h)\},\quad
 A(h)=h-2(1-e^{-h})+\tfrac12(1-e^{-2h}),\quad
 B(h)=h-\tfrac12(1-e^{-2h}).\] For fixed \(h=1/2\), \(A(h)>0\), so this grows as \(x^{6}\), whereas the printed right side is \(O(x^{5})\). No constant independent of \(x\) repairs that inequality. analysis: The double-well derivatives in (188)–(189), and the parameters asserted on page 8, are incorrect.

For the verification’s \(\alpha=\beta=1\) potential \(U(x)=|x|^{4}/4-|x|^{2}/2\), direct differentiation gives \[\begin{aligned}
 \nabla^2U&=(|x|^{2}-1)I+2xx^\top,\\

analysis: Location and classification. Theorem 3.4 on p. 6 and Appendix \(C\) on p. 16. Major: the stated ground-truth uniqueness guarantee is not established by the supplied proof.

The theorem assumes that the oracle rationale is smaller than its complement and is minimal for the label: every proper subgraph of that oracle loses label information. Minimality within the oracle does not imply the opening proof assertion that every predictive-optimal candidate contains it; another informative subgraph or redundant copy is not excluded by this condition. A stronger global identifiability assumption would be needed for that reduction. The architecture also feeds complementary topological features to the classifier, so prediction sufficiency cannot simply be identified with the selected-edge set without accounting for that channel.

Even granting the proof’s containment reduction, its subsequent graph identities fail. For a finite graph, \[\beta_0=|V|-|E|+\beta_1,\] not the edge-count relation used in the proof. On the common vertex set \(\{0,1,2,3\}\), let the rationale edges be \(\{01\}\) and the noise edges be \(\{12,23\}\). Then \(|E_\epsilon|>|E_X|\), yet \(\beta_0^\epsilon-\beta_0^X=2-3=-1\), while \(|E_\epsilon|-|E_X|=1\). If isolated vertices are discarded, both subgraphs are connected and the component difference is instead zero, still not one. Thus neither conventional vertex treatment supports the printed equality. This counterexample already uses an acyclic connected full graph, so excluding cycles would not repair the displayed sign/count identity.

Nor does a larger edge count imply more finite zero-dimensional bars: use rationale edges \(\{03,13\}\) and noise edges \(\{01,12,02\}\) on four common vertices. The noise has three edges versus two, but both have exactly two component-merging events. The extra noise edge creates a cycle rather than another \(H_0\) death. The independent union-find calculation records these counts.

The proof additionally asserts a bottleneck distance proportional to a difference of Betti numbers. Bottleneck distance minimizes a maximum matching cost and does not add up multiplicity differences. Let \(P_n\) contain \(n\) copies of \((0,1)\) and let \(Q\) be empty. Every copy can match the diagonal at cost \(1/2\), hence \(d_B(P_n,Q)=1/2\) for all \(n\geq1\). The independently enumerated partial matchings give exactly 0.5 for \(n=1,2,4\). A positive constant times the number of unmatched bars cannot represent this distance. These finite examples avoid complications from essential bars; if essential bars are retained at infinity, the convention must also be stated before the proof’s finite bound is meaningful.

Finally, Definition 3.2 is Wasserstein distance between distributions of diagrams, whereas the proof concludes from per-graph counts and an asserted weighted sum of homology-degree distances. The later finite-function lower bound need not preserve the maximizers of the original distance. An arbitrarily large learned scale is not automatically compatible with the one-Lipschitz requirement. None of these bridges is supplied. Consequently repairing a sign or bounding the first Betti number alone is insufficient. A valid replacement theorem would need explicit identifiability, diagram conventions, a justified objective and a proof for its actual surrogate. Such a theorem has not been established in this review; the finding concerns the proof, not a claim that every empirical fit must fail.

analysis: Location and classification. Proposition 3.3 and the Rational Hat construction in Section 3.1, p. 6. Major for the claimed tractable lower bound.

Proposition 3.3 itself is valid when its functions really are one-Lipschitz under \(d_B\): for any coupling, the difference of expectations is bounded by the expected distance, and taking the infimum yields the result. The problem is the proposed realization. Set the allowed learnable parameters \(c=(0,0)\), \(r=1\), take \(P_\varepsilon=\{(0,\varepsilon)\}\) and \(Q=\varnothing\). The printed kernel gives \[\varphi(P_\varepsilon;c,1)-\varphi(Q;c,1)
 =\frac1{1+\varepsilon}-\frac1{2-\varepsilon}
 \longrightarrow\frac12,
 \qquad d_B(P_\varepsilon,Q)=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\longrightarrow0.\] Its ratio to \(d_B\) diverges. For \(\varepsilon=10^{-6}\) the ratio is approximately \(999997.5\). No finite constant \(C\) makes this displayed map \(C\)-Lipschitz over the stated diagram space; multiplying by \(1/C\) therefore does not fix it. The problem is sensitivity to creation/deletion of a near-diagonal bar, not differentiability of the pointwise kernel. A common persistent component can be added to both diagrams without changing this argument. The variable-cardinality diagram setting is relevant to the paper’s variable-size graph rationale setting.

A restricted diagram domain, a diagonal-vanishing construction with proven cardinality control, and explicit norm constraints could support a different guarantee. Those conditions are not stated here. The sum of two individual maximizers also need not remain a lower bound with constant one: even two identical valid witnesses can yield twice the distance. An average or a separately justified Lipschitz bound would be required; learned attention does not establish this automatically. These are limitations of the asserted theoretical approximation, not evidence against the possibility of using the feature map as an empirical regularizer.

analysis: Assessment: Minor, limited to the optional pairwise-judge scoring branch. Section 2.2, p. 3, uses pairwise comparisons to obtain scalar scores for selecting preference pairs. Appendix B, pp. 12–13, defines the battle matrix and says scores are obtained by maximizing an unregularized logistic likelihood. No connectivity condition, penalty, score bound, or finite-iteration fallback is specified. Valid, unanimous comparison outcomes can make this optimization lack a finite solution.

Let \(B_{mn}\) count wins of response \(m\) over response \(n\) across the two presentation orders. The printed objective is \[\ell(s)=\sum_{m,n}B_{mn}\log\sigma(s_m-s_n),\qquad
 \sigma(u)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-u}}.\] Take two responses for which the judge prefers response 1 in both orders. This gives \(B_{12}=2\) and \(B_{21}=0\), with no ties or parse errors. If \(d=s_1-s_2\), \[\ell(d)=2\log\sigma(d),\qquad
 \ell'(d)=2(1-\sigma(d))>0\] at every finite \(d\). The supremum is zero as \(d\to+\infty\), but it is unattained. Fixing \(s_1+s_2=0\) removes translation ambiguity without curing this separation.

The issue also applies to the paper’s usual eight candidates. Suppose both presentation orders agree with the strict ranking \(1\succ2\succ\cdots\succ8\). Then \(B_{mn}=2\) for \(m<n\) and zero otherwise. Choose centered scores \[s_i=t\left(\frac72-(i-1)\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,8.\] Their sum is zero, and \[\ell(t)=2\sum_{m<n}\log\sigma(t(n-m))<0\] for every finite \(t\), increasing to zero as \(t\to\infty\). No finite maximum exists. Such an outcome is allowed by the described procedure and does not require a pathological empty comparison graph.

An independent scalar script evaluates this eight-candidate likelihood as \(-38.8162\) at \(t=0\), \(-6.5919\) at \(t=1\), \(-0.09456\) at \(t=5\), and approximately \(-2.89\cdot10^{-8}\) at \(t=20\). These computations confirm the analytic argument; they do not execute an author solver.

Specify a well-defined estimator and its exact hyperparameters. For example, \[\ell_\lambda(s)=\ell(s)-\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_i s_i^{2},\qquad \lambda>0,\] is strictly concave and tends to \(-\infty\) as \(\|s\|\to\infty\), hence has a unique finite maximizer. A bounded-score optimization or an explicitly documented fallback is another possibility. The chosen method must be stated because it can affect length-penalized scores and preference pairs.

This is an analytic existence repair, not a verified replication or a modification of supplied code. The frequency of separable comparisons and the impact on STE-trained models remain Needs Evidence. The default scalar-score results are outside the demonstrated impact.

analysis: Appendix C, page 16, Equations (9)–(13), contains two mathematical inconsistencies in the coefficient-estimation prescription to which Section 4.5 directs the reader.

The source defines \(L(N,D)=E+A/N^\alpha+B/D^\beta\) and states \[\log L=\operatorname{LSE}(\log E,\log A-\alpha N,\log B-\beta D).\] Equation (13) then minimizes a sum of Huber losses of \(\log L(N^{(i)},D^{(i)})-L^{(i)}\), where the following sentence defines \(L^{(i)}\) as the loss achieved by the \(i\)th run, rather than its logarithm. Parameters are not tied; positive \(A,B,E,N,D\) and positive exponents suffice for the following tests. The source uses \(\delta=10^{-4}\) and a grid of initializations in log parameters. The last sentence extends a similar procedure to the other scaling-law forms.

By the definition of exponentiation, \(\log(A/N^\alpha)=\log A-\alpha\log N\). Exponentiating the right side of the displayed formula instead yields \(E+Ae^{-\alpha N}+Be^{-\beta D}\), a different family from the stated power law. All quantities are positive in the example \(N=4,D=9,A=B=E=1,\alpha=\beta=1/2\). The correct value is \(\log(11/6)=0.6061358036\); Equation (12) gives \(\log(1+e^{-2}+e^{-4.5})=0.1366652219\). The example tests the asserted algebraic identity, not an unperformed four-parameter language-model experiment.

The discrepancy also occurs at the actual grid scale: \(N=41{,}000{,}000,D=300{,}000,A=B=e^{6},E=1,\alpha=\beta=1/2\) satisfies positivity and the specified coefficient-initialization grid. The correct log loss is \(0.5875432061\), whereas the printed expression is indistinguishable from zero at double precision because both exponentials underflow. The exact expression remains different from zero. The independently written `check.py` and `check_output.json` give the inputs and results.

The residual inconsistency is separate and survives correction of Equation (12). Fix \(N=4,D=9,A=B=1,\alpha=\beta=1/2\) and take one observed loss \(y=2\). The feasible choice \(E=7/6>0\) fits it exactly, but the printed residual is \(\log2-2=-1.3068528194\), with Huber loss \(0.0001306802819\). The feasible choice \(E=e^{2}-5/6>0\) predicts \(e^{2}\) and makes that residual zero. This finite diagnostic establishes that the displayed objective favors the wrong target even when an exact fit exists. It does not reproduce the 125-point experimental fit.

 L_{\rm MI}=\log\sum_{j=1}^M e^{s_j}
             -\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M s_i
 \ \geq\ \log M.\] Jensen’s inequality gives equality whenever all matched-pair scores are equal. A common additive score shift leaves the loss unchanged; its score gradient is \(\operatorname{softmax}(s)_i-1/M\), zero at equality.

Take two equally likely inputs \(H_1^{1}=(1,0)\) and \(H_1^{2}=(0,1)\), and set both learned representations to the same nonzero unit vector \(u=(1,1)/\sqrt2\). With either dot-product or cosine similarity, both scores equal \(1/\sqrt2\) and the loss attains its global minimum \(\log2\), although the representation is constant and its mutual information with \(H_1\) is zero. The informative choice \(\widehat H_{\rm inv}^{\,i}=H_1^i\) also attains \(\log2\) while retaining \(\log2\) information. For constant \(Y\), the same distinction applies to the conditional information in Eq. 11. No undefined cosine or numerical approximation is involved.
Finite batch M>=2. Printed denominator contains matched \(j\),\(j\) scores. Nonzero unit vectors for dot-product or cosine demonstration.
result: The supervised term can oppose collapse; this does not prove collapse of the complete predictor. An intended anchor-versus-negative formula is a plausible correction, but no appendix correction or acquired implementation supplies it. The demonstrated failure concerns the contrastive/MI mechanism central to the invariant-learning argument, so Major does not require showing benchmark loss.

A candidate repair compares anchor \(\widehat H_{\rm inv}^{\,i}\) against every \(H_1^j\) in its denominator. A bound on the conditional information of Eq. 11 additionally needs appropriate conditioning and negative sampling. An index change alone does not prove that bound or invariance. For deterministic \(w\), moreover, \(I(w(H_1);H_1\mid Y)=H(w(H_1)\mid Y)\); maximizing it can retain nuisance variation. If \(H_1=(Y,C)\) for independent fair bits, retaining \((Y,C)\) preserves more conditional information than retaining \(Y\) alone, despite equal predictive information. This limits the noise-removal interpretation.

Loss>=logM with equality at any equal matched scores, including zero-MI collapse; no anchor-negative discrimination. Central MI/invariance mechanism is mathematically unsupported as published; no benchmark loss required for this assessment.

analysis: Major. The discrepancy affects a central conditional modeling module and its claimed derivation.

The prose on p. 13 instead mentions \(p(z\mid e)\). Granting that intended prior still does not justify equality for arbitrary \(q\). In the same joint, \(q=N(0,1)\) gives a proper ELBO of \(-1.4189385332\), below the evidence by \(0.1534264097\). The correct decomposition is \[\begin{aligned}

 \log p_\theta(x\mid e)
 &=\mathbb E_q\log p_\theta(x\mid z,e)
   -\mathrm{KL}\{q\Vert p_\theta(z\mid e)\}\\
 &\quad+\mathrm{KL}\{q\Vert p_\theta(z\mid x,e)\}.\nonumber\end{aligned}\] This refutes the particular asserted marginal-likelihood identity. It does not claim every data-conditioned prior in a different generative model is invalid.

Negating likelihood-minus-KL for minimization changes both terms, giving negative log likelihood plus KL. Equations 6/24 change the reconstruction sign but retain negative KL. The appendix repeats this discrepancy.

Set \(x=0\), comparison prior \(N(0,1)\), \(q=N(0,v)\) and fixed reconstruction variance parameter \(\sigma^{2}=1\). This explicitly separates posterior and reconstruction variances; the paper gives no equation binding them. With its reconstruction coefficient, \[K(v)=\tfrac12(v-1-\log v),\quad
 J_-(v)=-K(v)+v,\quad J_+(v)=K(v)+v.\] Independent symbolic calculations give:
\(v | K(v)\) | Printed \(J_-(v)\) | Corrected \(J_+(v)\)

Both satisfy \(\mathrm{KL}<0.4\), yet the losses order them oppositely. Without a hard KL bound, \(J_-(v)=\frac12(v+1+\log v)\to-\infty\) as \(v\downarrow0\). If \(\sigma^{2}\) is tied to \(v\), the reconstruction term itself has another degeneracy; that alternative is not used to attribute all unboundedness to the KL sign. The identity and sign findings do not depend on this diagnostic’s variance interpretation.

The published derivation does not establish its ELBO interpretation or prior-matching regularization, undermining MCVAE’s theoretical justification and Proposition 4.2. This supports Major independently of a benchmark rerun. It does not prove historical training used these signs or diverged.

the displayed formula restores the exact decomposition. A coherent minimized objective is \(-\mathbb E_q\log p_\theta(x\mid z,e)+\gamma\mathrm{KL}(q\Vert p_\theta(z\mid e))\), \(\gamma>0\); \(\gamma=1\) gives the usual negative ELBO. Specify decoder, prior and variance roles. These local repairs do not prove predictive sufficiency or OOD invariance and were not tested in a neural implementation.
claim:
Equations 5–6 (pp. 5–6), A.2 Equations 21–24 (pp. 12–13), and Proposition 4.2 (p. 7) motivate a conditional evidence objective. Writing \(x=\widetilde H_1\), Eq. 23 claims \[
 \log p_\theta(x\mid e)
 =-\mathrm{KL}\{q(z\mid x,e)\Vert p_\theta(z\mid x)\}
   +\mathbb E_q\log p_\theta(x\mid z,e).\] Equations 6/24 combine negative KL with a positive reconstruction/variance penalty, and enter the minimized loss the displayed formula.

Constant environment, normalized Gaussian joint with positive variances. Literal Eq23 counterexample uses \(q\) equal to true posterior, satisfying every positive KL threshold. Sign diagnostic explicitly separates reconstruction variance1 from posterior variancev.
result: Literal RHS exceeds log evidence by 0.0965735903; intended prior version still omits posterior gap; negativeKL plus positive reconstruction reverses the correct sign. Invalid mathematical basis for core MCVAE and Proposition4.2; historical divergence or benchmark loss not established.

claim:
A.1 (p. 12), Eqs. 14–20, assumes a Lipschitz predictor with constant \(L_f>0\), bounded nonnegative loss \(B\), and \(\widetilde H=\lambda H_1+(1-\lambda)H_2\), \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). It asserts \[
 \mathcal E_{\rm mixup}(\lambda)
 \leq \mathcal E^*+c_2\sqrt{I(\widetilde H;C_{\rm nuisance})},\] where \(\mathcal E^*\) is optimal achievable error and \(c_2>0\) depends on \(L_f,B\).

Let \(Y\) be a fair bit and set \(H_1=H_2=e_1=e_2=Y\). Then \(\widetilde H=e=Y\) for every \(\lambda\), including a Beta-distributed one. Use prediction/target domains \([0,1]\), squared loss, \(B=1\), and \(f(h)\equiv1/2\). This satisfies the displayed Lipschitz inequality with \(L_f=1\). Let \(C_{\rm nuisance}\) be an independent fair bit. Then \[I(\widetilde H;C_{\rm nuisance})=0,\quad
 \mathcal E^*=0,\quad
 \mathcal E_{\rm mixup}=\mathbb E(1/2-Y)^{2}=1/4.\] The zero optimum is attained by \(f^*(h)=\min(1,\max(0,h))\), also globally 1-Lipschitz. the displayed formula therefore requires \(1/4\leq0\), independently of \(c_2\).

A one-hot version removes any concern about environmental encoding. Let \(Y\) be uniform on the two unit vectors in \(\mathbb R^{2}\), set all four representations/labels equal to \(Y\), predict \((1/2,1/2)\), and use half squared Euclidean loss on the probability simplex. The loss is bounded by one and the risk is \(1/4\); Euclidean projection onto the simplex is 1-Lipschitz and attains zero risk on the support. Both versions are in the independent calculation record.
Lipschitz predictor Lf1. Squared loss bounded \(B=1\) on [0,1]. H1=H2=e1=e2=fair bit; any lambda. Independent nuisance; evaluated f constant1/2. One-hot vector extension also supplied.

No replacement upper bound is verified: substantive assumptions and an excess-risk or approximation term would be required.

analysis: Equations (20)–(21), p. 5, produce a non-intersecting boundary for an ordinary pair on the positive unit hyperboloid.
The curve \(x(t)=(\cosh t,\sinh t)\) has unit intrinsic speed. Consequently the genuine midpoint is \(x(1/2)\) and its angle satisfies \(\cot\theta_{\rm true}=\tanh(1/2)\simeq0.462117\).

Both supplied `manify/predictors/_midpoint.py` snapshots use a different expression, whose relevant branch is \[\cot\theta_{\rm code}=\frac{-V-\sqrt{V^{2}-4}}{2}.\] For this example it equals \(\coth1-\operatorname{csch}1=\tanh(1/2)\). The independent check inspected the actual source and typeset p. 5, excluding an extraction artifact. The code is therefore important counterevidence to any claim that the erroneous printed formula generated the benchmarks.

The published formula nevertheless directly drives the stated candidate construction in Algorithm 1 and the hyperbolic specialization in Section 3.2. This supported derivation defect is Major. A correct value for this example does not certify the code generally: its intermediate formula has a singularity when the two angles sum to \(\pi\), and dtype-specific behavior was not tested by running author code. result: The projected radii are \(1\) and \(1/2\). Equal angular deviations would imply equal distances on a normalized projected circle, but do not imply equal distances in the original sphere. Neither the main statement nor Appendices \(B\)–C restricts all samples to equal projection radii. Both inspected code snapshots implement arithmetic spherical averaging. Thus this is a Major failure of an explicit central geometric guarantee, not an observation that a benchmark score must decrease. The resulting great-circle split may still be useful and convex in the usual non-antipodal sense.

A limited pairwise repair is available. For unit-norm, non-antipodal sphere points with nonzero projected sum, take \(\theta_*=\operatorname{atan2}(u_0+v_0,u_d+v_d)\). The boundary then has \(n_*^\top(u+v)=0\), so \(|n_*^\top u|=|n_*^\top v|\) and their distances in the displayed formula are equal. This verifies only the specified pairwise property; degenerate cases, candidate ordering, and the entire tree algorithm are not certified by this repair.
Distances pi/4 approximately 0.785398 and asin(1/(2\(\sqrt{2}\))) approximately 0.361367 differ. Core five-desiderata guarantee fails; useful convex splits and empirical performance may survive.
analysis: Equation (22), p. 6, and Table 5 prescribe \(m_S(u,v)=(\theta_u+\theta_v)/2\). This does not generally satisfy the equidistance desideratum in dimension two or higher.

Work on the unit sphere \(S^{2,1}\) and choose \[u=(1,0,0),\qquad v=(0,1/2,\sqrt3/2).\] Both have norm one. Select \(d=1\). Their angles are \(\pi/2\) and \(0\), so Eq. (22) chooses \(\theta=\pi/4\). The resulting great-circle boundary \(B\) has unit normal \(n=(1,-1,0)/\sqrt2\). The two points are strictly on opposite sides because \(n^\top u=1/\sqrt2\) and \(n^\top v=-1/(2\sqrt2)\).

For a point \(x\) on the unit sphere, the shortest distance to \(B=\{y:\|y\|=1,\ n^\top y=0\}\) is \[
d_S(x,B)=\arcsin|n^\top x|.\] Indeed, normalizing the orthogonal projection of \(x\) onto \(n^\perp\) maximizes its dot product with a unit point on \(B\), giving cosine \(\sqrt{1-(n^\top x)^{2}}\) and hence the displayed formula. It follows that \[d_S(u,B)=\frac{\pi}{4}\simeq0.785398,\qquad
d_S(v,B)=\arcsin\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\simeq0.361367.\] The asserted equality fails. The independent script `c.py` checks norms, angles, and both distances in `calc.json`; the analytic argument does not depend on floating-point tolerance.
claim: Angular spherical mean provides original-manifold geodesic equidistance.

On the unit sphere \(S^{2,1}\), take \(u=(1,0,0)\), \(v=(0,1/2,\sqrt3/2)\), and select coordinate \(d=1\). The training set consists only of these two points. Both have unit norm and nonzero selected projections, and the resulting split places them on opposite sides; thus they are the nearest samples on their respective sides, without an antipodal or wraparound convention.

analysis: Assessment: Minor.

The main text explicitly says the predicted horizon state becomes the next reference; Figure 3 supports the same intended recurrence. Thus the most defensible interpretation is an incomplete or erroneous listing. It is not evidence that the experiments actually used unavailable future targets or teacher forcing.

A self-contained recurrence is as follows. Initialize \(v=U^{t_i}\) and \(t=t_i\). While \(t<t_o\), set \(\Delta=\min(t_h,t_o-t)\), predict \[v\leftarrow F_\theta(v,\text{coordinates},t,t+\Delta),\qquad
t\leftarrow t+\Delta,\] then return \(v\). For \(t_o=t_i\) it returns the input. This handles remainders and exact multiples without a future-state input. Under the stated restriction that each call advances at most \(t_h\), any rollout over \(H=t_o-t_i\geq0\) needs at least \(\lceil H/t_h\rceil\) calls; this recurrence attains that bound. That proof establishes minimal call count, not smaller forecasting error.

The reviewer-authored toy flow \(du/dt=1\), \(t_h=3\), checked horizons \(0,1,3,6,7,20\), including both boundary cases and remainders. Its outputs and call counts match the corrected recurrence (). No author implementation was run or repaired. The manuscript’s unambiguous prose supplies counterevidence against a central algorithmic failure; the supported problem is local reproducibility of the listing. Actual rollout semantics and historical results remain unverified.

claim: SCENT encodes irregular observations into latent tokens, evolves those representations, and decodes requested coordinates. Sparse attention limits each of \(N\) observation or query tokens to \(S\) attended tokens. The cost discussion uses \(L_s\) sparse-attention layers, \(M\) latent tokens, \(L_m\) latent self-attention layers, latent width \(d\), and \(W\) forecasting calls. The Warp-Unrolling Forecasting (WUF) description advances by at most the trained horizon \(t_h\), feeding the predicted state into the next call. Its call-count claim is distinct from any claim about accumulated forecasting error.

Algorithm 1 in Appendix \(B\), p. 15, is intended to implement the WUF procedure described on p. 4 and in Figure 3. It computes a prediction at \(t_c\) and advances \(t_i\) to \(t_c\), but never assigns the predicted state as the next input state. It defines a remainder \(t_r\) but tests \(r>0\). Its final call uses \(U^{t_i+t_r}\), which is a state at the target time, rather than the currently available predicted state. For an exact multiple of the horizon, the final output variable is not explicitly assigned. These are literal listing defects confirmed in the rendered original.

claim: SCENT encodes irregular observations into latent tokens, evolves those representations, and decodes requested coordinates. Sparse attention limits each of \(N\) observation or query tokens to \(S\) attended tokens. The cost discussion uses \(L_s\) sparse-attention layers, \(M\) latent tokens, \(L_m\) latent self-attention layers, latent width \(d\), and \(W\) forecasting calls. The Warp-Unrolling Forecasting (WUF) description advances by at most the trained horizon \(t_h\), feeding the predicted state into the next call. Its call-count claim is distinct from any claim about accumulated forecasting error.

Appendix L, pp. 23–25, presents a computational-complexity analysis and labels the sum of sparse, cross, and latent self-attention costs as the final Big-O complexity: \[
O\bigl(WL_sNSd+WNMd+WL_mM^2d\bigr).\] Appendix F, p. 19, specifies a feed-forward multiplier of four and varies latent dimension from 128 to 1024. The suspect step is treating attention-interaction costs alone as all contributions without stating a bounded-width or attention-dominated regime.

Conventional dense feed-forward block \(d\) to \(4d\) to \(d\) as suggested by multiplier4. Positive fixed \(W,L_s,N,S,M,L_m\) while varying latent width d. Encoder/decoder dimensions distinguished from processor width. No implementation available to exclude undocumented structured layers.
analysis: Assessment: Minor; practical cost comparisons need evidence.

For the conventional dense feed-forward block indicated by the multiplier, a token passes through matrices of dimensions \(d\times4d\) and \(4d\times d\). At \(M\) latent tokens, the two matrix products require \(8Md^{2}\) multiply-accumulate operations per block. Thus the latent processor alone contributes \[
8WL_mMd^{2},\] before biases, nonlinearities, or query/key/value and output projections. With \(W,L_s,N,S,M,L_m\) fixed and positive, the displayed formula is \(O(d)\) whereas the displayed formula is \(\Theta(d^{2})\). An unrestricted full-cost statement cannot omit this dependence. For \(L_m=2\), \(M=128\), one call gives 33,554,432 such operations at \(d=128\), and 2,147,483,648 at \(d=1024\). These are analytic counts, independently evaluated in and , not measurements of a released implementation.

This argument assumes ordinary dense feed-forward matrices, as suggested by the stated multiplier. An undocumented structured implementation could change the count; no code is available here to verify that alternative. Encoder and decoder widths need not equal latent width, and this calculation does not conflate them.

Substituting Table 6 into the paper’s own interaction proxies independently reproduces Table 7. Writing \(A\) for one SCENT call and \(B\) for one FNO step gives \[\begin{aligned}
A&=6(2000)(500)(128)+(2000)(128)^{2}+2(128)^{3}\\
 &=804{,}962{,}304,\nonumber\\
B&=4(2000)\log_2(2000)(60)+4(2000)(16)^{2}(60)\\
 &\simeq128{,}143{,}576.46.\nonumber\end{aligned}\] Here FNO’s Fourier-mode symbol is 16, whereas SCENT’s latent-width symbol is 128; the two uses of \(d\) in the source are not identified. With \(t_h=3\) and \(W=\lceil T/3\rceil\), these proxies give \[\frac{WA}{TB}\geq\frac{A}{3B}\simeq2.09391.\] At \(T=1\) the ratio is 6.28172; at \(T=20\) it is 2.19860. The shrinking gap in Table 7 is reproduced. These proxies do not demonstrate a crossover to a cheaper SCENT model, nor are Big-O expressions with unspecified constants numerical runtime measurements.
result: Appendix L explicitly acknowledges that SCENT is the most expensive of its three listed models at the selected training scale and that the gap shrinks with unrolling. Its long-horizon efficiency wording can reasonably refer to fewer model calls. This review does not attribute a categorical FNO crossover claim to the authors.

The expression remains a valid description of attention interactions. With widths and \(S\) fixed, adding dense-layer terms still permits linear scaling in \(N\). Figure 4 reports empirical error versus parameter count; no dependency of that curve on the incomplete cost derivation was established. Consequently the verified defect is an insufficiently qualified cost model, rather than a demonstrated invalid central accuracy or fixed-width scalability result. That dependency analysis, not appendix location or repair difficulty, supports Minor.

A correction should either label the displayed formula as an interaction-only proxy and specify its regime, or include all layer costs with their respective widths. Hardware timing, memory, and measured operations are needed to establish practical relative cost. This review does not certify the baseline architectures’ complete cost formulas.

Omitted quadratic width term; proxy ratios reproduce6.28172 at \(T=1\) and 2.19860 at T20. For horizon3 asymptotic proxy ratio bounded below by 2.09391. Supported local cost-model defect; complete practical cost advantage unresolved. No established core dependency warrants upgrading to Major.

analysis:
The restoration formula on p. 6, Equation (9), and minimization in Algorithm 1, p. 18, specify \[
L_{\rm paper}=\frac1{|E|}\sum_{e\in E}\log(1-p_e)
+\frac1{|E_{\rm inject}|}\sum_{e\in E_{\rm inject}}\log p_e.\] The released `experiment.py`, lines 240–250, instead minimizes binary cross-entropy with target one for original edges and zero for injected edges: \[
L_{\rm BCE}=-\frac1{|E|}\sum_{e\in E}\log p_e
-\frac1{|E_{\rm inject}|}\sum_{e\in E_{\rm inject}}\log(1-p_e).\]

Take one equally weighted positive and one negative prediction sharing \(p=\sigma(z)\). In the released decoder, final weights can be zero and the common bias can be \(z\), with equal directional predictions and zero symmetry penalty. A bias is not needed for the literal paper architecture either: in Equations (4)–(7), take identical node features with \(H_i^{(0)}=e_1\), let \(W_e\) copy only the first endpoint’s zero-hop coordinate into \(e_1\) and annihilate all other inputs, including higher-hop coordinates, and set \(W_d=ze_1\). The ELU activation used by the released configuration fixes 0 and 1, so all directed scores are \(\sigma(z)\) and the symmetry penalty is zero. The two objectives reduce to \[L_{\rm paper}(p)=\log p+\log(1-p),\qquad
L_{\rm BCE}(p)=-\log p-\log(1-p).\] At \(p=1/2\) their values are \(-1.38629436\) and \(1.38629436\); at \(p=0.9\) they are \(-2.40794561\) and \(2.40794561\). Moreover, \[\frac{dL_{\rm paper}}{dz}=1-2p,\qquad
\frac{dL_{\rm BCE}}{dz}=2p-1.\] At \(p=0.9\) the derivatives are \(-0.8\) and \(0.8\): minimization moves the shared logit in opposite directions. The first expression tends to \(-\infty\) at either boundary; the second has its unique shared-probability minimum at \(1/2\). These identities were independently evaluated in `independent_checks.py`; actual output and source excerpts are retained in `verification/0171/independent_checks.json`.
claim: The paper predicts link probabilities \(\widehat A_{ij}\in(0,1)\) using sigmoid outputs. The positive set \(E\) contains original edges; \(E_{\rm inject}\) contains sampled nonedges. These roles are explicit in Section 5.1 and in the training code. Bidirectional predictions are averaged; a symmetry penalty compares the two directions. The iteration in Equation (12) is \[A^{t+1}=(1-\alpha)A^t+\alpha f_\theta(A^t,X),\qquad 0<\alpha\leq1.\] If \(f_\theta\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(L<1\), on a closed invariant domain, the relaxed operator has Lipschitz constant at most \(q=1-\alpha(1-L)<1\). This triangle-inequality calculation in Appendix A.2 is valid. On a closed ball about a fixed clean graph \(A_\star\), the conditions \(f_\theta(A_\star)=A_\star\) and uniform contraction throughout that ball imply invariance and linear convergence. Mere local contraction at an initial point does not itself supply invariance. The explanatory fixed-point condition on p. 4 provides a possible intended setting, so this review does not assert a false convergence theorem. The empirical maximum of 100 sampled pairwise ratios in Section 6.2 is a lower bound on the supremum defining a Lipschitz constant, not a certificate of a uniform upper bound. It is evidence for the sampled behavior. Likewise, Theorem 3.1’s maximization decomposition is valid for a fixed partition whose unaffected losses remain constant over the entire perturbation set. A partition defined separately for each candidate graph cannot automatically be pulled outside the maximum. This quantifier issue is recorded as a scope clarification, not an established counterexample or an additional severity-bearing Problem.

Paraphrase: Minimize the sum of positive-edge \(\log(1-p)\) and injected-edge \(\log(p)\), plus symmetry loss.

p in (0,1) from sigmoid. Original edges positive, injected nonedges negative. Equal mean contributions; shared final decoder bias is an admissible parameter restriction. Directional equality makes symmetry penalty zero.

result: For independently adjustable positive and negative scores, minimizing the printed terms pushes each score toward its correct boundary. Thus a claim that every individual gradient has the wrong class direction would be false. The demonstrated discrepancy concerns the objective under parameter sharing. Reversing only the optimization sign or only the edge labels does not make the specifications identical. claim: The paper predicts link probabilities \(\widehat A_{ij}\in(0,1)\) using sigmoid outputs. The positive set \(E\) contains original edges; \(E_{\rm inject}\) contains sampled nonedges. These roles are explicit in Section 5.1 and in the training code. Bidirectional predictions are averaged; a symmetry penalty compares the two directions. The iteration in Equation (12) is \[A^{t+1}=(1-\alpha)A^t+\alpha f_\theta(A^t,X),\qquad 0<\alpha\leq1.\] If \(f_\theta\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(L<1\), on a closed invariant domain, the relaxed operator has Lipschitz constant at most \(q=1-\alpha(1-L)<1\). This triangle-inequality calculation in Appendix A.2 is valid. On a closed ball about a fixed clean graph \(A_\star\), the conditions \(f_\theta(A_\star)=A_\star\) and uniform contraction throughout that ball imply invariance and linear convergence. Mere local contraction at an initial point does not itself supply invariance. The explanatory fixed-point condition on p. 4 provides a possible intended setting, so this review does not assert a false convergence theorem. The empirical maximum of 100 sampled pairwise ratios in Section 6.2 is a lower bound on the supremum defining a Lipschitz constant, not a certificate of a uniform upper bound. It is evidence for the sampled behavior. Likewise, Theorem 3.1’s maximization decomposition is valid for a fixed partition whose unaffected losses remain constant over the entire perturbation set. A partition defined separately for each candidate graph cannot automatically be pulled outside the maximum. This quantifier issue is recorded as a scope clarification, not an established counterexample or an additional severity-bearing Problem.

analysis: Rating: Major. Locations: Figure 2, p. 4; Section 3.3, p. 5, Eqs. (8)–(10); Algorithm 1, p. 6; Table 8, p. 16; `trainers/GL_SVDMSE.py:129–165` and `trainers/GL_SVDMSE_HE.py:131–169`.

The paper specifies a global prompt \(P_g\in\mathbb R^{T_g\times d}\) and a full SVD \(P_g=USV^\top\) with \(V\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\). It selects the last \[d'=\lfloor(1-\rho)d\rfloor\] columns as \(V_2\). Algorithm 1 instead takes the slice \(V[:,d(1-\rho):d]\), retaining approximately \(\rho d\) columns. The release calls `torch.svd(global_ctx)` with its default reduced SVD, then uses `cutoff=int(S.shape[0]*(1-ratio))` and `V[:,cutoff:]`. Thus it counts from \(\min(T_g,d)\) singular directions, not from \(d\) full-SVD directions.

The locally installed primary PyTorch documentation explicitly states `some=True` by default and \(\min(m,n)\) columns in \(V\). A small installed-library shape diagnostic used PyTorch 2.9.0+cu128, with no author import. This checks available-library behavior; it is not asserted to identify the historical training environment.

Use standard dimensions \(T_g=16\), \(d=512\) and \[P=[\operatorname{diag}(16,15,\ldots,1)\mid0_{16\times496}].\] This is an allowed real global prompt, with rank 16 and nullity 496. Its nonzero singular values are distinct; \(V=I_{512}\) is a valid full right basis and the reduced basis is \((e_1,\ldots,e_{16})\).
At the default \(\rho=4/5\):
- Eq. (9) selects the last 102 full-basis columns; \(Q\) has rank 102 and \(PQ=0\).
- Algorithm 1 starts at index 102 under floor indexing and keeps 410 columns, also with \(PQ=0\) on this example. A ceiling convention changes this count to 409, not to 102.

- The release cuts the 16 reduced directions at index 3 and keeps \(e_4,\ldots,e_{16}\). Its rank-13 projector lies in the global row space and \[\|PQ_{\rm release}\|_F^{2}=1^{2}+\cdots+13^{2}=819,
 \quad \|PQ_{\rm release}\|_F\approx28.618176.\]
A local prompt row \(p=e_{16}^{\top}\) is preserved by the released projector and annihilated by both full-basis alternatives. It can be repeated to any legal local prompt length.

At \(\rho=1\), explicitly tested in Table 8, rounding ambiguity disappears: \[Q_{\rm equation}=0,\qquad Q_{\rm Algorithm\,1}=I_{512},\qquad
 Q_{\rm release}=\text{projector onto the row space of }P.\] The latter two give \(PQ=P\ne0\), with \(\|P\|_F=\sqrt{1496}\approx38.678159\). More generally, Algorithm 1 returns the identity for every nonzero \(P\) at this setting; its range cannot lie in \(\ker P\). The equation and pseudocode thus prescribe opposite operations at a legal evaluated parameter.

These identities were checked analytically and with independent reviewer calculations. The independent check recomputed all ranks, squared norms and boundary cases; no learned-prompt distribution or benchmark execution is needed to refute the general construction claim.

If an exact null-space projector is intended, let \(V_r\) contain right singular vectors for nonzero singular values. Then \[Q_{\rm null}=I_d-V_rV_r^\top,\quad
 Q_{\rm null}^{2}=Q_{\rm null}=Q_{\rm null}^\top,\quad
 PQ_{\rm null}=0.\] This fixes the linear-algebra property. It does not preserve an arbitrary selected null-subspace dimension or settle differentiation/rank-tolerance choices and empirical behavior. If an approximate row-space filter is intended, it should instead be named and specified consistently with its \(\rho\) semantics. Merely requesting a full SVD is insufficient while the cutoffs disagree. No corrected FedPHA model was trained or certified.

analysis: Rating: Minor, pinned-release scope. Locations: `GL_SVDMSE_HE.py:47--56,103--127,178--205,259--270,284--302`; heterogeneous sequence construction, p. 5, Eq. (7).

Token IDs are created using the maximum prompt length \(T_{\max}\) and retained. The text encoder pools at `tokenized_prompts.argmax`, the EOS position in that maximum-length tokenization. The embedded sequence, however, concatenates the common prefix, a shorter learned context, and the shared suffix. EOS moves earlier by \(T_{\max}-T_i\), and zero-padding is appended only at the end. The pooling IDs are not adjusted.

For a class name with one token and a punctuation token, \(T_{\max}=32\) gives fixed zero-based pooling index 35. A length-four context has actual EOS at index 7; a length-16 context at index 19. Both are still pooled at index 35. Only length 32 has matching EOS and pooling positions. Other class-token lengths change the absolute indices but not the displacement.

This is a deterministic sequence-bookkeeping discrepancy, independently reconstructed without executing CLIP. A later padding-position hidden state may still attend to preceding content, so it is not evidence of an empty representation or a measured accuracy loss. A deliberate shared readout position is another possible design, but it would need a consistent description rather than mismatched token and embedding sequences. Historical experimental impact remains Needs Evidence. Updating each pooling index consistently is a local implementation correction, not a validated method repair.
