analysis: Judgment: Needs Evidence / inferential scope qualification.
Consider seven token representations at each layer i. For tokens A and B set a_A = a_B = 2; for each other token set a_x = 1/2. Let

Code:
u(i,x) = (a_x, z(i,x)), with -1 <= z(i,x) <= 1.
score(i,x,y) = u(i,x) dot u(i,y), for distinct x and y.

Every A–B score is 4 + z(i,A)z(i,B), hence at least 3. For a pair containing exactly one of A/B, the score is at most 1 + 1 = 2. For a pair containing neither, it is at most 1/4 + 1 = 1.25. Thus the selected distinct pair is always A–B, strictly and without a tie.

A changing finite search state can be encoded by distinct bounded values of z(i,C) for another token C, with downstream computation reading that coordinate and ignoring the fixed first coordinate. For example, three successive states can be assigned 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3. Each layer may still correspond to one search step, while the observed maximum pair never changes. The decoder reports a constant pair; the encoded state changes.

This construction satisfies the stated raw-inner-product definition, bounded finite representations, and a layerwise state progression. It grants exclusion of self-pairs, which is favorable to the decoder. It is an abstract countermodel to an unrestricted proxy-to-state implication, not a construction of the inspected pretrained Llama weights and not a refutation of the authors’ explicitly conditional assumption. No assumption that the model must place algorithmic state in its dominant similarity component has been established.

An independent finite check evaluated all 3^7 = 2,187 assignments with z in {-1, 0, 1}. The minimum A–B score was 3, the maximum competing score 2, and the minimum margin 1. The inequalities above establish the continuous case; the grid is only a check on their implementation.

A separate attention boundary follows from the standard head output A V, where A = softmax(Q K-transpose / sqrt(d_k)). [R5, Eq. 1, p. 4] Setting a head’s value output to zero makes its contribution zero for every attention pattern permitted by its queries, keys, and mask. Such heads can influence an unweighted attention average without contributing to the answer. Multi-head output projection further separates attention weight from causal contribution. This does not imply that the actual models contain such zero-value heads.
claim: Section 4, p. 6, assumes a layer-to-search-step correspondence. Section 4.2, p. 7, selects the node pair with greatest representation inner product at each layer and compares that sequence with BFS/DFS rollouts. Figure 2, p. 6, labels the comparison as hypothesis rejection. The interpretation on p. 8 extends the attention observations toward absence of exhaustive search or a full world model. [R1]

The missing link is necessity: if a model implemented a particular search procedure, must the chosen maximum-inner-product pair or attention summary reveal its state? A mismatch rejects the procedure together with its assumed observable encoding. It cannot separately reject every implementation of the procedure.
result: The paper is substantially more cautious than a universal exclusion theorem: p. 6 states the correspondence as an assumption; p. 7 calls the sequence possible; p. 8 uses tentative interpretation and requests further mechanism verification; p. 5 includes causal intervention in the proposed framework. Figure 6 also treats geometric changes as a candidate signature. These qualifications preserve a useful exploratory case study. The cited attention literature likewise does not justify a blanket claim that attention can never explain a model. [R6]

The defensible conclusion is that the extracted sequences show poor agreement with the tested rollouts under the chosen decoder. A stronger exclusion requires validated state decoding or causal evidence, with sensitivity to representations, token occurrences, layer grouping, stopping rules, and candidate implementations. Positive controls with known algorithms and tests of value/output contributions would help distinguish the possibilities; none was performed in this review.
Limits case-study mechanism inference; central research program unaffected.

claim: Section 4.1, p. 7, counts 14 layers favoring the correct pathway and three favoring the incorrect pathway. Appendix A.1, p. 20, describes Bonferroni correction over layer tests but does not explicitly give sidedness, alpha, or separate directional families. [R1]

Let T have Student’s t distribution with 31 degrees of freedom. Recomputing P(T >= abs(t)) from each printed statistic approximately reproduces the Tables 2–3 p-values, allowing for rounded t values. This is a one-sided tail in the observed direction. For a single two-sided family of 32 layers at an explicitly assumed alpha = .05, the required raw two-sided threshold is .05/32 = .0015625; the two-sided p is twice that tail.
Layer and direction | Printed t; df | Recomputed one-tail p | Two-sided p | Bonferroni 32 adjusted p

These two layers do not pass that two-sided family criterion. Every other listed layer does. Among the published significant layers, the resulting counts are 13 positive and two negative. This is not a reanalysis of omitted layers or a claim that the paper specified the assumed test family.

For a symmetric null, selecting the one-sided tail after observing the sign covers both tails. Controlling a combined family requires accounting for both directions. Equivalently, the two-sided 32-test calculation uses a one-tail threshold .05/64. Bonferroni does not require independence, although the validity of each original t-test still depends on its sampling/model assumptions.
analysis: Judgment: Needs Evidence, with a fully specified conditional recalculation.

Two separately prespecified directional families could justify a 32-test correction within each family. This would not by itself provide a single .05 bound for their union. The published description does not resolve the intended claim, so the reviewer cannot infer the authors’ prior decisions or declare the 14/3 result unconditionally false. The original observation unit, pairing, full p-value vector, and handling of dependence also require the underlying data and analysis specification.

Table 1 is consistent at the level that can be checked: t = 4.51, df = 2015 yields two-sided p = 6.85561e-6, agreeing with the rounded 7.0e-6. The displayed coefficient .33 and SE .07 need not divide to exactly 4.51 because they are rounded; their rounding intervals permit ratios from about 4.33 to 5.15. No extra error is inferred from that ratio.

Defensible resolution: disclose the planned hypotheses, sidedness, alpha, family definition, analysis unit, and raw/adjusted p-values. If the intended claim is one two-sided 32-layer family at .05, the conditional changes above follow from the printed statistics. If separate directional families were intended, describe them and limit the associated error-control statement.
result: Two marginal classifications depend on family; aggregate-model tail consistent; algorithm identification still unproven.

claim: The p. 10 emission-efficiency paragraph presents half a liter of cooling water and gasoline-equivalent emissions for one interaction, then compares projected global water use with UK consumption, citing Li et al. (2025). [R1]

A defensible local revision is to preserve the source’s response count and combined operational-water scope, explicitly distinguish withdrawal from consumption, and remove or separately substantiate the gasoline-equivalent number with a workload-specific calculation. analysis: Minor; high confidence. The final sentence of Appendix C, p. 19, says the binary evals attain the specified correlation rho; p. 20 describes an example with marginal accuracies 0.6 and 0.9 and rho=0.7. Thresholding correlated Gaussians preserves the stated Bernoulli marginals, but generally changes Pearson correlation. Writing Phi2 for the bivariate standard-normal CDF, the induced correlation is:
> Corr(Y_A,Y_B) = [Phi2(Phi^-1(theta_A),Phi^-1(theta_B);rho) - theta_A theta_B] / sqrt[theta_A(1-theta_A) theta_B(1-theta_B)].

For theta_A=theta_B=1/2 and latent rho=1/2, the binary correlation is (2/pi)arcsin(1/2)=1/3. More decisively, the paper’s 0.6 and 0.9 Bernoulli marginals permit correlation at most [0.6-0.54]/sqrt(0.6*0.4*0.9*0.1)=0.408248, so binary correlation 0.7 is impossible. Independent quadrature gives approximately 0.339587 for that latent model.

claim: Extra normalization in the importance estimator.
analysis: Minor; high confidence. Appendix E, p. 21, Eq. (55) defines normalized weights w_hat[k] = w[k]/sum_i w[i], which sum to one. Equation (60) then places a further factor 1/K outside the weighted sum. The correct self-normalized estimate is:
> E_hat[theta | Y] = sum_k theta[k] w_hat[k] (no additional 1/K).

Complete witness: with a uniform Bernoulli prior, one success and one failure, take proposal values 1/4 and 3/4. Both likelihoods equal 3/16, so normalized weights are 1/2 and 1/2. The corrected weighted estimate is 1/2, also the exact Beta(2,2) posterior mean. The printed Eq. (60) returns 1/4. For proposals in [0,1], the printed estimate is bounded by 1/K and therefore cannot consistently estimate a positive posterior mean as K grows.
result: Written expectation derivation incorrect; resampling code normalizes once and does not establish corrupted coverage.

analysis: Minor; high confidence in code behavior, conditional attribution to the published run. Section 3.2 and Figure 3 (pp. 5–6) target the global theta in Eq. (8), with cluster probabilities drawn around theta. In no_clt_paper, eval_lib/src/intervals_clustered.py, bootstrap_subtask_confidence_interval (lines 120–200, especially 159–176 and 191), the algorithm resamples observations within each existing cluster and averages the cluster means. A fixed-cluster conditional target would be a possible alternative interpretation, but Eq. (8) explicitly targets a global mean over random clusters. analysis: Source claim and location. Appendix D.2.3, p. 50, in the boxed Verus example, identifies failure to preserve the original ring-buffer elements as an omitted postcondition. The same box displays the branch-sensitive whole-sequence relation below. The source page was visually inspected. [E1, E5-E6]

Complete analytic check. Let q be the old logical sequence, q’ the post-state sequence, and n the length of q. If ret is true, the displayed clause gives q’ = q.push(val). By the indexed definition of sequence append, q’[i] = q[i] for every integer i with 0 <= i < n; q’ has length n+1 and its last element is val. If ret is false, the clause gives q’ = q, so every previous element is again retained. These are the only two Boolean branches. Thus the exact omission alleged in the prose is already excluded by the displayed postcondition.

\[\forall\,i\in\mathbb{Z},\quad 0\le i<|q|\ \Longrightarrow\ q'_i=q_i.\] Assumptions and independent source check. In the linked prepublication implementation, View for RingBuffer<T> has V = Seq<T>; its view enumerates the stored elements from head to tail modulo capacity. The inspected implementation also writes preservation as an explicit indexed equality in its enqueue contract. The two formulations agree on this property. This is a semantic argument about the printed contract, not a claim that the printed implementation was mechanically verified, or that all necessary preconditions are printed in the box.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. A different, unfaithful view abstraction could make a postcondition irrelevant to physical contents; the linked view explicitly maps to the active stored elements, so that escape does not explain this example. A client using only a weaker trait-level contract may know less, but that is different from the concrete contract shown in the paper. The box could still omit other requirements, including a particular capacity policy; this review does not assert complete specification adequacy. The precise preservation accusation fails.

Impact and repair status. The example does not demonstrate the stated autoformalization failure. This is a local defect in evidence supporting D.2.3’s recommendation to refine specifications interactively. No downstream theorem or quantitative result depends on the alleged omission, and the separate argument that formal specifications can fail to capture intent is not contradicted. Remove or replace this example, or explicitly discuss a genuinely missing property. The preservation implication is analytically verified; a replacement example and its model provenance are not verified. Supported judgment: Minor.

claim: Issue #14181 introduces an input format; writing is implicit and models only implement reading.
analysis: Source claim and location. Appendix C.3, p. 38, in the serializer-deserializer box, describes astropy #14181 as requesting a new reStructuredText input format, treats writing as an implicit requirement, and reports that models implemented only reading. The source page was visually inspected. [E1, E3-E4]

Complete source comparison. The primary issue is titled ’Please support header rows in RestructuredText output’. Its reproducer first successfully calls tbl.write with format=’ascii.rst’, then requests header_rows for that same output format. The failure is an unexpected header_rows argument. Output is therefore explicit, and basic support for the format already exists. This does not match either the claimed input direction or the claimed introduction of a new format.

PR #14182 strengthens and limits the conclusion. Its patch adds configurable header rows and adjusts both read and write paths, with a round-trip test. Consequently the example may have a repairable directional reversal: reading may be the implicit companion to an explicitly requested writing feature. That possibility is counterevidence to any claim that the broad serializer-deserializer principle itself fails.

Unresolved model provenance. The issue and human-authored PR establish what was requested and repaired. They do not identify the exact model, prompt, patch or evaluation run underlying the paper’s behavioral allegation. This review does not infer whether a published model implemented only read, only write, or both. A mistaken issue identifier or reversed narration could explain the discrepancy, but neither is demonstrated.

Impact and precise supported correction. Correct the description to an explicit request for header-row support in an existing reStructuredText output writer. That textual correction is supported by the primary issue. It does not by itself restore the alleged model-failure example; that requires the actual evaluation patch and a faithful comparison with the request. The existing narration cannot support an inference about missing implicit writing behavior. This bounded evidentiary defect is Minor; the unverified model behavior remains Needs Evidence and does not raise the paper’s supported severity.

analysis: Source claim and location. Section 2.1 and Figure 2, p3, use the equally weighted mixture of Bernoulli parameters zero and one as the first central contrast: disagreement/MI is maximal, while the cited Wimmer axiomatic view is asserted to yield approximately zero EU. The proposed explanation is that only two models remain possible. The questionable step is treating this intuition as a consequence of the cited axioms.

Primary-source check. Wimmer et al., UAI 2023, printed p2285 (PDF p4), A2 makes the uniform distribution on the simplex a global EU maximum. A3 requires a mean-preserving spread not to decrease EU, with a strict alternative also stated. Footnote 3 defines the spread through conditional mean-zero noise. A1 applies to a single Dirac measure; an endpoint mixture is not a single Dirac measure.

\[U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],\quad B\mid U=u\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(u),\quad Q_B=\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\delta_1.\qquad \mathbb E[B-U\mid U=u]=0.\] Complete assumption check. Both distributions are valid distributions over the binary probability simplex, represented by the scalar Bernoulli parameter. Integrating P(B=1|U=u)=u gives P(B=1)=1/2. Both means are 1/2. Setting Z=B-U supplies exactly the conditional mean-zero noise required by the source definition, so \(Q_B\) is a mean-preserving spread of \(Q_U\), with no approximation or limit involved.

\[\mathrm{EU}(Q_B)\geq\mathrm{EU}(Q_U)\geq\mathrm{EU}(Q_B),\qquad \mathrm{EU}(Q_B)=\mathrm{EU}(Q_U)=\max_Q\mathrm{EU}(Q).\] Under the strict A3 reading, this nontrivial spread instead exposes incompatibility with A2 on the same pair. Neither reading gives the nontrivial near-zero value asserted in the reviewed paper. This argument does not claim to construct a functional satisfying an inconsistent full axiom set, and does not use inconsistency to infer arbitrary conclusions.

Independent finite/numerical checks confirm MI(\(Q_B\))=1 bit and MI(\(Q_U\))=1-1/(2 ln 2), approximately 0.27865248 bits; variances of the parameter distributions are 1/4 and 1/12. These checks illustrate the example; the conditional coupling above is the decisive proof.

Alternative reading and counterevidence. Wimmer’s p2286 discussion does support the intuition that knowing the parameter is an endpoint can convey more knowledge than a uniform distribution does. The philosophical tension about knowledge and disagreement is real. It does not establish the reviewed paper’s stronger zero-versus-maximum claim as an axiomatic necessity.

Impact and correction scope. This invalidates the first central technical demonstration used to motivate reassessment, warranting Major. It leaves open independent conceptual disagreements and all empirical questions about useful uncertainty for agents. A defensible revision must remove the purported axiomatic near-zero implication or provide an explicitly specified measure with verified assumptions. No replacement axiom system is claimed to have been repaired or validated. Evidence: independent_math_memo.json, independent_math_checks.py/results.json, and the archived Wimmer PDF and p2285 image.

Converts number-of-remaining-models intuition into a consequence of Wimmer A2/A3. Wimmer discusses knowledge-versus-disagreement intuition, but does not derive near-zero. No claim to construct metric satisfying inconsistent full axioms.

Binary probability simplex; bothQ valid; \(Q_U\) uniform; \(Q_B\) equal endpoints; mean-preserving spread defined by conditional mean-zero noise.

claim: Bengs infinite-data requirement forces modelbias to be AU.
analysis: Source claim and location. Section 2.2, p4, contrasts a restricted model class with a richer data-generating mechanism. It then invokes Bengs et al.’s infinite-sample requirement as a corollary forcing remaining model bias out of EU and into AU. Figure 3 and the theoretical framing make this an evidentiary step in the second principal example, not just an unrelated terminology aside.

Actual cited requirement. Bengs et al., NeurIPS 2022, p8, Section 4, Definition 1(A2), considers iid categorical observations with true probability parameter theta*. It requires the learned second-order distribution \(Q_N\) to converge in probability to the Dirac measure at theta*. The original simplex contains the true parameter. This is a consistency requirement used to assess second-order loss functions, not a universal theorem that reclassifies arbitrary model misspecification.

\[Y_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.8),\quad \Theta_{\mathcal H}=\{0.5\}\ \Longrightarrow\ Q_N=\delta_{0.5}\ \forall N.\qquad \int\theta\,dQ_N=0.5\ne0.8=\int\theta\,d\delta_{0.8}.\] This is an applicability check, not a counterexample purporting to satisfy Bengs A2. The fixed test-function gap proves the restricted sequence cannot converge to the required true-parameter target. Moving the target to the best approximation would define a different requirement and must be stated. Failure to express the truth does not itself imply that residual model bias must be labeled AU.

Counterevidence and faithful terminology. Hullermeier and Waegeman do call the risk minimizer within a hypothesis class a Bayes predictor; that phrase alone is not an error. Their discussion distinguishes it from the pointwise Bayes predictor, groups model and approximation uncertainty with EU, and assumes correct specification when setting model uncertainty aside. Schweighofer et al., arXiv:2410.10786v1, pp2-3, genuinely offer an alternative selected-model entropy definition of AU. The reviewed quotation is accurate. That source also retains a selected-versus-true KL term, and its setup states representability of the true predictive distribution.

Impact. Legitimate differences between uncertainty conventions therefore survive. What fails is the specific argument that the cited consistency axiom forces misspecification bias to be AU. The inference is central to the paper’s second theoretical example and thus supports Major under the task’s core-derivation standard. This judgment does not assert that all of Section 2.2, Table 1, or the proposed agent agenda is false.

analysis: Locations: Section 3.2, Eqs. (8)-(14), p.4; combined coefficient, Eqs. (15)-(16), pp.4-5; Algorithm 1, p.14. Algorithm 1 initializes both policy and reference to the same SFT model. Equation (8) defines a beta-scaled policy/reference log-ratio gap. The text following Eq. (14) explicitly initializes its running mean to zero. Equation (9) divides every gap by that mean, and Algorithm 1 calls Eqs. (9)-(11) before its first gradient or running-state update.

Exact witness satisfying the operative setup: use N=16, K=12, beta=0.1 and momentum gamma=0.9, as in the reported configuration. For each batch item, let both identical models assign preferred-response probability 1/4 and rejected-response probability 1/8, with the remaining 5/8 assigned to other responses. These are normalized distributions with positive probabilities and finite log ratios. A finite data-aware factor, including alpha_D=1, is allowed. Every reward gap is exactly zero; the initial running mean is exactly zero. The required normalized gaps are therefore 0/0.

Consequently the distance mask, selected-batch statistic, model-aware factor and combined beta are not defined by the printed procedure at the first update. The later EMA update cannot resolve a value already needed to compute that update. This is not a counterexample using an inadmissible distribution, a zero response probability or an unmentioned asymptotic regime.

The severity follows the role of the missing definition: the model-aware factor is one of the two principal contributions and is required to operate the training rule. A first-step convention and the actual estimator must be specified to make that contribution reproducible. No convergence or universal-performance theorem is invented or challenged here; the demonstrated failure is in the central algorithm as written.
\[\pi_\theta=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}=\pi_{\mathrm{SFT}}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad R_i=\beta[\log 1-\log 1]=0,\qquad \bar R_0=0,\qquad \widetilde R_i=\frac{0}{0}.\]

Equation (10) retains distances no greater than the K-th smallest distance. With distinct distances it retains K items, as also labeled in Figure 3. Equation (11), however, divides their sum by N-K. At N=16 and K=12, that is a division by four instead of twelve.

A separate positive-state arithmetic check sets Rbar=1 and normalized gaps \(r_i\)=0.80+0.01i for i=1,...,16. All distances from one are distinct, so the mask retains indices 5,...,16. Their sum is 10.86: the actual retained mean is 0.905, while Eq. (11) gives 2.715. With gamma=0.9 the next state is 0.9905 for the retained mean but 1.1715 for the printed statistic. This checks Eq. (11) on a finite input; it does not claim that the undefined first-step algorithm reaches this state.

Replacing the denominator by the actual retained count verifies the mean for a fixed mask. Ties at the K-th distance can retain more than K examples, so exact cardinality also requires a tie rule. The retained-count error supports Major within Problem 1 on its own core dependency: the incorrect statistic enters the model-aware sigmoid factor in Eq. (12), the combined training coefficient in Eqs. (15)-(16), and the next running state in Eq. (14). The finite positive-state witness therefore changes the central update, not just a displayed label. The simplicity of the denominator repair does not make this defect peripheral. It remains grouped with the startup failure as one method-specification finding, without asserting that the undefined startup reaches the diagnostic state.
A denominator correction alone does not define the zero-state normalization, decide which gap scale the EMA tracks, or reconcile the different selection and sigmoid-aggregation rules in the release.
\[\sum_i M_i r_i=\frac{543}{50},\qquad \frac{\sum_i M_i r_i}{N-K}=\frac{543}{200},\qquad \frac{\sum_i M_i r_i}{\sum_i M_i}=\frac{181}{200}.\]

The active source is sources/0080/DAMA/DAMA/llava/train/train_dpo.py, especially lines 1220-1291, 1343-1349 and 1361-1391. It constructs detached raw log-ratio gaps A, without the paper’s multiplication by beta and division by the running mean. analysis: Claim and dependency. Lemma 1 in Section 4.4, p. 5, asserts an exclusivity relation between sparse, concentrated attention and consistent low-precision robustness. Appendix A, p. 16, Eqs. (5)–(6), is its proof. Case 2 drops every non-dominant term because \(e^{z_j-z_i}\) is small, even though that term is multiplied by \(e^{\delta_j-\delta_i}\). This theoretical explanation is advertised in the abstract and introduction and used to interpret sensitive layers in Sections 4.4–4.5 and Appendix E. No bound on \(u\), on the projected errors, or on their size relative to logit margins is supplied.

A finite counterexample to the actual quantization argument. Use two keys in dimension three, per-token asymmetric quantization with \(B=2\), and \[K_1=(0.49,0,1),\quad K_2=(0.48,0,1.2),\quad u=(1000,0,0).\] These groups have positive ranges and no rounding ties. The original query in Eq. (1) can be \(q=\sqrt3\,u\), so the scale convention causes no discrepancy. The two group scales are \(1/3\) and \(0.4\). Thus \[\widehat K_1=(1/3,0,1),\qquad \widehat K_2=(0.4,0,1.2).\] The original logit margin is \(490-480=10\), whereas the quantized margin is \(1000(1/3-0.4)=-200/3\). Consequently \[a_1=0.9999546021313,\qquad
 \widehat a_1=1.11438315784\times10^{-29},
 \quad \operatorname{TV}(a,\widehat a)=0.9999546021313.\] The initial attention is extremely concentrated, but the quantized distribution is almost reversed. All coordinates and errors are finite. Replacing 1000 by \(c\to\infty\) makes the original attention arbitrarily concentrated while the quantized attention converges to the other token. This is not a rounding-level discrepancy. Values such as \(V_1=(0,0,1)\), \(V_2=(1,0,0)\) are exactly representable by the same per-token rule and transmit the attention reversal to the output. This construction is an attention-level counterexample, not a claim that these exact activations occurred in a tested LLM.

The Gaussian assumption does not rescue the derivation. Appendix A also models coordinate errors as Gaussian with \(\sigma=(\max K-\min K)/(2^B-1)\). This is an additional stochastic model, not the distributional law of deterministic rounding. Even granting independent Gaussian coordinates, take \(K_1=(0.001,0)\), \(K_2=(0,1)\), \(u=(10000,0)\), \(B=2\), and \(\sigma=1/3\). Again \(a_1=0.9999546\). Now the noisy margin is \[10+Z,\qquad Z\sim N(0,2(10000/3)^{2}).\] Its probability of reversing sign is \[\Phi\!\left(-\frac{10}{\sqrt2(10000/3)}\right)=0.4991537163.\] Thus even a natural interpretation of the appendix’s own noise assumption gives almost one-half probability of overturning the dominant token. The two examples test separate interpretations and are not conflated.

Necessity, alternatives, and scope. For finite logits, equality of the entire two softmax distributions holds exactly if and only if every \(\delta_j\) is the same: compare their pairwise probability ratios. The paper acknowledges this as Case 1 but dismisses it as atypical without an assumption that excludes it. For instance, \(K_j=(x_j,0,1)\), \(0<x_j<1\), and \(u=(0,0,1)\) give a uniform, non-concentrated distribution that is preserved exactly for every such \(x_j\) and every positive integer bit width, although the first coordinates may have nonzero rounding errors. This is a whole family with a nonzero query, not only \(q=0\).

A fixed, bounded perturbation becomes harmless when a margin tends to infinity. That restricted reading is correct; it is precisely the missing condition. Empirical correlations in Figures 4 and 11–19 may still hold for the measured models. They do not prove the exclusive or general robustness statement. The finding is Major because the paper’s central theoretical explanation is invalid as derived, without requiring a failure of its entire search framework or a lower benchmark score.

Verified correction bound. If \(z_i-z_j\ge m\) and \(\delta_j-\delta_i\le\rho\) for every \(j\ne i\), then (1.1) gives \[\widehat a_i\ge \frac{1}{1+(S-1)e^{-m+\rho}}. \tag{2.1}\] Each denominator ratio is at most \(e^{-m+\rho}\), proving the bound directly. The sufficient condition must therefore compare the margin with projected error and sequence length. With \(|\delta_j|\le\eta\), one may use \(\rho=2\eta\). This repairs a conditional single-head statement only; it proves neither prompt-independent layer sensitivity nor full-model accuracy preservation. Targeted inspection of arXiv v5, dated 20 November 2025, found the same Lemma 1 and Case 2 approximation still present [later]; no full-version diff or author correction is asserted.

paragraphs: With original margin >=m and pairwise projected error differences <=rho, \(\widehat a_i\ge1/(1+(S-1)\exp(-m+\rho))\). Bound proved; only conditional single-head guarantee, no full-model or prompt-independent result.

analysis: Location and assumptions. Section 5.3 and Appendix D.1.2 group layers to define one precision pair per layer. In the supplied `search_optuna_adaptive.py`, lines 37–43, the Qwen2.5-14B per-channel configuration repeats layer 25, and the Qwen2.5-32B per-channel configuration repeats layers 22, 24, and 25. The independent static audit checks all twelve model/mode combinations; these are the two failures.

For the 14B setting, 49 memberships are used for 48 distinct layers. Lines 218–228 construct a dictionary that overwrites a repeated layer, but accumulate bit cost over every membership and divide by \(2L\). If every group uses KV4, the actual dictionary assigns four nominal bits per element while the returned objective is \[\frac{49(4+4)}{2\cdot48}=4.083333\ldots.\] Thus even the uniform configuration’s reported objective and constraint value are wrong.

For the 32B setting, the group at zero-based index 2 contains 22, 24, and 25 outside its designated special candidate set. Assuming required dependencies are available, the explicit consistency condition at lines 176–185 raises `ValueError` before the search starts. This is a static control-flow deduction, not an executed author program.

Impact and correction bounds. These defects obstruct or mismeasure the released extensions to these settings. They do not establish that the main 3B/7B/8B results used these groups, and they do not invalidate the separately reported uniform-precision 14B/32B measurements. That limited impact supports Minor. For 32B, removing 22, 24, and 25 from group index 2 yields a complete disjoint 64-layer partition compatible with the supplied special sets; this exact data-level repair was checked. For any setting, computing the nominal bit sum from the final distinct-layer mapping avoids double counting, but the grouping still must be made unambiguous. No corrected search performance has been verified.
result: Local reproducibility and nominal memory objective affected, not a general algorithm impossibility.

 \tag{1.1}\] Section 3.2, Eq. (2), quantizes each selected group by \[\widehat x=z+s\,\operatorname{round}((x-z)/s),\qquad
 z=\min x,\quad s=(\max x-\min x)/(2^B-1).
 \tag{1.2}\] The method searches layer precision pairs using calibration accuracy and average nominal bit width, then reuses the chosen configuration online. The arithmetic mean bit objective is appropriate as a nominal payload measure when the layers have equal KV tensor sizes; it is not itself an accounting of metadata, residual tokens, packing, or peak allocations.

analysis: Claim and source. Section 5.3, p. 7, and Appendix E.1, p. 23, emphasize applying quantized KV during prefilling. In `flexible_quant/flexible_quant/flexible_quantized_cache.py`, lines 173–190, the `force_quant=True` path with nonzero residual length \(R\) computes \(r=S\bmod R\), passes the slice `:-r` for quantization, and retains `-r:` at full precision.

For \(S=64,R=32\), \(r=0\). Python’s `:-0` is empty and `-0:` is the entire sequence. Hence this path sends zero tokens to quantization and retains all 64, rather than quantizing the complete prefix and retaining an empty suffix. If a backend rejects the empty input, it can fail earlier; that runtime outcome was not tested. The source-level slice defect is independent of such backend behavior.

Alternatives, impact, and bounded repair. The defect is confined to this flag and boundary condition, and does not occur for the same reason when \(r>0\) or \(R=0\). The released search file itself sets `force_quant=False`; its historical relation to the prefilling-enabled paper runs is unresolved. Therefore no numerical table damage is asserted, and the supported severity is Minor. Computing \(c=S-r\), using prefix `:c` and suffix `c:`, restores the intended partition at this boundary. Only the slicing identity is verified; backend empty-input handling and complete inference behavior require separate evidence.
result: Localized implementation defect; no numerical historical table damage demonstrated.

analysis:
Section 6, Q1 (p. 7), interprets Fig. 8 as having vector directions toward CEC or CEC-Finetune in both task settings and uses this as evidence of robust cross-algorithm generalization. Appendix A.8 (p. 19) identifies Fig. 21 as the original-task payoff matrix. With order IPPO, E3T, FCP, CEC, CEC-FT, that matrix is \[A=\begin{pmatrix}
 .51&.29&.77&.47&.49\\
 .29&.43&.41&.38&.33\\
 .77&.41&.55&.58&.71\\
 .47&.38&.58&.61&.67\\
 .49&.33&.71&.67&.78
 \end{pmatrix}.\] On the IPPO–FCP edge, putting IPPO mass \(p\) gives payoffs \(.77-.26p\) and \(.55+.22p\). They agree at \(p=11/24\), so \[x^*=(11/24,0,13/24,0,0),\qquad x^{*\top}Ax^*=781/1200.\] The E3T, CEC, and CEC-FT payoffs are \(71/200\), \(1271/2400\), and \(731/1200\), respectively. Their invasion growth rates in the displayed formula are \[-71/240,\qquad -97/800,\qquad -1/24,\] all strictly negative. The tangent eigenvalue on the IPPO–FCP edge is \(-143/1200<0\). Thus \(x^*\) is locally asymptotically stable, including against small positive invasions by every excluded strategy. It is not merely a zero-mass absorbing boundary point.

The conclusion is robust to independent symmetric rounding errors of at most \(.005\) per displayed payoff. The perturbed edge equilibrium has \(p\in[.42,.50]\). Its resident payoff is at least \(.635\), while CEC-FT’s payoff there is at most \(.6226\), and CEC’s is at most \(.5388\). The negative invasion margins persist. This rounding bound does not account for empirical sampling uncertainty.

The abstract and contribution 2 (pp. 1–2) advertise solvable coordination challenges. Appendix A.1 (p. 14) claims that making at least one facility of each required type reachable by at least one agent guarantees a solvable task. Algorithm 1 (p. 15) implements that criterion. The missing step is reachability of the material flow from onions to pots: separate access to each facility does not ensure that ingredients can move between the agents’ disconnected walking regions.

Forced Coordination \(5\times5\) wall pattern. two empty-inventory agents at 6 and 8 (zero-based row-major). empty pots. mandatory cells [7,5,3,17] in plate/onion/pot/goal order. additional cells [12,10,9,19]. all 8 placements distinct and permitted. no-rotation/no-flip case; wall padding. held-out set can consist of five canonical tasks, none equal to this layout.
analysis: Use the \(5\times5\) Forced Coordination base with zero-based row-major cell index \(5r+c\). Its free cells are \(\{6,11,16\}\) and \(\{8,13,18\}\). Put agents at 6 and 8. Choose facilities as follows:
Facility | Mandatory cell | Supplemental cell
Plate pile | 7 | 12
Onion pile | 5 | 10
Pot | 3 | 9
Delivery goal | 17 | 19

These are eight distinct wall cells. The mandatory sequence \((7,5,3,17)\) is an admissible ordered selection from the source’s `need_one` set \[\{1,5,10,15,21,17,12,7,3,9,14,19,23\}.\] The supplementary sequence \((12,10,9,19)\) uses distinct remaining wall cells. Agent 6 is an allowed left-side start and agent 8 an allowed right-side start. These facts follow directly from `layouts.py`, lines 815–883; the independent script additionally checks them as finite set statements.

Every facility is reachable by at least one agent. In particular, both onion piles touch the left walking component, both pots touch the right one, the two plate piles touch both components, and the goal at 17 touches both. Take the permitted no-rotation/no-flip choice and pad with walls. Neither operation creates a passage. Empty inventories and empty pots are the ordinary reset setting, explicitly supported by `overcooked.py`, lines 451–455 and 500–508. The arrangement differs from the five canonical held-out tasks, so Algorithm 1 with those tasks as its held-out set accepts it. This is an admissible input to the stated generation procedure; the argument does not assert that this exact task appears in the authors’ additional 100-task sample.

Proof. Let \(L=\{6,11,16\}\) and \(R=\{8,13,18\}\). Walls prevent an agent from moving from \(L\) to \(R\). The only wall cells adjacent to both components are \(\{7,12,17\}\). They contain, respectively, a plate pile, a plate pile, and a goal. None is an empty counter, onion dispenser, or pot.

Initially there is no onion in \(R\), in either pot, or in the right agent’s inventory. An onion can originate only at cells 5 or 10, adjacent solely to \(L\). Movement preserves the component containing its carrier. Dropping an onion across the cut is impossible because all shared cells are permanent piles/goals, and those facilities are not empty counters. No direct transfer between agents exists across a wall. Therefore the stated absence of onions on the right is an invariant of every action sequence. Both pots remain empty, and no completed soup or delivery is reachable, even with an unlimited horizon. ◻

The exact interaction conditions are `table_is_empty` at line 825 and `successful_drop` at line 862 of `overcooked.py`; pile pickup preserves the pile at lines 866–872. The proof is analytic. The reviewer-written script validates the coordinates, permitted selections, walking components, and shared boundary; it does not run or emulate the author’s training code. Its output is `independent_results.json`.
result: A shared pot or shared onion dispenser can make some split layouts solvable without an empty counter. Neither occurs here. Random initial food could also defeat this invariant, but the counterexample uses the supported empty initialization. The rule’s two copies of each facility are present; the example does not exploit missing objects, duplicate placement, or an inaccessible mandatory item.

This is Major because the constructive solvability guarantee is a named core contribution and differentiator from generators permitting impossible tasks. It does not require proving that the average reward changes. The empirical benefit of environmental diversity may survive. The proportion of generated unsolvable tasks and their effects on the published comparisons require new enumeration or experiment records. Individual reachability must be replaced or supplemented by a condition certifying feasible ingredient transfer and delivery; no complete corrected generator is claimed or verified here.
Stated: solvable. unsolvable for every horizon. Invalidates universal solvability guarantee; does not estimate prevalence or overturn measured CEC benefits.

analysis: Claim and location. Appendix B, p. 13, estimates finetuning as about 5% of computation and calls a 12,600-attempt fixed-model search a match to one SOAR improvement cycle: 6,000 attempts before training, 6,000 after, and additional training. Section 3.4, p. 5, specifies three epochs; the pinned trainer defaults to three (lines 112–116).

Conditional calculation. Using the paper’s own dense-model coefficients, equal completion length \(T\), \(D\) selected examples per task, and \(e\) epochs gives \[\frac{C_{\mathrm{train}}}{C_{\mathrm{search},6000}}
 =\frac{6N eDT}{2N\,6000T}=\frac{3eD}{6000}.\] At the permitted upper value \(D=100\) and \(e=3\), training is equivalent to 900 generation attempts, or 15% of one search and 7.5% of two searches. The corresponding total is 12,900, rather than 12,600. This is a consistency diagnostic under explicit assumptions, not a measurement of the actual LoRA training FLOPs.

Counterevidence and bounds. The paper specifies up to 100 examples, so actual \(D\) can be smaller; for example \(D=200/3\) under the simplified accounting would give 600 equivalent attempts. LoRA/QLoRA computation, varying prompt and response lengths, shared prompt processing, and the disclosed early stopping at sufficient visible-example successes also affect costs. The nominal 6,000 attempts are consequently not complete observed token counts. The source-data defect in Problem 1 must not be used to justify a historical training-size assumption.

Thus the current evidence does not establish an exact match, but the diagnostic also does not prove that a corrected fixed-model curve catches SOAR. Provide actual per-stage task counts, selected examples, epochs, processed tokens, cache assumptions, adapter-training cost convention, and cumulative compute across iterations and pooled models. The result remains Needs Evidence for the specific equal-compute assertion; nominal-budget accuracy improvements are a separate reported result.

claim: Location: Sections3.3/4.2 pp4,6; Table2; Section4.5; process_sample_for_training.py36-48,117-134; tuto_expe.md155-167.
Paraphrase: The core greedy-diverse dataset selects up to 25 high-performing and 25 low-performing candidates per task; the released default implements that selection.

Ordinary finite well-formed candidate records reach the selected helper. The pinned source uses an initially empty dictionary whose sole write is guarded by preexisting key membership. Default requested sample count is 50. Historical producing revision is not established.
analysis: Claim and exact source. Sections 3.3 and 4.2 (pp. 4 and 6) define a sampling dataset with up to 25 high-performing and 25 low-performing candidates per task. Table 2 favors that greedy-diverse strategy, and Section 4.5 links retained solution diversity to continued self-improvement. The default released path calls `get_sample_task_greedy_div`; the supplied tutorial calls the corresponding `greedy_div` option (lines 155–167).

In `soar/post_process/process_sample_for_training.py`, lines 36–48, the output-deduplication helper initializes an empty dictionary. Its only insertion is guarded by the condition that the output key is already in that dictionary. There is no alternative branch inserting unseen keys. Lines 117–134 then use the helper’s result to construct the diverse sample.

Decisive argument and assumptions. Assume ordinary finite, well-formed candidate records that reach this function. Initially the dictionary is empty. At every loop iteration, the membership guard is false because no earlier iteration can have inserted a key. By induction the dictionary remains empty, regardless of whether the candidate outputs are distinct or duplicated, and the helper returns an empty list.

Consequently the residual pool at line 118 is empty; all three passes intended to collect low-performing candidates add nothing. With the default request of 50 records, the initial greedy branch can retain at most 25, and the diversity branch contributes zero. The same helper is reached after majority-based greedy selection for test-time data. This is not normal deduplication of a repetitive pool. For a witness pool containing 25 eligible high-performing and 25 distinct eligible low-performing candidates, the promised second half is lost even though all of its inputs exist.

The independent script parses the source as text and verifies the empty initialization, sole guarded write, and absent alternative branch. It does not import the file, execute the helper, load a model, or launch an author pipeline. The semantic invariant itself supplies the decisive proof.

Counterevidence and core impact. An earlier experimental revision may have had a different condition. The released tree includes later demo options, so this finding is not evidence that Table 2 or the 52% run definitely used this defect. Remaining greedy examples can still be unsuccessful on some original tasks and can still support hindsight learning; the finding does not eliminate all synthetic training or all refinement training.

Nevertheless, the inspected default implementation omits an expressly central training-data component and cannot implement the claimed greedy-diverse experiment. That supports Major for the pinned implementation and its reproducibility link to the core contribution. No score degradation is required to demonstrate this control-flow failure, and no unmeasured degradation is claimed.

Correction and verification bounds. Insert unseen output keys, with an explicit first- or last-representative policy. Check that a nonempty unique residual pool survives and that, when enough eligible candidates exist, the intended number is added. This corrects the empty-pool invariant but does not prove a performance improvement or resolve any other selection-policy choices. The original source was preserved; no author-code patch was applied or executed, and historical datasets or ablations were not rerun.
result: The pinned default cannot implement the claimed greedy-diverse data construction; no author function was executed. Major scoped implementation failure of a central contribution and its reproducibility link; no numerical score loss is asserted.

GroupA has 10 programs with accuracy.2; B has 1 with accuracy1; C has 1 with accuracy.8. Five visible examples permit these accuracies. \(c\)=1000 as specified. analysis:
Claim and exact locations. Section 3.2, p. 4, assigns each output pattern the sum of its programs’ visible-example accuracies. Appendix D.1 and Algorithm 1, p. 17, instead use pattern count plus \(c\) times `train_accuracy`. They define the latter as a generated program’s mean accuracy on its training examples, but do not specify how accuracies are combined across different programs sharing a pattern. For the homogeneous groups used below, either a mean or representative-program interpretation gives \[W_{\mathrm{appendix}}(g)=n_g+c\,\overline a_g,\qquad c=1000,\] where \(n_g\) is the pattern count and \(\overline a_g\) is the common example accuracy within that group. Thus the witness does not depend on choosing among unequal program accuracies. The pinned `soar/llm_utils.py`, lines 745–766, adds \(1+c a_i\) for each response, implementing \[W_{\mathrm{release}}(g)=n_g+c\sum_{i\in g}a_i
                       =n_g+c n_g\overline a_g.\] Thus the missing multiplicity factor is not a constant common to all patterns.

Decisive calculation. Consider three valid output groups. Group A has ten programs of accuracy \(0.2\); B has one of accuracy 1; C has one of accuracy \(0.8\). These accuracies are possible with five visible examples. Their scores are \[\begin{array}{c|rrr}
 & A&B&C\\ \hline
\sum_i a_i &2&1&0.8\\
n_g+1000\,\overline a_g &210&1001&801\\
n_g+1000\sum_i a_i &2010&1001&801
\end{array}\] so the appendix selects B and C as its top two, while the main-text and released rules select A and B. This avoids ties and does not depend on unknown test labels. The released rule also differs slightly from a pure accuracy sum because it adds counts; no exact equivalence of those two prescriptions is asserted.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. An intended sum over programs, or a missing count multiplier, could reconcile the appendix with the released aggregation; that convention would need to be stated explicitly. The release is closer to the main-text weighted-frequency explanation. Both choices are legitimate heuristic aggregators; this review does not claim one always predicts better. When counts are equal, or under some special accuracy patterns, they may give the same ordering.

Core dependency and precise impact. Voting chooses the two submitted output patterns and supplies group weights to the test-time data selector (Appendix D.2; source lines 99–104). The discrepancy can therefore alter the reported evaluation algorithm and subsequent learning data. This is Major for the specification of those core pipeline decisions. The example proves a changed top-two set, not an observed error in any historical ARC prediction or a lower corrected score.

State the exact group weight, its aggregation convention, count term, tie rule, and grouping across multiple test inputs. Identify the scorer that produced the published predictions and link it to the search archives. A consistent written rule can be supplied analytically, but numerical impact requires those archives; no revised benchmark score is available here.
result: The written pseudocode and pinned release can implement different evaluation and adaptation decisions. Major core algorithm-specification discrepancy, demonstrated by a changed top-two set; historical numerical impact remains unknown.

analysis: Equation (9), p. 4, does not implement the paired alignment described in Section 2.1.1. The supported assessment is Major for this central mathematical definition.

For any strictly positive probability vector \((p_1,\ldots,p_B)\) summing to one, concavity of the logarithm gives \[-\sum_{k=1}^B\log p_k\geq B\log B,\] with equality exactly at \(p_k=1/B\). Applying this to every row in both directions yields \[L_{\mathrm{align}}\geq B\log B.\] Equal cross-modal similarities attain the bound. In particular, setting all normalized embeddings equal is allowed and is a global minimizer. Independently permuting text examples only permutes entries/rows in the full sums, leaving the objective unchanged. It therefore contains no information about which EEG belongs to which text.

A complete admissible finite example has \(B=2\), \(d=256\), \(\tau=0.3\) and \[\hat e_1=\hat l_1=(1,0,\ldots,0),\qquad
\hat e_2=\hat l_2=(-1,0,\ldots,0).\] All norms are one, all cosine similarities lie in \([-1,1]\), and the correct-pair probability is \(q=(1+\exp(-2/\tau))^{-1}\). the displayed formula gives \[-\log q-\log(1-q)=6.6692103160.\] Setting all four unit vectors equal gives \(2\log2=1.3862943611\), strictly lower. Minimizing the stated objective thus favors losing discrimination rather than retaining the strongly correct pairings in this legal example. Parent calculation output: .

\(B=2\),\(d=256\),unit EEG/text vectors,\(\tau=0.3\). ELMe,l lacks the separate ELMl orthogonal restriction.

\frac{1}{2B}\sum_{j=1}^B
[-\log p_{jj}-\log\widetilde p_{jj}]\] gives \(0.0012718247\) for the aligned example and \(\log2=0.6931471806\) for collapse, restoring the intended distinction in this check. The release’s `models/loss.py`, lines 59–65, instead constructs similarity-derived soft targets for ELM\(_{e,l}\). The defect is not merely an inconsequential symbol: it changes the optimum and removes pair information from a central representation-learning strategy. The MIL extension and other empirical observations may survive independently; no whole-paper failure or empirical score decrease is asserted.

analysis: Equations (10)–(11), p. 4, and the pinned loss implementation apply different objectives to multiple positives.

For an anchor with \(m\geq1\) positive samples \(\mathcal P\) and softmax probabilities \(p_j\), the paper uses \[L_{\mathrm{paper}}
=-\log\left(\frac1m\sum_{j\in\mathcal P}p_j\right).\] In `models/loss.py`, lines 90–100, masked `log_softmax` values are averaged, giving \[L_{\mathrm{release}}=-\frac1m\sum_{j\in\mathcal P}\log p_j.\] The configured MIL training route calls this class (trainer/configuration evidence is bound in verification). \frac{\exp(100a_i)}{\exp(100a_i)+\exp(100b_j)}.\] `generation.py`, lines 101–105, thresholds this statistic. Equal scores give \(0.5\) for every sample count, so that feature is rejected. analysis: The temporal implication underlying the asserted novelty guarantee is invalid. The supported impact is Major for this core benchmark interpretation; actual contamination remains unestablished.

Let \(t_r\) be recognition under the selected taxonomic status, \(t_p\) the first availability of relevant visual or descriptive records, and \(t_c\) the model’s latest training cutoff. The rule requires \(t_r>t_c\). It does not require \(t_p>t_c\). The ordering \[t_p<t_c<t_r\] satisfies the rule while allowing pretraining on an older record, including a photograph captioned with a historical subspecies name. Construct a model whose pre-cutoff training corpus contains that record. Its cutoff and the species’ recognition date meet the stated selection conditions, yet the underlying appearance has been encountered. Section 4 imposes no condition excluding this case.

The paper’s own example illustrates the distinction. The primary study published on 29 January 2024 groups previously recognized subspecies, including L. t. pardinoides and L. t. oncilla, as the clouded tiger cat, using historical museum and photographic material [taxonomy]. Recognition of a grouping is not creation of its underlying visual information. This evidence refutes the claimed implication; it does not identify an image in a particular closed training corpus.
claim: For target and confusing classes \(C_T,C_M\), Section 3.2 defines a sum of pairwise CLIP-score ratios and uses a fixed cutoff of \(0.6\). Section 4 claims that selecting concepts discovered after the latest component-training cutoff guarantees novelty. Formal recognition date, first availability of relevant records, and actual training-corpus membership are distinct quantities.

The abstract and introduction (pp. 1–2), Section 4 (pp. 5–6), and Section 5.1 (p. 6) assert that species selected after a model’s cutoff were never encountered during training. Section 4 offers the date rule specifically as a guarantee despite unavailable corpora. Figure 1 and Section 3.1 motivate the approach with the clouded tiger cat, Leopardus pardinoides.
Recognition date later than cutoff. No earlier-record/synonym exclusion.
result: A task of learning a newly adopted label or taxonomic distinction remains meaningful, as does low-resource adaptation. Those narrower interpretations support useful experiments but cannot provide the advertised unseen-concept guarantee. Conversely, unavailable corpora do not prove contamination.

NovelSpecies is an explicit principal contribution and the central unseen-concept test. The invalid implication thus affects a core interpretation. It does not invalidate the numerical accuracy tables, SUN/iNaturalist results, or the usefulness of CoDA. A supported correction is to describe recently recognized taxa under documented cutoffs and remove the unconditional guarantee. Establishing stricter novelty requires record dates, synonym-aware checks, and training provenance; no such comprehensive audit was performed here.
Universal inference invalid; evaluated-model contamination not demonstrated. Major for guarantee only.

analysis: The passage following Eq. (16), p. 6, identifies its normalized expected denoising error with a score function, then uses this identification to motivate Eq. (17). This derivation is invalid. Assessment: Major for the mathematical rationale of the central flow loss.
claim: The paper writes the total deformation Jacobian as \(J_t=J_t^P+J_t^R\), where \(J_t^P\) is the spatial component and \(J_t^R\) is the temporal correction. Equations (12)–(13), p. 5, use a learned ODE and prescribe \(J_0^R=0\). The auxiliary loss in Eq. (18), p. 6, compares scores associated with the total and spatial-only sequences and adds a squared correction penalty. Equation (19) combines it with video SDS.

For a Gaussian perturbation \(Y=X+n\), \(n\sim N(0,c)\), a denoiser \(D(y)\) is a pointwise map, its mean squared error is an expectation, and a score is the derivative of a log density with respect to its argument. These objects must not be interchanged. The diffusion check below uses fixed kernel mean, differentiable positive covariance for \(t>0\), zero drift, and spatially homogeneous noise, exactly the specialization invoked in Appendix C.3.

In scalar notation the quantity in Eq. (16) is \[R(c)=\frac{1}{c}\mathbb E\left[(D(X+n;c)-X)^{2}\right].\] The following paragraph treats it as the score \(\nabla_X\log p(X)\); the next paragraph introduces a difference of scores to preserve dimension and invokes detailed-balance inspiration.

Take independent \(X\sim N(0,1)\) and \(n\sim N(0,c)\), with \(c>0\), and the optimal denoiser \(D(y;c)=y/(1+c)\). This is a smooth data density, positive scalar Gaussian covariance, and a valid denoised estimate satisfying the definitions in the passage. Since \[D(X+n;c)-X=\frac{n-cX}{1+c},\] independence gives \[R(c)=\frac{c+c^{2}}{c(1+c)^{2}}=\frac1{1+c}.\] However, the noisy-data density is \(N(0,1+c)\), whose score is \(s_c(y)=-y/(1+c)\). At \(c=1\), \(R(c)=1/2\), while \(s_c(0)=0\) and \(s_c(1)=-1/2\). The clean-data score, if intended instead, is \(-y\) and also differs. More generally a scalar expected risk cannot equal a pointwise vector field.

The correct Gaussian Bayes-denoiser relation is \[
 D(y;c)-y=c\,s_c(y).\] It can be verified directly here; generally it follows by differentiating the Gaussian convolution under suitable integrability. It relates the residual, not its expected squared magnitude, to the score. The independent arithmetic in `independent_check_results.json` reproduces the values above; the algebra, not finite testing, is decisive.
X~N(0,1), independent n~N(0,c), \(c>0\). \(D(y)\)=E[X|\(Y=y\)]=y/(1+c). Smooth positive Gaussian densities and scalar covariance.
result: The loss is described as inspired by GFlowNet rather than a formal implementation of its transition probabilities. A score-comparison regularizer can therefore be used as a heuristic even though the stated derivation fails. Nevertheless the explicit transition from Eq. (16) to Eq. (17) is the paper’s justification of a named core component, not peripheral notation. This supports Major without requiring a decline in benchmark performance.

There is a related exact limitation: setting the permitted neural vector field \(f_R\) to zero, with the prescribed \(J_0^R=0\), gives \(J_t=J_t^P\) and makes both terms of Eq. (18) zero for every spatial trajectory. Thus zero auxiliary loss alone does not certify removal of temporal artifacts. Joint optimization with SDS could still be useful; failure of the full optimizer is not established. the displayed formula repairs the mistaken identity only. It does not by itself prove dimension preservation, GFlowNet detailed balance, or the proposed neural ODE’s claimed denoising behavior. Those stronger conclusions need additional evidence.
Claimed mathematical identification false. Invalid mathematical rationale explicitly used for named central flow objective.

 \partial_t p=\frac12\partial_{xx}p=-\frac{p}{4}
 =-0.07052369794346953.\] The printed right-hand side is zero. All hypotheses remain satisfied, so this is a counterexample to the displayed derivation, not a boundary-case objection. The original formula was visually confirmed on p. 14.

For fixed mean and spatially homogeneous covariance the correct calculation retains the kernel derivatives: \[\partial_t p=p_0*\partial_t\kappa
 =\frac12\sum_{ij}\dot C_{ij}\,\partial_{ij}p.\] For its interpretation as an Itô diffusion one additionally needs \(\dot C\succeq0\). This restores the standard Gaussian-convolution identity and shows that the final condition \(GG^\top=\dot C\) is itself correct. Consequently this finding does not refute the standard probability-flow ODE.

abla\cdot(f\kappa)=(
abla\cdot f)\kappa+f\cdot
abla\kappa\). Its interchange of spatially varying drift multiplication and convolution also needs restrictions. analysis: Static source inspection establishes inactive score-related gradients and nonzero first-frame corrections in the pinned release. Assessment: Major for the disabled central score-related objective in this released implementation; Minor for the nonzero initialization. Impact on the historical published experiments remains Needs Evidence.

At `animate_clipart.py:211–218`, the code obtains `logp` and `logp_p`, detaches the latter, and adds their mean squared difference to SDS and an L1 Jacobian penalty. In `losses.py:136–198`, both log-probability tensors are constructed and returned inside `torch.no_grad()`. The ordinary backward graph therefore does not contain this score-related term [torch]. The SDS implementation separately constructs a gradient-bearing surrogate at lines 214–215; there is no analogous construction for `logp`. The score-related MSE contributes zero parameter gradient, although the SDS and Jacobian penalties can train the model. This removes the training contribution of the named central score-comparison component in Eqs. (17)–(18), whose gradient is explicitly required on p. 6. That direct dependency supports Major within the pinned implementation; it does not require a demonstrated decrease in benchmark scores or proof that this release generated the historical experiments.

Independently, the quantity returned at `losses.py:177–193` has the form \[y=m+sz,\qquad
 \ell=-\frac{(y-m)^{2}}{2s^{2}}-\log s-\frac12\log(2\pi)
      =-\frac{z^{2}}{2}-\log s-\frac12\log(2\pi),\quad s>0.\] The predicted mean cancels. This is a Gaussian transition log density evaluated at its own sampled point, not the data score in Eq. (17). With \(s=0.5,z=0.7\), changing \(m\) from 0 to 2 leaves the computed result at approximately \(-0.4707913526447274\). Removing a detach or no-gradient context alone would not establish the intended objective.

In `painter_clipart.py:917–928`, the first correction is initialized with \(F\) identity blocks and then normalized and added to the spatial Jacobian. At the initial integration time the correction per face is \(I_2/\sqrt{2F}\ne0\), contrary to \(J_0^R=0\). The layered branch repeats this at lines 1033–1046. This is a statement about the Jacobian passed to reconstruction; it does not quantify visible distortion after constraints and reconstruction.

The inspected release has not been established as the code that produced Tables 1–4. This uncertainty limits claims about those experiments; it does not change the demonstrated inactivity of a core objective in the inspected release. The correction penalty still operates, so a flow-loss ablation could change results even when the score surrogate is inactive. No author code was run, and no empirical performance correction is proposed. A defensible implementation repair requires a specified differentiable score objective, compatible initialization, and separate validation.

claim: Exact \(z_full=(0,2,-1)\); fixed removal increments (0,-3/2,2),(0,-1,-2),(0,-1/10,1/10). Original ranks[2,3,1,1], promotions[-1,2,0]; influential order2,3,1 gives ranks[2,2,2,1]. All6mixed logit differences exactly0.
Three nonzero fixed additive head contributions, binary presence masks; no target ties; same head set; signed successive target-rank promotions sorted descending as confirmed by released notebook.
analysis: Section 4, p. 6, and Appendix C.3.1, p. 23, measure each removed head’s target-rank improvement along an initial trajectory, sort heads by these improvements, and repeat removal from the full model. The stated premise is that independent heads would make this influential ordering accelerate the switch to target-token dominance. The observed delay then supports the interdependent-pathway interpretation.
Fixed additive head contributions must be distinguished from an additionally assumed, context-independent effect on token rank. The latter does not follow from the former.

Complete counterexample. Order logits as target \(T\) and competitors \(A,B\). Let the full logits and fixed head-removal increments be \[z_\varnothing=(0,2,-1),\quad
 \delta_1=(0,-3/2,2),\quad
 \delta_2=(0,-1,-2),\quad
 \delta_3=(0,-1/10,1/10).\] For every removed-head set \(S\), set \[z_S=z_\varnothing+\sum_{i\in S}\delta_i.\] All contributions are nonzero. Equivalently, binary present-head masks give \(z(m)=b+\sum_i m_i a_i\), with \[b=(0,-3/5,-9/10),\quad
 a_1=(0,3/2,-2),\quad a_2=(0,1,2),\quad a_3=(0,1/10,-1/10).\] Every mixed discrete logit difference is identically zero: \[z_{S\cup\{i,j\}}-z_{S\cup\{i\}}-z_{S\cup\{j\}}+z_S=0
 \quad(i,j\notin S).\] Thus no head contribution depends on another head’s presence. The initial order \(1,2,3\) gives:
Removed heads | \(z_A | z_B\) | Target rank
Signed rank improvements, previous minus new rank, are \((-1,2,0)\). Descending order is \(2,3,1\), giving:

The reordered trajectory has a better early rank, yet persistent top -1 starts at removal three instead of two. There are no target ties, zero contributions, or changed removal sets. This reproduces the qualitative combination reported by the paper without logit interactions. ◻

The source confirms the signed convention: zero-based cell 18 of `playground.ipynb`, lines 4–5, negates successive rank differences and sorts descending. Absolute-change sorting would be a different protocol. Initial learned priorities can be any strictly ascending values for heads \(1,2,3\); the diagnostic supplies no condition excluding this case. Rational trajectory arithmetic and all six mixed-difference checks are in `calc.json`.

Rank effects depend on which competitors cross the target at the current point. An additive logit system can therefore have nonadditive rank effects. If independence instead meant invariant marginal rank gains, the experiment could reject that stronger rank-level assumption, without thereby identifying neural interactions.

Table 6 establishes group importance; Figs. 4–5 establish representational resemblance. Neither identifies interaction edges or excludes this null explanation. Co-movement during joint training also does not identify computational dependence. Actual LLM interactions are not disproved. The invalid inference directly supports the central pathway interpretation, warranting Major. A repair needs an operational interaction null and conditional interventions, such as mixed differences of specified logits across inputs. No repaired empirical mechanism is verified.
result: Better early rank with delayed persistent top 1 occurs without any logit interaction. Independence of contributions does not imply additive/context-independent rank effects. Demonstrated invalid inferential step directly supports second central contribution, interdependent functional pathways; Major without claiming whole-paper collapse.

Nevertheless, the undisclosed unit changes a published comparison and cannot be treated as the standard token comparison implied by the reported metric. Unlike the PPL issue below, this is not a monotone change of scale. It materially compromises the scoring evidence supporting the third contribution, warranting Major. It does not establish decreased average semantic translation quality.

The release additionally chooses the generated paragraph with the highest score against the gold reference. This exceeds reference-free cleanup and can interact with response style, although both branches use it. Cell 19 has a null execution count and no retained outputs. Matching single-paragraph examples do not prove that this oracle selection affected historical Table 8 runs. Its historical effect and the corrected aggregate Table 8 ranking remain Needs Evidence.

The positive controls are retained: scaling was selected on XNLI; IWSLT is an additional dataset; Appendix C.5 acknowledges explanation-style effects and attempts cleanup. claim: Parent exact rational outcome enumeration and independent corrected count recurrence.

Two actions, binary outcomes, \(K=2\), \(\gamma=1/5\), equal hypothesis priors. \(H_0\) Beta57,1083; \(H_1\) A Beta1,999 and \(B\) Beta56,84. Thresholds10 and1/10; shared-parameter integrated likelihood.
analysis: Equation (7), p. 5, defines \[J(x_{1:K})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\gamma^k r(n_k),\qquad 0<\gamma<1,\] where \(n_k\) counts interventions in the first \(k\) positions. Equation (8), used by Algorithm 2 lines 10 and 16, instead applies \[J_k(n)=r(n)+\gamma\max_{a:n_a>0}J_{k-1}(n-e_a).\] Starting from zero, this weights the final reward most strongly and the first reward by \(\gamma^{K-1}\). It is not a constant rescaling of the stated objective.

Admissible finite witness. Take actions \(A,B\), binary outcomes, \(K=2\), \(\gamma=1/5\), equal hypothesis priors, and the paper’s thresholds \(k_0=10\), \(k_1=1/10\). Under \(H_0\), let \(Y\mid\theta_0\sim\operatorname{Bern}(\theta_0)\) independently of the action, with \(\theta_0\sim\operatorname{Beta}(57,1083)\). Under \(H_1\), use conditionally independent Bernoulli outcomes with independent action parameters \[\theta_A\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,999),\qquad
 \theta_B\sim\operatorname{Beta}(56,84).\] All prior parameters are positive. The means match one possible observational table: one success in 1,000 observations at \(A\) and 56 successes in 140 at \(B\). The conditional means are \(0.001,0.4\) and the marginal mean is \(57/1140=0.05\). The paper does not specify enough of its categorical fitting procedure to claim that it would return these exact concentrations; the witness satisfies the stated Beta-prior family.

Use precisely the shared-parameter integrated likelihood in Appendix B.1, equations (14)–(15). If an action-specific Beta\((a,b)\) parameter produces \(s\) successes and \(f\) failures, the probability of that ordered outcome subsequence is \[E[\theta^s(1-\theta)^f]
 =\frac{(a)_s(b)_f}{(a+b)_{s+f}},\] where \((a)_s=a(a+1)\cdots(a+s-1)\). Under \(H_0\) there is one shared factor over all observations; under \(H_1\) the factors for \(A\) and \(B\) multiply. Enumerating the two or four possible outcomes yields \[r(A)=\frac1{40},\quad r(B)=0,\quad
 r(AA)=\frac{278}{5705},\quad
 r(AB)=r(BA)=\frac{1083}{45640},\quad
 r(BB)=\frac{19}{235}.\] For \(AA\), at least one success gives decisive correct evidence under \(H_0\); for \(AB\), only \((Y_A,Y_B)=(1,0)\) does so; for \(BB\), only two successes give decisive correct evidence under \(H_1\). The strict threshold tests have no boundary ties.
Sequence | Equation (7) | Equation (8)’\(s\) value

The unique maximizers are \(AA\) and \(BB\). Algorithm 1 executes the first intervention of the optimized sequence, so the disagreement changes its immediate action. This is a concrete core dependency, without requiring a demonstrated loss of benchmark accuracy.

Counterevidence and repair scope. Proposition 4.1’s symmetry of each individual \(r(n_k)\) is valid under the joint likelihood. However, \(AB\) and \(BA\) have the same terminal counts and different Equation (7) values. The claim that the whole \(J(x_{1:K})\) is merely \(J(n_K)\) is therefore false. Count states still suffice if they store the best prefix value: \[V_0(0)=0,\qquad
 V_k(n)=\gamma^k r(n)+\max_{a:n_a>0}V_{k-1}(n-e_a).\] This is consistent with Appendix B.2, equation (16). Independently authored rational enumeration verifies that it recovers \(AA\) in the witness. Thus a local recurrence correction is available; adoption, actual implementation, and experimental consequences remain unverified. Replanning after each observation does not remove the first-action discrepancy.

claim: Analytic Beta moments and exact rational verification n2,56,100.
H0 Beta2,2; H1 action parameters independent Beta1,1. Equal hypothesis priors; repeated successes at one action. Nondegenerate shared parameter across trials.
analysis: Section 4.2, p. 4, explicitly freezes parameter priors fitted from observational data. Its posterior recursion then multiplies the previous hypothesis posterior by the fixed one-observation predictive from equations (2)–(3). Appendix B.1, equation (14), instead places a single shared latent parameter outside the product of all observations. These define different evidence accumulations for nondegenerate priors.

For a fully specified categorical example, take equal hypothesis priors, \(\theta_0\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)\) under \(H_0\), and independent \(\theta_A,\theta_B\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)\) under \(H_1\). Intervene repeatedly at \(A\) and observe successes. Every frozen single-observation predictive is \(1/2\), so \(B^{\rm fixed}_{01}=1\) after any number of observations. But after two successes, \[L_0=E[\theta_0^{2}]=\frac3{10},\qquad
 L_1=E[\theta_A^{2}]=\frac13,\qquad
 B^{\rm joint}_{01}=\frac9{10}.\] The corresponding posterior probability of \(H_0\) is \(9/19\), not \(1/2\). In general, for \(n\) successes, \[B^{\rm joint}_{01}=\frac{6(n+1)}{(n+2)(n+3)}.\] At \(n=56\) this is \(171/1711<1/10\), crossing the paper’s decisive threshold within its budget of 100, while the printed frozen-predictive update still reports no preference. This is evidence-model inconsistency, not an assertion about the true causal direction in a particular realized dataset.

Core consequence and counterevidence. The discrepancy directly affects posterior causal belief, stopping/evidence interpretation, and the probabilities used to plan future interventions. The deliberate decision not to refit parameter priors is disclosed, so this is not alleged to be an accidental missing code update. One can retain the original prior and recompute the integrated joint likelihood correctly; equivalently, sequential predictive probabilities must condition on previous outcomes.

A fresh independent parameter draw on every observation would make the fixed-predictive multiplication coherent, but changes Appendix \(B\)’\(s\) shared-parameter model. The empirical-Bayes point-mass alternative explicitly allowed in Appendix B.5 also makes the two products agree. The finding is therefore restricted to the nondegenerate shared-parameter formulation. No claim is made that a point-estimate implementation has this defect, or that the observed curves use one particular variant. The necessary full repair is a consistent probabilistic specification and its verified implementation.
result: Fixed BF1; joint BF9/10 at n2,171/1711 at \(n=56\) below .1. Core causal evidence and posterior are inconsistent as specified; experimental implementation unknown.

claim: Let \(\mathcal S\) be a vocabulary of size \(m\), and \(x:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^d\) an embedding shared across queries, keys, and values. With \(X_i=x(s_i)^\top\), the model is \(\operatorname{SA}(X)=XCX^\top XW^V\). The desired output is \(y_i=\sum_{j=1}^L F_{s_i,s_j}w_{s_j}\). When \(d=m\), one-hot embeddings represent any \(F,w\) exactly. At smaller dimension, the repeated embedding imposes joint subspace constraints. \(\mathcal S={a,b}\); \(d=d_2=1\); \(L=2\); \(F=[[0,1],[0,0]]\); \(w=(1,1)\); arbitrary real shared embedding.
analysis: Claim and location. Theorem B.2, pp. 17–18, claims one embedding and parameters with uniform sequencewise error at most \(\zeta_1L\sigma_{d+1}(F)\) when \(d_2\le d<m\). Main p. 5 invokes it to justify a small approximation gap below full vocabulary dimension.

Complete counterexample. Take \(\mathcal S=\{a,b\}\), \(d=d_2=1\), \(L=2\), \(w_a=w_b=1\), and \[F=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Its singular values are \(1,0\), so the asserted bound is zero. Write arbitrary real embeddings as \(x(a)=u\), \(x(b)=v\), and scalar parameters as \(C=c\), \(W^V=q\), with \(t=cq\). The output is \(t x(s_i)\sum_{j=1}^2x(s_j)^{2}\). For \((a,a)\), the target is zero, hence exactness requires \(2tu^{3}=0\), implying \(tu=0\). For \((a,b)\), the target at the \(a\) position is one, while the model gives \(tu(u^{2}+v^{2})=0\). No choice meets the bound. Repeated symbols and these dimensions are allowed. The contradiction also applies with a normalized embedding column.

Invalid step and dependency. Page 17 calls \(\widetilde C=BCB^\top\) an arbitrary rank-at-most-\(d\) matrix. Page 18 treats rank as its only constraint and independently chooses a low-rank approximation of \(W\) in the form \(BW^V\). Both row and column spaces of \(\widetilde C\), and the column space of \(BW^V\), must instead lie in one \(\operatorname{col}(B)\). In dimension one \(BCB^\top\) is symmetric, whereas this \(F\) is not. Independent truncated singular-value decompositions need not meet the shared-subspace constraints.

Counterevidence and impact. The full-dimensional exact result survives. This does not refute every practical low-dimensional approximation. It falsifies the uniform guarantee, even at zero singular tail, and removes the stated theoretical justification for extending the central representation claim to smaller embeddings.
result: No embedding and parameters satisfy the stated bound. Invalidates low-dimensional extension used to justify central representation theory.
