claim: A date trend does not identify representation obsolescence.
Mixture examples show logical nonidentification, not actual mixture estimates; release historical equivalence is unproved; answer-span failure prevalence unknown.
analysis: The abstract, Section 4.2 (p. 7) and Section 4.3 (p. 8) attribute residual gold-article decline to outdated representations and infer that continuous pre-training is still needed. Severity: Major. The experimental controls do not identify this mechanism or necessity, materially weakening a central scientific conclusion without invalidating the benchmark or its reported accuracy differences.

For a fixed model \(g\), let \(D_t\) be the distribution of generated questions, choices and supplied contexts at date \(t\). Observed accuracy is \[A_t=\mathbb{E}_{D_t}[\mathbf1\{g(X)=Y\}]
     =\sum_z\pi_t(z)a_t(z).\] A change in \(A_t\) does not distinguish changed mixture weights \(\pi_t\) from changed conditional accuracies \(a_t\). For example, keep accuracy on remembered outcomes at \(0.9\) and on unseen forecast questions at \(0.5\). Reducing the remembered fraction from \(0.8\) to \(0.2\) changes accuracy from \(0.82\) to \(0.58\) with unchanged forecasting ability. The paper itself explicitly distinguishes pre-cutoff historical questions from post-cutoff future questions (Section 4.1); combining them does not measure a single invariant ability. This example does not assert the actual memorization fractions or erase the practical cost of stale knowledge.

Even complete gold articles do not remove question difficulty, changing entities, distracting content, answer extraction or generator effects. Hold gold-context accuracy fixed at \(0.95\) for easy questions and \(0.70\) for hard questions. Reducing the easy fraction from \(0.8\) to \(0.2\) changes aggregate accuracy from \(0.90\) to \(0.75\) without any change in either conditional ability. This is an explicit nonidentification example, not an estimated decomposition of Figure 5. The generator/filter models also change from GPT-4/GPT-3.5 to GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini around October 2024 (p. 4, footnote 6). That creates a design change near the end of the time axis; it cannot explain the entire earlier decline, but it must be controlled when interpreting the final months. A roughly stable category histogram in Figure 8 does not establish stable within-category difficulty.

There is also a concrete implementation obstacle to the claimed full-context control. In `evaluation/eval.py`, lines 127–128, gold articles pass through `get_first_k_words`, whose default at lines 183–187 is 512 words. The generation code in `qa-generation/utils.py` passes the whole article to prompts after accepting texts between 800 and 10,000 characters. A 5,644-character synthetic article with its answer at word 513 is therefore admitted by that length rule but loses the answer under the released gold preprocessing. This independent construction proves that the implementation does not guarantee answer-containing gold context. It does not prove any particular dataset item was affected, nor that this code version generated Figure 5. Historical configuration and per-question answer-span coverage are necessary to settle those questions.

The authors provide relevant counterevidence: Figures 9–11 show that declines remain after excluding refusals, and gold accuracy is often near \(0.9\). Thus refusal alone is not a sufficient alternative explanation, and many questions are answerable. The limitation section acknowledges generator and event-selection bias and the short post-cutoff horizon. Those concessions do not turn the gold experiment into a causal isolation of internal representations. Calling gold retrieval an “upper bound” also requires an operational assumption: additional or differently arranged context can change an LLM’s answers, so correctness is not monotone in context inclusion.
result: Fixed conditional ability with changed mixture gives declining accuracy; release truncates gold to 512 words while full article generates questions, so answer-preserving context is not guaranteed. The abstract and pp.7-8 Gold/Need for Continuous Pre-training paragraphs connect date-related performance loss to outdated representations and the need for continued pre-training, whereas both the question distribution and generation system change. Section 4.1 distinguishes pre-cutoff historical questions from future questions; footnote 6 discloses a GPT-3.5/GPT-4 to GPT-4o-mini/GPT-4o generator switch after September 2024. The released eval.py truncates gold text to 512 words, while generation utils accepts 800-10000-character articles and supplies full text. These lines establish release behavior, not historical equivalence to Figure 5. Fresh total-probability constructions with unchanged conditional performance give 0.82 to 0.58 closed-book accuracy as remembered-item fraction moves 0.8 to 0.2 (accuracies 0.9/0.5), and 0.90 to 0.75 gold accuracy as easy-item fraction changes identically (0.95/0.70). Independently constructed an admissible 5644-character, 513-word article whose only answer is word 513; the 512-word prefix loses it. The first construction disproves identification of representation deterioration from aggregate drift; the second disproves an automatic answer-preservation guarantee. Major retained for a central explanatory/necessity conclusion, while descriptive benchmark declines remain supported. Repair requires frozen generators and evaluators, answer-span/full-context checks, matched items/difficulty, and a continued-pretraining intervention compared with retrieval/adaptation; alternatively weaken the causal/necessity wording. Report status updated to reflect this acceptance and exact final TeX rebuilt. Actually inspected Figure 5's high gold scores and p.18 Figure 11's decline after refusal exclusions: the problem is not that all questions are unanswerable or that refusals alone explain the trend. The generator switch cannot explain the entire earlier decline. Authors' p.9 limitations and category distributions are meaningful but do not identify matched difficulty or the causal mechanism. No estimate of actual mixture shift/truncation prevalence or historical released-code identity is asserted. Gold reading comprehension is also not itself future forecasting. High gold scores establish many answerable items; refusal-excluded declines persist; authors acknowledge generator/selection limits. None isolates mechanism.

Without these controls, the defensible conclusion is descriptive decline on this retrospectively constructed distribution; the proposed mechanism remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated necessity.

claim: The expanding slope is not a local rate of deterioration.
analysis: Section 4.3 and Figure 6 use increasingly negative expanding-window coefficients as evidence of faster decline near and after the cutoff. Severity: Minor for the statistic itself; it reinforces the identification problem above. An expanding-window slope does not estimate the derivative at its last month.

For the specified monthly decay \(\lambda=0.995\), an observation 59 months old retains relative weight \(0.995^{59}=0.744\), and the weight half-life is \(\log(1/2)/\log(0.995)=138.28\) months. The fit therefore remains strongly influenced by earlier levels. As an independent check, let raw accuracy be \(0.8\) for months 1–36 and \(0.6\) for months 37–60. After a trailing five-month mean, expanding weighted slopes are approximately \(-0.000225\), \(-0.003078\), \(-0.004954\) and \(-0.005197\) at months 37, 42, 48 and 60. They become more negative although the post-change raw series is exactly constant. These are accuracy fractions per month; they are illustrative values, not digitizations of Figure 6. The paper’s moving-average alignment is not specified, so the calculation declares its own trailing alignment.

An expanding fit is a valid descriptive summary of accumulated data, but its coefficient cannot by itself establish ongoing local acceleration or a cutoff-induced change. Report unsmoothed monthly denominators and uncertainty, specify smoothing/alignment, and compare segmented or local models with separate level and slope changes. Multiple QA pairs share an article and event, so treating every question as independent understates uncertainty; article/event or date blocks are appropriate for sensitivity analysis. No significance calculation was reproduced without the raw data.

Table 3 also needs an explicit definition of the YoY observations, weights and cutoff masks. If Pre and Post exhaustively partition the same nonnegatively weighted observations, their combined mean must satisfy \[\min(\bar y_{\rm pre},\bar y_{\rm post})\leq\bar y_{\rm all}
 \leq\max(\bar y_{\rm pre},\bar y_{\rm post}).\] TF GPT-3.5 reports \((-4.33,-3.43,-2.84)\), and MC Claude reports \((-6.26,-11.78,-5.03)\), in Pre/Post/Avg order; both violate that interpretation. Excluding cutoff-straddling intervals or using different masks can explain the numbers. Consequently this is an unresolved definition/reproducibility problem, not a proved arithmetic error. Annual means are insufficient to reconstruct monthly YoY changes.
result: Monthly \(\lambda=0.995\) has 138.28monthhalf-life; a single step with constant post-level yields increasingly negative expanding slopes. Several All means lie outside Pre/Post convex hull under exhaustive partition interpretation. Section 4.3 describes a five-month moving average and expanding weighted linear regressions with \(\lambda=0.995\) after the initial ten months. These are accumulated coefficients, not local derivatives. The Table 3 convex-hull check assumes Pre/Post are an exhaustive disjoint partition of the same nonnegatively weighted observations used for All. Fresh standard-library WLS on accuracy 0.8 in months 1-36 and constant 0.6 thereafter, using a trailing five-month mean and dropping the first four incomplete means, gives slopes -0.0002252373, -0.0030777340, -0.0049540611, -0.0051969334 at end months 37,42,48,60. Post-change raw slope is zero. The monthly weight half-life is 138.282573 months and the 59-month-old relative weight is 0.743980862. Table 3 TF GPT-3.5 (-4.33,-3.43,-2.84) and MC Claude (-6.26,-11.78,-5.03) violate the convex-hull implication under the stated partition interpretation. Minor retained. Disclose monthly series, masks, denominators, weight/alignment conventions and uncertainty accounting for questions clustered within articles/events; distinguish level shifts from later slope changes. Evidence supports interpretive and reproducibility limits without negating the observed aggregate drop. The synthetic alignment is explicitly declared and is not a reconstruction of the authors' Figure 6. Expanding regression remains a valid descriptive statistic. Distinct masks, weights or omitted cutoff-straddling intervals can explain the table; no raw-data arithmetic error is established. Annual means cannot recover monthly YoY values. Headline relative reductions were independently recalculated at about 21.5523% and 11.3379%, preserving the published descriptive effect. Expanding coefficients valid as descriptive summaries; omitted straddling intervals/different masks could explain table. No raw-data arithmetic error proved.

claim: Date boundaries and released configuration need reconciliation.
analysis: Section 4.1 says retrieval reaches the day before resolution, while its half-open interval and the release exclude that day. Severity: Minor; the direction is less recent context, not demonstrated future leakage.

In `evaluation/rag.py`, lines 34–36, the bound is `article_date < yesterday`. For resolution on 10 January, an article dated 8 January passes and one dated 9 January does not. The fixed-cutoff branch similarly uses a strict inequality. This agrees with the printed half-open formula but differs from an inclusive reading of the accompanying prose. State an unambiguous timestamp/timezone rule and recompute boundary-sensitive comparisons if the intended interval differs. The retrieval script obtains ten candidates, but `eval.py` selects the first five; that is consistent with the paper’s top-five evaluation and is not a ten-versus-five defect.

Table 5 specifies `gpt-3.5-turbo-0125`, whereas the released model mapping uses the unversioned `gpt-3.5-turbo` alias. Exact endpoint versions, run dates, response parsing/refusal rules, random seeds and historical prompts are required to reproduce the aggregates. The release’s random distractor-ordering and article-selection paths are not all seeded. No observed score change is attributed to those differences without runs.

The original figures support real benchmark differences, heterogeneous benefits from newer retrieval, and remaining errors with gold context. The forecasting-market comparison also supports the practical advantage of denser, more uniform sampling; smoother plots do not prove a more valid forecasting construct. The authors appropriately avoid claiming that all LLM-generated questions are inherently higher quality. Overall assessment: Major, driven by the unsupported central explanatory inference in Problem 1. The other issues warrant specification and validation repairs rather than a claim that the reported accuracies are fabricated or the entire dataset is unusable.

analysis:
Source claim and location. Equation (5), p. 4, defines \[L_{\mathrm{edit}}(z)=\|s(z)-q(z)\|_2,\qquad
s(z)=f(z,t,C_{\mathrm{src}}),\quad q(z)=f(z,t,C_{\mathrm{tgt}}).\] Equation (6) and the adjoining paragraph propose minimizing \[
F(z)=\|a-s(z)\|_2+\lambda\|s(z)-q(z)\|_2\] with respect to the current latent, with \(a=z_{t-1}\) fixed during that refinement. Algorithm 1 on the same page instead computes \(z^e_{t-1}=q(z^{(0)})\) before entering the \(K\)-step loop. Within the loop it recomputes only the source branch and updates \(z_t\). Read as a cached numerical target, it uses \[
G(z)=\|a-s(z)\|_2+\lambda\|s(z)-q(z^{(0)})\|_2.\] The rendered original confirms this placement; it is not an extraction artifact.

Assumptions and decisive calculation. Fix one inversion step, use the ordinary Euclidean norm exactly as printed, and consider differentiable points with nonzero residuals. There is no assumption in the paper that the target branch has zero Jacobian. For the alignment residual \(r=s(z)-q(z)\), the gradient of its norm is \[(J_s-J_q)^\top r/\|r\|_2.\] Treating the target output as fixed removes the \(J_q\) term and, after updates, also evaluates the residual against a stale target value.

A scalar affine diagnostic makes the consequence exact. Let \[s(z)=z,\quad q(z)=2z+1,\quad a=0,\quad z^{(0)}=1,\quad\lambda=10.\] The weight is the default reported in Appendix C. In a neighborhood of \(z=1\), \[F(z)=|z|+10|z+1|,\qquad G(z)=|z|+10|z-3|,\] so \(F'(1)=11\) and \(G'(1)=-9\). For a small refinement step \(\eta=0.01\), cached-target descent gives \(z^{(1)}=1.09\), with \[F(1)=21,\quad F(1.09)=21.99,\qquad G(1.09)=20.19<G(1).\] It therefore increases the claimed objective while decreasing the cached surrogate. This is a direction error, not a large-step overshoot. The global minimizers also differ: \(F\) is minimized at \(-1\), whereas \(G\) is minimized at \(3\); the latter has \(F(3)=43\). If the displayed norm was intended to be squared, the same example gives derivatives \(42\) and \(-38\), again with opposite signs. The independent script checks both readings using finite differences and explicit loss values.

This diagnostic is admissible for the method definition: at a fixed nontrivial DDIM step, Equation (3) has the form \(A z+B\epsilon_\theta(z,t,C)\), with nonzero \(B\), so affine prompt-conditioned maps are not excluded by its algebra. It is not an assertion that a particular trained Stable Diffusion network realizes these maps or that an observed benchmark sample exhibits this trajectory.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. The target assignment might be an omitted recomputation in the pseudocode, while the implementation actually differentiates both current branches. Alternatively, the authors may intend a deliberately frozen target and a different surrogate objective. Either could define a useful empirical method, but they are distinct methods and the paper does not identify which produced the tables. Retaining an old computational graph is also not a specification of repeated evaluation of \(q\) at the current iterate. Even moving the target evaluation inside the loop while stopping its gradient would generally differ from the full gradient of the displayed formula. The example establishes non-equivalence of the printed prescriptions, not failure of all these possible algorithms.

Core dependency, impact, and correction bounds. The target-conditioned refinement is the central new operation, and the update direction and optimization endpoint can change. This supports Major for the mathematical specification as printed. It does not imply that background-preservation gains, CLIP scores, or qualitative edits are fabricated or numerically false.
claim: Location: p4 Eq5-6 and Algorithm1.
Paraphrase: Minimize a loss with both current prompt branches, while algorithm computes target output before \(K\)-step loop.

One fixed DDIM inversion step and fixed previous latent. Literal cached-value semantics of target assignment outside loop. Nonzero residuals and ordinary L2 norm as printed. No constraint requiring target-branch Jacobian to vanish. Local affine diagnostic; not an actual trained-model trajectory.
result: Printed algorithm is not generally descent on the printed central objective. Major core-method specification discrepancy; empirical gains are not disproved.

The actual refinement limit \(K\), threshold \(\tau\), and optimization settings are not settled by the inspected implementation section and appendices. The discrepancy is between the printed objective and update; which historical results used either interpretation remains unresolved.

claim: Eq9 defines complete replay distribution.
Nonempty RL buffer, \(\beta=1/2\), unsuccessful negative-reward terminal refinement permitted by gate.
analysis: Assessment: Minor, published specification. Historical implementation handling and empirical consequences remain Needs Evidence.

Equation (7), p. 4, defines \[I_v(\tau)=\mathbf1\{\widehat r(s,\widehat a)\ge0
                  \ \land\ \neg d(\widehat s')\}.\] Equations (8)–(9), p. 5, then define \[w_r(\tau)=
 \frac{\exp(\widehat r(s,\widehat a)/\beta)}
      {\exp(r(s,a)/\beta)}\] and, with \(Z_{\rm LLM}=\sum_{\tau'\in D_{\rm LLM}}I_v(\tau')w_r(\tau')\), \[
 p_{\rm mix}(\tau)=
 \begin{cases}
 (1-\beta)/|D_{\rm RL}|,&\tau\in D_{\rm RL},\\
 \beta I_v(\tau)w_r(\tau)/Z_{\rm LLM},&
                          \tau\in D_{\rm LLM}.
 \end{cases}\] The buffer components are interpreted as tagged replay entries. Algorithm 1, p. 5, lines 21 and 27, invokes this distribution for RL updates and construction of the fine-tuning buffer. The practical refinement process allows at most five attempts when proposed actions remain inferior (Section 4.3, p. 6). A finite attempt limit does not ensure a valid refinement.

Take a nonempty RL buffer and \(\beta=1/2\). Let the LLM buffer contain one unsuccessful refinement with \(r=-1\), \(\widehat r=-1\) and terminal flag \(\widehat d=1\). Negative rewards and terminal outcomes are explicitly part of the gate’s domain, and unsuccessful finite refinement attempts are not excluded. Then \[w_r=1,\qquad I_v=0,\qquad Z_{\rm LLM}=0.\] The LLM branch in the displayed formula is \(0/0\). Meanwhile, summing the RL branch gives only \(1-\beta=1/2\). The displayed rule therefore does not define a probability distribution.

Discarding invalid candidates before storage does not by itself complete the specification. In that case \(D_{\rm LLM}\) can be empty, but the stated RL branch still carries only mass \(1-\beta\) unless an explicit fallback changes it. The issue also applies before any valid refinement has been collected.
result: An actual implementation could delay mixed updates, fall back to RL-only replay, or adapt a separate mixture weight. No available executable source establishes whether it did so. The finding is not an observed crash and does not show that published trajectories used an invalid distribution.

For nonempty \(D_{\rm RL}\), a sufficient mathematical completion is to use \[p(\tau)=|D_{\rm RL}|^{-1}\quad(\tau\in D_{\rm RL}),\qquad
 p(\tau)=0\quad(\tau\in D_{\rm LLM})\] when \(Z_{\rm LLM}=0\), retaining the displayed formula when \(Z_{\rm LLM}>0\). This fallback has total mass one, while the positive-normalizer branch has component masses \(1-\beta\) and \(\beta\). This completion does not require substituting \(\beta=0\) into the exponential temperature expression.

In `defame/eval/evaluate.py`, `compute_metrics` counts refusals and returns \[\widehat A_{\rm release}=\frac{C}{M-R},\] where \(M\) is the number of saved predictions and \(R\) the number marked `REFUSED_TO_ANSWER`. `compute_accuracy` uses the same exclusion. An independent ten-claim example with eight correct decisions, one wrong decision, and one refusal yields \(8/9=88.89\%\) under the release formula, compared with \(8/10=80\%\) over all attempts. This is an exact denominator effect, not a reconstruction of the paper’s runs. Selective accuracy is legitimate if explicitly named and accompanied by coverage and a common abstention policy. Here it must not silently stand in for the ordinary accuracy and micro-F1 population discussed in the paper. If all historical runs had full coverage and no refusals, their accuracy values would be unaffected; that remains a plausible alternative requiring the run artifacts.
result: The release reports accuracy conditional on saved non-refusal outputs rather than all requested claims. With complete historical coverage and no refusals those values would coincide; the historical coverage remains unresolved.

claim: 0.0436332313 rad vs 0.3 rad; closed 64-gonal prism gives theta=0.0981747704 rad and satisfies complexity/unit-sphere/manifold assumptions.
analysis: Source claim and location: section 4.1, p.8, defines high curvature at an adjacent-normal angle exceeding 0.3 rad, specifies a neighborhood width t=0.035 times the minimum bounding-box dimension, allocates at least 25% of the samples near qualifying edges, and ultimately selects 10,000 points. Static check: sample_mesh.py line 75 uses np.deg2rad(2.5); line 89 applies that threshold. Lines 104-112 interpolate on the edge at spacing 0.001. Complete analytic witness: consider the convex regular 64-gonal prism with vertices (0.5 cos(2 pi j/64), 0.5 sin(2 pi j/64), +/-0.5), j=0,...,63. It has 66 planar BREP faces and is therefore complex under the paper’s face-count criterion. Its closed convex boundary has no self-intersections, every edge has exactly two incident faces, and vertex links are single cycles. All vertices have norm sqrt(1/2), so the whole convex prism lies inside the unit sphere. Triangulate each planar face without altering its surface. Along each vertical prism edge, adjacent outward normals differ by 2 pi/64.

\[0.0436332313 < \theta = 2\pi/64 = 0.0981747704 < 0.3.\] The released threshold selects those vertical edges; the written threshold does not. This verifies a difference on an input satisfying the stated geometry assumptions. It does not predict a published table entry. In particular, no trained model or author sampler was executed.

A later subsampling step could reconcile the point count. The inspected release does not identify that step or connect any commit to the reported tables. claim: \(D_r\)(aP,aQ)=\(a^r\) \(D_r\)(P,Q); r=1, extent2 and four-inch object yield 0.058in and factor11.6.
analysis: Source claim and location: Table 1 and section 2.1, p.5, compare normalized Chamfer values with the absolute tolerances on p.3 and in Appendix Table 5, using a four-inch object as an illustration. The metric equation, power of distance, bidirectional aggregation, and per-object inverse scale are not given. The adjacent prose refers to a median, while Table 1 explicitly reports averages and standard deviations. No released evaluation script resolves these choices. Evidence E1-E2.

Check: for the following explicitly defined illustrative family, scaling follows directly by factoring the norm in every nearest-neighbor term. Here r>0 is the power, a>0 is a uniform scale, and P,Q are nonempty finite point sets.

\[D_r(P,Q)=\frac{1}{|P|}\sum_{p\in P}\min_{q\in Q}\|p-q\|^r+\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q\in Q}\min_{p\in P}\|q-p\|^r,\qquad D_r(aP,aQ)=a^rD_r(P,Q).\] Linear conversion is valid for r=1; r=2 has squared-length units until an appropriate square root is taken. Fitting inside a unit sphere does not, by itself, specify the object’s normalized longest dimension. An average nearest-neighbor value also cannot certify a worst-case tolerance bound or identify the failing manufacturing feature.

Counterevidence: if the actual statistic is an unsquared distance and the normalized longest extent is 2, scaling to four inches gives a=2. Then 0.029 becomes 0.058 inches, 11.6 times 0.005 inches. Thus a plausible interpretation supports the stated order-of-magnitude comparison; this audit does not demonstrate a wrong numerical conversion. Judgment: Needs Evidence. Supply the metric equation, dimensional inverse transforms, exact summary statistic, and feature-appropriate deviation measures. No correction to the table or experimental result is proposed.
result: Dimensional comparison not reproducible as stated; no wrong result established.

claim: Original trial GAD-7 between-arm P=.581; completers improved across both groups P=.004.
analysis: Source claim and location. Section 3, p.4, describes Woebot as having shown efficacy in alleviating depression and anxiety, citing Fitzpatrick et al. (2017). The relevant distinction is improvement observed over time versus a benefit attributable to the intervention compared with its control [E1, E3].

Complete source check. The source randomized 70 young adults to a two-week Woebot intervention or information-only control. Its Results, Table 2, reports a depression difference (PHQ-9, P=.017) but no significant anxiety difference (GAD-7, P=.581). The Completer Analysis reports anxiety improvement over time in both groups (P=.004). A within-time improvement shared by both arms does not establish an intervention-specific anxiety effect. The Methods describe a decision-tree conversational system with embedded NLP, so the study also cannot directly validate generative-LLM efficacy.

Counterreading, impact, and precise clarification. If the target sentence means only that participants’ anxiety improved, the source supports that narrower descriptive reading. The target also introduces Woebot under conversational AI, so merely including this older system is not independently treated as a model-category defect. Replace the efficacy summary with preliminary comparative evidence for depression, alongside anxiety improvement in both arms without a demonstrated between-arm benefit. Nonsignificance is not proof of no anxiety effect. Judgment: Minor bounded overstatement of this study’s efficacy evidence; no change to the general case for evaluating collaborative tools.
result: Specific anxiety-efficacy evidence, not whole collaborative-care thesis.

claim: Section 4.2, p.5, describes approximately 29% of baselines as having reported recruitment quality control. Section 4.3, p.6, describes approximately 88% and 76% as displaying differences in UI and instructions. Tables 3 and 6, pp.41-42, disclose defaults; Appendix B, pp.45,47-48, defines the coding. The concern is the main-text interpretation, not a hidden imputation procedure. [Wei-PMLR (2025)]
analysis: The independent checker reads the XLSX ZIP/XML directly and counts raw, non-formula cells. It does not execute the author notebook or any workbook formula. The following categories reproduce from the pinned raw workbook:
Item and cell range | Yes | Partial | No | Unknown | N/A
Recruitment QC, D34:DN34 | 13 | 0 | 82 | 20 | 0
UI equivalence, D54:DN54 | 7 | 7 | 37 | 62 | 2
Instruction equivalence, D57:DN57 | 23 | 5 | 21 | 66 | 0
All ranges are on Final_Data, and each row totals 115. [Wei-data (2025/06); independent_results.json]

Recruitment QC: the explicit-Yes proportion is 13/115 = 11.30%. The stated default-Yes rule adds 20 unknowns, yielding 33/115 = 28.70%, which explains the main-text 29%. That value describes the classification after imputation; it cannot simultaneously be the proportion that explicitly reported QC.

Instructions: 21/115 = 18.26% are explicitly No, and 66/115 = 57.39% are unknown. Defaulting unknowns to No produces (21+66)/115 = 75.65%, explaining 76%. Five Partial records are separate and are rounded upward under the authors’ rule. This calculation does not establish that 76% were observed to use different instructions.

UI: 37 records are explicitly No, 62 are unknown, and two are N/A. The published Table 6 has 14 Yes and 101 No. Its No total numerically equals 37+62+2; thus it also includes the two N/A records. The explicit-No share is 37/115 = 32.17%, whereas the table’s residual-No share is 101/115 = 87.83%. The formula path that allocated N/A was not inspected. Retaining 115 as the denominator matches the published table; removing N/A would create a different analysis. [Wei-PMLR (2025), Table 6; Wei-data (2025/06)]

Severity: Major. The dependency is explicit: the abstract presents the systematic 115-baseline review as a contribution; sections 4.2 and 4.3 use these rates to describe observed recruitment and evaluation practices; Tables 3 and 6 and the coding defaults generate the cited summaries. Treating unknown records as observations changes the estimand and materially overstates what the released annotations establish about these practices. This is a defect in the core audit’s quantitative evidence, even though the textual correction is bounded. The raw categories establish documented evidence and missingness, not the true practices in unknown cases. The disclosed defaults and the continued support for transparency remain valid counterevidence against stronger accusations.

A verified descriptive repair is to report the explicit counts and missing counts separately, while labeling the 28.70%, 75.65%, and 87.83% values as summaries after the specified coding defaults. A corrected estimate of actual practice cannot be obtained by relabeling unknowns; it requires source re-examination or author information. This repair is arithmetically checked against the frozen workbook, not adopted by the authors.
result: The authors openly disclose imputation and deliberately choose different defaults for different variables. For example, tool-access unknowns default to Yes. Appendix B frames these defaults as assumptions about prevailing practice; this is evidence against an allegation of concealed or uniformly pessimistic coding. The discrepancy concerns the semantic move from an assumed label to a reported or observed practice.

If the intended outcome is an assumption-dependent assessment of likely rigor, the imputed summaries are interpretable with that qualification. They do not directly measure actual reporting rates or demonstrated procedural differences. The many unknown records independently support concern about transparency.

The abstract's stated systematic audit contribution depends on main-text descriptions of recruitment QC and UI/instruction differences. Raw observed categories plus imputed unknowns cannot support the same estimand as explicitly reported/observed practices; three headline rates materially overstate what the annotations establish.

claim: Section 4.1, p.4, first correctly says that power analysis depends on significance level and a prespecified relevant effect. It then invokes a sample near 1,000 for a survey margin of error and, explicitly conditional on that standard, characterizes the baselines as vastly underpowered using their median sample size of eight. The numerical precision reference does not establish test-specific power across heterogeneous outcomes and effects. The wording must preserve that conditional standard; it is inaccurate to attribute an unqualified universal power theorem to the source. [Wei-PMLR (2025), p.4]

The released data reproduce the descriptive median of 8 and mean of 89.8272 (rounded to 90), using 81 numeric entries in Final_Data!D16:DN16. These are not calculations over 115 fully observed participant counts. The descriptive numbers themselves are not the issue. [Wei-data (2025/06); independent_results.json]
analysis: Consider eight independent, uniformly sampled humans from a large target population. Each answers one fixed binary task under identical conditions. Let Y_i be independent Bernoulli(p) outcomes and K their sum. Treat the AI reference probability p0 = 0.5 as known; no additional estimated-AI uncertainty is present. Test H0: p=0.5 against a two-sided alternative at nominal alpha=0.05.
The conventional nonrandomized equal-tail exact test rejects at K=0 or K=8:

Every stipulated sampling assumption holds, and the design is a valid human-baseline comparison. Thus n=8 can provide greater than 92% power for a sufficiently large effect even with a conservative exact test. A normal-approximation survey half-width of 1.96*sqrt(0.25/1000) = 0.03099 describes a different target: precision for a proportion near one-half. [Independent analytic calculation; independent_checks.py]

This exact example shows that small sample size alone does not force low power. It uses a known AI probability, independent Bernoulli outcomes, and a very large prespecified alternative. It does not meet a demand for roughly three-percentage-point survey precision and therefore does not refute the source’s conditional precision standard. It is not a counterexample to a theorem asserted in the paper, nor a power estimate for any of the audited studies.
result: The explicit qualification to the stated standard supports reading the sentence as a warning about survey precision. The earlier effect-specific power-analysis sentence, the sampling-bias discussion on p.5, and the context-dependent framework on p.9 reinforce that reading. The precise supported concern is conflation of precision and statistical power, plus an unestablished transfer of that survey target to heterogeneous baseline studies; the example does not prove those studies adequately powered.

Severity: Minor within this demonstrated scope. The issue bears on the audit’s sample-size diagnostic, but the source’s express precision condition and correct effect-specific guidance prevent the example from establishing a materially false power conclusion under matching assumptions. The descriptive median remains verified. Retain the sample-size evidence, distinguish precision from power, and state the estimand, effect, variance, dependence, sampling design, and test needed for a power assessment. No actual-study power reanalysis was performed.

The sample-size diagnostic requires precision/power clarification; median8 remains verified. No materially false design-specific power conclusion has been demonstrated under matching precision/effect assumptions.

claim: Appendix B.3, Q3.5, p.48, asks whether humans and AI have the same technical tools but instructs coders to count Internet-trained AI without Internet access as equivalent to humans with Internet access. Appendix D, p.53, argues that such an asymmetric comparison can be fair because the model has encountered Internet information. Table 6, p.42, and section 4.3, p.6, use the resulting tool-equivalence variable. [Wei-PMLR (2025)]
Conditions: Independent post-training fair bit posted online; human allowed retrieval; fixed Internet-trained model without retrieval; identical prompt reveals URL not bit.
analysis: Prior training does not supply a live retrieval tool. Let model weights Theta be fixed. After training, draw B uniformly from {0,1}, independently of Theta, and publish B at a known URL. Both participants receive the same task identifying the URL but not B. The human is permitted live retrieval; the model has no retrieval or other channel containing B. Model randomization R is independent of B.

For any binary prediction Y=g(Theta,prompt,R), independence gives P(Y=B)=1/2. An idealized human who successfully retrieves and correctly copies the page obtains B with probability 1. The example deliberately assumes successful lookup; it does not assert measured human performance.

All conditions of the codebook exception hold: the human has Internet access, the AI does not, and the AI was Internet-trained. The rule nevertheless labels unequal operational access as equal. The failure of equivalence is already present in the allowed tools; the bit example additionally shows why prior exposure cannot resolve every information-access difference.
result: The authors’ fairness argument can be reasonable for a specified research question. Fairness of an asymmetric design, however, is distinct from literal equality of permitted tools. The report does not claim that every such comparison is scientifically inappropriate.

Severity: Minor within the demonstrated scope. This is a construct-labeling defect in one audit variable: its operational rule permits different live tools while the question asks about the same tools. The rule can instead be understood as a proposed fairness proxy; the report does not disprove that normative choice. No affected observed row or materially changed aggregate rate has been established, so the analytic example does not establish a false corpus-level result. The released row59 has 34 Yes, 12 No, and 69 Unknown/Unreported; default Yes yields 103/115 Yes. The number of explicit-Yes records using the exception and any corrected percentage remain undetermined.
One construct needs separate operational-access and fairness fields; no source-level recoding or corrected prevalence is claimed.

claim: On p.5, section 4.3, the text gives ICLR 88,220 active users and describes this as approximately six times the NeurIPS count. Figure 5 on the same page displays active users as orange bars against the left logarithmic count axis. [Yang-PMLR (2025), p.5]
analysis: The exact source page was rendered with pdftoppm. The NeurIPS orange bar is unambiguously above 10^4.5, or approximately 31,623, rather than near 14,700. Only this conservative graphical bound is used:

Code:
NeurIPS count implied by sixfold statement = 88,220 / 6 = 14,703.3333.
Conservative lower bound from plot = 10^4.5 = 31,622.7766.
Therefore ICLR / NeurIPS < 88,220 / 31,622.7766 = 2.7897614.

Thus the sixfold comparison and the plotted count cannot both describe the same active-user metric, reporting window, and filter. Reading the wording as sevenfold rather than sixfold does not resolve the disagreement. The figure crop is preserved as sources/0017/figure5_crop.png, derived from the hashed original. [Independent arithmetic; independent_results.json]
result: Possible explanations include different reporting windows, filters, or a mistaken comparator. None is specified in the compared text and caption. The check does not establish which representation contains the correct raw count.

Judgment: Major. Section 4.3 presents this comparison as quantitative validation of community interest across review modes. Under the common measure and population implied by the text and caption, a claimed factor of six is incompatible with the conservative graphical upper bound below 2.79. This materially overstates a core empirical comparison, even though the displayed direction of the association survives. The bound establishes inconsistency, not which raw representation is correct. A precise numerical repair requires both counts for the same population, window, and filters; no exact replacement ratio is inferred from pixel heights. Repair verification remains pending.
The factor-six narrative contradicts the conservative below-2.79 bound in Section 4.3 Community Interests Validation, materially overstating a core empirical comparison of review modes.

claim: At the opening of p.7, section 4.3, the discussion contrasts extended open-review dialogue with a categorical characterization of fully closed models as allowing a single rebuttal phase. The suspect implication is that non-public reviews necessarily prevent iterative author-reviewer communication. [Yang-PMLR (2025), p.7]
analysis: The paper classifies ICML in its closed category for the historical period ending in 2024. The official ICML 2024 Author Instructions, under Reviewing and Author Response, specify private reviewing, an initial rebuttal, a subsequent discussion period involving authors, reviewers and area chairs, and permission for multiple responses per submission. This is an example within the paper’s own historical scope, rather than a policy introduced only after publication. [ICML-2024, Reviewing and Author Response]

The relevant variables are distinct: public visibility, number of allowed responses, duration of discussion, and eligibility to participate. A private process can allow multiple exchanges, while excluding the broader public.
result: Open public commenting can still expand participation beyond the author/reviewer group. Nothing here establishes equal interaction volumes or quality across review modes. A charitable reading is that the text intended a particular closed venue, but it did not specify that restriction.

Judgment: Major. The paper defines review modes by public disclosure on p.1 and places ICML in the fully closed category in Figure 5. The within-scope ICML 2024 counterexample therefore invalidates the categorical premise used in Section 4.3 to explain iterative clarification as an advantage of open over closed review. Public visibility and permission for repeated author responses are distinct policy variables. This is a failed core explanatory inference, not an assessment that public participation has no value. Repair by identifying venue/year, response rounds, discussion duration, and eligible participants separately from disclosure. The policy evidence verifies this distinction; it does not estimate the contribution of each variable to the observed reply differences.
Invalidates a central explanatory premise used to attribute iterative clarification to public disclosure; the paper's own closed ICML category admits repeated private author discussion.

claim: Section 6, p.8, Disclosure Policy, describes the U.S. first-to-file system as requiring no public disclosure before filing. The adjacent statement that an open submission can jeopardize patent protection is conditional and broader. [Yang-PMLR (2025), p.8]
analysis: USPTO MPEP section 2153.01, revision R-01.2024, explains 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)(A): qualifying inventor-originated disclosures made no more than one year before the effective filing date are excepted from the specified prior-art rule. This pre-existing exception disproves an unconditional U.S. prohibition on all prefiling disclosure. [USPTO-2153.01 (2024)]

For a concrete logical instance, assume an otherwise qualifying inventor-originated disclosure occurs six months before the effective filing date and satisfies the statutory provenance and subject-matter conditions. The paper’s absolute statement would exclude it solely because disclosure preceded filing; the cited exception does not treat that qualifying disclosure as prior art under 102(a)(1). This does not establish patentability under all other requirements.

Judgment: Minor. The defect is local to the legal premise used in the confidentiality discussion. A defensible repair acknowledges the defined U.S. exception and conditions the risk on jurisdiction, timing, disclosure origin, and subject matter. The general concern about disclosure risk remains. No particular invention, application, or filing strategy was evaluated.
result: Corrects a local absolute premise; general disclosure risk remains.

claim: Sections 4.3 and 5, pp.5-8, attribute engagement and oversight advantages to review openness. Website traffic and accepted-paper discussion distributions are offered as supporting observations. [Yang-PMLR (2025)]
analysis: The comparisons vary venue and review mode together. Venue identity also carries topic, audience, calendar, available content, search visibility, and review procedures. The site’s ability to show live information differs by mode. Restricting discussion data to accepted papers introduces venue-specific selection. Similar submission counts do not remove these differences.

A minimal identification argument makes the limit explicit. Let m_c be an observed mean engagement value for venue c and O_c its disclosure indicator. In the decomposition m_c = beta*O_c + gamma_c, gamma_c represents unrestricted venue effects. For any beta, choosing gamma_c = m_c - beta*O_c reproduces every observed mean. The reported cross-venue means therefore do not identify beta without additional assumptions or design information. This is an analytic identification check, not a fitted model or evidence of a zero effect.
result: The paper is a position paper and can legitimately use descriptive patterns to motivate policy. Some explanations are tentative, and p.9 acknowledges voluntary-selection bias. Its traffic data can support interest in the particular information service. Those points limit the concern.

Judgment: Needs Evidence. The direction or size of a causal effect, the quality of discussion, the reduction of overconfidence, and population-wide policy preferences are unresolved. They are not elevated into supported Major damage. A verified wording repair would describe associations and hypotheses. A causal repair requires a defensible design or assumptions and relevant data, not merely a new label.
Observed associations remain usable; causal size and direction unresolved.

claim: On p.7, section 6.2 describes seven ordered stimuli A through G and novel test pairs that exclude the terminal elements. Section 7.3 on the same page reports tests at symbolic distances 2-6. The distance definition in Figure 2, p.8, is rank separation. [Rane-PMLR (2025)]
Distance is rank separation as defined. Endpoint exclusion applies to Experiment2.
analysis: After removing A and G, the available ranks are B, C, D, E, F. Enumerating all unordered nonadjacent pairs gives exactly:
Pair | Distance
B,D | 2
B,E | 3
B,F | 4
C,E | 2
C,F | 3
D,F | 2

Thus the admissible distance set is {2,3,4}, with maximum 4. Distance 5 requires A,F or B,G; distance 6 requires A,G. All of those pairs contain a terminal element. Reversing the display order of a pair does not change its rank separation. The finite enumeration was independently executed using the standard library and saved in verification/0018/independent_results.json.

Judgment: Minor, a bounded methods/results incompatibility. Endpoint exclusion matters because endpoints have uniformly reinforced status, so choices involving them can be answered without general nonadjacent inference. The inconsistency prevents a precise reconstruction of the intended control. It does not show that the reported 0.40 accuracy is false.

If endpoint exclusion describes the implementation, the admissible range is 2-4; this conditional mathematical correction is verified. If distances 5 or 6 were actually tested, the method description and endpoint-free interpretation require revision. The actual pair list must determine the repair, followed by recalculation of any affected summaries. No empirical repair has been verified or adopted.
result: The reported range could be a carryover from Experiment 1, which includes all pairs. Alternatively, the actual Experiment 2 tests may have included endpoints. The abbreviated Figure 1 schematic is not a trial log and cannot decide between these possibilities.

A nearby statement assigning B an always-incorrect status is also inconsistent with B being an interior member of the adjacent chain; it plausibly intends G. This is treated as related descriptive ambiguity, not as a second independent defect or evidence that the experiment used incorrect labels.
Bounded design/reporting ambiguity; endpoint control interpretation affected, not proof accuracy0.40 is false.

claim: Section 7.3 characterizes Experiment 2 performance as at chance and reports no distance differences. Table 1 gives accuracy 0.40 and SD 0.50. Figure 2 presents 95% intervals and fitted lines for Experiment 1. The text specifies ten task iterations and sixty training trials per iteration, but does not establish the independent test-response denominator or the SD’s aggregation unit. The inspected materials also do not identify a reproducible model snapshot, inference settings, complete response history, or sufficient GLM family/link and uncertainty details. [Rane-PMLR (2025), pp.6-8]

Ten iterations cannot automatically be equated with ten test observations, and the six hundred training presentations are not test responses. An SD near 0.50 can be compatible with binary outcomes near accuracy 0.4; it is not evidence of an arithmetic error. The Experiment 2 paragraph’s pointer to Figure 2 does not supply its missing trial data because that figure describes Experiment 1.
analysis: To illustrate dependence on the missing denominator, consider hypothetical independent Bernoulli responses under a known null probability 0.5. An exact two-sided binomial test sums probabilities no greater than the observed probability. Two hypothetical samples have identical accuracy 0.40:
Hypothetical sample | Accuracy | Exact two-sided p-value

These are independently calculated illustrations, not reconstructions of the paper’s data or its SD. They prove that an accuracy value alone does not determine its statistical relation to chance. Actual observations may also be clustered within conversations or task instances, so an independent-binomial calculation could be inappropriate even after obtaining a raw count.
Failure to reject a chance null is not, by itself, an equivalence result. A formal equivalence claim would additionally require a justified tolerance and suitable uncertainty calculation.
result: Judgment: Needs Evidence for independent statistical verification. The authors may intend a descriptive characterization of 40% as roughly near a 50% baseline; that reading is acknowledged and is not disproved. Likewise, all six displayed fitted slopes are visually positive, consistent with their sign claim. No contrary numerical result is asserted.

The unresolved material is needed to assess sampling uncertainty, distance effects, and reproducibility. Release the actual test pairs and responses, independent units, aggregation rules, model/inference metadata, and uncertainty procedure. Reanalysis should respect dependence and distinguish estimation, a difference test, and equivalence. The published estimates, intervals, and fitted coefficients have not been independently reproduced.
Statistical and reproduction uncertainty; no verified numerical error.

claim: Multi-race Census answers are simplified into single-label categories in ACS PUMS; this is invoked as a data-availability obstacle.
analysis: Source claim and location. Section 4, Approach E, PDF p. 4, states that multiple-race responses collected by the Census are subsequently simplified into single-label categories in ACS PUMS, and invokes this as a data-availability obstacle to multi-label treatment. Appendix C, p. 19, describes the coarse folktables race categories. The suspect step is extending the properties of the RAC1P recode to the information available in the underlying public microdata.

Complete check. The official 2022 ACS 1-year PUMS metadata independently defines RACWHT, RACBLK and RACASN as binary indicators for White, Black and Asian membership respectively, including membership in combination with other races. Each has distinct 0/1 values. RAC1P is a different variable with a combined multiple-race category. The public schema therefore retains combination-capable information in parallel with the coarse recode. These are metadata for a pre-publication data year, not a hypothetical newly proposed representation. [S2-S5]

The sampled public folktables implementation, acs.py lines 84-102, configures ACSIncome with RAC1P as its group variable. This supports the narrower statement that the default benchmark uses a coarse group label. It does not support a claim that PUMS itself lacks the separate indicators. The exact inspected code bytes are saved and hashed; the snapshot was retrieved from the current main branch and is not evidence of which historical revision the paper’s authors used. [S6]

Alternative reading and impact. Read strictly as a statement about a particular RAC1P-only benchmark export, the criticism is reasonable. Read as the stated property of ACS PUMS, it is false. The demonstrated impact is bounded: one practical argument against multi-label analysis is overstated. This check neither proves that all mixed identities are adequately represented nor refutes the paper’s ethical critique or establishes the performance of any alternative fairness method. result: Local practical premise incorrect; no demonstrated failure of normative thesis.

claim: Answer-choice absence offered as likely explanation of observed accuracy gap.
analysis: Source claim and location. Section 4.1, p. 7, paragraph below Figure 5, proposes the contrived MedQA format as a likely explanation of the accuracy drop, specifically referring to answer choices being absent in real-world clinical reasoning. Appendix B, p. 12, instead describes pairing the retrieved EHR note, after removing its Plan section, with the extracted MedQA question and its answer choices [S1].

Complete check. Under the appendix protocol, the benchmark condition uses an MCQ clinical vignette, while the EHR condition uses an MCQ with a retrieved clinical context. Both retain answer choices. Therefore, the comparison changes context and case construction, but does not implement removal of choices. Its accuracy difference cannot identify the effect of a format intervention that was not performed. Figure 5’s separate answer-count experiment does not establish that the EHR comparison lacked choices.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. The main-text sentence can be read as a general ecological criticism of medical MCQs; that criticism is not refuted. It becomes unsupported when used to explain this particular accuracy drop. The appendix could describe a protocol different from the one actually used, but neither execution logs nor prompt records were available to decide that. The displayed measurements themselves have not been disproven.

Judgment and impact. Minor, confined to the methodological interpretation of the accuracy gap. The actual executed protocol is a Needs Evidence subitem, not an additional demonstrated error. If Appendix B is accurate, a supported repair is: ’The comparison shows a performance drop when MedQA questions and choices are paired with EHR-derived contexts; this design does not isolate the effect of removing answer choices.’ This is a conditional interpretation repair, not a validated experimental repair. A paired evaluation with and without choices would be new work.
result: Local interpretation only; no proved invalid measured accuracy.

claim: Listings5 and 6 give standardized formats used respectively for Brainfuck and Befunge evaluation.
Interpret Listing6 as the documented Befunge protocol per main-text cross-reference. Use the language semantics supplied in A.5 itself.
analysis: Source claim and location. Section 3.1, p. 4, says models are prompted with the standardized formats in Listings 5 and 6, respectively, including the full language rules and example code. Appendix A.5 is headed ’Befunge Prompt’ (pp. 16-17), but Listing 6 ends with instructions to generate Brainfuck programs for ’ey’, ’ez’ and ’hi’, and the first two programs use Brainfuck arithmetic/loop syntax. The caption also repeats the Brainfuck label. [E1]

Complete check. A.5 first defines Befunge’s ’.’ as numeric output, ’,’ as character output and ’@’ as termination. The appended Brainfuck demonstration programs contain neither ’,’ nor ’@’. Under the very rules supplied in the listing, those programs therefore cannot act as terminating demonstrations that print the stated letter pairs. More directly, the task instructions explicitly ask for the wrong language. Comparing A.4 and A.5 shows the same demonstration tail repeated. This is more than a misspelled heading: the documented executable task and examples conflict with the claimed evaluation language.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. The appendix may contain a copy-and-paste documentation error while the actual evaluated prompts were correct. Indeed, several high reported Befunge printing accuracies make it particularly unsafe to infer that the displayed Brainfuck tail was used verbatim. The released text does not identify the submitted prompt logs or evaluator needed to distinguish the possibilities. The visual source check establishes the published discrepancy only.

Dependence and impact. The listing is explicitly linked to the protocol of the original esoteric-language experiment, a supporting empirical contribution. The inconsistency compromises faithful reproduction and interpretation of that protocol. claim: Controlled experiments isolate whether RL training from scratch is the major factor and rigorously evaluate whether passive pretraining impairs escape from local minima.

Use only the documented RPT versus SPT-then-RFT designs and their explicit KL distinction. Do not assume measured Go scores are false or actual local minima absent. The cached one-state bandit is an identification illustration, not an instance of the Go experimental environment. No matched-objective isolation control is reported in the checked Section4.1/AppendixB.1.
analysis: Source claim and location. Section 4.1, p. 5 (bottom-right), presents the Go comparison as a controlled isolation of whether training with RL from scratch is the major source of the performance gain, and as a rigorous test of whether supervised pretraining impairs escape from local minima. Figure 2 and p. 6 (top-left) interpret the comparison as evidence that passive pretraining restricts exploration. This is an actual interpretation of an executed experiment, not an experiment requirement imposed on a prospective recommendation. [E1]

Design and invalid inference. The comparison changes the initial policy and the KL-anchored objective: p. 6 explicitly introduces a KL penalty for SPT-then-RFT, with coefficients 0.1 and 0.5 in Figure 2. The reported win rates therefore compare complete pipelines. They do not isolate an initialization-created local-minimum mechanism, because the anchoring can change which policy optimizes the objective. Appendix B.1 describes the training stages but supplies no matched-objective control that resolves this distinction.

Decisive identification check. The existing independent mathematical audit provides a strictly concave one-state, two-action illustration, reused here without re-execution. Let q be the probability of the action with reward 1, let the other action have reward 0, let the reference probability p lie strictly between 0 and 1, and let beta > 0. The regularized objective is:

\[J_\beta(q)=q-\beta\left[q\log\frac{q}{p}+(1-q)\log\frac{1-q}{1-p}\right].\] \[J_\beta''(q)=-\beta\!\left(\frac1q+\frac1{1-q}\right)<0,\qquad q_\beta=\frac{p e^{1/\beta}}{1-p+p e^{1/\beta}}<1.\] Thus a lower reward than the unregularized optimum q=1 can arise at the unique global optimum of the regularized problem, with no suboptimal local maximum. This is a witness to non-identification by the reported contrast, not a model of the Go dynamics, a counterexample to the win rates, or proof that the actual Go runs never encountered local minima.

Counterevidence and surviving result. The paper explicitly discusses KL strength, reports 66% and 92% RPT win rates against the two KL-constrained pipelines, and states that removing KL with an infinite training budget can yield the same optimal policy. Those qualifications support the narrower complete-pipeline comparison. They do not establish the stronger claimed isolation of an initialization or local-minimum mechanism. The LLM experiment separately starts all conditions from a pretrained Qwen base and is expressly a finetuning proxy; F02 does not reinterpret it as scratch pretraining or allege false scores.

Dependency, severity, and repair. Section 4.1 uses this inference as a central empirical argument for replacing passive pretraining. The demonstrated invalid causal-isolation inference is therefore Major under the saved calibration standard. Whether initialization-induced trapping actually occurred remains unresolved. Restrict the conclusion to the evaluated pipeline comparison, or provide a comparison that separates initialization from the anchored objective together with evidence specifically identifying optimization trapping. No experiment is demanded for the broader normative proposal, and no corrected scores or fully repaired empirical claim are certified.
result: papers/0038/0038.pdf pp5-6,19. verification/0038/math/independent_math_audit.json M38-03 and analytic_illustration. Source p6 explicitly adds KL to SPT-then-RFT and Figure2 varies its coefficient. The contrast identifies combined pipeline behavior. Existing strictly concave KL illustration shows the same direction of reward gap can occur at a unique global optimum, so the contrast alone does not identify optimization trapping. Inferring an isolated initialization/local-minimum mechanism from a contrast that also changes the KL-anchored training objective. KL penalty is openly introduced to mimic realistic LLM finetuning, and its coefficient dependence is reported. Source p6 states no-KL/infinite-budget convergence to the same optimum. claim: All KEs have no inference overhead and unchanged latency.
analysis: Source claim and location. Section 2, p. 2, states that KEs introduce no inference overhead and therefore leave edited-model latency unchanged. This follows a taxonomy that includes memory-based and in-context methods, and is presented as a distinction from PEFT. Table 1 on p. 3 includes IKE. [E1]

Complete check. The rendered table itself marks IKE with minimal inference overhead, while the MEND, MALMEN, ROME and MEMIT rows are marked none. The original IKE study constructs an inference prompt containing the edited fact and demonstrations, commonly 32 demonstrations and 16 for a shorter context window. Those input tokens must be processed at inference. A lack of additional model parameters therefore does not imply zero inference work or guaranteed unchanged latency. No timing experiment is needed to reject the universal zero-overhead statement; the paper’s own table already records the exception. [E4]

Counterevidence and impact. Weight-only edits that preserve the forward architecture can have no additional inference operations, and Table 1 acknowledges IKE’s exception. The defect is the blanket prose and its latency-based rationale, not a demonstrated failure of the low-cost editing methods or their attacks. The evidence supports Minor: scope the claim to the relevant parameter-modifying methods, and separate edit-time computation, added parameters, prompt length and deployment-time latency. No measured slowdown or reliable timing detector is asserted.

Related comparison limits. ROME optimizes an internal edit value with Adam, so a few forward passes is not a complete cost description; no training may instead mean no conventional base-model retraining. LoRA can merge its update into the original weight matrix without additional inference latency. An unmerged-adapter implementation could explain a nonzero overhead entry, but that deployment assumption must be stated before treating latency as a general KE-versus-PEFT discriminator. These are scope clarifications, not separately counted findings. [E3,E5]
result: Overgeneralized method comparison and latency-based argument; no claimed measured slowdown or loss of attack validity.

claim: Let H denote candidate configurations, J-hat_t(h) the selection score of h over t steps, and J_n(h) its independent full-horizon evaluation score. The relevant selections are h_short in argmax over H of J-hat_j(h) and h_life in argmax over H of J-hat_n(h). The paper instead reports a comparison involving h_default, an externally supplied configuration. This notation formalizes the comparison; it is not a theorem attributed to the authors.
SAC tests impact of k-percent and lifetime tuning with similar outcomes.
analysis: Source claim and location. In the upper-right paragraph of p. 2, immediately before Section 2, the paper describes the SAC study as an extension to another algorithm and continuous actions that tests the impact of k-percent and lifetime tuning, with similar outcomes. Section 7, p. 6, actually specifies comparison to previously reported default values; Figure 6 on p. 7 labels the reference curve Default. Table 3 defines the short-horizon search and Table 4 gives the configurations. [E1]

Suspect step. The default-versus-short-tuned contrast is used as evidence about the effect of restricting tuning duration. The reference configuration is not a full-horizon selection over the reported short-horizon candidate family. This is not an unknown code-provenance inference: the mismatch follows directly from the reported tables.

Complete finite check. Table 3 contains seven learning rates, five batch sizes, three replay-buffer sizes, two beta2 values, and two Adam epsilon values. Its Cartesian product has 7 x 5 x 3 x 2 x 2 = 420 configurations, if all combinations are used. The conclusion requires only coordinate membership and does not assume all 420 were executed. Exact rational arithmetic confirms the following. [E4]

P0.18P0.32P0.19P0.19 Coordinate & Table 3 candidate values & Table 4 default & Default admissible?
Learning rate & 0.02, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001, 0.00001, 0.000001, 0.0000001 & 0.0003 & No
Batch size & 16, 32, 128, 256, 512 & 256 & Yes
Replay buffer & 512, 1,000, 10,000 & 1,000,000 & No
Adam beta2 & 0.9, 0.999 & 0.999 & Yes
Adam epsilon & 0.00000001, 0.1 & 0.00000001 & Yes

The one-percent-selected configuration is learning rate 0.001, batch size 512, buffer size 10,000, beta2 0.9, and epsilon 0.00000001; every coordinate belongs to the stated search. The default learning rate 0.0003 is absent and its buffer is 100 times the largest available buffer. Thus h_default is not in H, whereas h_short is in H. No increase of tuning duration within H can select h_default. These assertions use printed values, not assumptions about hidden code.

The desired contrast is Delta_duration = J_n(h_life) - J_n(h_short). The reported contrast is Delta_reported = J_n(h_default) - J_n(h_short). Subtraction gives Delta_reported - Delta_duration = J_n(h_default) - J_n(h_life). The reported SAC experiment does not determine this last term. The identity establishes the attribution gap without inventing learning curves or claiming that the observed direction must reverse. [E4]

Alternative reading and counterevidence. Section 7 is explicit about defaults, and Figure 6 labels the curve correctly. As a comparison of transferred defaults against limited-tuning configurations and mitigations, the experiment is legitimate. Historical defaults could themselves have been chosen using long experiments; that does not make them the full-horizon optimum of the same candidate family on the switching quadruped task. If p. 2 is interpreted only as an imprecise roadmap, the appropriate action is to narrow that claim to the default-transfer comparison. The report does not label the Figure 6 legend or descriptive comparison erroneous.

Impact and judgment. The affected dependency is: advertised SAC corroboration across algorithm/action domains -> interpretation of the default gap as an effect of limiting tuning -> claimed empirical support beyond DQN. The second step is unsupported by the actual design, so that specific central extension fails. Major applies to this invalid empirical attribution. A position-paper label, surviving DQN results, or easy textual narrowing does not restore the missing comparison.
result: Measured SAC curves not disputed. SAC mitigation improvements relative to short-tuned base. Separate DQN and JBW comparisons. Normative recommendation.

claim: References concatenated before overlap calculation.

Use one valid instance ID, an unrelated nonempty input, and one training document. Let the two references each contain seven distinct lowercase, tokenizer-stable words separated by single spaces, with no punctuation; their fourteen-token concatenation is the training document. Set \(n=13\). The reference-boundary convention is the only difference being tested.
analysis: Source claim and locations. Appendix B.1, p. 19, concatenates references; Appendix C, p. 21, computes reference n-gram intersections; Appendix D.2, p. 22, converts those intersections into scores. The official repository is linked directly in the caption of Table 2, p. 7. [E1]

Suspect implementation step. In the pinned compute_data_overlap_metrics.py, lines 100-108 index each reference separately. Lines 174-186 only record matches against that index, and lines 239-249 emit the recorded entries. By contrast, compute_metrics_from_ngrams.py, lines 278-294, processes emitted entries and joins references at line 292 before computing scores. Therefore the matcher omits cross-reference n-grams that the paper and downstream denominator include. [E2]

Complete case A. Let r1 be ’alpha beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta’ and r2 be ’theta iota kappa lambda mu nu xi’. Set n = 13 and let the sole training document be their fourteen-token concatenation. Under the paper’s definition, the concatenated reference has two 13-grams, both present in training. Binary overlap is 1, n-gram fraction is 2/2 = 1, and the union of their token positions covers all fourteen tokens, giving token overlap 14/14 = 1. Each separately indexed seven-token reference has zero 13-grams. The released matching stage therefore emits no reference-overlap entry for this instance. Missing output is the demonstrated static consequence; it is not mislabeled as a numerical zero returned by a helper. [E3]

Complete case B avoids short individual references. Use the twenty-six-token sequence ’alpha beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta iota kappa lambda mu nu xi omicron pi rho sigma tau upsilon phi chi psi omega aleph beth’. Split after token thirteen into two references, and use the entire sequence as the training document. The paper’s concatenation has 26 - 13 + 1 = 14 distinct 13-grams, all overlapping, so its n-gram fraction is 1. Per-reference indexing retains only two 13-grams. A reference entry now exists, but downstream scoring uses the concatenated denominator fourteen and only two recorded matches: 2/14 = 1/7. Binary and token coverage remain 1 in this case. All tokens are distinct and both references have length thirteen, so neither zero denominators nor multiplicity conventions explain this discrepancy. [E3]

P0.18P0.32P0.19P0.19 Independent case & Paper convention & Static release consequence & Method
A: two 7-token references & Binary 1; n-gram fraction 1; token coverage 1 & No reference-overlap entry & Set arithmetic plus control-flow inspection
B: two 13-token references & N-gram fraction 14/14 = 1 & N-gram fraction 2/14 = 1/7 & Set arithmetic plus static score tracing

Alternative reading and counterevidence. Preserving reference boundaries is a legitimate design that avoids artificial matches between separate answer choices. It is not the convention stated in B.1, and it should not be combined silently with a concatenated downstream denominator. The finding is a specification/implementation mismatch, not an assertion that concatenation is scientifically preferable.

Impact and severity. Minor is supported for the inspected release. The official link establishes relevance, but neither the paper nor the retrieved repository proves this exact commit generated Writer’s results or every overlap example. No Table 1 classification is shown to change. The missing publication-run linkage remains Needs Evidence; it is not filled by assuming current public code is the historical executable. The appendix location is not the rationale for Minor.

Paper. Binary: 1. Checks. Paper. Ngram fraction: 1. Checks. Paper. Token overlap: 1. Checks. Release: No reference entry emitted; not a returned zero. Checks. References: 13. Checks. Training: Joined26tokens. Checks. Paper. Ngram fraction: 14/14=1. Checks. Release. Binary: 1. Checks. Release. Ngram fraction: 2/14=1/7. Checks. Release. Token overlap: 1. Officially linked release is relevant, but exact commit-to-published-Writer-run linkage not established.

claim: Codeforces example establishes significant overlap contribution to published breakthroughs.
analysis: Source claim and location. The Introduction, p. 1, and Section 3, p. 3, connect the published GPT-4 Codeforces evaluation to a separate report of success on ten pre-2021 problems and failure on recent problems. Section 3 then states that overlap reporting would have made overlap’s significant contribution to the described breakthroughs clear. The issue is this inference and the linked evaluation populations, not a claim that the anecdotal counts are fabricated. [E1]

Primary-source check. The GPT-4 Technical Report’s Table 1, p. 5, reports a Codeforces rating of 392, below the fifth human percentile. Appendix A.6, p. 25, describes ten recent contests, about six problems each, with ten attempts per problem. Table 9, p. 30, already reports zero measured contamination for that evaluated set. This is a different evaluation from ten old problems. The source’s own contamination test is not treated as proof that every possible form of overlap is absent. [E4]

Complete inference check. Let A be the report’s recent-contest evaluation and B the separate historical-problem comparison. Evidence about scores on B does not establish membership of A in the training data or the causal contribution of overlap to A’s scores. Even accepting the paper’s old/new accuracy numbers, time also changes the sampled problems and potentially their difficulty and selection. The reported comparison contains no identification argument that holds these factors fixed. Furthermore, the specific assertion that missing reporting prevented understanding A is not supported when the cited report already supplies an overlap analysis.

Alternative reading. The historical-problem result can be a useful warning signal and motivation for more transparent evaluation. The original cited social-media source was inaccessible in this review, so the counts were not independently authenticated. Low human percentile also does not by itself rule out best performance among contemporary language models. Neither of those stronger accusations is made here.

Impact, repair, and judgment. Minor is supported for this bounded empirical illustration: the survey count and the protocol definition are not derived from this anecdote, and the demonstrated failure is a local population/causal attribution. A faithful narrowing would present the anecdote as a separate concern about historical problems and avoid treating it as proof that contamination caused the published result. This logical narrowing is supported; no causal effect has been estimated, no author correction has been adopted, and no new experiment was run.
result: Published GPT-4 recent-contest evaluation A differs from separate historical-problem comparison B; scores on B do not establish training membership or causal effect on A. Original report already reports measured contamination forA. Anecdote may motivate transparency. Original anecdote inaccessible, counts not independently authenticated or alleged false. claim: Patient-inclusive co-design in the cited healthcare case reduced diagnostic bias and enhanced trust.
analysis: Source claim and location. Section 6, p. 6, presents a healthcare co-design case involving patients, clinicians, and ethicists, with enhanced accountability. Table 1, p. 7, specifies iterative design with patients and clinicians and lists reduced diagnostic bias and enhanced trust as achieved impacts. Appendix B(e.1), p. 20, again invokes Zicari et al. (2021) for collaborative diagnostic-bias tools. These are concrete claims about a cited case, not merely recommendations for future participation. [E1]

claim: kappa <= \(p_o\) <= 1-|a-b|=.71; with rounding <=.72 <.775.
Same evaluated items for both rater-model accuracies and inter-rater kappa. Final nominal categories. Unweighted defined Cohen kappa.
analysis: Source claim and assumptions. Appendix D.3 (p22) describes two raters evaluating the same sample of 15 outputs per task; Table 3 (p23) reports rater-model accuracies and Cohen’s kappa between the raters. The Conspiracy (Bad) row gives a=0.73, b=0.44 and kappa=0.78. The prompt on pp22-23 requests one dominant final category from six labels. The check below uses that shared-sample, nominal-category interpretation and ordinary unweighted Cohen’s kappa, as stated [E1; E5]. The values were visually confirmed in the PDF.

Complete check. Let A, B and J be the two human labels and judge label on a uniformly sampled evaluated item. If A and B agree, their agreement indicators with J are equal. Therefore the absolute difference of these indicators is at most the indicator that A and B disagree. Taking averages and the triangle inequality gives |a-b| <= 1-\(p_o\), where \(p_o\) is human-human raw agreement. For a defined Cohen kappa, the chance agreement \(p_e\) lies in [0,1), so kappa <= \(p_o\). Hence the reported accuracies require kappa <= 0.71, contradicting 0.78.

Rounding cannot explain this. With conventional rounding to two decimals, a is at least 0.725 and b is at most 0.445, so kappa is at most 0.72; a displayed 0.78 requires kappa at least 0.775. The contradiction does not depend on n=15. Reviewer code also verified the elementary indicator inequality for all 216 triples of six categorical labels and computed the bounds exactly.

Alternative readings and impact. Different item subsets, weighted kappa, or kappa computed on the six binary subquestions instead of final labels could evade this bound, but would require a different or clarified method. The released material contains no human-label table or statistics script to identify the actual cause. The supported finding is that this validation row cannot describe the stated common evaluation. Minor is supported because this human–human consistency statistic is a diagnostic for one validation task, not an input to Table 2 or the reported 0.75 human–model mean. The bound also does not force corrected kappa below the authors’ 0.5 convention. Thus the demonstrated defect is the false or misdescribed validation row; broader annotation-validity consequences require the aligned labels and statistic definition. This dependency judgment does not require a change in model ordering.
\[\left|\mathbf{1}_{A=J}-\mathbf{1}_{B=J}\right|\leq\mathbf{1}_{A\ne B},\qquad \kappa=\frac{p_o-p_e}{1-p_e}\leq p_o\leq1-|a-b|.\]
result: False or misdescribed validation row under the stated common-item, final-label, unweighted-kappa method. Broader annotation-validity effects remain Needs Evidence; no ranking-change condition is imposed.
